News.title: Man who 'stabbed Brit toddler in Alps and tried to kill 12 others' faces trial
News.content:
Man who 'stabbed Brit toddler in Alps and tried to kill 12 others' faces trial

Abdalmasih Hanoun will go on trial for attempted murder after he allegedly stabbed a British toddler at a playground in the French Alps - he is also charged with the attempted murder of 12 others

View 3 Images Police gather at a cordoned-off area following the knife attack in Annecy, France, in June 2023 (Image: JEAN-CHRISTOPHE BOTT/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock)

A man who allegedly stabbed a British toddler at a playground in the French Alps will go on trial charged with attempted murder, prosecutors have said.

‌



‌



Abdalmasih Hanoun faces attempted murder charges relating to 12 other people too after the alleged knife attack at a lakeside park in Le Paquier, Annecy, south-east France, in June 2023. He is also charged with armed resistance.

‌



The British girl was three at the time of the attack and was named locally as Ettie.

‌



She had been visiting the area with her parents, officials said, and was one of four children, aged between 22 months and three years, who were wounded. Two elderly adults were also hurt.

View 3 Images Police officers work inside a cordoned-off area following the incident in Annecy (Image: JEAN-CHRISTOPHE BOTT/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock)

At the time, French prosecutors said the girl suffered a single stab wound but her condition was never “vital”.

‌



In an update provided on Wednesday, the French public prosecutor’s office said Hanoun would face trial at Haute-Savoie Assize Court in Annecy within the next year.

The announcement came after the defendant’s mental state was assessed by a panel of experts who found he was not “suffering from a psychological or neuropsychological disorder” at the time of the attack.

The translated statement read: “By a decision dated October 6 2026, the Indictment Chamber of the Chambery Court of Appeal ordered that Abdalmasih Hanoun be back before the Haute-Savoie Assize Court in the case known as the ‘paquier’ case.

‌



View 3 Images A rescue helicopter is pictured in Annecy (Image: AP)

“The defendant will have to answer charges of attempted murder in respect of 13 victims, violence with a weapon without total work incapacity in respect of two victims, and armed resistance.

“The Indictment Chamber considered that since the person under investigation was manifestly not, at the time of the events and according to the second panel of experts, suffering from a psychological or neuropsychological disorder abolishing his discernment or ability to control his actions, there could be no grounds justifying the decision not to indict Mr Abdalmasih Hanoun.”

Article continues below

The decision to order a trial to proceed can be subject to appeal at the French Court of Cassation, the statement added.

Shortly after the attack, French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte visited the British child and other victims in hospital before travelling to the lakeside town where the attack took place.

News.title: Serial violent offender jailed for murdering ex days after early prison release
News.content:
Serial violent offender jailed for murdering ex days after early prison release

Robert Sabat, 60, was handed a minimum term of 17 years and one month for murdering ex-partner Dickiesha Nurse, 42, at her flat days after being sentenced to a year in jail

View 5 Images Robert Sabat was freed early when he killed (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

A serial violent offender who repeatedly targeted women has been jailed for life for fatally stabbing a mother-of-two days after being released from prison early.

‌



‌



Robert Sabat, 60, was handed a minimum term of 17 years and one month for murdering ex-partner Dickiesha Nurse, 42, at her flat in Tulse Hill, south London, in October last year.

‌



Sabat had been released on licence from Wandsworth jail four days earlier after being sentenced the day before to 12 months in prison at Kingston Crown Court. He had been in prison on remand since May.

‌



Dickiesha is the latest in a string of women to be murdered by violent men who had previously been bailed or released on licence. They include Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins who were killed by serial sex offender Simon Levy while he was on bail and being monitored.

Chaos and confusion in court which released double killer Simon Levy READ MORE :

5 View 5 Images Sheryl Wilkins was murdered by serial sex offender Simon Levy (Image: PA) 5 View 5 Images Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo was killed by Levy

‌



Zara Aleena, 35, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney in Iford, east London in June 2022, nine days after his release from prison on licence.

View 5 Images Zara Aleena, 35, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney (Image: PA)

Sabat had been convicted of possession of a bladed article and harassment relating to an incident on May 1 2025 when he banged on the door of an ex-girlfriend armed with two knives.

‌



Sabat has convictions dating back to 1987 including harassing two former partners, burglary, assault, wounding with intent and knife possession. In 2023 he was given a restraining order after being cleared of attempted murder when the victim– his landlady – failed to attend court.

In 2013, Sabat was made subject to a non-molestation order of a former partner. On being arrested on suspicion of Dickiesha’s murder, he claimed he had killed before and said: “I’m gonna go on a murder spree”, a court has heard.

View 5 Images Jordan McSweeney was released nine days before he murdered Zara Aleena (Image: PA)

‌



When told what he was being detained for, he said: “Not suspicion. Murder. Murder, yeah. I’ve murdered three people so far. I’m gonna go on a murder spree.”

Begging to be sent back behind bars, he said: “I stay jail. I’ve been let out a week. Let me back. I’m happy in there, I’ve done wrong. I killed before and got away with it.”

Sentencing him at the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Sarah Whitehouse KC said the victim, who was known as Keisha, was “adored” by her family and acknowledged the “terrible and devastating pain brought about by her death”.

‌



Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Sabat, from Balham, south London, and Dickiesha had previously been in a relationship and they had known each other for many years as the defendant was brought up by her father.

Two days after Sabat was released from prison, Dickiesha’s children visited her and on returning home, told their father her “friend or cousin” had been there.

On October 22, Dickiesha told a neighbour Sabat was at her address and would not leave and another neighbour saw her shouting in the street “get out of my house”.

‌



Two days later, a neighbour heard a single scream coming from the victim’s home which sounded as if a woman was in distress and possibly being attacked, the court heard.

Dickiesha was last seen on CCTV the next day.

Her secondary school-age children tried to visit on Sunday October 26 but got no response when they knocked on her door.

‌



Ms Farrelly said their father thought it was odd so contacted her mother and siblings.

Family members raised concern on Monday October 27 and paramedics went to her flat to carry out a welfare check accompanied by her sister and mother.

After getting no response at the door, an ambulance crew member got in through an open window and opened the door to allow access.

‌



Ms Farrelly said: “As they moved into the hallway, an internal door was flung open, and the defendant came through it, charging towards them, whilst brandishing a red-handled knife.

“The London Ambulance Service crew and family members withdrew from the property and police were called.”

Soon after, armed officers forced entry to the property and used tasers as they detained Sabat, who smelt strongly of alcohol.

‌



Ms Farrelly said officers found Dickiesha on a bed with a pillow over her face and with multiple stab wounds to the face.

She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A post-mortem examination found she had sustained around eight stab wounds, including to the left side of her face, neck and hands.

‌



Police recovered a knife with the victim’s blood on it, a bag marked “HMP valuables”, and prison records in Sabat’s name from the flat.

After being arrested on suspicion of murder, Sabat made a series of comments.

In a victim impact statement, Dickiesha's sister Samantha Carvalho described Sabat as a “menace to society”, saying the “heartlessness” of the killing was “impossible to comprehend”.

‌



She said: “The defendant intentionally cut her again and again, overwhelming her as she struggled for her life.”

Each cut to her face was an expression of Sabat’s “ballistic rage” and he left her on the bed “like a rag doll”, she said.

Her mother Claudette McBean described her daughter as kind, loving and the “life and soul of the party”.

‌



Referring to Sabat, she said: “I do not know what he was thinking about but I keep thinking about the fact he was staying in that address all that week.

“If he was here now, I would ask him why he had to do what he did and why he stayed so long in that address.

“I could put my hands on him but I know he is another person’s child. I know there is something wrong with him.”

‌



In mitigation, Alisdair Williamson KC said the defendant had lived “on the margins” with spells in jail and had struggled with his mental health, depression and anxiety.

Following his arrest, Sabat said: “What have I done? I’m sorry.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Dickiesha Nurse who have suffered immeasurably. This was a horrific crime and it is right that this offender faces the full force of the law. The Probation Service has been carrying out a thorough investigation to see what happened in this case.

Article continues below

“We are determined to always have the prison places needed to keep dangerous offenders locked up. That is why we're building thousands more prison places and tagging offenders at record levels to track and manage those in the community."

News.title: Leap second that crashed Reddit and LinkedIn plus knocked out Qantas's booking system
News.content:
Sixty-six million years ago, days were about twenty-three-and-a-half hours long. Professor Claire Nichols, associate professor of the geology of planetary processes at Oxford University, said: "Tyrannosaurus Rex had half-an hour less than us to go about his business. The planet was rotating faster because the Earth had more energy.

"Earth formed around 4.5 billion years ago, and there was a lot more energy in the solar system then. So everything was rotating very, very rapidly. The moon was much closer to us. But Earth has slowed down and the Moon has moved further away over the last 4.5 billion years as the solar system loses energy. The energy is being dissipated basically by the interactions between all the bodies in the solar system. It's really surprising that we're currently speeding up and the days are getting fractionally shorter. This means that the days and months have been getting longer and longer over geological time."

By fractionally shorter, Prof Nichols means a shift of around a millisecond and a half, which doesn't sound like a massive problem. Even Earth's fastest day on record, set in July 2024, was only 1.66 milliseconds short of 24 hours. And this month, turning back the clocks to British wintertime will not be the only changing time we need to be concerned about.

The horrendous storm that killed 43 and how brave woman rescued nine survivors READ MORE :

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 6 Images Professor Claire Nichols, associate professor of the geology of planetary processes at Oxford University (Image: Supplied)

For, between October 13 and 15, at the 28th meeting of the General Conference on Weights and Measures, international timekeepers will address the future of the leap second at the Palais des Congrès de Versailles in France The leap second that delegates from around the world are due to vote on retiring is the extra second that’s been added to the world's clocks every few years since 1972, to keep them in step with the Earth's uneven spin.

Throughout most of human history, the sun set the length of a day. That changed with the railways, when Britain adopted a single standard time, so that a timetable in Bristol matched a timetable in London. In 1955, scientists at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington built an atomic clock based on the vibrations of caesium atoms, accurate to within a second every 300 years. By 1967, the second itself had been redefined around caesium, ending thousands of years of timekeeping by the stars.

Mathematician Kit Yates says it is easy to confuse leap seconds with leap years, though the two work differently. Leap years, he said, adjust the calendar for the Earth's orbit around the sun, while leap seconds adjust the clock for the Earth's rotation on its own axis. Over a hundred years, Kit said, losing 24 days to the calendar would be hard to miss, but a midday shift of a minute or so from leap seconds would not.

‌



View 6 Images Mathematician Kit Yates (Image: INTERNET)

Setnam Shemar, principal scientist at the National Physical Laboratory, said it brings forward a decision the world's measurement authorities already made in 2022, when they agreed leap seconds would stop by 2035. Meanwhile, applying the leap second hasn't always gone smoothly. Setnam said different systems can apply it slightly differently, causing timing conflicts between networks.

The last time it went badly was in 2012, when the extra second crashed Reddit and LinkedIn, and knocked out Qantas's booking system for around two hours, forcing staff to check passengers in by hand. Accurate time is used across the country, Setnam said, by telecommunications, electrical grid operators, banks timestamping financial transactions, transport, positioning and emergency services, much of it critical national infrastructure.

Most of those users get their time from satellite navigation systems such as GPS, he said, but the most critical ones get it directly from the lab. Until now, every leap second has worked the same way, adding a second because the Earth was running slow against the clocks.

‌



View 6 Images Setnam Shemar, principal scientist at the National Physical Laboratory

Setnam said it has become more urgent because the Earth's rotation has been speeding up, meaning the next adjustment would have to go in the opposite direction from normal, a negative leap second that has never been applied before. One estimate puts the odds of that happening by 2035 at 30 per cent.

At midnight on New Year's Eve, Setnam said, a negative leap second would mean skipping the 59th second entirely, jumping straight from 58 to the next minute. What's on the table in October would avoid that altogether, by letting the gap between atomic time and the Earth's spin grow far wider before anyone has to touch the clocks at all, from one second to as much as an hour. Setnam said that would take thousands of years to add up.

Why it's happening now comes down to what's going on deep inside the Earth. "This kind of wobble will have happened before," Prof Nichols said. "Lots of things slightly change the rotation rate of the Earth.

‌



"We have a solid inner core and a liquid outer core, and there's observations that suggest that the solid inner core is actually kind of rotating slightly, either ahead of the rest of the planet or behind the rest of the planet. And it seems to do that on kind of a 70 year time scale, roughly. And so if it gets slightly ahead of us, it makes the days go slightly faster. And if it gets slightly behind us, it makes the days go slightly slower."

View 6 Images Earth and the Moon (Image: Getty Images)

Tectonic plates shifting across the surface change how the planet's mass is spread out too, alongside the ice sheets and oceans moving around it. "You can imagine it being like an ice skater spinning," Prof Nichols said. "If you stick your arms out compared to kind of crouching inwards, that will change how quickly you spin."

The same core also generates the Earth's magnetic field, which plays its own part in changing the length of the day. "I guess it's either speeding up or slowing down always, but it's really interesting that it's actually causing enough of an issue now that we're kind of having to fix the length of the day. And it's also actually manifest in what the magnetic field is doing. So the magnetic north pole has been wandering very, very rapidly from Canada over to Siberia. We've had to keep updating the model of the magnetic field so we can all still navigate using our phones. So actually we're seeing lots of effects of this in real life. So it's always nice to feel like we have a purpose."

‌



Prof Nichols also points to why any of this matters outside a lab. "We rely on the fact that the day and the night happen at predictable times, the months match with the changing seasons, for all manner of things. From kids being able to walk to school in the daylight, to ensuring we have enough fuel for heating when the weather gets colder in the winter."

View 6 Images The leap second could be scrapped (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Looking further ahead, Prof Nichols expects the balance to tip back the other way. "We should start slowing down again in the next few decades. So over our lifetime, we'll probably go back to having a slightly slower day. It will take a lot, lot longer. But there are more sinister consequences for the whole solar system before we actually stop rotating. It's a pretty slow process."

Even though the changes are tiny, Professor Nichols say they help remind us what an incredible place the solar system is. She added: "As a planetary geologist, the thing I would like people to remember is that we're on a planet that's rapidly spinning and hurtling around the Sun in space. We very rarely have reminders of the fact that we're part of a very complex, dynamic and fast moving solar system, so I think this is a nice reminder."

News.title: Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
News.content:
Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

News.title: Chris Mason: Tories united behind Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
News.content:
It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.

Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.

It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.

The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.

Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland.

Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.

The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax â which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people, external but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax, external.

Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.

But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it.

Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.

The Institute For Fiscal Studies said the "biggest beneficiaries" would be "a very well off group, external, mainly living in London and the south east of England".

It also said it would "encourage wealthy people to buy (or stay in) more expensive homes in their later years".

The proportion of estates subject to inheritance tax is rising rapidly, the IFS said, but forecasts are uncertain because it depends on, among other things, what happens to house prices.

The Conservatives estimate their inheritance policy change would cost around Â£6bn a year.

They claim to have identified Â£71bn pounds worth of cuts that can be made to government spending, including Â£36bn a year from benefits and welfare.

The largest savings are projected to come from reforming sickness and disability benefits, where the party believes it can save Â£13.7bn a year, with Â£9.5bn a year from ending access to benefits for non-EU nationals, Â£4.5bn from changes to housing benefit, and Â£3.1bn from reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit.

But Work and Pensions Minister Torsten Bell said "history is very clear that promising this scale of tax cuts ends one way, external: trashing your public finances".

News.title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
News.content:
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.

Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.

The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rent rate - but she wasn't able to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.

"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding that her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".

Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.

Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.

However, a legal glitch allowed her landlord, investment company UrbagestiÃ³n, to raise her rent from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension.

Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.

Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.

That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.

News.title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
News.content:
Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (Â£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.

Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.

Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.

The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.

Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.

It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.

In its most recent annual results, Boots generated Â£7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.

Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".

She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.

The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.

Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".

News.title: Man charged with 13 attempted murders including British child after Alps attack
News.content:
A man accused of attacking 13 people, including a British three-year-old and three other children, with a knife at a playground in the French Alps will go on trial charged with attempted murder, prosecutors have said.

Abdalmasih Hanoun is also charged with armed resistance after the attack at a park in Le Paquier, southeast France, in June 2023.

In addition to the four children, who were aged between 22 months and three years, two adults were wounded in the attack.

The three-year-old British child was visiting the area with her parents. She suffered a single stab wound, French prosecutors said, but was later confirmed to be in a stable condition.

Hanoun will face trial at Haute-Savoie Assize Court in Annecy within the next year, the French public prosecutor's office said on Wednesday.

The prosecutor's statement said: "The defendant will have to answer charges of attempted murder in respect of 13 victims, violence with a weapon without total work incapacity in respect of two victims, and armed resistance."

It added that the defendant's mental state had been assessed by a panel of experts, who found he had not been "suffering from a psychological or neuropsychological disorder" at the time of the attack.

This means there could be "no grounds justifying the decision not to indict Mr Abdalmasih Hanoun".

The statement also said that the decision to order a trial to proceed could be subject to appeal.

Shortly after the attack on 8 June 2023, officials confirmed that the four young victims were in stable condition, including the British toddler.

One of the children was a Dutch national and the other two were confirmed to be French nationals from the eastern region of Haute-Savoie.

Two adults were also hurt in the attack, but were later said to be out of danger.

News.title: Family tribute to 'kind and loving' GP found dead at home
News.content:
The family of a GP who was found dead at her home say they have been "devastated" by her death.

Police discovered the body of Hannah Cain, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, at her home in Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday morning.

"She was kind, generous and loving; a beloved mother, daughter, sister, auntie, daughter-in-law and friend," the 45-year-old's family said in a statement.

Her husband, Mark Cain, 45, of Fern Hill in Dersingham, appeared before magistrates in Norwich earlier, accused of her murder.

He did not enter a plea during the hearing and will return before a judge on Thursday.

"We are devastated by the loss of our beautiful Hannah," the family said.

They added: "We are incredibly proud of the woman she was and of the great care she took of all her patients who knew her as Dr Terry.

"We would ask people to respect our privacy at this difficult time."

News.title: Watch: Stop firing stun grenades on protesters, French police told
News.content:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests after a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off earlier this week in Lens.

Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said he had requested the pause until the facts of the incident had been "clarified".

Rights groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers who have been protesting against old buildings, a lack of teachers and overcrowded classrooms all week.

Police unions have said they need non-lethal options such as stun grenades to protect officers in these increasingly violent situations.

More on this story.

News.title: Fraudster jailed over multi-million pound PPE scam
News.content:
A fraudster has been jailed for helping to scam medical companies out of millions of pounds through bogus personal protective equipment (PPE) deals during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Craig Morris, 43, and Jogesh Bhandari, 60, bought luxury cars, holidays and a new home after pretending they could supply millions of boxes of nitrile gloves in the US and Germany.

They were convicted of two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation as well as concealing and transferring criminal property at Leicester Crown Court in July.

On Wednesday, Morris received three years and nine months in prison. Jogesh, of Mitchell Drive, Loughborough, Leicestershire, will be sentenced later.

Jogesh told his counsel he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" after having a pacemaker fitted last week and was not able to travel to Northampton, where the sentencing hearing took place.

His wife, former pharmacist Meenakashi Bhandari, 58, also of Mitchell Drive, did attend the sentencing hearing.

She was found guilty of concealing and transferring criminal property. She was given a two-year prison sentence, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity.

Judge William Harbage KC said there was "no medical evidence" to properly explain Jogesh's absence and said a bench warrant would be issued. He is expected to be sentenced on 16 October.

News.title: Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss as Spygate ban suspended
News.content:
Tonda Eckert is free to continue as Southampton manager after being given a suspended ban for his role in the Spygate scandal.

A Football Association (FA) independent regulatory commission handed the German a six-week ban from all football, but suspended it until the end of next season.

Eckert has also been given a Â£28,000 fine and reprimand but avoided a lengthy ban that could have cost him his job.

The FA had proposed a three-month ban, but the commission gave credit to Eckert for what they called "considerable mitigation in this matter, most particularly around the genuine contrition".

The FA is yet to confirm whether it will appeal.

In a statement, Southampton welcomed the decision.

"We hope this now brings a conclusion to a regrettable period of our history, and measures have been put in place to ensure that such errors in judgement never happen again at our club," the club said.

"We want to take this opportunity to thank the supporters for their unconditional backing throughout this process."

Saints owner Dragan Solak said the club had "already suffered enough".

"We appreciate the panel's recognition of that," he said.

"We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role.

"I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe's most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season."

Solak said the FA process had been a "positive experience", but criticised the English Football League (EFL), saying "the way they have treated us is not something we will forget".

Saints were expelled from the Championship play-offs in May after admitting spying on training sessions involving Oxford United, Ipswich Town, and Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.

They were also handed a four-point deduction for this season.

An English Football League (EFL) independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

The 33-year-old apologised in June - claiming he was unaware the practice was banned and that it had no impact on his team's performances - but the FA charged him with misconduct, and a hearing took place at the end of last month.

Eckert has been sanctioned for three breaches of FA Rule E3.1. The six-week ban from all football activity would be triggered if he was found to be involved in any other spying between now and the end of next season.

Eckert was appointed permanent Southampton manager in December 2025 after taking interim charge when they were 21st in the Championship. They finished the season in fourth place.

Saints, who face local rivals Portsmouth this weekend, are 13th in the Championship this season with four wins from their eight matches so far.

The FA did not charge Leeds United's former manager Marcelo Bielsa after the club were found guilty of spying on Derby in 2019, instead issuing a formal warning.

The EFL fined Leeds Â£200,000 - which Bielsa said he paid - and introduced a rule prohibiting any club from observing a rival's training session within 72 hours of a match between them.

The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year after opponents New Zealand were spied on.

News.title: Man jailed for killing ex days after early release
News.content:
When he was arrested on suspicion of Nurse's murder, Sabat claimed he had killed before and was planning a "murder spree".

He told officers: "I'm a murderer, I don't want to come back out, I wanna go to jail... I've been let out a week.

"Let me back... I'm happy in there, I've done wrong. I killed before and got away with it.

"I've murdered three people so far. I'm gonna go on a murder spree."

Outlining the facts of the case, prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Sabat and Nurse had been in a relationship and had known each other for many years as the defendant was brought up by her father.

Two days after Sabat was released from prison, Nurse's children visited her and on returning home, told their father her "friend or cousin" had been there.

On 22 October, Nurse told a neighbour Sabat was at her address and would not leave. Another neighbour saw her in the street shouting: "Get out of my house."

Two days later, a neighbour heard a single scream coming from the victim's home, the court heard.

Nurse was last seen on CCTV on 25 October. Her children tried to visit the following day but got no response when they knocked on her door.

Her family raised concerns on 27 October and paramedics entered the flat, where the defendant, armed with a knife, charged at a paramedic, the court heard.

The London Ambulance Service crew and family members withdrew from the property and police were called, Farrelly said.

Soon after, armed officers forced entry to the property and used Tasers as they detained Sabat.

Farrelly said officers found Nurse on a bed with a pillow over her face and with multiple stab wounds to the face. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A post-mortem examination found she had sustained about eight stab wounds, including to the left side of her face, neck and hands.

News.title: Greens investigate party member behind Zionism motion
News.content:
Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green Party conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The motion - which was approved by party members by 1,022 votes to 813 - also called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

The motion attracted criticism from opposition parties and some Jewish groups, who labelled it an "attack on the Jewish community".

Four out of five Green Party MPs also opposed the motion.

Adrian Ramsay, a former party leader and Green MP for Waveney Valley, said the motion was an "unhelpful distraction" and "wrong in principle" as "the Green Party has always supported the right to self-determination and that has to apply to all peoples".

Asked if he would consider leaving the party, Ramsay told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live he was "not ruling anything in or out at this stage".

"What I'm doing at this stage, and we're only a few days after the motion, is to talk carefully with colleagues to reflect both with Jewish Greens but also with Green MPs and other people in leading roles in the party to look at how best can we get things back on track," he said.

On Tuesday, the Jewish Chronicle reported, external the existence of a 2015 letter from Speitan in which she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham.

US prosecutors said Pham had been directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him.

He was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.

In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" who could provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state".

In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem".

She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that I and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed".

She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known."

There is no suggestion in the documents Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other.

Following the emergence of the letter on Tuesday afternoon, a Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate."

On Wednesday, the party released an updated statement adding "an investigation is under way".

The spokesperson said: "Lubna Speitan holds no party positions other than being a member."

News.title: Eleven arrested as pro-Palestinian marches held in London
News.content:
Eleven people were arrested as several pro-Palestinian demonstrations were held in London on Wednesday, the Metropolitan Police has said.

Among them were five people arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London.

The force said the other arrests were made at student-led pro-Palestinian protests elsewhere in the capital, which went ahead despite calls for them to be postponed so they did not fall on 7 October. One of those arrested was part of a counter-protest.

Wednesday marked three years since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken as hostages by the militant group.

Israel responded to the attack by launching a military offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

Footage from the demonstration outside the Board of Deputies' Camden office showed a few dozen protesters, several of whom were wearing face coverings.

In a statement following the arrests, the Board of Deputies, the UK's largest Jewish community group, said it "would not be threatened or intimidated" and thanked police for their "swift" response.

Slogans "calling for intifada" were chanted during the protest, according to the Met. The five arrested remain in custody.

The term intifada came into popular use during the Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1987.

Jewish groups have described the term as a call for violence against Jewish people. Pro-Palestinian groups have said it is a call for peaceful resistance to Israel's occupation.

The Board of Deputies held a vigil in Whitehall, central London, later on Wednesday to remember the victims of the 7 October attack.

News.title: Masked 15-year-old stabbed schoolgirl, court told
News.content:
A masked 15-year-old who was captured on CCTV stabbing a schoolgirl had written notes saying he hated women, a court has heard.

Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back.

The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder - but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.

The boy brought a knife to school, dressed in black with a face mask and had an "intention to kill", prosecutors told King's Lynn Crown Court.

Police were called to reports of the stabbing at 10:24 GMT, not long after parents had gathered at the gates.

Opening the prosecution case, Chris Paxton KC said the defendant armed himself with a kitchen knife and "went to school not to learn, but to kill".

He was "dressed in black, masked up and tooled up", jurors heard.

News.title: Notorious gangland enforcer Paul Ferris dies aged 62
News.content:
A Glasgow gangland enforcer who wrote books about his underworld experiences has died at the age of 62.

Paul Ferris is believed to have died on Tuesday night at the city's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital after a short illness.

He was cleared of the murder of crime boss Arthur Thompson's son, Arthur Thompson Jnr, in 1992, before being jailed for seven years in 1998 for gun-running.

His first book, The Ferris Conspiracy, was published in 2001.

It was later made into a 2013 film, The Wee Man, featuring Line of Duty star Martin Compston as Ferris.

News.title: Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed
News.content:
Five former Barclays traders sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis have had their convictions overturned following a long-running legal battle.

Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham were convicted following trials for manipulating the interest rates used for loans between banks.

But their convictions were quashed on Wednesday by the Court of Appeal. The ruling came after two other former City traders had their convictions overturned last year, which paved the way for others to appeal.

The traders were cast by prosecutors as a symbol of banker greed amid public backlash and anger during the 2008 financial crisis.

Merchant, Mathew, Pabon and Bermingham have all served various jail terms. Moryoussef was sentenced in his absence in 2018, never returned to the UK to serve time after France refused to extradite him.

The prosecutions were over the manipulation of two key interest rate mechanisms: Libor and Euribor, which at the time were used to set borrowing costs on a range of loans such as mortgages and car finance deals.

Mathew said the "strain" of what he had gone through had been a burden on him for the last 10 years.

"Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it's about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened," the 45-year-old said.

"I now have two children and this means a great deal to have the record corrected for their sake as well."

Merchant, 55, added that he looked forward to moving on with his life, but said part of that would be "ensuring that those responsible for what happened are held fully accountable".

Lord Justice Edis said full reasons behind the overturned convictions would be given later on Wednesday.

News.title: Katie Price messaged ex's rape accuser, court told
News.content:
Katie Price messaged a teenage girl allegedly raped by her then-husband, telling her: "I will make you a little star," a court has heard.

Price's ex-husband, Kieran Hayler, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault against the then 13-year-old girl in 2016 in West Sussex, all of which he denies.

Jurors saw messages sent between Price and the girl, then aged 14, in which Price said she had heard Hayler and the girl had kissed and that he had "tried it on" with her.

"I'm only asking as this is a serious allegation," Price had then asked, to which the teenager replied that it was "just a flirt thing" and that "nothing happened".

In the messages shown in court, Price also asked: "Did he kiss you? I won't bring up anymore just want truth. I will make you a little star."

In addition, she asked the girl if Hayler had ever said he liked or fancied her, to which she replied: "Yes, but I took it as a joke."

Asked in cross-examination as to why she said nothing happened, the complainant, now an adult, replied that she was "trying to brush it off".

Pressed on what she took Price to mean by: "I will make you a little star", she told the court: "I don't think I said anything. I think I just ignored it."

News.title: Thousands protest in Spain after death of woman, 87, who was evicted from home
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An 87-year-old woman whose removal from her home triggered housing protests across Spain has died, Madrid's tenants' union announced on Wednesday.

Maricarmen Abascal had been hospitalised since being carried out on a stretcher from the flat where she had lived for seven decades.

Ms Abascal was expected to return home following her discharge, having agreed terms with the firm that owned the property.

Her eviction last month sparked demonstrations, including activists camping in a major Madrid square amid growing anger over the country's housing crisis.

open image in gallery Protesters gathered in Madrid on Wednesday evening following the death of Maricarmen Abascal ( REUTERS/Violeta Santos Moura )

Trade unions on Wednesday announced there will be a nationwide general strike over housing issues on November 11.

Those protests, along with parliament's rejection last week of decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting ⁠rent pressures, prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an early ​election ⁠for November 29.

Mr Sanchez is seeking to shift the political narrative from his government's handling of a migrant crisis in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta and a series of corruption cases involving his Socialist Party and his family to the housing crisis, an area in which he can harness growing resentment about rising rents.

In a statement on X, Sanchez said: "All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”

Angel Victor Torres, Spain's territorial policy minister, said Maricarmen had become a symbol of what was happening to many families as elderly and young people struggled to obtain their own homes or stay in them.

"Now, following ⁠her passing, we are left with the example of the fight she waged and the legacy Maricarmen has left behind. And, above all, we will honor what she always asked of us: 'Fight, keep fighting for what is yours,'" the tenants' union said in a statement.

A wave of indignation swept Spain when Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her apartment after police cordoned off the street.

“I haven’t managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what’s theirs,” Abascal said in a video recorded from a hospital bed after the eviction.

Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the southern European country.

The Spanish real estate company which had insisted on evicting her in order to rent the property at a much higher price ended up reaching an agreement for her to return to the apartment, her lawyer said, adding Abascal was “happy.”

Even with a satisfying resolution for “Maricarmen,” as Abascal is now widely known, she remains the embodiment of the struggle against suffocating rental costs.

Protesters have carried signs with slogans such as “Not even one more Maricarmen!" and demonstrations have been cropping up in cities across the country.

“The housing crisis will sweep this government away,” left-wing parliament member Gabriel Rufián of the ERC party said when she was evicted, urging Sánchez to act.

News.title: NASA chief has hilarious response to NFL player who doubts whether astronauts really landed on the Moon
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

One giant leap for mankind is a point of skepticism for New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye – and NASA's chief had a hilarious response to his doubts.

Maye, 24, was asked by a fan Monday on WEEI Sports Radio 93.7 Boston to name a conspiracy theory he “actually kind of secretly believes in.”

After briefly contemplating one that wouldn't be “too controversial,” Maye named on the moon landing.

“I don’t know about the moon,” Maye said.

“I think I can see back in the day why we would put on the mask if we went there, but I’m not really sure 200% if we went there or not,” he continued. “I wouldn’t say I’m leaning one way or the other. I just know I’m a little bit skeptical.”

open image in gallery New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye said Monday that he is ‘a little bit skeptical’ of the 1969 moon landing ( AP )

His comments caught the attention of NASA chief Jared Isaacman, a billionaire entrepreneur, pilot and commercial astronaut, who became the agency's 15th administrator in December 2025.

“I quite literally have the receipts,” Isaacman responded Wednesday on X, sharing his response to a news story about Maye's comments.

The quarterback's skepticism taps into one of America's most enduring conspiracy theories: the idea that NASA never actually put astronauts on the moon and instead staged the historic Apollo 11 mission on Earth.

One version of the theory, brought up during Maye’s interview, claims legendary filmmaker Stanley Kubrick helped NASA fake the landing, with believers pointing to similarities between the Apollo footage and his 1968 film “2001: A Space Odyssey.”

open image in gallery Jared Isaacman, a billionaire entrepreneur and NASA’s 15th administrator, offered a hilarious response to Maye’s remark on X ( Reuters )

There is no credible evidence that Kubrick was involved in staging the moon landing.

Maye isn't the first NFL player to publicly question the moon landing. Former Rams and Dolphins defensive end William Hayes said in 2017 that he believed the moon landing was fake, while Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver A.J. Brown questioned whether humans had actually been to the moon in 2023. Brown's teammate, tight end Dallas Goedert, also questioned whether the footage of the landing was legit.

NBA star Stephen Curry also made similar comments in 2018 but in 2022, he said he was joking and that he believes the moon landing happened.

Maye, at least, has been less skeptical on the football field. The quarterback had his best game of the new 2026 season Sunday, throwing for a season-high 269 yards and three touchdowns in the Patriots’ 29-26 win over the Buffalo Bills.

The Patriots will host the Las Vegas Raiders this Sunday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts.

News.title: Scott Bessent spat in his food and exploded at DC restaurateur after being confronted by protesters: report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly spat in his food in a rage after being confronted by protesters at a Washington, D.C., restaurant at the end of last year.

The alarming new detail was one of many revelations in a Wall Street Journal account of Bessent’s conduct over the last 20 months at the helm of the Treasury, where he reportedly regularly yells at staffers and is known for losing his temper.

President Donald Trump has told advisers that he likes Bessent’s “feisty public persona,” according to the Journal. The report comes amid growing skepticism about the Trump administration’s handling of the economy ahead of the midterm elections.

Bessent was dining at a Brazilian-Italian restaurant in D.C. last December when he was confronted by activists from Code Pink who were protesting economic sanctions. They accused Bessent of “oversee[ing] the deaths of 600,000 people due to sanctions annually.”

After the public shaming, the Treasury chief blew up at the restaurant owner for not removing the activists, and spat in his food before he stormed out, according to the Journal, citing the owner and a nearby diner.

open image in gallery Revelations have emerged about the conduct of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, including one incident when he reportedly spat in his food in a rage at a restaurant after protesters interrupted his dinner ( AFP/Getty )

Bessent’s tough management style has led to staffers reportedly trading advice on how to handle the secretary’s mood before they meet with him, while others described feeling relieved when he was not in the office.

Some told the outlet that Bessent’s behavior “was a factor in the departure of multiple key officials” during his tenure.

When Bessent was asked by Trump to investigate alleged fraud in Minnesota’s Somali community, he reprimanded - John Hurley, the former undersecretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, in front of staffers for “dragging his feet.”

Bessent reportedly yelled profanities at Hurley, and was so loud that staffers working nearby overheard. Hurley left the Treasury in February. In a statement to the Journal, Hurley praised Bessent as “a brilliant and fearless warrior for President Trump and the American people.”

In another incident last year, Bessent picked up a binder full of papers and hurled it at a wall after he became angry about the way his daily briefing book was organized, according to the Journal. Bessent denied the incident to the outlet.

A Treasury spokesperson did not directly address the reports of Bessent’s temper when reached for comment, but said the secretary “approaches the job with a deep sense of responsibility and urgency” after working in “some of the most demanding roles in global finance.”

“He has high expectations of the United States Treasury’s performance because the American people deserve the best outcomes,” the spokesperson told The Independent.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump reportedly told advisers that he likes Bessent’s ‘feisty public persona,’ according to the Journal ( Getty )

The White House also defended Bessent in a statement to the newspaper, and touted “the level of professionalism and accountability” he has brought to the Treasury as “one of the great accomplishments of this administration.”

Reports of Bessent’s hot temper first emerged early in Trump’s second term, when he had a physical altercation with Elon Musk.

Bessent and the world’s richest man, who for six months oversaw the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency, got into what observers described as a professional wrestling-style shouting match over who would be placed in charge of the Internal Revenue Service.

Since then, he has confronted Bill Pulte at a private dinner in 2025, reportedly “physically threatening” him, and clashed with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at an event last year, according to the Journal.

Bessent “enjoys cultivating a tough-guy image,” former Treasury officials told the newspaper, and has found reports of the altercations “humorous.”

MAGA stalwart Steve Bannon, Trump’s former White House chief adviser, described Bessent as a “good person” but warned, “he’s got a tripwire and he’s got a temper.”

In response to the report, the Treasury spokesperson also touted several policies ushered in under Bessent.

“He championed the Working Families Tax Cuts and is overseeing their implementation, directed the search for a new Federal Reserve chairman,” the spokesperson began.

“Delivered the most successful tax filing season in American history while improving IRS efficiency, launched Trump Accounts, enacted sweeping bank regulatory reform, leads the China economic relationship, designed Operation Economic Outcast to cut off Iran from the international financial system, and helped to secure more than a dozen major economic agreements that expand U.S. market access and advance strategic investment.”

News.title: 9/11 victims’ families challenge Saudi Arabia in appeals court hearing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An appeals courtroom was filled to the brim with family members of victims of the 9/11 terrorist attacks as three judges heard arguments over whether legal claims against Saudi Arabia can proceed on Wednesday.

The New York City judges revealed through questioning that there still appear to be many legal issues that need to be decided in the lawsuit, despite it being dragged on for nearly a quarter-century.

The judges didn't say when they might rule on whether claims can proceed to trial alleging that Saudi Arabia provided aid to at least two of the 19 men who hijacked planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field that day.

Still, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom Strada was killed in the attacks, said she was encouraged that more than 100 family members of 9/11 victims turned out and by the judges' questions.

“It really was a good day for us,” she said afterward. “The judges asked really meaningful questions and hammered the Saudi attorneys and didn’t let up. They weren’t buying what the Saudis were selling.”

Hundreds of victims’ relatives and injured survivors, along with insurance companies and businesses claim in lawsuits that employees of the Saudi government knowingly assisted the hijackers and other plotters and fueled al-Qaida’s development into a terrorist organization by funding charities that supported them.

Brett Eagleson, president of 9/11 Justice, speaks outside the hearing ( Reuters )

Some defendants, including Iran, the Taliban and al-Qaida, have already been found in default.

On Wednesday, lawyers from both sides were questioned repeatedly by the appeals judges who seemed unsure exactly how they would respond to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's claims that it should be dismissed as a defendant on sovereign immunity grounds.

Lawyers for Saudi Arabia say the nation and the U.S. were partners in the 1990s against terrorism, al-Qaida and its founder, Osama bin Laden.

Although 15 of the 19 attackers on 9/11 were Saudis, the Saudi government has long denied any involvement in the attacks.

Lawyers for victims' relatives claim that a group of extremist religious leaders in Saudi Arabia aided the hijackers.

The appeal by Saudi Arabia stemmed from an August 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge George B. Daniels, who decided that the case could proceed in federal court, though he did not rule on the merits of the claims.

News.title: Political candidate in Arizona reports she was raped while out mending campaign signs
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democratic candidate running for Congress in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, is speaking out publicly after she says she was sexually assaulted over the summer while repairing campaign signs near Sun City.

Greene-Placentia reported the incident to the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office roughly two weeks after it occurred, according to a report published Wednesday by the Phoenix New Times. A spokesperson for the sheriff confirmed to The Independent that a report was filed August 31 and remains active. No additional information was available.

The assault occurred around 2 a.m. on a Friday morning, according to records and interview accounts provided to the Phoenix New Times. Greene-Placentia pulled her Jeep Grand Cherokee into a parking lot near 99th Avenue and Bell Road to fix a damaged sign — a frequent late-night routine intended to avoid daytime heat and traffic.

Per the newspaper, shortly after stepping out of her vehicle, she says an unknown man struck her over the head, causing her to lose consciousness. She awoke on the asphalt to find a man on top of her, assaulting her.

“It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia said in an interview with the Phoenix outlet. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.”

open image in gallery Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona’s 8th District, reported being sexually assaulted near Sun City during the early morning hours late this summer while repairing campaign signs. She formally reported the attack to local police more than two weeks later, and the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office confirmed the investigation is active ( Ballotpedia )

The newspaper reports that a second man wearing black boots then approached, but backed away after Greene-Placentia kicked at him, saying, “Not even worth it.”

The two men left her face down on the pavement while her vehicle’s engine and music were still running. Suffering from memory loss likely linked to a head injury, she drove back to her Sun City apartment and had little recollection of the immediate aftermath, per the newspaper.

Following the assault, Greene-Placentia withdrew from her normal routine for two days, she says. Her husband, Alex Placentia, told the Phoenix New Times that he called her several times while she stayed at her Sun City residence, noting she seemed unwell and was taking frequent baths. Police reports indicate she experienced vaginal bleeding for three days following the attack and sustained extensive bruising across her body.

Her landlord, Annarose Lily, recalled seeing her outside the apartment looking as though “she was gonna fall over,” though Greene-Placentia did not share what had happened until days later.

On the following Sunday morning, campaign staff noticed her physical distress at a canvass launch event in Chandler, Arizona. Campaign manager Isaiah Lopez and communications director Craig Beckman pulled her aside, where she disclosed the assault, per the newspaper.

open image in gallery Greene-Placentia, a long-haul trucker who moved to the Phoenix area in 2017, is challenging Republican Representative Abe Hamadeh in the heavily conservative district — it covers parts of the northwest Valley, including north Glendale, Peoria, Surprise, Sun City and Anthem ( Reuters )

“I spent quite a lot of time explaining to her that this isn’t her fault,” Beckman told the publication. “Just because she put herself in a vulnerable position doesn’t give a man an excuse to physically or sexually assault her.”

Greene-Placentia disclosed the attack to her husband the following day.

“Being a husband, I wanted to beat the hell out of somebody,” Placentia told the Phoenix New Times, recalling his initial reaction.

The candidate described feeling intense anger after the attack, recalling how she told her husband and campaign team, “I want a f***ing rematch.”

“I want to call them out,” she said. “I want to like go on TV and say ‘Let’s go again and don’t come at me from behind.’”

She added: “I know that sounds crazy, but I was just mad.”

Greene-Placentia, a long-haul trucker who moved to the area in 2017, is challenging Republican Representative Abe Hamadeh in the heavily conservative district. The district covers parts of the northwest Valley, including north Glendale, Peoria, Surprise, Sun City and Anthem.

Despite her initial hesitation to report the attack out of embarrassment, Greene-Placentia decided to speak out to encourage other survivors to come forward.

“I need to let women know that it’s okay to talk about it,” she told the Phoenix New Times. “We’re asking people to stand up and donate or volunteer. We’re asking those folks to be uncomfortable, as Secretary Fontes says; then I have to be willing to be uncomfortable too.”

The Independent has contacted Greene-Placentia’s office for comment.

For those affected by rape and sexual abuse, if you are in the United States, you can call Rainn on 800-656-HOPE (4673).

Rape Crisis also offers support. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk.

News.title: Hegseth visits the long-deployed USS Lincoln to bestow a top award before the ship returns home
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln a high-level award during a visit to the aircraft carrier Wednesday, a day before the ship returns home to San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war.

The Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat, was bestowed upon the Lincoln and accompanying ships for “40 days of combat operations and an ironclad maritime blockade against Iran in support of Operation Epic Fury,” Hegseth said, referring to the Trump administration’s code name for the Iran war.

The carrier endured a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea, and its extended deployment drew national attention following reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products. After more than 10 months deployed, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Pentagon chief visits the crew and acknowledges long time at sea

Hegseth, who flew out to the ship before its arrival Thursday in San Diego, acknowledged to the crew that “I’m the only thing standing between you and home” and that his intention was “once they pull up to the dock, we’re getting out of the way.”

Long deployments can tax service members who are away from their families for extended periods while facing threats, and can add wear to the aircraft carriers, which have been used for President Donald Trump's military operations in the Middle East and South America.

The Lincoln is the second carrier that has endured an unusually long and arduous deployment to support the war against Iran and the second to receive the top unit award afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

As for the Lincoln, it departed San Diego in late November, arrived in the Middle East in January and now will be back in its home port.

Hegseth said Wednesday that Trump “tracked your activities from day one and couldn’t be more proud of what you executed.”

Issues had been reported aboard the USS Lincoln

The Navy initially played down early reports of supply problems on Lincoln and Trump said its lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough,” Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

Navy officials also said that while combat operations led to delays in scheduled resupply shipments, they prioritized the delivery of hygiene products and established a rotation to streamline distribution to different squadrons.

More recently, the service told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide while on the long deployment. Experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”

He said that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”

Aircraft carriers have been key to Iran war operations

According to the award that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and the strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

There are now two aircraft carriers assigned to the Middle East. The USS George Washington, though usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August.

The other aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could join the Washington and the Bush as early as the end of October.

News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.

News.title: Weight loss jabs are safe for obese teenagers, WHO announces
News.content:
Obese teenagers can safely be given weight-loss drugs and undergo bariatric surgery, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

The recommendations form part of the first set of global guidelines released by the WHO for the treatment of obese children and adolescents.

Previously, the WHO only recommended weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy and bariatric surgery, which alters the stomach and reduces appetite, for the treatment of obese adults – defined as someone with a body mass index of 30 or above.

However, the new guidelines say children over the age of 10 can safely be given the drugs, as well as undergo weight-loss surgery, if all other options, like managed exercise and diet programmes, have been exhausted. Children under that age should not be given drugs or surgery.

Obese children in the UK are currently not eligible for weight-loss drugs or surgery on the NHS, although specialised clinics may offer them to children over 12 under very strict conditions.

The WHO recommends first and foremost that obese children and teenagers undertake a structured diet programme and physical activity, which for children over five should include an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous activity across the week.

According to Unicef an estimated 188 million children and adolescents are obese, and last year, the number of overweight children exceeded the number of underweight children for the first time in history.

While obesity rates are beginning to plateau in many rich countries, childhood obesity is rising rapidly in the developing world, including in sub-Saharan Africa, which is home to nearly a quarter of the world’s overweight children.

The drivers of obesity are complex, but experts believe a switch from traditional, fibre-rich diets to cheap, high-fat, high-sugar food has played a significant role in growing global obesity rates.

Obesity at any age carries significant health risks – but the consequences are thought to be more acute if obesity begins in childhood, accelerating the development of severe and life-threatening conditions, including type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and liver disease.

The WHO guidelines also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health issues that are often associated with obesity and contribute to unhealthy eating patterns – including anxiety and depression, low self-esteem, and bullying.

“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” Dr Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, WHO.
