News.title: Russia’s plague shouldn’t scare us – its secretive bioweapons should
News.content:
The facts about the laboratory accident in Russia are scant.

A lab technician at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Siberia is dead, 200 people have been quarantined, and the state security services are saying “nothing to see here, folks”.

Denials from the country that has run a covert biological weapons programme since the Cold War have done nothing to quieten speculation about what is really going on in the vast Siberian tundra.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, demanded on Tuesday that Russia be “transparent” about the situation, which he said Washington was monitoring “very closely”.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Mr Rubio said during a trip to Iceland.

A death from plague is a tragedy, but should not be something we need to worry about. We have moved on from the Middle Ages, when the Black Death laid waste to much of Europe.

It’s treatable with antibiotics and does not spread as fast as diseases like Covid. Its replication or R number does not get above 1.5 – measles, for example, has an R number of 12 to 18.

News.title: Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first
News.content:
One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

MANCHESTER UNITED were one of four clubs who were handed Manchester City’s guilty verdict EARLY.

Arsenal, Liverpool and Tottenham also got advance notice before other Premier League clubs.



The quartet had given City legal notice of their intention to ask for the right to seek compensation and the decision to allow them prior sight of the outline findings appear related to those claims.

Last week, the three-man independent commission found City of substantive rule breaches over contracts and payments, including booking £830m in “sham” sponsorship deals.



City have vehemently denied the verdict and launched an appeal.

It comes as it emerges City were investigated over potential tax issues by HMRC in 2018.



The probe was launched as a direct result of the leaked emails published by German magazine Spiegel – and which were the main evidence of the Prem’s case that saw the club found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.

And the inquiry – which did NOT involve any allegations of fraud – was never actually closed, it has now emerged, although HMRC has taken NO action against the club.

According to the Financial Times, tax officials opened the investigation to see if City had used complex arrangements to underpay money owed to the Government.

The civil investigation was a direct result of the email “hack”, with City instructing external lawyers to argue there was nothing untoward in the club’s commercial arrangements.

Tax expert Dan Neidle has reported he believes City may owe HMRC £12m over the extra contracts paid by Abu Dhabi-based entities to Roberto Mancini during his period in charge of the club.

Meanwhile, Amanda Staveley, who was involved in Sheikh Mansour’s takeover of City in 2008 and was then part of the Saudi-backed consortium that gained control of Newcastle, urged the club and Prem to find a solution.

Staveley said: “English football is the most watchable in the world and we should nurture this asset, our league, our fans and do everything we can to try and make a resolution to the issues that exist.

Harry Kane and Lamine Yamal are the two leading contenders to be crowned the world’s best player.



Kane is hoping to become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the Ballon d’Or.

The Three Lions captain was Europe’s top goalscorer last season, bagging 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern Munich.



Kane’s exploits played a major part in Bayern’s success as the German giants claimed an emphatic league and cup double.

The former Tottenham striker continued his fine domestic form into the World Cup, where he led England to third place – the nation’s best finish on the global stage since 1966.

Elsewhere, Yamal scored 24 goals and made 18 assists in all competitions for Barcelona, helping his side to a second consecutive LaLiga title.

The wonderkid also became the fourth-youngest player in history to win the World Cup as Spain secured their second global crown with victory over Argentina.

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Ousmane Dembele is nominated once again after his brilliant season with Paris Saint-Germain.

The exhilarating winger won the Champions League and Ligue 1 titles, while also helping France to a fourth-place finish at the World Cup.



Despite a trophy-less season, Real Madrid superstar Kylian Mbappe was the leading scorer in the Champions League and LaLiga, plus he left the World Cup with the golden boot this summer.

Sports.title: Winners and losers from England’s international break as Scott and Hall shine but Rice left looking over his shoulder
Sports.content:

THERE were major winners and sorry losers from England’s first set of matches after the World Cup.

The biggest surprise is that Declan Rice, a mainstay of the England team with 80 caps and one of the best midfielders in Europe, was still one of the losers simply because he is now looking over his shoulder.



Finally, he has some proper competition.

Rice was one of five players who withdrew from the squad for the four Nations League games along with Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento.



Due to various reasons, 12 of Tuchel’s World Cup squad did not feature in this camp which featured a loss to Spain, two wins over the Czech Republic and a 7-0 hammering of Croatia.

Considering Rice played 69 games for club and country last season, his decision to have a rest was understandable. While he remains a clear first choice, he will not have been watching at home comfortably as Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott took his chance with both hands against Croatia.



Although Rice and Elliot Anderson are terrific players, they are maybe too similar whereas Scott – always looking to move the ball forward – has different qualities.

Scott combines well with his former England under-21s team-mate Anderson and there is an obvious chemistry between the two.

It is a shame that Scott was injured for Tuesday’s 3-0 win over the Czechs and he now looks set to miss next month’s final two games against Croatia and Spain.

Equally, Rice’s team-mate Myles Lewis-Skelly did well enough in his three starts which could also impact other players hoping to return to the squad.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

WINNERS

Tuchel came out of this four-game spell with a smile on his face as there was a lot of pressure on him.

Some fans will never forgive him for the 2-1 loss to Argentina but looking forward, the Three Lions are in decent shape.

England are certain to feature in the Nations League quarter-finals in March but everything is about Euro 2028.

Scott and Lewis Hall were the big successes. Left-back Hall did really well and must now be the first choice.



Tuchel said: “I was very impressed with both of them. Alex looked at another level.

“We missed him (against the Czech Republic) because he was super strong and Lewis was also very, very good. He got the chance and stepped up three matches in a row.”

Trent Alexander-Arnold, who missed out at the World Cup, also got his first two starts under Tuchel so will have some renewed hope while James Trafford will be reasonably pleased with his two starts.

But the fact he was given this trial shows you that he has a chance of replacing Jordan Pickford.



Lewis-Skelly will be satisfied with three starts but he still passes the ball sideways or backwards too much.

Jude Bellingham was also a winner simply because he enhanced his reputation as one of the best midfielders on this planet and red-hot Anthony Gordon underlined the fact he is England’s best attacker on the left



Harry Kane continues to rewrite history.

LOSERS

Quite a few.

Palmer, although not selected for the World Cup, looks as though he has ruined his chances by making himself unavailable with Tuchel clearly not impressed. There also seems no way back for Phil Foden. Remember him?

Asked whether Palmer or Foden can fit into his aggressive style of play, Tuchel said: “I don’t know, is the honest answer.

“They are not here. This team took another step and it’s always about the guys who are here.”



The players missing from the Nations League, who were at the World Cup, were Rashford, Mainoo, Livramento, Reece James, Djed Spence, Noni Madueke, John Stones, Dean Henderson, Jordan Henderson, Dan Burn and the Saudi Arabian-based forwards Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney.

Rashford, who has a history of withdrawing for England, once again faces a battle to be in the squad.



Mainoo, who did not play a minute at the World Cup, looks out in the cold because of Scott and Lewis-Skelly.

Spence has been hit by the performances of full-backs Hall and Jarell Quansah. The same goes for Nico O’Reilly who started against Spain but returned to Manchester City injured. Although he will return to the squad, he will lose his starting place to Hall. And in any case, he would rather play in midfield. There will come a point when Tuchel will just give up on injury-jinxed James.

Arsenal winger Madueke could also struggle to get into the next squad along with Chelsea midfielder Henderson who was not selected due to a fitness issue but on the same day of the announcement, he still played against Brentford.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin will be annoyed at only being introduced as an 82nd-minute substitute for Kane on Tuesday.

So it looks as though either Toney or more probably, Watkins, will return next month. But either way, they are being kept on their toes – like many others.

FORMER Spurs defender Ramon Vega says he wants to stand against Fifa President Gianni Infantino.

As European football’s top brass prepared to meet in Berlin to plot the next move in their fight against the world governing body, ex-Switzerland centre-back Vega, 55, became the first to actually put his head above the parapet.



Vega accused Infantino and the current Fifa leadership of “demoralising” the game, blasting that “weak governance has damaged Fifa’s credibility and eroded trust across the global football family.

“We must stop this conflict from escalating.”



Infantino’s plot to sell off the World Cup to private investors has sparked the latest battle for Fifa power, although he remains favourite to win a final term of office in Morocco in March.

Candidates have until the middle of next month to declare, although they also need to prove they have had a role in football for two of the past five years, be endorsed by five national associations and pass the Fifa eligibility check.



That may prove a bar too far for Vega, whose bid for the role in 2015 failed to reach the lift-off stage.

Nevertheless, Vega said: “Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family

“Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution. It is the people’s game and belongs to everyone.

“The players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life, every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and billions of supporters.

“I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs.”

With Uefa still struggling to find a credible candidate, today’s meeting of the 55 European associations in the German capital is expected to see a new approach to the Infantino issue agreed.

Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin slammed Infantino in a speech in Copenhagen last week, insisting: “It’s time to say enough.”

The Berlin meeting comes a week before Fifa’s ruling Council gathers in Zurich.

KIERAN MCKENNA has landed a new job working as a technical observer for Uefa just months after leaving Ipswich.

The former Manchester United coach caused a surprise by departing Portman Road despite leading the team to Premier League promotion.



He spent nearly five years with the Tractor Boys and secured five promotions but decided to quit in June to seek a new challenge.

And McKenna has now landed a role with Uefa, which will see him analyse Champions League games and select a man of the match.



He will also help choose team, player and goal of the season along with other observers.

McKenna told the Guardian about his new role: “I wanted to give myself the best possibility to learn before taking on the next challenge.



“I’m always going to want to be somewhere where I can improve players, play attacking football and win games.

“But beyond that I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community, trying to build something memorable.”

Ipswich were 12th in League One when McKenna took over and he said he was keen to leave on a high.

He added: “I had a lot of different opportunities to leave, could have left in many different circumstances really.

“But I was always aware I wanted to depart in the best way possible, with the club on a high, back in the Premier League and with a great chance to build for what will hopefully be a really successful period.

“It was a really special opportunity at Ipswich and you want to do that again in your career. But you have to be ready to come in somewhere and get some short-term success as well.

“What’s right for me, after two decades coaching, might be different for a manager who only stopped playing three years ago.



“I want to enjoy the time we have now, take this period to reflect and be in the best position I can for the next role’.”

McKenna was a youth player for Tottenham but was forced to retire aged 22 due to a serious injury.

Sports.title: Why Sprint in Singapore adds new twist to F1's toughest race
Sports.content:
Formula 1 stages its sixth and final Sprint event of the year this weekend to conclude the first flyaway triple header of the sport's busy 2026 season run in.

And, for the first time, the Sprint format is being used at the Singapore Grand Prix and its Marina Bay street track, home of the sport's original night race.

But on a track not known for its overtaking, what kind of weekend can we expect with two qualifying sessions and two races?

How the Singapore GP weekend will be different to normal

When the Sprint format was first introduced at three races for the 2021 season, the tracks selected - Silverstone, Monza and Interlagos - were ones deemed to be particularly good for racing so to justify the addition of a 100km race on the Saturday as an appetiser to the main Sunday Grand Prix.

That has generally continued to be the case in the selection of Sprint venues up to this year, with perhaps the inclusion of Imola in 2022 the surprise exception.

Street tracks, which by their nature traditionally aren't as overtaking-friendly as conventional permanent tracks, have generally not featured on that yearly list.

Azerbaijan did host a Sprint in 2023, but Baku's wall-lined street track features the longest straight on the calendar and so allows passing.

Singapore certainly falls more into the category of conventional street track - there are no long straights of note and overtaking opportunities are severely limited around the confined, twisty layout.

Image: The Singapore GP takes place this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1 (HOCH ZWEI/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)

The floodlit race is instead most known for its physicality owing to the hot and humid conditions of the Asian country and the fact the 62-lap race pushes towards the two-hour limit around a 19-corner lap that features plenty of 90-degree turns.

So, holding a second race this weekend appears counterintuitive in one sense to the original purpose of the Sprint format. However, there are flip sides to the decision.

The first relates to qualifying. Given the lack of passing opportunities in the race, qualifying is always considered absolutely essential at Marina Bay and, like all street tracks where the walls are so close, the Saturday spectacle is often spectacular.

The circuit was the scene of one of the most famous qualifying laps in the sport's recent history when Lewis Hamilton surged to pole position for Mercedes in 2018, while numerous drivers have come a cropper against the barriers over the years when pushing for a decisive, grid-defining lap.

This year there will be two such sessions - Sprint Qualifying on Friday followed by Grand Prix Qualifying on Saturday - which means double the qualifying challenge and, therefore, double the jeopardy for drivers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from qualifying at the 2025 Singapore Grand Prix.

The Sprint format also means drivers and teams will have two-thirds less time to hone their cars' set-ups and settings for the competitive sessions given there is only a single one-hour session of practice running instead of the usual three.

Building up rhythm and confidence is crucial on a street track so drivers know they will have to shortcut that process this time in Singapore. However, that is clearly easier said than done, increasing the likelihood of mistakes in sessions that count and teams going down set-up cul-de-sacs.

A further potential twist comes in the scheduling of the sessions.

That sole practice takes place in the hours before sunset at 4.30pm local time (9.30am BST) whereas Sprint Qualifying is at 8.30pm (1.30pm BST) when the floodlights will be in full effect and temperatures will be a little cooler, creating a set-up conundrum for teams as cars, engines and tyres won't necessarily behave the same in different conditions.

Parc-ferme conditions mean teams can't then touch the cars again for Saturday's Sprint, which takes place during the late afternoon like practice.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2025 Singapore Grand Prix from the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

A precursor to Monaco 2027

Next season the Sprint format is being expanded to 10 events and, when the full 2027 calendar was published last month, the surprise news came from the fact that Monaco had been selected to host one of them.

The Principality's street circuit is even narrower and harder to pass on than Singapore's, which has increasingly made qualifying the standout aspect of that particular race weekend as cars have become wider and more reliable.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player F1 drivers share their opinions following the announcement that the Monaco Grand Prix will get a Sprint race next year.

Staging two races there next year therefore appears to be as counter-intuitive as it does in Singapore, yet the opposite thinking in terms of doubling up on qualifying and building in the potential for more unpredictability now appears to be a balancing factor.

It will be interesting to hear what drivers, who have mostly been supportive about bringing the Sprint to Monaco next year, make of the Singapore Sprint experience as it unfolds.

A four-team fight for Singapore victory?

Irrespective of how much unpredictability there is this weekend on Singapore's Sprint debut, the weekend promises to be competitive in the battle for victory at the front.

Max Verstappen's impressive win for Red Bull last week in Malaysia means F1's 'Big Four' teams have now all won at least one race in the first year of the sport's new regulations, with Mercedes' early-season dominance a thing of the past despite the Silver Arrows' continued command of both world championship races.

Marina Bay was actually one of only two races that Mercedes won last year although George Russell, who dominated that weekend, already knows his hopes of going back-to-back are effectively over thanks to a grid penalty for excessive engine usage that will send him to the back of Sunday's grid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains why George Russell's Singapore GP grid penalty could end his chances of a world title this season.

Russell will still hope to be a factor at the front in Saturday's Sprint, though, where the grid penalty does not apply.

But it is clearly championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who dominated Monaco but crashed in Baku qualifying, who will be carrying Mercedes' front-running hopes into Sunday on a weekend the team bid to get a handle on why their big aerodynamic upgrade brought to Malaysia did not deliver the expected step forward.

Who has won on 2026's Sprint weekends so far? Race weekend Sprint winner Grand Prix winner China George Russell Kimi Antonelli Miami Lando Norris Kimi Antonelli Canada George Russell Kimi Antonelli Britain Kimi Antonelli Charles Leclerc Netherlands George Russell Lando Norris

The in-form Verstappen will also likely be a factor at the front for resurgent Red Bull as he finally looks to win the Singapore Grand Prix - at the 10th attempt.

Marina Bay is the one long-standing track on the current calendar (Madrid, where Verstappen finished second last month, only joined the schedule this year) that the Dutchman has yet to win at.

Verstappen has qualified and finished second in each of the last two years, so has certainly been knocking on the door to do so. Red Bull will hope their recent performance gains elsewhere transfer to the unique demands of Singapore.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the F1 Show podcast, David Croft looks at Red Bull's strengths following Max Verstappen's dominant win at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

Then there is McLaren, who claimed dominant victories with Lando Norris on F1's last visits to high-downforce tracks in Hungary and Zandvoort but have hitherto not enjoyed great success across the first two legs of the Azerbaijan-Malaysia-Singapore triple header.

The absence of long straights is good news for Ferrari, who will hope the race pace that allowed Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to recover strongly from the team's disastrous slick-tyre strategy at the start of last Sunday's delayed Sepang race will transfer to the slower-speed streets of Singapore.

Sports.title: What's next for Littler? Can he still qualify for Players Championship Finals?
Sports.content:
Two-time world champion Luke Littler can still qualify for the Players Championship Finals in Minehead – but what else can he win?

His unprecedented 12-month clean sweep may be over following a crushing 10-4 defeat by Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam and a shock first-round exit at the World Grand Prix, but he can still qualify for next month's Players Championship Finals.

The world No 1 had won the first six premier events of the season following his World Championship triumph at Alexandra Palace in January with the World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup of Darts and World Matchplay.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Dawson discusses Luke Littler's early World Grand Prix exit

Darts in 2026 Event Winner Dates World Championship Luke Littler Dec 11-Jan 3 World Masters Luke Littler Jan 29-Feb 1 UK Open Luke Littler March 6-8 Premier League* Luke Littler Feb to May World Cup* Luke Littler and Luke Humphries June 11-14 World Matchplay Luke Littler July 18-16 World Series of Darts Finals* Ross Smith September 17-20 World Grand Prix Luke Humphries Sept 28-Oct 4 European Championship October 22-25 Grand Slam of Darts November 14-22 Players Championship Finals November 27-29 *Non-ranking event

He had been hoping to add the World Series of Darts Finals, World Grand Prix, European Championship, Grand Slam of Darts and Players Championship Finals trophies to complete a historic clean sweep of the year. But his bid was derailed by Clayton, who reeled off seven of the final eight legs to defeat the teenager before overcoming Luke Woodhouse in Leicester, where he suffered a 2-1 defeat in the double-in, double-out tournament.

At the weekend 19-year-old Littler lost in the semi-finals of the World Youth Championship to Cam Crabtree.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Paul Nicholson has backed Littler's reduced schedule for the rest of the season

Had he gone on to win the title, Littler would have become the first player to hold both the World Championship and World Youth titles.

The final will take place on Sunday, November 29, in Minehead as part of the Players Championship Finals, a tournament Littler won last year but has yet to qualify for this time around.

What could the rest of Littler's year look like? Players Championship 33 (Leicester) November 4 Players Championship 34 (Leicester) November 5 Grand Slam of Darts* (Wolverhampton) November 14-22 Players Championship Finals* (Minehead) November 27-29 World Championship* (Alexandra Palace) December 11-January 3 *denotes major

With just two floor events remaining before the Players Championship Finals, Littler can still earn enough prize money to qualify for the tournament - but will he make the trip to Leicester on November 4 and 5?

The top 64 players on the ProTour Order of Merit qualify for the Minehead showpiece, with the projected cut-off expected to exceed £30,000 after all 34 events. Littler currently sits in 126th place with £10,500, while Mike De Decker occupies the final qualifying spot in 64th with £29,250.

That leaves 'The Nuke' with a slim route into Minehead, but he would likely need to reach the final of at least one - and potentially both - of the final two ProTour events to force his way into the field.

Littler won the 2025 title, defeating Nathan Aspinall 11-8 in the final.

Sports.title: Rahm to quit LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms
Sports.content:
Jon Rahm is set to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms proposed to him for the relaunch of the series “unacceptable”; Rahm is reportedly owed up to $150m (£113m) from the contract he signed three years ago, with both sides now working towards a separation agreement

Jon Rahm withdrew from this week's Open de Espana as he expects the birth of his fourth child

Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series “unacceptable”.

LIV Golf is currently going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the US after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its support at the end of the season, having invested $5bn (£3.7bn) over four years.

While players including Sergio Garcia successfully petitioned the court to lift the automatic stay on their contracts, effectively freeing them to explore other opportunities for next year, Rahm was not granted the same route out.

The Spaniard is one of LIV Golf's two biggest names, alongside Bryson DeChambeau, and is reportedly owed up to $150m (£113m) for the remainder of the contract he signed almost three years ago.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm says he's willing to honour his contract with LIV Golf but his future beyond that remains a doubt.

"Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0," attorney John Beck told a bankruptcy hearing.

The Athletic has also reported that Rahm and LIV are working towards a separation agreement, with a deal expected to be finalised by October 15.

Rahm withdrew from this week's Open de Espana in Madrid to remain at home with wife Kelley, who is expecting their fourth child.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Geraint Hughes explains what is next for LIV Golf and what will happen to their players after they filed for bankruptcy.

The 31-year-old has already taken steps towards a potential return to the traditional tours. In May, he ended his dispute with the DP World Tour and paid around £2.21m in fines for playing in conflicting events, securing conditional releases for 2026 and making him eligible for the Ryder Cup.

Rahm previously declined the PGA Tour's offer of reinstatement through a specially created Returning Member Program, which was made available to him, Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka. Koepka was the only player to accept.

As a result, Rahm would face a mandatory one-year suspension before being eligible to return to the PGA Tour, meaning he could not play on the circuit until late August next year.

Sports.title: Garcia targets Ryder Cup return
Sports.content:
Sergio Garcia is desperate to be involved in next year's Ryder Cup, either as a player or vice-captain, with his time on LIV Golf appearing to be coming to an end.

The Saudi-backed breakaway league filed for bankruptcy last month, with its restructuring plan likely to release players from their existing contracts ahead of a potential LIV 2.0 relaunch.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Garcia is Europe's all-time leading points scorer at the Ryder Cup

This week, Garcia successfully secured a court ruling to lift an automatic stay on his contract, allowing him to seriously consider his options for 2027.

Europe's all-time leading Ryder Cup points scorer now has his sights firmly set on Adare Manor next September.

"I think everything is an option," he told a press conference at the Open de Espana in Madrid.

"That doesn't mean I won't go or that I'll definitely stay with LIV, but settling the LIV 1.0 matter now avoids potential repercussions related to that contract.

"I don't really know how things will end up with the DP World Tour regarding LIV 2.0, we'll have to see, [but] I want to try and give myself the best chance of making that team.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Garcia was successful in getting a court to lift an automatic stay on his contract and can now assess his options in 2027

"Everyone knows how much I love the Ryder Cup and the possibility of playing in another one, or if not, finding some way to help in another way, as vice-captain or something like that could be something very interesting."

Garcia, who has spoken to European captain Luke Donald, added: "I told him that I'm going to do everything possible to see if I can get into that team and I also told him that if I don't get into that team, I'll help in any way I can."

The 2017 Masters champion would first need to regain his DP World Tour membership.

Garcia resigned his membership in 2023 after being sanctioned for playing in conflicting LIV events. He later paid around £750,000 in fines in an unsuccessful bid to qualify for the Ryder Cup at Bethpage last year, but ultimately lost his card after failing to meet the minimum number of events.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm has previously said Sergio Garcia should be allowed to play at the Ryder Cup

Garcia has also not ruled out a return to the PGA Tour, although under its rules he would have to serve a suspension until August.

"It's definitely a possibility. I turn 47 in January, and the Champions Tour is a possibility," he said.

"Besides, I'd like the chance to play some of those tournaments, especially the big ones on the Champions Tour. These are things that I'm starting to consider at my age."

Sports.title: Verstappen: F1 'less stressful' without Horner
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says the Formula 1 paddock is "less stressful" following Christian Horner's exit because "it is not nice when you constantly have tension between people".

Verstappen, who secured his first victory of the season, and the 72nd of his career, at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, won all four of his world championships at Red Bull while Horner was at the helm as team principal.

Horner has been consistently linked with a return to the sport, saying he has "unfinished business" and that leading Ferrari would be a "dream".

Any comeback could see him spar with fellow bosses Toto Wolff (Mercedes) and Zak Brown (McLaren) once again.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jacques Villeneuve comments on the likelihood of Horner joining Ferrari following his comments that working with the team would be a 'dream role'

In an interview with the Press Association, Verstappen said: "To be honest, I like to see people get on. It is not nice when you constantly have tension between people.

"Of course, from the outside, people like it, but honestly between the teams, it is better when you have just a friendly relationship.

"It is not as spicy, but I obviously quite like how things are going at the moment with everyone's behaviour, let's put it like that.

"It is less stressful. We are all leading a stressful life and when you can take a bit of stress out at times, it is good."

On Horner's potential return, Verstappen said: "He has shown he did a good job. Of course, people spread a lot of rumours and I don't know how much of that is true.

"I don't want to sound rude, but it is also not my problem or concern. He wants to come back and if there is a good opportunity I am sure he will but I don't know where that is going to be."

Image: Horner left Red Bull in 2025

Verstappen: Rebuilding Red Bull is what's driving me

Verstappen recently signed a new four-year deal at Red Bull having spoken with other teams including McLaren - but did he fancy a switch to Ferrari?

The Dutchman said: "I only want to win.

"I am not a nostalgic type. Do I have a lot of respect for the [Ferrari] brand? Absolutely. But if that means you then commit yourself, and you are driving P5 or P6, what's the point?

"I am very performance-driven, and I have won a lot with this team already. It is a second family at Red Bull, and the challenge of rebuilding is what's driving me."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Verstappen jokes about getting Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar on his private jet

Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso has penned a deal to stay in F1 beyond his 46th birthday but Verstappen, 29, does not expect to still be around at that age.

"Staying here until then would mean I have dedicated more than half of my life to Formula 1, and that is probably a bit too much," he added.

"I have extended for a few more years, and then I will look again and say to myself, 'can I commit 100 per cent?' If not, or there are other fun things around that deserves more time, then maybe I don't continue.

"I also want to spend more time at home and see the kids growing up."

Sports.title: Southampton manager Tonda Eckert given six-week suspended ban for Spygate scandal
Sports.content:
The Southampton head coach, Tonda Eckert, has escaped a ban from the Football Association for his part in the Spygate scandal that led to the club being expelled from last season’s Championship playoff final and denied the chance to win promotion to the Premier League.

The German has been given a six-week suspended ban and £28,000 fine by an independent commission after admitting all charges of misconduct, but the FA could appeal against the sanction after its lawyers demanded a three-month ban from all football.

Quick Guide How do I 

Eckert was charged with misconduct in July after Southampton admitted they had spied on three Championship clubs last season in a breach of English Football League regulations, including their playoff semi-final opponents Middlesbrough before the first leg.

Southampton beat Middlesbrough over two legs to reach the final, but were subsequently found guilty of a “contrived and determined plan” to spy on Oxford, Ipswich and Middlesbrough by an EFL independent disciplinary commission, who removed the club from the playoffs and imposed a four-point deduction for this season.

While Southampton appealed against that punishment it was upheld by the league arbitration panel two days before the playoff final at Wembley, where Hull beat Middlesbrough to reach the Premier League.

In their written reasons for imposing a suspended ban the independent commission makes clear they disagreed with many of the findings of the EFL panels, describing Eckert as a “particularly impressive witness” who showed “genuine contrition”.

In contrast the original EFL commission that kicked Southampton out of the playoffs had condemned Eckert’s “deplorable” behaviour in pressuring junior members of staff to spy on their opponent’s training sessions, while they also said they were “unimpressed” with his testimony.

The commission hearing the FA charges concluded there was no evidence of Eckert pressurising staff however, adding that “although there are three rule breaches, we do not consider there was a systematic or organised course of conduct”. With Eckert having admitted three breaches of FA Rule E3.1, most of the hearing, which took place last month, was devoted to determining the sanction.

In their submission to the commission the FA’s lawyers initially argued for a ban from football of “at least nine months”, citing the 12-month ban given to Canada Women’s coach, Bev Priestman, for using drones to spy on New Zealand during the 2024 Olympics, which they reduced to a suggestion of three months allowing for mitigation.

View image in fullscreen Tonda Eckert can continue in his role after receiving a suspended ban. Photograph: Matt Watson/Southampton FC/Getty Images

The commission accepted Eckert’s evidence regarding the three incidents in question, namely that he suggested observing Oxford’s training session before a Championship game last December, accepted video footage from an Ipswich session later in the season without commissioning the spying and requested that someone watch Middlesbrough train before the playoff semi-final to determine whether Hayden Hackney was fit to play.

Eckert’s claim that he did not know such acts were a breach of EFL regulations was also accepted by the commission, which concluded that a 16-week ban from football was proportionate before mitigation.

The commission noted what they described as Eckert’s “genuine contrition”, however, including consulting a psychologist to determine how his behaviour could affect other members of staff, and the fact that a lengthy ban would almost certainly cause him to lose his job, which led to their proposed ban being reduced to nine weeks.

A further three-week reduction was applied in recognition of Eckert’s guilty plea before the commission opted to make the six-week ban suspended because of the wider impact such a punishment would have on Southampton as a club and their fans.

In response to the verdict, the Southampton chair, Dragan Solak, gave his backing to Eckert and praised the FA’s handling of the process, but was extremely critical of the EFL. “We have already suffered enough, and we appreciate the panel’s recognition of that,” Solak said. “We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role.

“I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe’s most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season. I’d like to thank our fans for standing by us and showing the team so much support during a time when we have needed them more than ever.

“The FA process has been a positive experience. Tonda has been given the opportunity to be open and honest with the panel, and the panel has been able to see that he is simply a good person who made poor decisions.

“The same cannot be said for the EFL process, and the way they have subsequently treated us is not something we will forget. However, now is the time to look forward to what I believe will be a great future for our club.”

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery | Marcela Mora y Araujo
Sports.content:
“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.

Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidents we all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.

Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time as Argentina captain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.

View image in fullscreen A giant number 10 shirt was displayed on the pitch before Messi’s farewell apperance. Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/AP

Despite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.

“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”

Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentina came against Benin on Tuesday – a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.

View image in fullscreen An 18 yr old Lionel Messi grapples with Hungary’s Vilmos Vanczák and is sent off after 44 seconds on his Argentina debut. Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Getty Images/Allstar

Messi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?

Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.

But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.

View image in fullscreen Adoring fans cheer for Messi before the match against Benin. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

But the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When he quit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.

Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspiring the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.

Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.

View image in fullscreen An electric atmosphere at Estadio Monumental. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

But against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.

To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and then clad himself in the same flag that fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.

But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi salutes his adoring fans after his final match for Argentina. Photograph: Roberto Tuero/ZUMA/Shutterstock

The cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.

“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.

As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.

Sports.title: England ready to level up and embrace ‘calculated risks’, claims Tuchel
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel believes England have unlocked a new level after moving forward with his tactical tweaks in the opening Nations League fixtures. The head coach wanted the players to retain their aggression, especially in the high press, to step on to the front foot and to harness the chaos often seen in the Premier League. But he has also tried to get them to play with greater freedom, to trust and follow their instincts more – while being alive to the need to cover for their teammates.

The results have been positive. After losing to Spain at Wembley, England recorded three wins: two against Czechia either side of the 7-0 victory against Croatia in Rijeka. They have in essence guaranteed their progress into the quarter-finals of a competition regarded as a tune-up for Euro 2028, while putting a bit of distance between themselves and the heartbreaking World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in July.

“I have never done a big tournament or a big camp after a tournament,” Tuchel said. “It was new for me and brilliant to see how everyone bought in to the idea of the next steps and the details needed to adjust to maybe unlock the next level.

“It was football on a very high level, football that suits us, attacking football. It was a lot of high-ball wins and we took some calculated risks in the ‘man-man’ approach in the opponents’ half. We did it in all four games and we had four good performances if unfortunately not four wins. We didn’t beat Spain but it was always about the reaction and that was on a high level.”

Tuchel’s assistant, Anthony Barry, talked on Monday about adding more flexibility and fluidity to the game model. Tuchel was asked to elaborate. “We had the feeling that it was the next step because we saw them in training and we said sometimes we were missing the transfer [from the training pitch] into the game,” he said.

“So we made some slight adjustments to how we trained – not big ones because we always believed we had something to build on – but slight adjustments in the structure of how we build up and also how we defend. I am happy that what we did worked. We finally had two weeks with the team which helped a lot because we can do reviews of matches and training and we have a chance for a common language to sink in, for the patterns to sink in.”

View image in fullscreen Jarell Quansah has urged his England teammates to be ‘relentless and ruthless’. Photograph: Charlotte Wilson/Offside/Getty Images

The defender Jarell Quansah said the style had evolved since the World Cup and felt more aggressive and front-footed. “It’s exactly that,” he said. “I think it’s going all out. We can really dominate teams with the lads playing in the Premier League at such a high level and high intensity.

“It’s being relentless and ruthless. As soon as we score a goal, it’s not easing off, it’s going again, going again, trying to get the next goal, trying to put the next player under pressure. Everyone’s working for each other. If someone gets outplayed, the next person is into a tackle.

“We’ve put together a few performances now where we’ve fully gone for games and not tried to sit back. That’s what we wanted to do in this camp. We’ve shown how aggressive and dominant we can be against top nations in a tough group. There’s a lot more to come.”

Quansah also opened up on the pain of his World Cup red card. He was sent off in the last 16 against Mexico at the Estadio Azteca for catching Jesús Gallardo with a high and late tackle. It was the 54th minute and England led 2-1. They went further in front before being pegged back to 3-2 and digging in for a famous victory. Quansah was suspended for the quarter-final and semi-final.

“It was horrible,” he said. “I went into the tackle quite fast so it was a bit unlucky to end up the way it did. Being inside [the dressing room] and watching the team pull through was gut-wrenching but an unbelievable moment as well.

“It was tough. And obviously the two-game ban wasn’t ideal. You’re not just going to move on and forget about stuff. Obviously, it hurts so much. It’s not easy to get over something like that and it’s not been too long after.”

Sports.title: ‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal deal
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has promised “this is only the beginning” of what he can achieve as Arsenal manager after signing a new long-term contract that would take his reign at the club beyond a decade if he sees it out.

The Spaniard is understood to have signed a four-year deal worth more than £20m a season, making him the best-paid Premier League manager. That is a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait to be crowned champions after three successive runners-up finishes.

Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City. After losing the Champions League final last season to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout, the 44-year-old is targeting more success as he seeks to build a winning dynasty at Arsenal, where he previously served as captain under Arsène Wenger.

“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” Arteta said. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”

Arteta’s previous contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season, was believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal, to June 2030, cements his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world. His coaching staff have also signed extended deals.

“It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship,” said Arsenal’s co-chairs, Stan and Josh Kroenke. “Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.

“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019. He has a deep understanding of Arsenal’s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.”

Arsenal confirmed this week that they have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. His side face Leeds on Saturday as they attempt to bounce back from a surprise 3-0 defeat at Brighton before the international break that ended the champions’ 100% start to the new campaign.

Sports.title: Portuguese authorities took 83 days to tell Rui Pinto his witness protection was ending
Sports.content:
Portuguese authorities kept Rui Pinto in the dark for almost three months about their decision to end his status as a protected witness and notified the Manchester City whistleblower 10 days before it was due to expire, it can be revealed.

According to documents seen by the Guardian, the special security programmes commission (CPES), which oversees Portugal’s witness protection programme, met on 8 and 9 July to discuss Pinto’s case. It concluded that the threat level against him was low and that the special protection measures were no longer warranted.

Yet it was not until 30 September that Pinto, who has been a protected witness since 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest, was informed of the decision – 83 days after it had been made.

With 10 days’ notice, Pinto was left with little time to address a number of immediate issues. He needs to find somewhere safe to live and establish a way of supporting himself in a new location, while avoiding contact with family members.

The Guardian contacted the CPES on two occasions seeking details of the criteria and evidence used to determine that Pinto’s protection should be withdrawn. On Wednesday, the commission was also asked to explain the 83-day gap between its decision and the notification. None of the inquiries received a response.

On 30 September, the day Pinto was informed his protected-witness status was coming to an end, the Premier League’s guilty verdict against City, which had been confirmed 24 hours earlier, was dominating headlines around the world. The authorities stood by the decision reached nearly three months earlier despite protestations from Pinto and his lawyers that he fears for his life.

Pinto entered Portugal’s protection programme after cooperating with the country’s justice authorities. His revelations have subsequently been used by judicial, tax and sporting authorities across Europe, including the Premier League’s investigation into City’s alleged financial irregularities. Pinto’s lawyers argue that the authorities should take into account his cooperation with the justice system and the continuing risks associated with his disclosures before ending his protection.

Mounting pressure appears to have prompted a rethink. Last Saturday Portugal’s justice minister, Rita Alarcão Júdice, was questioned by journalists about the decision. She said the authorities would review Pinto’s case and promised to respond by Saturday, the date on which his protection is due to end.

“I have received various requests and we are examining them very carefully,” Júdice said. “If there has been any irregularity, or if any procedure was not handled as it should have been, that will, of course, be taken into consideration.”

The Guardian understands that, as it first reported, Pinto remains willing to cooperate with British authorities in the City case and in other investigations stemming from his findings. He handed over millions of documents to investigators in France, which can now be shared with other nations – including the UK – under international cooperation and bilateral ties.

Pinto’s lawyer, Francisco Teixeira da Mota, told the Guardian an appeal against the decision would be filed this week. “The most shocking thing is the fact that he wasn’t heard before the decision was made,” he said. “It’s something that goes against the European court of human rights.”

In a press release last week, Pinto’s defence team called the decision “an act of state terrorism”. Their outrage has intensified after they learnedtheir client had been kept in the dark for almost three months. “It says a lot,” Da Mota added.

Sports.title: Robertson rant and the wrong system? Pocognoli’s Scotland start raises questions
Sports.content:
What is the general situation after four games?

Scotland are staring at a third-place finish in Group B1 of the Nations League, which will have repercussions for their seeding in Euro 2028 qualifying. More striking, though, was the general standard of performance over Sébastien Pocognoli’s first four games as manager.

Scotland were dismal for a half in Slovenia before a decent but scoreless recovery. They capitulated after an early sending-off against Switzerland, failing to register a shot on target in a meek 3-0 loss. North Macedonia were as poor an international team as Scotland have faced in recent times, rendering the 2-0 win in Skopje worthy of little more than a shoulder shrug. Pocognoli’s men rounded off this extended window by being played off the Hampden Park pitch by Slovenia. Andy Robertson, the captain, strikingly questioned the attitude of his teammates. There has been no new manager bounce.

Pocognoli was given only a two-year contract, which was odd given the pedestal he was placed on by the Scottish Football Association when hired in August. The likelihood remains host-nation status will secure the Scots a place in the next Euros, but the country cannot arrive at the event under the cover of darkness. The alarming nature of the performance against Slovenia – it really had no redeeming qualities – places a huge emphasis on November’s fixtures.

Are Scotland suited to the way Pocognoli wants to play?

It does not look that way. The manager deploys a three-man backline as routine, with an emphasis on pressing high and wingbacks being crucial to attacking phases. Scotland do not have an obvious two-man central defensive pairing, meaning they most definitely struggle when the number is increased by one. Time and again, they leave far too much space in behind and look woefully exposed. Counterattacks bypass Scotland’s midfield all too easily. Pocognoli’s Scotland are a dream to play against.

Success for the Scots under Steve Clarke came from being well-drilled, compact and difficult to beat. Unsexy perhaps, but effective. Playing with gay abandon is all well and good when having a level of security Scotland simply do not possess currently. Scotland allowed Slovenia to be just as menacing as Morocco and Brazil, top-quality opposition they faced at the World Cup. Pocognoli’s desired methods may be impossible to implement without day-to-day involvement with players. Ideology is fine when club football permits an overhaul of personnel.

When Scotland switched to a defensive four in the closing stages of the Slovenia clash, players appeared generally confused. This was a bad look for Pocognoli, who has insisted he is “flexible” in a tactical sense and disputed the idea he had a touchline row with Robertson. Scott McTominay’s return for the next set of fixtures would provide an iota of hope, were it obvious where the Napoli man fits in. The setup as is will not maximise the abilities of McTominay, John McGinn, Ryan Christie and Billy Gilmour.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli consoles Billy Gilmour after Scotland’s feeble defeat at home against Slovenia on Tuesday. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

Didn’t fans want a revolution?

A reality is Scotland have qualified for three of the last four major tournaments. Noise directed towards Clarke underappreciated the scale of his work. That said, after seven years, Clarke’s tenure had run its course.

The obvious move at that point was to turn towards a coach who had succeeded in tournament football with a similarly sized nation. With the level of available talent dropping or ageing, there was also a requirement for pragmatism and realism. Instead, Scottish FA officials spoke of a data-led search for Clarke’s successor, which led them to a coach who had never managed in international football before. Trying to be too smart by half? This team was not fundamentally broken, it just needed to progress.

Nobody of sane mind should insist upon Scotland morphing into the Ajax team of the 1970s. The baseline, created by Clarke, is now tournament participation. This summer’s World Cup was the latest example of how finals involvement positively alters attitudes within and outside Scottish football to an unparalleled level. That is the important thing. The rest is fluff.

There were 34,000 at Hampden for Slovenia’s visit; hardly disastrous in broader Nations League context but almost 20,000 short of capacity. The public are yet to buy into Pocognoli and the blue-sky vision sold by his employers.

How does Pocognoli handle Ben Gannon-Doak?

Some in Scotland would have us believe Gannon-Doak is the tartan equivalent of a young Ryan Giggs. The truth is that at 20 Gannon-Doak is a player who is lightly raced at club level and, at this point, looks unlikely to make a first-team impact at Bournemouth. He has searing pace and a directness that scares defenders, which is offset by woeful decision making. Whether these shortcomings can he improved upon very much remains to be seen.

What is clear is that Gannon-Doak cannot operate as a right wingback for Scotland against credible opposition. Deploying him there also denies a start to Aaron Hickey, who is undeniably one of Scotland’s best players. Gannon-Doak is a winger (as are Josh McPake and Findlay Curtis). Pocognoli’s first-choice method does not involve wingers. Something has to give.

View image in fullscreen Ben Gannon-Doak, pictured holding off Slovenia’s Erik Janza, is not a wingback. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

What is the wider scenario that Pocognoli is part of?

The Scottish FA suddenly has a chief football officer in Craig Mulholland, and a head of strategy, operations and performance in Graeme Mathie. The latter was plucked from the Scottish second tier and the former was present in the dressing room during Scotland’s Nations League fixtures. The move to insert this level of middle management carrying wishy-washy job descriptions is strange, not least when neither of the individuals in question can provide working examples of markedly improving the big picture with an equivalent nation. Meanwhile, the new Scotland Under-21s manager, Tony Docherty, who is fielding teams in the same formation as Pocognoli, last took charge of a plummeting Ross County.

Scottish football in general has a reluctance to let others mark its homework. Those in high office, typically very pleased with themselves, fail to convince on umpteen levels. Scotland have to work far, far harder at finding resource for the men’s A team. Six starters against Slovenia were 30 or older. Clarke could be obstinate but there was no raft of exciting footballers he chose to ignore.

There is no question of the Scottish FA becoming anxious towards Pocognoli. Indeed, as was the case with Clarke, they seem beholden to him. If this goes wrong, however, there will be significant questions to be answered about a chosen direction of travel.

Sports.title: Arsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World Cup
Sports.content:
The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to the Club World Cup, with Arsenal and Chelsea likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month.

The Guardian revealed last week that the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup is set to be awarded to the US, with transatlantic travel to cause additional problems for European sides, while the proposed dates of 5-30 January will clash directly with the WSL.

Fifa has yet to confirm the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup but the Guardian has learned Arsenal are guaranteed to be involved as 2025 Champions League winners and Chelsea are likely to join them, although they would lose their place if Manchester City win this season’s Champions League. Based on this season’s schedule, an extended run in the Club World Cup would mean the two English clubs missing up to four WSL match weeks plus the fourth round of the FA Cup, playing havoc with the fixture list and causing major congestion at the end of the season.

Uefa will be granted places for six clubs: five to qualify automatically and one to take part in a six-team qualifier before the tournament, with the three highest-ranked clubs joining 13 automatic qualifiers to form a 16-team competition. While the process has still to be ratified by the Fifa council, it is understood Uefa’s spots will be given to the Champions League winners between 2024 and 2027 – currently Barcelona as the two-time champions and Arsenal, with this season’s title still up for grabs – topped up by the highest-ranked clubs in Uefa’s Champions League coefficient table.

Chelsea are third in that table for the current four-year cycle, behind Barcelona and Lyon with a 17-point lead over fourth-placed Bayern Munich, and cannot be caught. Based on the current rankings, Bayern and Wolfsburg are next in line to qualify, although the latter have not qualified for this season’s Champions League and will not accumulate additional points, so are likely to be overhauled by Real Madrid or Paris Saint-Germain. Fifa plans to cap the number of participants from each country at two, so City winning the Champions League would cost Chelsea their place.

The WSL declined to comment as it has yet to be told of Fifa’s plans for the tournament, but sources conceded its impact is likely to prove challenging. The WSL has a winter break, which is scheduled for 21 December to 10 January this season, and although that could be pushed back slightly, aligning it with the Club World Cup is not viewed as practical due to the congested calendar.

As well as creating a lopsided ­season, moving the winter break would result in a backlog of WSL fixtures during the period when the Champions League knockout stage begins at the beginning of February. The issue of fixture congestion is a growing area of concern in the women’s game and 2028 will be particularly problematic due to the Olympic football tournament taking place in Los Angeles in August, just before the start of the European domestic season.

The International Olympic Committee has expanded women’s football to 16 nations at the 2028 Games, and unlike the men’s version which is restricted to players under 23 with three overage exceptions, senior internationals are permitted to take part.

Fifa’s imposition of the Club World Cup in the middle of the European season has exacerbated the problem, and last month European Leagues, a lobby group, extended its legal complaint to the European Commission about the world governing body’s alleged “abuse of power and dominant position” to include the women’s game.

Sports.title: Bochum ban fans from jumping in unison over sickness fears
Sports.content:
The German club Bochum have banned their supporters from ⁠jumping up and down in unison in part of their stadium as ⁠the ⁠movement of the stand ​makes some spectators feel unwell.

Engineers ⁠investigated the structure as part of a Ruhrstadion upgrade plan and cleared its load-carrying ⁠capacity. Their report, however, also highlighted the fact that synchronised jumping during ‌matches created what they called a “trampoline effect” ‌in the stand that could trigger discomfort among those who are not used to it.

The 2. Bundesliga club said on Wednesday that, from 11 October, any synchronised movement in the East Stand’s standing area ‌would be banned. The stadium has a capacity of about 26,000.
