World.title: Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi detained over election chief protest
World.content:
Rahul Gandhi has been arrested several times at protests demanding the resignation of poll body chief.

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has been detained for the third time in two days during a protest demanding the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were apprehended by police on Wednesday as they marched towards Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in India’s capital, New Delhi.

A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi’s Congress Party showed police taking him into a vehicle and driving away. Authorities also detained several other opposition lawmakers and protesters.

Opposition parties, their student units and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the poll body he heads of benefiting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

India’s Election Commission has so far removed more than 130 million names from the voter lists, with millions appealing the removals. About 969 million people were eligible to vote in the 2024 election.

Protesters allege the changes disproportionately removed voters who support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters more likely to back Modi’s party.

The commission and government deny the allegations. They say the revision has no political motive but is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain registered.



Opposition lawmakers led by Gandhi protested on Tuesday as well, before police broke up their gathering and ‌‌briefly detained them.

Speaking before his detention on Wednesday, Gandhi said protesters showed up unannounced after Delhi police “stopped” their gathering the day before.

“We will go to the designated protest site, sit there, and tell the country that, for us, Gyanesh Kumar is not the legitimate commissioner,” he told reporters, referring to Jantar Mantar.

“The people who have done this [vote theft] are traitors … Gyanesh Kumar will have to resign,” he ⁠⁠added.

There was no immediate comment from the police on the detentions.

The demonstrations present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party ‌‌youth ‌‌movement forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.

The “Cockroach” protests, one of the most visible signs of public dissent against Modi’s government in recent years, reflected growing anger over job scarcity, corruption and a lack of government accountability.

World.title: Ultra-Orthodox rabbi’s anti-Zionist remarks stir Israel election row
World.content:
Comments by one of Israel’s most senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis postulating that Jews may have been better off without a state have prompted controversy in the country.

In footage broadcast by Channel 12 on Monday, the 96-year-old Rabbi Dov Lando, the spiritual leader of the Degel HaTorah party, also said that soldiers adhering to “Religious Zionism” killed in Israel’s wars were dying because of what their rabbis had taught them. The remarks, made at a closed meeting at his home in Bnei Brak, have set off a political storm three weeks before Israel’s October 27 parliamentary election.

“They are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah,” Lando said, adding that many military operations are carried out “not for saving lives, but for the honour of the state”.

Lando’s comment came in response to a question about admiration among some ultra-Orthodox Jewish men – who have traditionally refused the military draft – for religious Zionists who combine Torah study with military service.

His comments aren’t new – they were first published in February 2025. However, their reemergence this week comes amid an election campaign in which ultra-Orthodox military service has become one of the sharpest fault lines in Israeli politics.

The Israeli Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that there was no legal basis for ultra-Orthodox seminary students to have exemptions from military service, and the government has since not been able to pass legislation restoring the exemptions. The issue has led to large protests on both sides of the divide.



“The question is not what he said, but why this discourse has been placed at the heart of the Israeli debate three weeks before the election,” Ehab Jabareen, a researcher on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera.

Better ‘without a state’

Lando’s party is one of the two factions of the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance, which won seven seats during the last election in 2022, and had been part of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government before its ministers resigned last year.

The bloc did continue to intermittently support the coalition government, however, and Netanyahu has been wary of removing the military exemption – despite widespread opposition to it from many in Israel – out of fear that the UTJ and similar parties would remove their support completely.

Along with his role within Degel HaTorah, Lando is also one of the spiritual leaders of Israel’s Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community, which makes up roughly a third of the country’s estimated 1.45 million ultra-Orthodox Jews, also known as Haredim.

In May, he said he no longer trusted Netanyahu and called for parliament to be dissolved.

In the footage, he goes further. “It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state,” he says, adding that international or Palestinian rule would have been “the best situation”.

Zionism, he argues, “caused the Arabs to hate us” and brought physical as well as spiritual disaster on the Jewish people. He describes secular Israelis as having built “a state of apostasy and heresy”.

The comments reflect non-Zionist and anti-Zionist positions that used to be dominant within ultra-Orthodox Judaism, but take on an overt reference to the possibility of living within a non-Zionist state, something that is even more controversial in Israel.

Ibrahim Khatib, a conflict studies scholar at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said Lando’s remarks drew a line between Zionism and Judaism “from inside the Jewish community itself”, at a time when the official Israeli establishment “tries to bind them together”.

They also put to the test the narrative that Jewish communities in Arab societies were in danger and threatened, and that the Zionist movement came to “save them” at the formation of the state of Israel in 1948, he told Al Jazeera. However, Khatib cautioned that the ultra-Orthodox polity in Israel “is right-wing, its leaders hold right-wing positions, and some of them have made clearly offensive statements about Arabs and Palestinians”.

Political ammunition

Israeli opposition leaders moved quickly after the footage of Lando emerged this week, taking it as an opportunity to attack a figure from a party within Netanyahu’s electoral bloc.



Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – one of Netanyahu’s main challengers in the upcoming elections – called the remarks “anti-Semitic, anti-Zionist and anti-[Israeli military]”, but aimed his fire at Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who he said “back [Lando] and funnel tens of billions of shekels to him and his friends”.

Gadi Eisenkot, another opposition leader whose Yashar party has campaigned on enforcing the military draft, urged every Zionist party to pledge not to sit with Lando’s party.

Netanyahu, who publicly rejected Lando’s remarks in July when the rabbi accused the Religious Zionism movement of “incitement to murder” for its support of the drafting of religious seminary students to the military, has not yet commented.

Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, put it bluntly: “Netanyahu is silent because without Rabbi Lando and his emissaries, he has no government.”

Jabareen sees Netanyahu’s silence as “calculated”.

“If Netanyahu attacks Lando forcefully, he pays a price with the Haredim he needs to form a government,” he said. “If he stays silent, he hands his rivals material to tell right-wing voters that the man who speaks of Zionism and security depends on a religious leadership that doubts Zionism itself.”

Who fights and who dies

The military draft of the ultra-Orthodox, Jabareen added, has turned “from an old dispute over religion and state into a question about the Israeli [social] contract itself: Who fights? Who dies? And who gets the exemptions, the budgets and the political influence in return?”

Mohammad Abu Rumman, an academic adviser at the Politics and Society Institute in Amman, said the significance of Lando’s remarks lay in the question that prompted them. The example of a young religious man who combines Torah study with military service, he said, “raises a question inside the ultra-Orthodox world itself: Why don’t we do the same?”

“When Lando describes their teaching as a distorted Torah, he is trying to close the door on emulating them,” Abu Rumman told Al Jazeera. “His words are aimed at his own audience as much as at his opponents.”

But Jabareen argued that the row exposes a rift more dangerous for Netanyahu than the familiar clash between secular and religious Israelis, because it runs through the right itself. Religious Zionists have paid a heavy human price in the war, while the ultra-Orthodox leadership still rejects conscription. Caught between those who pay the price of war and those who refuse to, Netanyahu needs both, and cannot satisfy them at once.

Whether the outrage over Lando’s comments translates into votes is less clear. Abu Rumman expects the remarks to “reinforce existing positions more than change voters’ choices”. The space where they could matter, he said, lies among right-wing voters who serve in the army and resent Netanyahu’s protection of ultra-Orthodox demands.

“If Netanyahu needs these parties to build a majority, that need will not disappear because of a rabbi’s remarks, however shocking,” Abu Rumman said. Netanyahu is also not the UTJ’s only suitor: Channel 12 reported that, frustrated by his failure to secure a law exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, the party would not rule out or oppose a government led by Eisenkot.



“The Israeli right has managed to bring under one political roof two currents with almost contradictory visions of the Jewish state,” Jabareen said. “One sanctifies the state and the expansion of its sovereignty. In the other, one of its most important rabbis can say it might have been better had the state never been founded.”

World.title: Witnesses spot Eritrean troops inside northern Ethiopia as tensions flare
World.content:
Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving through a northern town inside Ethiopia, witnesses tell the Reuters news agency, days after the neighbouring countries severed ties.

At least two witnesses told Reuters they saw “dozens” of Eritrean soldiers drive through Adigrat in two trucks on Wednesday. The town is located 25km (15 miles) south of the border with Eritrea.

The witnesses said they could identify the soldiers as Eritrean by their off-white camouflage uniforms.

Another Adigrat resident who was not in town at the time said family members had told him they had also seen Eritrean troops, according to Reuters, which could not independently verify their accounts.

“The Eritrean army has entered Tigray in uniform, equipped with heavy weaponry,” said Gebreigziabher Beyene, commander of the Tigray Peace Force, a pro-government militia that has fought alongside the federal army.

“This force is being struck by drones,” he said, adding Eritrea was “deliberately deploying its forces so that the fighting takes place inside Tigray rather than spilling into Eritrea”.

Last week, the chief administrator in Ethiopia’s northeastern Afar region said Eritrean troops were fighting in the area, but Reuters was unable to confirm the claim.

In a statement on X, Eritrea’s Information Minister Yemane Meskel did not deny that troops had crossed the border, but said Ethiopia’s government was creating “a fallacious narrative of ‘self-defense’ to rationalise and camouflage its war of aggression”.

If confirmed, it would mark the first time Eritrean forces have been seen inside Ethiopia since the renewal of fighting between Ethiopian forces and a seven-group armed alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), on September 23.



Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, as well as Egypt and Sudan of backing the armed alliance which is fighting to remove the government. All three countries have denied involvement.

Eritrea announced it was severing ties with Ethiopia on Thursday after Addis Ababa announced it would close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats.

In a statement, Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Ethiopia’s actions had left it with “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”.

On Monday, Ethiopian forces captured Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle, days after the TPLF confirmed that it had withdrawn from the city and moved its regional administration “temporarily” to another location.

It happened as Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five-year term, during which he insisted that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea.

On the same day, Eritrea joined Somalia, Sudan and Egypt in issuing a joint declaration calling for a political and peaceful solution to the war in Ethiopia.

The declaration appeared to push back against several policies pursued by Ethiopia in recent years, highlighting widening rifts between Addis Ababa and its neighbours.

World.title: At least 24 killed as Russia launches massive attack on Ukraine
World.content:
At least 24 killed as Russia launches massive attack on Ukraine

NewsFeed At least 24 killed as Russia launches massive attack on Ukraine

Ukraine says Russia launched a massive overnight barrage of 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, with air defences intercepting 161 targets. At least 24 people were killed across several regions, including four children in the northern city of Pryluky.

World.title: Kenya on high alert amid concern over screening after first Ebola death
World.content:
Kenya on high alert amid concern over screening after first Ebola death

NewsFeed Kenya on high alert amid concern over screening after first Ebola death

Kenya’s government has intensified Ebola preparedness efforts following the death of the country’s first confirmed Ebola patient, amid growing concern over lapses in border screening measures.

World.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks on airports killed three foreign nationals
World.content:
Share Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks on airports killed three foreign nationals on social media

Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Abha and King Khalid international airports on Tuesday and Wednesday, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation.

The attack on Abha international airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, it added.

The attack on King Khalid international airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said it is working, “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities”, to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.

On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.

A day later, at least one explosion was heard near the airport on September 19 in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid international airport.

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swath of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait which connects the Arabian and Red Seas.

Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

World.title: LSD – from counterculture to clinical trials
World.content:
NewsFeed LSD – from counterculture to clinical trials

From early psychiatric research to counterculture and secret CIA mind-control experiments, LSD has had a turbulent history. Now, it’s finding its way back into the lab and quite possibly, medicine cabinets.

World.title: Most Americans oppose Trump’s taxpayer-funded ‘golden age’ ads: Poll
World.content:
Trump says he will pay for future s, but the White House says taxpayers will not be reimbursed for past ones.

The Trump administration says its taxpayer-funded television s are about patriotism, reminding people why they should love the United States and why it is worth defending. But an overwhelming majority of Americans say they should not be paid for with taxpayer dollars.

A new Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested that 86 percent of Americans, including four out of five Republicans, believe it is inappropriate to use public money for election-related television s featuring US President Donald Trump or members of his cabinet.

The poll comes as Trump says he will stop using taxpayer money to fund the s. On Monday, he said he would instead pay for them himself and with money raised by MAGA Inc, his political action committee.

What remains unclear is whether he will reimburse taxpayers for s that have already aired. The White House said on Tuesday that the president would only pay for future s, but Trump later appeared to leave the door open to reimbursing the government, telling reporters, “The ads were really good. They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before. So, we’ll decide.”

The Trump administration faces mounting criticism about a number of government-funded s that have been airing in the run-up to November’s midterm elections, celebrating what they describe as a “golden age of America”.

In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”. The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.



All three end with a disclaimer saying they were “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The s have already cost taxpayers at least $1.4m, according to media tracking firm AdImpact, and have aired across network and cable television, including during high-viewership programmes, such as NFL games, as well as streaming services.

Democratic lawmakers have said the White House transferred $20m in Department of Homeland Security funds to pay for the campaign and have called for independent investigations.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticised the s in a Senate floor speech, saying, “Americans sat down to watch football, not to be force-fed Trump’s propaganda on their own dime.”

But criticism has also come from within Trump’s own party.

“It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters last month.

The White House has defended the s as public service announcements, pointing to government-funded campaigns under previous administrations promoting Medicare, Affordable Care Act subsidies and COVID-19 vaccinations. It says the Trump s are similarly intended to remind Americans to “love their country and understand what makes it worth defending”.

But critics say there is a key difference: those s were tied to specific government programmes or policies, while Trump’s are not.

“There’s nothing in here about a particular policy that’s at all focused,” Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told The Associated Press news agency.

Experts interviewed by The AP also pointed to potential legal issues, as the s may violate federal restrictions on using congressionally appropriated funds for “publicity or propaganda,” as well as rules limiting partisan political activity by government employees.

“You watch all three ads; they’re sheer propaganda,” said Painter. “This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders.”

World.title: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
World.content:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.

Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.

The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut.

Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has defended the police response, after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.

In an address to the nation on Wednesday evening, he denied security forces had "orders to confront" the young people.

He said the government would look into the demands made by students and promised they would present a set of proposals at the end of October, ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available. He gave no further details.

The "anger of young people does not come from nowhere," he said.

Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.

NuÃ±ez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.

World.title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
World.content:
As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.

It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.

The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.

"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.

The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.

Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.

And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.

"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.

World.title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
World.content:
Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.

It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.

On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".

Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to medical care.

A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.

Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.

Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.

The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.

That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so.

However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.

Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.

"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.

Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.

Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent.

Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.

Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.

In a statement, advocacy group Dying with Dignity called the government's decision "profoundly disappointing".

"We anticipate that a very small number of individuals with severe and persistent mental illness would be eligible for Maid under this criterion, but their suffering is no less real than those who live with physical illnesses," said Helen Long, the group's CEO.

But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.

"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.

World.title: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he has a call set up with Vladimir Putin about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.

Russian officials say they are investigating the death of the 28-year-old employee and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic.

Trump told reporters on Wednesday evening he did not believe it was a bioweapon, adding "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so,"

"If you listen to them, it's under control," he said, referring to Russian authorities.

"We hope it is," he added. Reports emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation after the death.

Referring to China's initial response to the Covid pandemic, Trump said: "Well, China didn't say much, and Russia is not saying much either. But they do say they have it very much under control."

Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.

Trump said the US was in "deep discussions" with Russia, but the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for more transparency from Russia, and requested further information on the lab tests on the individual who died.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, adding that the WHO was also seeking "verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause."

Ghebreyesus called on Russia to provide "timely, complete and transparent information" in order to clarify "conflicting reports" and help the WHO assess the potential public health risks.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information".

The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.

World.title: Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats
World.content:
A Russian missile has killed 19 people including five children in an apartment block in northern Ukraine, destroying 30 flats as families slept.

Three of the children were one-year-olds in the attack on Pryluky, east of Kyiv, early on Wednesday, and one of the boys died with his mother and grandmother, officials said.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky said it was one of Russia's "most vile strikes", and suggested the Russian military had carried it out as a "birthday gift" to Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on Wednesday.

Moscow made no mention of the attack on Pryluky but said its "massive strike" had targeted military industries in Kyiv and elsewhere.

Across the country, the death toll on Wednesday climbed to 25, as Russian strikes claimed two lives in the capital, two in Kremenchuk, and two more in Oleksandriya. More than 430 apartments and private homes were damaged and dozens of people were injured in the attack on the central city of Kremenchuk, the regional leader said.

Rescue teams in Pryluky spent hours searching for victims in the rubble of a five-storey block of flats.

Late in the afternoon rescuers said the body of a fifth child had been found at the scene. More than 50 residents were wounded in the attack that also damaged other residential buildings as well as a youth centre.

Chernihiv regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said the town was hit by five cruise missiles, one of which slammed into the apartment building.

Zelensky named the one-year-old victims as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, and said a boy of eight called Maxsym had also been killed.

Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a boy called Sasha had died with his mother, Kateryna and her mother Viktoriia, and only the boy's elder sister Olha had survived.

Local reports said they had lived on the fifth floor and that Viktoriia had been looking after her grandson while her daughter worked in a factory.

World.title: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
World.content:
Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital.

Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday.

They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; Â£22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital.

But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.

Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated.

She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.

Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred.

Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president.

But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine.

Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled.

Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.

Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand.

His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

World.title: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
World.content:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.

The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.

For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.

But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.

In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.

You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.

And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.

When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.

So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.

The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.

The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.

Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."

World.title: Ten people linked to Kenya's first-ever Ebola case quarantined as screening concerns grow
World.content:
Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say.

They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday.

This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected.

"We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.

"What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked.

The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities.

World.title: Whose archive, whose history? Reclaiming the African past, By Toyin Falola
World.content:
At its deepest level, therefore, “Whose History?” is a question about power. Who has the power to record history? Who has the power to preserve it? Who has the power to classify it? Who has the power to interpret it? Who has the power to teach it? And who has the power to define what the future generations will remember? These are not theoretical queries. They shape how societies perceive themselves and how they envision their future. In other words, the historical archive is also a political site since the ability to control memory can affect one’s identity.

I was impressed by the youth-dominated audience that attended my lecture on archives on 6 October, hosted by the G.A.S. Foundation in Lagos, as part of the MOWAA in Residence fellowship. Space does not allow me to speak elaborately on this public lecture, which attracted significant questions and concerns.

Before engaging with the history in an archive, it is first necessary to come to terms with the history of the archive. In other words, the question is not one of ownership alone. It is, more broadly, a question of power, memory, representation, evidence, silence, and authority. The temptation on approaching an archive looking for Africa’s history is to see the archive as nothing more than a repository of facts. But an archive is never a mere storehouse of facts. An archive is always a construction of history, a choice of what someone has found significant enough to collect, preserve, categorise, and pass on. And it is not an innocent construction.

An archive always reflects its historical context, institutions, technologies, politics, and structures of power. Every piece of documentation has an author, an institution, a purpose, an audience, and an historical context. A colonial report, missionary correspondence, government memo, newspaper, court document, photo, or museum inventory does not provide us with the entire past. It provides us with a representation of the past. For the African scholar, it would be wise to ask not only the question, “What does this document tell us?” but also the questions, “Who is the author, why was the document produced, and what was the structure of power at play here?” This is important because history can never be totally disconnected from the environment that produces it.

This problem is more important when dealing with the colonial archive. Colonial administrations collected immense amounts of data on African societies. Such information included taxation, agricultural practices, education, labour relations, migration patterns, religion, politics, conflicts, movement of population, and resistance. This material cannot be substituted by anything in reconstructing African history. However, it was primarily collected within administrative structures, the primary goal of which was to govern African populations. Africans were often seen in these documents as subjects of classification, measurement, administration, and control, rather than authors of their own history. Words like “native”, “tribe”, “custom”, “chief”, “primitive”, and “civilised” were not neutral terms. They were part of the terminology used by colonial powers to render African societies comprehensible and governable. In this way, colonial sources can tell us a lot about Africa, but also about colonial imagination of Africa.

It is for this reason that the scholarship of African studies, and historians like me, is relevant to anyone interested in the use of African archives. In my previous analysis of the colonial archives of Nigeria, I have made points that we should not approach the colonial archives just as a repository of data but as a product of a certain knowledge and power system. This treatment of the colonial archives in conjunction with other alternative perspectives shows the need to consider the official archives together with other forms of African historical memories such as oral history, indigenous systems of thought, rituals, chronicles, among others. It is not about discarding the colonial archive but considering it within a wider evidentiary world.

This demands, as often pointed out, reading against the grain, which is to do more than grasp the obvious meaning of the document and uncover the voices, experiences, political consciousness, and history hidden behind its language. A colonial official may term a people’s demonstration as a “disturbance.” But then the historian needs to ask himself, disturbance to whom? What caused such disturbance? Is it because of taxation, alienation of land, labour abuse, political marginalisation, religious conversion, or protest against the new administration system? Perhaps the colonial language converted politics into administration. And perhaps the language of the official hides the political consciousness of the people whom he talks about. The archive will reveal much more when its assumptions, contradictions, silence, and omissions are properly considered. At times, what a document fails to say could be just as historically important as what it says.

We must therefore rethink what we mean by an archive. The archive is not simply a room filled with files. A family album can be an archive. A traditional ruler’s palace can contain an archive. A photograph can preserve a history absent from government correspondence. Songs can act as a repository for political memories that span generations. Monuments represent a society’s understanding of its history. Museum objects hold information regarding technology, religion, aesthetics, social organisation, and identity.

This approach to methodology is also directly related to the wider concerns with regard to the sources and methods of African history. Previous works like Sources and Methods in African History: Spoken, Written, Unearthed, edited in collaboration with Christian Jennings, are useful because they combine various types of evidence in the construction of African history. This approach is important in many ways. It cannot be that African history can be constructed on the basis of the documentary record of the colonial administrations alone. Every archive always has its silences. Thus, the issue is not only about what is being stored but who has been silenced as well. Where are the voices of women whose lives were not deemed historically significant? Where are the rural people who could not access the institution of writing? Where are the workers, migrants, artisans, children, minorities, dissidents, religious groups, and common people? What became of the history of people who could not write and whose papers were not seen as valuable enough for storage? The absence of a certain community in an archive does not necessarily mean that the community has not played a historic role. It is possible that the priorities of the institution have led to it.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We must, therefore, resist the perilous inclination to mistake the lack of evidence for evidence of lack. This is where the question of oral history becomes important. African societies have preserved knowledge across generations through oral traditions, genealogies, praise poetry, songs, proverbs, rituals, performances, religious practices, storytelling, and collective memory. The inability to record an event in written form does not mean that the event disappeared from historical consciousness. Orality can preserve dimensions of African experience that official archives never captured. Here, analysis of indigenous knowledge and oral traditions in Nigeria becomes useful.

First, we must focus on the oral traditions as an important source of historical information and indigenous memory, which may be treated as an archive. Consequently, it becomes obvious that African historical studies need to treat the very knowledge systems which were used by African societies to remember and transmit their past. Nevertheless, oral history cannot be idealised. Memories are rather changeable; people often forget, misinterpret, reconstruct, and even transform their memories in accordance with the current needs. Some events become important for families, while other events are neglected. Communities tend to construct competing versions of the same event. Political considerations shape memory, just as institutional considerations shape written documents. The solution here is not to substitute oral tradition for written archives but to put them in dialogue. Contradictions between official documents and oral tradition should not be considered as problems at all. They could turn out to be productive points for historical analysis.

We must therefore rethink what we mean by an archive. The archive is not simply a room filled with files. A family album can be an archive. A traditional ruler’s palace can contain an archive. A photograph can preserve a history absent from government correspondence. Songs can act as a repository for political memories that span generations. Monuments represent a society’s understanding of its history. Museum objects hold information regarding technology, religion, aesthetics, social organisation, and identity. Buildings, fabrics, recordings, movies, maps, court documents, family archives, and even digital materials can turn into historical evidence. The expanded idea of the archive relates directly to questions about the limited ideas about what counts as legitimate knowledge and delves into other types of archives of memory, speech, imagery, pictures, materiality, and native intellectual tradition. It is important to make such an intervention not only because of its political significance but also due to the methodological one. If knowledge takes on many shapes, then the historian needs to develop the capacity to recognise them.

The goal of researching African archives is to give back agency to African history. In other words, Africans were not just the targets of colonialism, governed subjects, and studied people. Africans were thinkers, diplomats, traders, politicians, entrepreneurs, intellectuals, priests, artists, farmers, institutional builders, negotiators, and resistors. Hence, the study of African history is not just about the impact of colonialism on Africa but also about what Africans did in response to colonialism…

The question of archives eventually becomes a question of ownership. Much of the history and culture of Africa exists beyond the continent in European and North American museums, libraries, universities, archives, and private collections. These items from Africa’s past include documentation, manuscripts, photographs, ethnological artefacts, and more that have travelled through a process of colonial extraction and academic collecting. This creates difficult questions. Who owns a document produced during the colonial rule? Who owns an artefact removed from an African community? Who has the right to classify indigenous knowledge? Which group has the authority to categorise indigenous knowledge? Which group has the authority to characterise African cultural materials? Which group has the authority to decide on the return, digitisation, restriction, or exhibition of objects?

Digitisation brings about a further complication into the picture. Digital technology can enable scholars, students, journalists, filmmakers, and communities in Africa to gain access to materials that might not have been previously accessible to them. It can preserve materials that would otherwise fall apart and enable researchers to gain access to materials that might be miles away from them. Digitisation, however, does not necessarily settle the problem of control. Who controls the servers? Who controls the access? Who owns the digital materials? Who creates the metadata? In which language should an African material be described? Does digitisation equal restitution, or will it be just another form of control? Africans, therefore, have to be participants in the process of archiving practices in the future and not merely users of digitised materials.

The historian, therefore, has to be not just a documentarian but an interrogator of documents. Who produced this source? When was it produced? Under what circumstances? For whom? What vocabulary does it employ? What political interests shaped it? What other sources confirm or contradict it? What voices are absent? What does the document reveal unintentionally? What does the document show us accidentally? These sorts of questions make us methodologically humble. We enter the archive prepared not only to confirm something but to complicate our assumptions. Good archival research is not about finding documents that will confirm our thesis. Great archival research allows the evidence to change, improve, and even disprove our thesis.

The goal of researching African archives is to give back agency to African history. In other words, Africans were not just the targets of colonialism, governed subjects, and studied people. Africans were thinkers, diplomats, traders, politicians, entrepreneurs, intellectuals, priests, artists, farmers, institutional builders, negotiators, and resistors. Hence, the study of African history is not just about the impact of colonialism on Africa but also about what Africans did in response to colonialism, about what institutions and ideas existed in Africa before colonialism, and about how they envisioned their futures. In other words, it is for this reason that the archive must not be confined within the walls of public buildings. Historical knowledge must move beyond the university to schools, museums, communities, media; to professionals such as documentary filmmakers and authors; and, most importantly, to the youth. Archival documents can be turned into exhibitions, documentaries, web pages, educational materials, community histories, and dialogues. It is about transforming archival research from a scholarly endeavour to dialogue across time.

At its deepest level, therefore, “Whose History?” is a question about power. Who has the power to record history? Who has the power to preserve it? Who has the power to classify it? Who has the power to interpret it? Who has the power to teach it? And who has the power to define what the future generations will remember? These are not theoretical queries. They shape how societies perceive themselves and how they envision their future. In other words, the historical archive is also a political site since the ability to control memory can affect one’s identity.

Toyin Falola, a professor of History, University Distinguished Teaching Professor, and Jacob and Frances Sanger Mossiker Chair in the Humanities at The University of Texas at Austin, is the Bobapitan of Ibadanland.

World.title: Cardiologist warns military personnel of hypertension, heart disease risks
World.content:
A military cardiologist, Life Ajemba, has warned that hypertension, prolonged stress, and inadequate sleep could increase the risk of cardiovascular disease among serving military personnel and veterans.

Mr Ajemba, a major-general, said hypertension remains one of the most common cardiovascular conditions among serving personnel and military retirees.

Speaking in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria on Wednesday in Abuja, he urged military personnel and veterans to prioritise their heart health through regular medical checks, physical exercise, healthy diets and adequate rest.

He cited studies which showed that hypertension accounted for 15.31 per cent of cases treated among mainly military retirees between 2015 and 2020.

He also referenced another study which found a hypertension prevalence of 34.3 per cent among military personnel.

He noted that major risk factors included alcohol consumption, tobacco smoking, family history of cardiovascular disease and being overweight.

According to him, the demanding nature of military service could also increase cardiovascular risks due to physical stress, psychological trauma, irregular schedules and inadequate sleep.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Military duties affect heart health through a combination of extreme physical stress, psychological trauma and environmental exposures that increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” he said.

The military cardiologist explained that prolonged stress could increase the release of hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol, leading to increased heart rate and blood pressure.

He added that sleep deprivation, anxiety and other psychological pressures could further increase the risk of hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart attack and stroke.

Mr Ajemba stressed the importance of regular medical screening among military personnel, saying early detection could help identify silent conditions such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol levels and elevated blood sugar.

He said routine medical checks could include blood pressure and heart rate monitoring, blood tests, lipid profiles, electrocardiograms (ECGs), chest X-rays, and echocardiography where necessary.

“Early detection ensures that soldiers receive treatment while remaining fit for duty, preventing medical evacuation and safeguarding their long-term health,” he said.

He also encouraged military personnel to maintain regular physical exercise, saying fitness helped reduce blood pressure, improve heart efficiency and increase resistance to operational fatigue.

Mr Ajemba, however, advised personnel to combine physical fitness with healthy eating, adequate rest and avoidance of smoking and excessive alcohol consumption.

He said maintaining a healthy lifestyle could help military personnel reduce cardiovascular risks and remain fit both during active service and after retirement.

(NAN)

World.title: Funke Akindele, Tunde Olaoye top box-office chart with ₦1.32 billion
World.content:
Nigerian filmmaker and actress Funke Akindele and film director Tunde Olaoye have emerged as the top-performing Nollywood directors at the Nigerian box office in 2025.

StatiSense, a Nigerian and African data and visualisation company, disclosed this in a tweet on its X page on Wednesday.

The company said the ranking was based on data from the Nigeria Box Office Yearbook, which tracks the performance of films released in the country.

According to StatiSense, films directed by Akindele and Olaoye generated a combined ₦1.320 billion at the Nigerian box office in 2025, placing them at the top of the ranking.

Other ranked directors

Film producer and director Adebayo Tijani followed in second place with films that grossed ₦1.159 billion, while Tope Adebayo ranked third with ₦852 million.

Yehi Morafa, popularly known as Film Boy, came fourth, with his films generating ₦522 million.

Actress and filmmaker Toyin Abraham-Ajeyemi ranked fifth with ₦480 million, followed by filmmaker and director Kayode Kasum, whose films grossed ₦422 million.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Actor and filmmaker Muyiwa Ademola occupied the seventh position with ₦419 million, while Biodun Stephen ranked eighth with ₦341 million.

Adeoluwa Owu, a film director and cinematographer, came ninth with ₦248 million, while actor and filmmaker Daniel Etim Effiong ranked tenth with ₦193 million.

StatiSense said the top 10 directors were attached to films that collectively generated at least ₦5.97 billion at the Nigerian box office in 2025.

Funke Akindele

Among Akindele’s notable projects in 2025 was “Behind the Scenes”, which she produced and released theatrically on 12 December. The drama follows Aderonke Faniran, a real estate entrepreneur portrayed by Scarlet Gomez, and enjoyed a remarkable box-office run.

Akindele also produced “Finding Me”, a film that examines love, personal growth and the challenge of maintaining balance. Amazon Prime Video released the movie on its streaming platform on 16 March 2025.

In January, PREMIUM TIMES reported that “Behind the Scenes” had crossed the ₦2 billion mark at the box office, making it the first Nollywood production to reach the milestone.

The achievement further extended Akindele’s remarkable box-office streak. In 2023, “Battle on Buka Street” became Nollywood’s highest-grossing film after earning ₦640 million locally, while it also recorded more than $61,000 from cinema screenings in the United States.

Her winning run continued in 2024 when “A Tribe Called Judah” crossed ₦1 billion at the box office. “Everybody Loves Jenifa” later surpassed that figure, grossing ₦1.88 billion and setting a new West African box-office record.

Other films

Olaoye directed “Singleness Is Bliss”, which was produced by Fisayo Ajisola-Borokinni. Abraham-Ajeyemi has directed films including “Oversabi Aunty”, “Street Genius” and “Monetised Marriage”.

Etim, meanwhile, made his directorial debut with the crime thriller “The Herd”, which opened in cinemas across the country on 17 October 2025.

Ademola directed “Orí Rebirth”, a spiritual drama that was released on 1 May 2025. Stephen has also directed several films, including the cinema releases “Labake Olododo”, “Aso Ebi Diaries”, and “Unclaimed”, as well as several direct-to-digital and YouTube productions released on her platform.

World.title: Abducted NYSC members freed after one week
World.content:
About 19 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members kidnapped while travelling from Oyo State to orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states have been released.

PREMIUM TIMES gathered that the prospective NYSC members were released during an operation conducted by some military personnel and police operatives in Imo State, Nigeria’s South-east.

Apart from the NYSC members, a yet-to-identified civilian was also released.

Security sources told this newspaper on Wednesday evening that the rescued victims were taken to the facility of the State Security Service (SSS) in Owerri, Imo State.

“They were taken to the DSS (SSS) Hospital in Owerri for treatment,” the source, a police operative, confirmed.

It is unclear, for now, if ransom was paid for the release of the kidnapped victims.

The release of the victims occurred exactly one week after they were kidnapped.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Kidnap

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that gunmen abducted the prospective NYSC members at about 6:30 a.m. on Thursday along the Owerri-Onitsha Road by Umunoha in Imo State.

They were travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states.

The police later said 10 victims were rescued at the scene following the intervention of the police and other security agencies.
