World.title: Kenya: The Researchers Building Kenya's Cotton Industry From The Seed Up
World.content:
At Kirinyaga University, researchers are testing whether Kenya can produce quality Bt cotton seed locally. The trials could help improve supply and lower costs, but taking the research to farmers will require commercial investment and support across the cotton value chain.

Inside a laboratory at Kirinyaga University in central Kenya and on nearby fields, researchers are investigating a question that could shape what farmers plant in future: can Kenya produce its own Bt cotton seed?

Their work aims to establish whether the seed, currently imported, can be produced locally as Kenya seeks to strengthen its cotton industry.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

“The experiment is about more than producing seeds. It is about generating the evidence needed to determine whether a process can work locally before it is taken to farmers and commercial producers,” says Dr. David Kabata, one of the researchers involved.

According to Kabata, the trials started in September 2025 and seed from the trial plants is now ready for laboratory testing. The tests will assess whether the seed is true to type, viable and healthy, and retains the intended Bt trait.

Grace Wambui, the trials’ field assistant, says the process began when the team received approved and certified Bt cotton seed from Mahyco. They received seed for both male and female parent plants, which they planted on separate demonstration farms according to the trial requirements.

“With these trials we are trying to establish two things. First, whether it is possible to produce high-quality BT cotton seeds locally, and the second one is to see if cotton can become a perennial crop. We want to see if cotton plants can be retained for subsequent seasons and still remain productive instead of planting new seeds every season,” says Dr. Kabata.

According to Wambui, workers were trained to select suitable female plants for seed production using a sticky/non-sticky test. They took young cotton bolls from the female plants and rubbed them against the backs of their hands. Plants whose bolls felt sticky were considered unsuitable and uprooted, while those with non-sticky bolls were retained.

At the flowering stage, workers hand-pollinated the female plants to support seed production.

Kabata says the laboratory results will guide the next stage of research, whether the locally produced seed meets the required quality standards or falls short.

“If the seeds don't perform as expected, the team plans to identify what may have affected their quality and refine the production process before conducting further trials. The objective is not simply to produce seed once, but to establish a reliable process for producing quality cotton seed locally,” adds Dr. Kabata.

The research comes as Kenya seeks to revive its cotton industry, with access to adequate and affordable seed central to efforts to expand production. Kabata says local seed production could reduce costs if the trials succeed.

“If we are able to produce the seeds here, it means that the price can go down by half,” says Dr. Kabata.

Local production could also give Kenya greater capacity to align seed supply with farmers’ planting requirements. However, the Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) cautions that producing seed locally will not automatically make it affordable. Prices will depend on the efficiency and scale of the production and distribution system.

Dr. Paul Chege, a crop scientist and biosafety expert, says local production could also help the country build seed reserves and maintain sufficient stock as farmers seek to expand production.

According to AFA, demand for Bt cotton seed is increasing as Kenya expands cotton production and promotes improved varieties. The authority expects demand to grow further as more farmers adopt Bt cotton and the area under cultivation increases.

Supply, however, has not always been sufficient to meet potential demand. Kenya depends on imported certified Bt cotton seed, with delays associated with government procurement sometimes disrupting farmers’ access.

“Lack of a local seed production and supply system is one of the major constraints affecting cotton production and expansion in Kenya. Emphasis should be on strengthening local production, multiplication, distribution and availability of Bt cotton seed, while ensuring that farmers have access to seeds in adequate quantities and before the planting season,” reads a statement from AFA.

Chege says local seed production alone will not resolve the challenges facing cotton farmers. Other parts of the value chain also need investment.

In the short term, he says, Kenya needs to strengthen extension services tailored to cotton production, revive existing ginneries and establish new ones to ensure farmers’ harvests can be processed.

He also advocates support for cottage industries to create jobs and enable more people to benefit from cotton production beyond the farm.

“Local production of Bt cotton seed is one of the critical factors that can revive the cotton industry by bringing down the cost of production and improving the quality of the produce, but it should not be viewed in isolation; it is not a silver bullet. Sound extension, proper soil and water management, mechanization and other agronomic practices must also be adhered to,” says Dr. Chege.

According to AFA, local seed production requires a system that connects research to farmers and, ultimately, finished products.

That means developing suitable cotton varieties, producing sufficient quality seed, testing and certifying it, and distributing it in time for planting. Farmers also need support to grow the crop successfully, while processors need the capacity to gin the harvested cotton and supply industries making textiles and clothing.

Close 

If effectively implemented, such a system could provide a more sustainable foundation for expanding cotton production and strengthening links between researchers, farmers and processors.

At Kirinyaga University, the researchers are working with an already approved and certified variety rather than developing a new one. This could shorten the route to supplying farmers if the locally produced seed meets the required quality and performance standards.

Kabata says commercial seed companies will need to take the work forward if the trials yield positive results. The university’s role is to establish whether quality seed can be produced locally and generate evidence to guide the next stage. It cannot produce seed on a commercial scale.

“This is a research production centre, so our main goal is, first of all, to do research and know whether it is possible to produce these seeds locally or not. From there, the other part we can play is to train people on how to produce these cotton seeds wherever they are,” he says.

Moving beyond the university’s demonstration farms will therefore require commercial seed companies and other producers to invest in larger-scale production and distribution.

Kabata is also calling on other researchers to pursue similar work and on the government to support institutions investigating ways to strengthen Kenya’s cotton industry.

World.title: Somalia: Beyond Irro's U.S. Visit - Next Steps for Washington-Hargeisa Relations
World.content:
Addis Abeba — President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi 'Irro' spent nearly two weeks in the United States from 5 to 19 September 2026, engaging in Washington and New York to press Somaliland's case for deeper international engagement. His program includes discussions with lawmakers, policy institutions, and engagement with the Somaliland diaspora. The visit gave Somaliland access to audiences that matter in American foreign-policy debates, but access by itself is not a policy outcome

Read Travel Guides For Somaliland, the more important questions are what follows the meetings and whether political attention converts into sustained relations with Congress, policy institutions, and American business. Can discussions about the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden lead to practical cooperation? And can Somaliland make an economic case that stands alongside its long-running argument for international recognition?

Discover morenewsNewsRead Daily News Since re-declaring independence from Somalia in 1991, Somaliland has built its own governing institutions and held a series of elections while continuing its long-running campaign for international recognition. For decades, however, that effort has not resulted in formal recognition by any UN member state. This situation changed on 26 December 2025, when Israel became the first UN member state to formally recognize Somaliland. The decision also generated strong opposition. The African Union reaffirmed its support for Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity, while Somaliland rejected the recognition



Follow Politics Somaliland has also maintained an official representative office with Taiwan since 2020. Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the mutual establishment of representative offices in July 2020. This cooperation is in the areas of fisheries, agriculture, energy, health, education, and information technology. These relationships have increased Somaliland's external profile, but they have not removed their wider diplomatic dispute over its status.

Building Somaliland's case in Washington

A central event in the Washington Programme came when Irro delivered a keynote address at the Hudson Institute on 14 September, 2026, marking his first official U.S. visit since winning the November 2024 presidential election. During the event, President Irro framed Somaliland's value around regional maritime security, the strategic port of Berbera, and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb strait amid rising Red Sea tensions and Houthi threats.

Access by itself is not a policy outcome."

The port city of Berbera is situated on the Gulf of Aden, across from Yemen and near the maritime pathway that leads to the Red Sea. Continuing insecurity around the Red Sea has demonstrated how quickly regional conflict can affect commercial shipping and global trade. Recent attacks on commercial ships illustrate how rapidly the instability in these waters can influence international trade.

Discover moreNews subscription serviceInvestigative journalism reportsDaily news updatesCurrent events analysisRead NewspapersBreaking news alertsRead Local NewsBrowse MagazinesEthiopia election coverageBuy Maps Somaliland can point to Berbera, its coastline, and its strategic location. But geography alone will not build a partnership. Hargeisa also needs to show where practical cooperation could work, whether in trade, logistics, maritime affairs, or other areas of shared interest.

Irro also used the visit to strengthen contact with Capitol Hill. On 19 September, he met Senator Ted Cruz. According to Somaliland's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the discussion covered recognition, strategic cooperation, security, economic cooperation, and regional stability.

Senator Cruz had already made his position public. In August 2025, he wrote to President Donald Trump urging U.S. recognition of Somaliland, pointing to its position on the Gulf of Aden, relations with Taiwan, and possible security and economic cooperation. His position represents the view of a U.S. senator, not a change in U.S. recognition policy.

Congressional engagement with Somaliland also predates this visit in 2022; the Somaliland Partnership Act was proposed to require a review of aspects of the USA-Somaliland relationship, including security cooperation; it did not itself provide U.S. recognition of Somaliland.

The opportunity lies in what comes afterwards. Somaliland needs regular contact with lawmakers, congressional staff, and policy institutions. Those relationships have to continue when there is no presidential delegation in Washington.

From strategic interest to commercial reality

Security formed another part of the Washington program. On 17 September, Irro met with representatives from the Atlantic Council and the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. The Somaliland Foreign Ministry said the discussions covered the Horn of Africa, the Gulf of Aden, shipping lanes, international trade, and strategic cooperation.

The timing is understandable. Conflict in Yemen and attacks on commercial vessels have pushed Red Sea security higher on the international agenda. Somaliland sits beside this increasingly important maritime corridor. That gives Berbera both commercial and strategic relevance.

Somaliland should use this interest, but security should not become the entire basis of its relationship with Washington. Security priorities change. Trade, investment, technology, education, and business links can give the relationship a broader base that lasts beyond the current security concern.

This may be the harder test. Somaliland regularly promotes Berbera, livestock, fisheries, minerals, energy, and infrastructure as areas with economic potential. Getting those sectors discussed in Washington is useful. Getting companies to invest is another matter.

An American company considering it would first want a clear answer to practical questions--how easy is it to register and license a business? - Can the contract be enforced? - What taxes apply? - How are commercial disputes handled? -Can profit and capital be transferred? -And is there reliable information about the local market?

If the U.S. visit leads to interest from American business, Somaliland needs to be ready with credible information, clear procedures, and projects that investors can properly assess.

There is a difference between saying Somaliland has fisheries, minerals, or a strategic port and presenting a commercially workable opportunity. Diplomacy can open the door. The business environment will determine whether investors walk through it.

On 23 September, people from Somaliland, as well as those who support their cause, assembled in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York City (Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza), asking for global recognition of their country. Somaliland's Foreign Ministry reported the rally as a public call for international recognition.

The gathering took place during the UN General Assembly high-level week. It was a diaspora-led public advocacy event rather than an official united national event, but it gave Somaliland supporters in North America a visible platform at a time when diplomatic and media attention was concentrated on New York.

Diplomacy can open the door. The business environment will determine whether investors walk through it."

The following day, Irro appeared at the Council on Foreign Relations, where the announced discussion focused on Somaliland's recognition bid and the regional security landscape. The two events served different purposes; the rally sought public visibility, while the CRP meeting placed Somaliland's arguments before a foreign-policy audience.

Somalia remains central to the equation

Somalia rejects Somaliland's claim to independence and maintains that Somaliland forms part of Somalia. The African Union and United Nations have also continued to affirm Somalia's sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, even after Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025. The United States has likewise stated that its policy has not changed. Washington's approach therefore sits within a wider set of interests involving its relationship with Mogadishu, counterterrorism, maritime security, and regional stability in the Horn of Africa. Somalia does not recognize Somaliland as an independent nation; therefore, Somalia views Somaliland as being a part of Somalia. The UN briefing also recorded Somalia's rejection of Israel's recognition decision.

Close 

For Hargeisa, this means making more than a historical argument for recognition. It also needs to explain how closer international engagement with Somaliland would fit within the wider region. That question will remain part of the debate.

Conclusion: What happens next?

A presidential visit can secure meetings and create attention. It cannot do the follow-up.

Congressional offices need continued engagement. Policy institutions need reliable contacts in Hargeisa. Investors need clear information. Business inquiries need timely answers. Security discussions will also need to move from general interest to specific areas of cooperation.

The diaspora also has the potential to contribute. Somalilanders across North America work in business, education, technology, and many other fields. Their professional networks can help build trade links, attract investment, support research, and connect people and institutions instead of primarily being organized to advocate for recognition.

The real test of Irro's visit will therefore come later.

Six months or a year from now, are the relationships built in Washington still active? Have business discussions moved forward? Are U.S. companies looking seriously at opportunities in Somaliland? Have any of the meetings led to practical cooperations?

Those questions will tell us more than the number of meetings held in September.

President Irro's visits gave Somaliland a larger audience in Washington. That is useful, but it is only a beginning.

Somaliland has spent years trying to get its case heard. Now it has to give Washington a reason to keep listening. AS

Editor's Note: Zakarie Mohamed Abdi serves as a senior advisor at Somaliland's Ministry of Trade and Tourism. He can be reached at Zakarieabdi2009@gmail.com

World.title: Africa: U.S. Backs Stronger AU-UN Role in Africa Conflicts, Supports UN Financing for AU-Led Missions
World.content:
Nairobi — The United States has backed a stronger African Union-United Nations partnership to address conflicts across the continent, saying a UN framework for financing AU-led peace operations could provide a useful tool in responding to Africa's security crises.

U.S. Representative for UN Management and Reform Ambassador Jeffrey Bartos told the Security Council that closer AU-UN coordination was particularly important in Sudan, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and the Sahel, where conflicts and militant violence continue to threaten regional stability.

"Coordination and partnership between the UN and AU can help achieve peace, security, and prosperity in Africa," Bartos said.

Washington specifically pointed to UN Security Council Resolution 2719, which provides a framework for UN financing of Security Council-authorised, AU-led peace support operations.



Bartos said such missions could strengthen the AU's role in resolving conflicts on the continent while drawing on UN support and resources.

"The deployment of a peace operation under UNSCR 2719 will strengthen the AU-UN partnership and leverage the AU's comparative advantages to addressing conflict in Africa," he said.

The United States, however, said the mechanism should be applied selectively, with any operation kept small, time-bound and focused on clearly defined objectives.

Washington said it would assess on a case-by-case basis where the framework could be most effectively used.

The remarks come as the AU and UN seek closer coordination over some of Africa's most persistent conflicts.

On Sudan, the United States called for an immediate end to the fighting and backed efforts by the AU and UN, alongside other members of the Quintet, to promote an inclusive political dialogue.

Bartos also said the United States was considering measures to support efforts to end the Sudan conflict, including expanding the existing Darfur arms embargo to cover the whole country.

On eastern DRC, he said the AU and UN should continue supporting U.S.- and Qatar-led peace efforts aimed at ending the conflict.

The United States also condemned terrorist attacks, including drone attacks, in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, saying African leadership and AU-UN cooperation were essential to confronting insecurity in the Sahel and West Africa.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia Says Al-Shabab Amniyat Chief Killed in Nisa Operation
World.content:
Mogadishu — Somalia's intelligence agency said a former head of al-Shabab's Amniyat security wing was killed in a planned operation carried out with international partners in the southern town of Jilib.

The National Intelligence and Security Agency, or NISA, identified the man as Bashir Ahmed Haji Nunow and said he was killed during the operation on Oct. 1, 2026.

NISA said Nunow led the militant group's Amniyat unit between 2016 and 2024. The agency said he operated under several aliases, including Geescadde, Fanax, Gardhuub and Ali Dheere.

The agency accused Nunow of playing a senior role in planning and carrying out attacks against Somali civilians. It specifically linked him to several major attacks in Mogadishu, including the Oct. 14, 2017, bombing at the Soobe intersection.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

NISA also attributed the Ex-Control Afgooye attack and the attack known as Soobe 2 to Nunow, along with assaults targeting hotels and other locations around Mogadishu's Lido Beach.

The agency said the operation formed part of a wider campaign to pursue senior al-Shabab figures accused of directing attacks and maintaining the networks used to organise militant operations.

NISA said the killing could disrupt al-Shabab's leadership and the networks responsible for planning and executing attacks. It did not provide details on how Nunow was killed or whether other people were killed or wounded in the operation.

Al-Shabab, an al-Qaida-linked militant group, has waged an insurgency in Somalia for more than a decade and continues to carry out attacks despite military operations by Somali forces and their international partners.

The Somali government has increasingly focused on targeting the group's senior leadership and disrupting its command, intelligence and financial networks as part of efforts to weaken the insurgency.

World.title: Africa: How Africa Can Capture More Value From Its Cotton
World.content:
column

As World Cotton Day approaches on 7 October, Africa has an opportunity to consider how its cotton industry can contribute more to agricultural development, employment and economic growth. The opportunity extends far beyond producing and exporting raw cotton.

Africa's cotton industry has significant potential to support agricultural development, employment and economic growth. Yet the opportunity extends far beyond producing and exporting raw cotton.

Building a stronger, more resilient sector requires attention to the entire value chain – from farmers and ginneries through to spinning, textile manufacturing, clothing and, ultimately, consumers.

South Africa's experience offers practical lessons in supporting farmers, promoting sustainable production, protecting fibre quality and strengthening links between growers and downstream users.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A strong cotton value chain starts with farmers who can produce consistently, sustainably and profitably. Farmer development must therefore go beyond access to seed and markets. Training, mentorship, technical support and knowledge-sharing can strengthen both production and business management.

South African cotton farmer Frans Malela illustrates what can be achieved when these opportunities are combined with determination and a willingness to learn. Malela began farming in 1984 on four hectares while working full-time in Johannesburg. He later moved into commercial cotton production, expanding his operation to more than 200 hectares.

His practices include crop rotation, soil management, integrated pest management, good harvesting practices and field hygiene. His yields increased from approximately 800 kg of seed cotton per hectare to 1.2 tonnes, reaching an exceptional three tonnes per hectare in 2021/22.

Malela also shares his experience through farmers' days, demonstrations and research trials, while his operation provides seasonal employment for approximately 40 people. His story shows how farmer development can improve productivity and fibre quality while spreading knowledge and creating employment within farming communities.

Sustainability and fibre quality go hand in hand

Sustainability is increasingly important throughout global agricultural and textile supply chains. Good agricultural practices are also fundamental to producing consistent, high-quality fibre.

Cotton fibre characteristics such as length, strength and micronaire – a measure reflecting fineness and maturity – directly influence spinning performance and fabric quality. Production, harvesting, storage and ginning practices therefore affect the value of cotton lint.

Cotton SA's South African Cotton Standard (ZACS) provides a practical framework for responsible production, bringing together farm management, environmental stewardship, people and economic viability.

Good agricultural practices support fibre quality from the beginning of the crop cycle. Appropriate land preparation and timely planting encourage uniform development. Locally adapted cultivars, effective weed and pest management, and appropriate nutrient and crop protection programmes support mature, strong fibre.

Quality protection continues during and after harvesting. Clean picking, appropriate storage and careful transport help prevent contamination and moisture damage. Clean ginneries and well-maintained equipment further minimise contamination and mechanical damage.

Sustainability, quality and profitability should therefore be pursued together. Good practices can protect natural resources, improve fibre quality and strengthen the commercial value of the crop.

Making sustainability measurable

ZACS shows how sustainability principles can be translated into a structured, measurable process.

The standard rests on four pillars – Management, Environment, People and Socio-economic – covering continuous improvement, water stewardship, soil health, responsible crop protection, labour practices, worker protection, economic viability and resilience.

Participants complete a self-assessment, followed by an internal review and a farm or ginnery visit. External verification takes place before certification, providing a mechanism to monitor performance and encourage improvement.

The programme is being tested under South African cotton production conditions through a three-year pilot. Malela has joined as a leader farmer, contributing to discussions and sharing his crop rotation system with other smallholder farmers.

For Africa, ZACS offers an example of how locally relevant standards can turn sustainability objectives into practical action at farm level.

Connecting farmers to the textile industry

Another major opportunity lies in strengthening links between cotton production and downstream textile manufacturing.

Producing more cotton does not automatically mean retaining more economic value within a country or the continent. When cotton is exported as lint and processed elsewhere, much of the value generated through spinning, textile production, garment manufacturing and retail is captured outside the producing country.

South Africa has experienced this challenge, highlighting the need to develop capacity beyond the farm gate. Initiatives such as the South Africa Cotton Mark show how locally produced cotton can be connected more visibly to manufacturers, retailers and consumers, supporting efforts to retain more value locally.

The processing gap is particularly pronounced in West and Central Africa. The World Trade Organization reported in March 2026 that around 98% of cotton from the region is exported as raw fibre, highlighting the opportunity to expand regional processing and manufacturing.

Close 

Retaining more value within Africa

Capturing this opportunity requires investment in spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing, finishing and garment manufacturing, alongside the infrastructure, skills, finance and markets needed to make these industries competitive.

Regional cooperation could allow countries to develop complementary strengths, rather than each establishing every stage of the value chain independently.

Value addition must also benefit farmers. Stronger relationships between growers and downstream users, quality-based incentives, sustainability premiums, traceability and longer-term supply arrangements can help ensure that benefits reach producers.

There is no single solution to strengthening Africa's cotton sector. Farmer development, sustainability, fibre quality, processing capacity, manufacturing and market access are interconnected.

South Africa's experience shows the value of bringing these elements together: supporting farmers, applying practical sustainability standards and connecting local cotton with manufacturers and consumers.

The journey from farm to fashion is an opportunity to strengthen African agriculture, create employment, develop skills and ensure that a greater share of the value generated by Africa's cotton remains within the continent.

Erica Vogel is Senior Quality Control Officer at Cotton SA.

World.title: South Sudan: South Sudan Rejects Claims of Foreigners' Expulsion Order
World.content:
Nairobi — South Sudan has moved to dispel reports that foreigners have been given seven days to leave the country, with Juba County Caretaker Commissioner Kalisto Lado Faustino Nyigilo saying the government remains open to legally resident foreigners but wants them to stay out of small-scale retail businesses.

Lado made the clarification on Tuesday following reports circulating on social media claiming that he had ordered foreign nationals to leave South Sudan.

He said the reports were false and that he did not have the authority to expel foreigners from the country.

"The Commissioner has never said that, and it's even not the mandate of the Commissioner to actually evacuate people or to send people out of South Sudan," Lado said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He said South Sudan welcomes foreigners who enter the country legally for business, residence, humanitarian work and other legitimate activities.

"Our policy is welcoming. We are welcoming everybody from any country who want to come to be with us in South Sudan," he said.

However, Lado maintained his position that foreign nationals should avoid small-scale retail trade in Juba, including boda boda operations and the sale of everyday food items.

He said foreigners should instead invest in wholesale businesses, companies, factories and other ventures capable of creating jobs for South Sudanese.

Lado said his earlier remarks were aimed at protecting economic opportunities for local youth and women rather than discriminating against foreigners.

He questioned the growing involvement of foreign nationals in boda boda operations, asking what opportunities would remain for South Sudanese youth if foreigners dominated the sector.

He similarly raised concern over foreign women engaging in small-scale food vending, including selling chapati, potatoes, onions and tomatoes.

Lado rejected claims that his position amounted to a ban on foreign investment or hostility towards foreigners.

"There is nothing about sending of foreigners out of South Sudan. There is nothing about prohibiting foreigners from business. There is nothing about hating foreigners," he said.

He instead urged foreign investors to bring substantial capital into the country and establish industries and companies that could employ South Sudanese.

Lado also addressed the ongoing removal of roadside businesses and structures in Juba, saying the county was not conducting indiscriminate demolitions.

He said the exercise was intended to clear roads, remove garbage and relocate businesses operating on road reserves to designated areas.

Close 

"We are not demolishing structures. We are organising the road, taking garbage out of the road and sending those who are putting their booths on the road to be in the rightful places," he said.

Lado urged foreigners living in Juba to remain calm, saying those who obey South Sudanese laws had nothing to fear.

"Our foreigners who are here, be peaceful. No fear, no worry, unless if you commit any crime," he said.

World.title: Kenya: The Symbolism Behind Raila Odinga's Pentagon-Shaped Mausoleum
World.content:
Nairobi — The unusual pentagonal shape of the late former Prime Minister Raila Odinga's mausoleum at Kango ka Jaramogi in Bondo was deliberately chosen to reflect a key symbol associated with his political life.

The Kenya Defence Forces officers involved in guiding President William Ruto and other dignitaries through the facility during its handover to the Odinga family have explained the thinking behind the design.

Samson Malaki said the five-sided structure draws inspiration from the raised fist that became one of the most recognisable gestures associated with Odinga.

According to Malaki, the fist was not intended as a gesture of confrontation, but as a symbol of strength and a call for Kenyans to come together.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He said the five fingers of the raised hand informed the decision to adopt a pentagonal form for the mausoleum.

"In as much as he was raising that particular fist, he wasn't raising that fist in defiance, but he was raising that fist to call people to unity. It is five, which represents a pentagon, and it's actually what informed the design of this mausoleum," Malaki explained.

The design also establishes a visual connection between Raila's final resting place and that of his father, the late Jaramogi Oginga Odinga.

While Jaramogi's mausoleum has six sides, the structure housing Raila's remains has five. Mr Malaki said the architects deliberately worked with the two geometric forms to create a sense of continuity between the neighbouring structures.

"The Jaramogi Mausoleum is actually hexagonal in shape. The Raila Mausoleum is pentagonal in shape. And for the purposes of that architectural harmony, we tried to play around with the geometry of Jaramogi Mausoleum, which is hexagonal, and we came up with the Raila Mausoleum, which is pentagonal," he said.

The explanation adds a political dimension to what might otherwise appear to be an architectural choice.

The number five has featured at important moments in Odinga's political journey, most notably during the build-up to the 2007 General Election.

'Pentagon'

The term "Pentagon" became synonymous with the Orange Democratic Movement's senior leadership in the run-up to the 2007 presidential nominations.

It referred to a group of five prominent politicians who were positioning themselves for the party's presidential nomination before the contest at Kasarani.

Odinga eventually secured the ODM ticket, with the other members of the group supporting his presidential campaign as the party entered the 2007 General Election.

Close 

Nearly two decades later, the pentagon has acquired a different meaning at his final resting place.

The symbolism of the five-sided mausoleum, according to its designers, links Mr Odinga's familiar raised-fist gesture with the broader theme of unity that defined much of his political messaging.

The structure therefore serves not only as a burial site but also as an architectural representation of elements associated with his public life.

Its pentagonal form stands alongside Jaramogi's hexagonal mausoleum, creating what the KDF officer described as a deliberate architectural relationship between father and son.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 7, 2026
World.content:
press review

Mali Army Retakes Kidal With Russian Support

Mali's army, backed by Russian paramilitary forces, has retaken the northern town of Kidal after Tuareg separatists announced a "strategic and controlled withdrawal" from the area. The Azawad Liberation Front said its forces withdrew without direct fighting, attributing the move to what it described as the disproportionate use of air power by Russia's Africa Corps. Kidal has long been a stronghold of Tuareg separatists seeking an independent state in northern Mali. It was previously seized by the separatists and an al-Qaeda-linked group. The recapture is being viewed as a symbolic victory for Mali's military government, which has increasingly turned to Russia for military support after distancing itself from France. Analysts said, however, that the development is unlikely to be decisive in the broader fight against jihadist and separatist groups. Human rights organisations continue to accuse both Malian and Russian forces of abuses against civilians.

Anti-Immigrant Protesters Harass Asylum Seekers Queuing at South Africa Office



Asylum seekers queuing at the Home Affairs Refugee Reception Centre in Durban were harassed by a group of about 15 anti-immigrant vigilantes. Some of the protesters wore masks and carried sticks or knobkerries as they entered the centre's parking area, where they shoved people in the queue and shouted xenophobic insults before police intervened and removed them. The group said it wanted to prevent foreigners from applying for asylum. Members linked to the March and March movement questioned why Home Affairs was assisting refugees when many South Africans still lack identity documents. The confrontation came after Home Affairs reopened the asylum system to new applicants following a Constitutional Court ruling, ending a six-year closure. Hundreds of people had arrived from early morning, with some sleeping outside overnight, but only about 20 applications were processed by the end of the day. Many applicants said the lack of documentation has made it difficult to access services, earn a living and secure basic assistance.

Nigeria's Anti-Graft Agency Opposes Diezani's UK Acquittal Evidence

Nigeria's Economic and Financial Crimes Commission has asked a court to reject former Petroleum Minister Diezani Alison-Madueke's attempt to introduce her recent acquittal by a United Kingdom court as evidence in her legal battle to recover assets forfeited in Nigeria. Alison-Madueke was acquitted in June by London's Southwark Crown Court of bribery charges. This came after British prosecutors accused her of accepting lavish benefits from oil and gas interests seeking favourable treatment and contracts. She is now seeking to rely on that judgment in her Nigerian case. She is arguing that it is relevant to questions surrounding her lack of conviction, due process and the forfeiture of her property. The EFCC argued that the UK proceedings are separate from the Nigerian case and have no bearing on the assets at the centre of the dispute, which it says were forfeited and auctioned under Nigerian court orders. The agency has also accused Alison-Madueke of attempting to broaden the scope of her case through new filings. The court has scheduled the matter for hearing on 11 November.

Namibia Intensifies Response to Foot-and-Mouth Disease Outbreak

Namibia is stepping up measures to contain a foot-and-mouth disease outbreak in the //Kharas Region. President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah warned that the crisis threatens farmers, workers and businesses across the livestock industry. As of 5 October, surveillance teams had inspected more than 29,000 animals on 68 farms, with 127 confirmed cases across 15 farms. The government has introduced movement controls, roadblocks, surveillance, testing and tracing, while plans include creating a containment buffer zone and strengthening veterinary fencing along the borders with Botswana and South Africa. The outbreak has also disrupted Namibia's vital beef export industry, with the European Union temporarily suspending imports of fresh meat from cattle, sheep and goats. The European market accounts for more than 80% of Namibia's beef exports, meaning the suspension could affect thousands of jobs and cause significant financial pressure for farmers and businesses. The government said that it is engaging trading partners to limit the impact while maintaining strict disease-control measures and protecting Namibia's reputation as a reliable meat exporter.

Close 

Ebola Outbreak Leaves Thousands of Children Without Caregivers

The Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo is having a devastating impact on children. More than 1,900 have lost one or both parents or been separated from their caregivers since the outbreak was declared in May. UNICEF said that at least 2,017 children had been confirmed with Ebola by 29 September, with 1,062 deaths recorded. Children account for just over a quarter of confirmed cases but around a third of deaths, while the fatality rate among children under five has risen to about 70%. UNICEF said that many children are dying before the disease is detected or before they reach treatment centres. The organisation is supporting nurseries near Ebola treatment centres, where babies and young children can receive food, care, monitoring and rapid medical attention while their parents are treated or after losing caregivers. UNICEF is calling for such services to be expanded to all treatment centres. Meanwhile, neighbouring Kenya has confirmed its first Ebola case and death. The World Health Organization believes it was likely imported from the Democratic Republic of Congo.

World.title: Mike Waltz fights back tears revealing what Hamas hostage refused to do before release
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

UNITED NATIONS — Three years after the worst massacre in Israel’s history, Eliya Cohen — who survived 505 days in Hamas captivity — took the stage at the United Nations alongside his newlywed wife, Ziv Abud, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre, and tried to explain to some of the world’s top diplomats what he had endured.

"They didn't let me change clothes or to get a shower, even to eat or to drink," he said. "They chained me with heavy iron chains by my leg," Cohen said during an emotional discussion moderated by Dr. Phil McGraw at Israel’s U.N. commemoration Tuesday.

He said lights were kept on to prevent the hostages from sleeping and that captors would enter repeatedly during the night screaming in an effort to frighten them. Cohen said they were not permitted to use a restroom and that at times survival felt almost impossible.

FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY

But he described repeatedly forcing his mind away from the violence and toward the possibility of returning home.

"Don't think about the violence. Don't think about the torture. Don't think about everything," Cohen recalled telling himself. "Just continue, stay strong. And maybe one day, you will come back home to your family."

Cohen was among the 251 people abducted during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when about 1,200 people were killed in southern Israel in their homes and at the Nova Music festival. It was the deadliest single day in Israel’s history. He personally lost 48 people he knew that day.

His wife, Ziv, carried a different piece of the same story.

Abud and Cohen had arrived at the Nova festival shortly before dawn with her 19-year-old nephew Amit and his girlfriend Karin. When the attack began, they eventually took refuge in a roadside bomb shelter that Cohen said was designed for roughly eight people but became packed with 29.

HAMAS USED SEXUAL VIOLENCE 'DELIBERATELY AND SYSTEMATICALLY' ON OCT 7, COMMISSION REPORT FINDS

Abud told the audience that more than 40 terrorists later attacked the shelter with grenades and gunfire. One man inside repeatedly grabbed grenades and threw them back outside before he was killed, she said.

As the attack continued, Cohen covered Abud with bodies — an act that saved her life.

"I lost my consciousness. Eliya was kidnapped," Abud said. "And after seven hours, I woke up in the shelter. I found myself in a pile of bodies."

She paused, fighting back the tears. "It wasn't even bodies. It was body parts."

Abud said she then saw that Amit and Karin had been killed. "I needed to sit with the bodies for seven more hours," she said. She was eventually rescued, one of seven survivors from the shelter.

"We were four people that went to the festival from the same house," Abud said, "And I'm the only one that came back home that night."

FORMER HAMAS HOSTAGE COUNTERS HASAN PIKER’S UT AUSTIN EVENT WITH HER STORY OF SURVIVAL

For 505 days, she campaigned for Cohen’s return without knowing whether the man she loved would ever come home. Cohen, meanwhile, said he believed while in captivity that Abud had been killed.

The couple married weeks before Tuesday’s ceremony.

"But now he's here," Abud said. "And I can look forward to the future after we got married."

She said she hoped the years ahead would include "kids and family because we are here and we survived. And we need to live a normal life," she said.

Another Oct. 7 survivor who addressed the diplomats was Oriya Berlin, a young Israeli visual intelligence observer who had arrived at a base in the Gaza border area just two days before the attack.

Berlin said she woke on the morning of Oct. 7 believing she was hearing a thunderstorm.

"Outside, thousands of missiles were raining down with a single objective: to destroy my life and the lives of my friends," she said.

Berlin and four other soldiers ran barefoot and in pajamas into a small shelter. They were unarmed. She said the women initially believed the incursion would resemble scenarios they had studied during training — a small squad that Israeli forces could quickly contain.

Seconds later, she said, they heard vehicles and gunfire. Berlin described roughly 60 heavily armed terrorists attacking the base. At one point, she said, a message appeared in the unit’s WhatsApp group telling soldiers to shout "IDF" in Hebrew so Israeli troops could find them. The broken Hebrew immediately raised suspicions that a terrorist had taken a soldier’s phone.

They remained silent.

Berlin said they then heard another group shouting for soldiers to identify themselves, followed by a burst of gunfire and silence.

Ten hours after the attack began, she said, special forces finally reached them.

THE SENATE HAS REMEMBERED AMERICA’S OCTOBER 7TH VICTIMS. NOW IT’S TIME TO HEAL

Berlin said that after learning how many of her friends had been murdered or kidnapped, she could not remain at home. Although she was offered the opportunity to leave military service, Berlin said she refused and returned as an observer for another six months before later moving into the IDF Public Diplomacy Office.

"I wanted the world to see that the IDF is not just an intimidating military force on a television screen," she said. "It was also a 5'2" fake blonde girl like me who simply wanted to protect her home, her family, and her friends."

She said she has since spoken before audiences ranging from international organizations to high school students who told her "I was wasting their time because of their deep-seated anti-Israel hostility." "But I stayed," Berlin said. "I spoke because the truth demands a voice."

Berlin said her decision to continue speaking was rooted in the friends who did not survive.

Before the ceremony, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz met privately with Cohen and Abud, asking Cohen how he was feeling physically and telling the couple how good it was to see them "healthy and alive."

Minutes later, from the stage, Waltz became visibly emotional as he recounted a part of Cohen’s captivity that he said he had been unable to get out of his mind.

Waltz said that on the night before Cohen’s release, Hamas tried to make him record a propaganda video claiming he had been treated well. "He refused," Waltz said. "He held firm. He said no."

Waltz said Hamas again tried to turn Cohen’s release into propaganda the following day, placing him before cameras and instructing him to raise his hands.

"He refused again," Waltz said. "Eliya, we salute you. I salute you," Waltz continued. "You are a proud, strong Jew. You're undefeated, man" he said with his voice breaking.

The hostage crisis stretched over two years and several rounds of negotiations, releases and rescue operations. Waltz told Fox News Digital after Tuesday’s ceremony that he wanted the commemoration to acknowledge both the loss of Oct. 7 and how much had changed since.

"Oct. 7, 2023, was their 9/11, was their Pearl Harbor," Waltz said. "More Jews were brutally massacred that day than any day since the Holocaust."

ISRAELI OCTOBER 7 SURVIVORS CONQUER TRAUMA ALONGSIDE LEGENDARY ROCK ICONS IN POWERFUL NEW DOCUMENTARY

He said it was important "to recognize the loss" and "hear directly from the survivors," but also to take stock of the region three years later.

"We have President Trump's 20-point peace plan. We have a U.N. resolution establishing the International Stabilization Force," Waltz told Fox News Digital. "He's determined to not repeat what's happened so often in the past, where Hamas rebuilds, Iran rearms, they attack again, and you have this devastation all over again."

Waltz pointed to broader shifts across the Middle East.

"Iran is on its back foot. Lebanon has hope, Syria has hope. Iraq has hope," he said.

He said he hoped the commemoration could combine "remembrance, the perspective, and I think charting, trying to chart a path of hope and peace for the future."

From the stage, Waltz argued that Oct. 7 had produced the opposite strategic result from what Iran and its allies sought. "Oct. 7 completely, and I think irreversibly, has backfired on Iran and all of their terrorist proxies," he said, pointing to changes in Syria, Lebanon and Iraq and the expansion of Israel’s regional relationships.

He ended with a message to the audience: "America will stand with the Jewish people."

"Be strong. Be resilient. Be wise," Waltz said. "And know that what you're doing is right. Stand with your moral compass and know that this administration, the United States of America, stands with you."

Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon used the gathering — attended by ambassadors and diplomats from multiple countries — to turn his attention to the institution hosting it.

MOTHER OF OCTOBER 7 HOSTAGE WHO WAS EXECUTED UNPACKS HER GRIEF IN NEW MEMOIR

"Even in this building, the U.N. is trying to demonize and isolate Israel," Danon said. "They have turned the victim into the accused, comparing our IDF soldiers to Hamas terrorists."

Danon said he has been told by colleagues that he takes criticism of Israel at the U.N. ‘too personally’.

"Indeed, it is personal," he responded. "My daughter is serving right now in the IDF. My son served as an officer in the IDF," Danon said. "He was supposed to be on the Re'im base next to Gaza on Oct. 7. The last minute, he was released home for the holiday."

"That's why it's personal," Danon said. "The U.N. tries to demonize all of our sons and daughters, our lions and lionesses who give everything so we can freely live in our homeland. So yes, it is personal. It's personal for all of us."

For Cohen and Abud, however, the event eventually returned from geopolitics to something much smaller: the possibility of an ordinary future.

Abud said they hoped to have children and build a family despite knowing that Oct. 7 and the 505 days that followed would remain part of their lives.

Cohen, asked by McGraw what he would say if the terrorists who abducted and tortured him were watching, needed only a few words.

"I won," Cohen said.

"I won and I'm here."

He then turned his message outward.

"Stay proud to be Jewish," Cohen said. "And stay proud to be Israeli."

"We are here to stay."

World.title: The best defense against high-tech AI scams is low-tech skepticism, expert warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As artificial intelligence rapidly evolves to make financial scams hyperrealistic, cybersecurity experts warn that the best defense isn't sophisticated detection software.

It's good old-fashioned human skepticism.

While adversarial states like China and Russia leverage AI on a global scale, average Americans are most frequently targeted by cybercriminals looking to exploit personal vulnerabilities for a quick payout, according to cybersecurity expert Morgan Wright.

"Let's go back to around 1860, when Edgar Allan Poe wrote, ‘Believe nothing that you hear and only one half that you see,’" Wright told Fox News Digital. "That advice is as good now as it was 160 years ago."

AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE

AI technology has allowed bad actors to automate and scale personalized fraud schemes against everyday citizens. Generative tools eliminate language barriers, draft convincing phishing texts and generate hyperrealistic voice and video clones.

By capturing just a few seconds of audio — often scraped from social media — fraudsters can convincingly replicate the voice of a family member. Wright pointed to the case of Deborah Del Mastro, a California mother who lost thousands of dollars after scammers used AI to clone her daughter’s voice to stage a terrifying kidnapping hoax.

THE FAMILY GROUP CHAT IS A GOLDMINE FOR SCAMMERS

"It's my daughter's voice," Del Mastro recalled during an interview on The CyberGuy Report podcast. "And she's having a panic attack."

Convinced her daughter was in immediate danger, Del Mastro transferred more than $5,000 to the scammers before realizing she had been swindled.

FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS'

"When you can fool a mother, that's how good these things are getting," Wright said of the voice-cloning technology. "What they do is use manipulation, influence and deceit. The more urgent I can make it sound, the more you're going to lower your guard and take action."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS

Wright, who has trained federal, state and local law enforcement in behavioral analysis, interviewing and interrogation — including teams at the FBI and the National Security Agency — emphasized that every scam relies on basic psychological triggers.

His primary advice for anyone on the receiving end of a suspicious call or message is to pause before reacting.

"We're not storming the beaches at Normandy; you're not going to get arrested," Wright said. "No law enforcement agency sends you an unsolicited text saying you're about to get arrested."

While AI platforms roll out updated security features, scammers continuously find ways around them, making software-based detection a constant moving target.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We hear about all the different models from xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini. They change models constantly," Wright said.

"So, when the model changes, how effective is [detection software]? We don't know because this stuff is moving so fast. What you see today will be drastically different tomorrow."

World.title: Amy Klobuchar calls for major anti-terrorism investments after alleged Mall of America plot
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic nominee for Minnesota governor, praised law enforcement Wednesday after the FBI arrested an 18-year-old man accused of plotting an ISIS-inspired mass shooting at the Mall of America.

"I'm grateful for the heroic work of law enforcement that prevented a mass shooting and terrorist attack at the Mall of America," she said in a statement. "This shows why we continue to need major coordinated investments in anti-terrorism and local law enforcement to stop attacks like these. Our state must take terrorism and violent crime head on, working with our federal law enforcement and local police departments to keep Minnesotans safe."

Klobuchar, who has represented Minnesota in the U.S. Senate since 2007, is running against Republican Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth in the November gubernatorial election.

MALL OF AMERICA TERROR PLOT THWARTED, SUSPECTED ISIS SYMPATHIZER ARRESTED, FBI ANNOUNCES

Her statement came after federal authorities announced the arrest of Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, who investigators say pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America.

According to federal court documents, Mohamud allegedly spent months discussing plans for an attack before buying an AK-47-style rifle, four magazines and roughly 200 rounds of ammunition from an undercover FBI employee Tuesday. The rifle had been rendered inoperable, though the ammunition was live.

FBI Director Kash Patel said Mohamud "allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans."

PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING ISIS ATTACK ARRESTED WITH RIFLE AND 190 ROUNDS OF AMMUNITION: DOJ

President Donald Trump also praised the FBI’s handling of the case while speaking to reporters Wednesday.

"I did hear about it. And they did a great job. The FBI did a great job," Trump said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Mohamud is charged with knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and federal crime of terrorism.



Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace and Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

World.title: California education candidate tells college professors to teach students basic math, rejects SAT requirement
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

California state superintendent candidate Richard Barrera drew criticism Tuesday from his opponent and education advocates after telling UC professors it was their job to teach students who arrive without basic math skills and rejecting the return of standardized testing requirements as the University of California confronts growing concerns over college readiness.

Barrera, president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education and a senior policy advisor to state superintendent Tony Thurmond, made the comments during a Sunday interview with NBC Los Angeles political reporter Conan Nolan. Barrera was asked whether the SAT should return as a requirement for the UC system as professors raise alarms about students entering elite universities without foundational math skills.

"Absolutely not," Barrera said. "So math teachers at UCLA and Berkeley and every place else, part of your job that you get paid by the taxpayers to do is to teach our kids."

Barrera told Fox News Digital that concerns about UC students being unable to perform basic math were "completely overstated," arguing that some incoming students instead just need review in subjects they had not studied recently, and that universities shared responsibility for helping them catch up.

UNPREPARED COLLEGE STUDENTS FORCED TO RELEARN 'MIDDLE SCHOOL MATHEMATICS,' CALIFORNIA PROFESSORS REVEAL

"I do think that this idea that students are coming in not knowing fractions is completely overstated," Barrera said. "What we're seeing is students who take a placement test, in the summer before they attend their freshman year at UC, who might miss questions on algebra, on trigonometry, maybe subjects that they haven't had in a couple of years. That's just about review and acceleration."

"This is not about students who are incapable of doing the work," he added. "This is about students who need some review and acceleration, and it is the responsibility of UC to participate in that acceleration."

Chino Valley Unified School District Board President Sonja Shaw, Barrera's opponent in the November race for state superintendent of public instruction, told Fox News Digital that his response shifted responsibility away from California's K-12 education system.

"Richard Barrera heard professors at Berkeley and UCLA sound the alarm that incoming students can’t do elementary-school math and his immediate response was to blame the professors. Not the students. Not the system that passed them along. The professors," Shaw said.

"His brilliant solution? Force college faculty to teach remedial middle-school math on the taxpayer dime, and claim that bringing back the SAT is somehow ‘exclusionary,’" she added. "That’s not a plan. That’s a career politician scrambling to cover up a failure he helped create."

Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital that Barrera's opposition to standardized testing protected California's K-12 education system from accountability for students reaching college without foundational math skills.

"Richard Barrera’s answer tells you everything you need to know about who he works for. The California Teachers Association is bankrolling his campaign for state superintendent, and he is returning the favor by protecting the system from accountability," DeAngelis said.

WATCHDOG REPORT EXPOSES TEACHERS UNION 'POLITICAL MACHINE' FUNNELING MORE THAN $1 BILLION TO LIBERAL CAUSES

Nolan followed up by asking Barrera whether professors at some of the country's leading universities should be responsible for teaching students fractions. Barrera said some students had overcome significant obstacles to reach those campuses.

"Listen, we've got students who are coming up from incredible experiences, first-generation students overcoming so many barriers to be on the campus," Barrera said. "Those students are capable of learning quickly. What they need is a little support to be caught up. What they don't need is to be excluded."

Tina Descovich, CEO and co-founder of Moms for Liberty, told Fox News Digital that students arriving at college without foundational skills reflected problems that began years before they reached a university classroom.

"A child who can't do fractions at 18 was a child who couldn't do fractions at ten, and the system knew it," she said. "Richard Barrera's solution is to make it a college professor's problem and continue to cover up the failures of the status quo. Parents in California have watched their kids get passed along for years. Now they're being told the people who did the passing along deserve a promotion."

GAVIN NEWSOM AVOIDS QUESTION ON BRINGING BACK SAT SCORES AFTER UC OPEN LETTER, ASKS 'SHOW ME THE DATA'

The exchange came months after more than 1,400 faculty members signed an open letter calling for SAT and ACT math requirements to be restored for STEM applicants. By August, more than 3,000 faculty members had signed letters raising concerns about academic preparation.

California's state testing results show a similar proficiency gap before students reach college. According to the state's 2024-25 Smarter Balanced assessment results, 30.49% of 11th graders met or exceeded the standard in mathematics, compared with 56.96% in English language arts.

DeAngelis said that those results undercut the argument that students reaching college without foundational math skills merely need additional support once on campus.

"About 30 percent of California 11th graders meet math standards," he said. "That result is not a story about first-generation students who just need a little catch-up once they reach campus. That failure is a system that handed out diplomas without requiring mastery, then blamed the score for noticing."

Barrera defended his opposition to restoring the SAT or ACT requirements in UC admissions, saying that concerns about students needing additional academic preparation predated the university system’s decision to eliminate standardized tests and arguing the exams had historically excluded some applicants.

"It's not the elimination of the SAT, you know, that is what we need to look at," Barrera said. "The question that we all need to be asking ourselves is, what are the best strategies to get students prepared for college-level math? And simply having a placement exam like the SAT, which is historically discriminatory towards students of color, towards first-generation students — it's a tool that has historically excluded students."

"Why would we reinstitute that, knowing that that has shown no relevance in helping improve students' preparedness for college-level math?" he added.

The UC Board of Regents' current admissions policy prohibits SAT and ACT scores from being used in its comprehensive admissions review, but the university system is now formally reconsidering standardized testing.

Shaw said that the state should instead focus on whether students master core subjects before reaching college.

"Students are not helped by being lied to about their skills," she said. "They’re helped by actually learning to read, write, and do math before they get to college. That requires high standards in K-12 enforced consistently and measured honestly."

"It does not mean turning UCLA and Berkeley into expensive elementary schools and then blaming the faculty for noticing the problem," she added. "Lowering the bar one more time will not fix a decade of failure. It will just hide it longer."

World.title: Comedy stars lash out at Sebastian Maniscalco over SiriusXM shake-up
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sebastian Maniscalco has found himself in hot water with some comedians who are claiming that his new SiriusXM channel is taking away money and exposure from working-class comics.

Earlier this year, SiriusXM changed a long-running channel in its lineup called Raw Comedy that often featured lesser-known comedians to Sebastian Maniscalco's Comedy Radio. The new station more prominently features famous comedians now.

Stand Up for Stand Up, a nonprofit that supports comedians, recently wrote an article saying the rebranding has "drastically shifted from a wider pool of 800-plus comedians enjoying spins (and thus, royalties and exposure to the audience of listeners)" on the channel "to a narrower pool of comedians getting plays per month.

"And of those few hundred who are getting spins, over 75% of the plays are going to the top 50 artists, which results in a concentration of wealth among the top echelon, which is largely made up of big-name celebrity comics."

SEBASTIAN MANISCALCO IS A NO-NONSENSE FATHER, SAYS PARENTS NEED TO BE 'HALF-PSYCHOTIC' WITH THEIR KIDS

The nonprofit called the change "bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy," adding, "it hurts passive revenue, and discoverability, as well as the infrastructure that supports up and coming comedians."

Comedian Matt Ruby on his Substack page claimed the channel was "crushing middle class comedians who rely on payments from the company to pad income."

Liz Miele, another comedian, said in a video on her Instagram, "This year, the Raw channel on SiriusXM became Sebastian Maniscalco’s channel. Great. Fine. Celebrities have taken over channels before. Never been an issue. The problem is Raw went from playing 800 working-class comedians to now playing less than 300 celebrity comedians like Joan Rivers, Johnny Carson, Bob Hope, Norm Macdonald. Just dead comic, dead comic, dead comic, and then a plethora of very famous alive comedians that might not even know about this extra income that they’re about to receive."

She added that every "working-class comedian that has been kicked off the channel is quite aware" of the money they've lost.

Comedian Gianmarco Soresi posted a photo of Maniscalco on X with the caption, "Aren’t you embarrassed?"

Comedian Ashley Ray, who relied on the income, wrote on X, "Those checks went from covering a car payment to barely covering a quarter of weed, i hate this man."

COMEDIAN SEBASTIAN MANISCALCO JABS CANCEL CULTURE WITH ST PATRICK'S DAY MESSAGE

Famous names like Patton Oswalt, Michelle Wolf and Margaret Cho also implored Maniscalco to do something this week.

"I know you didn’t mean to do anything bad by doing it. You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel," Oswalt said in a Facebook video. "Let them get those checks."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Wolf also pleaded with Maniscalco in a Facebook video, saying, "Comics, we’re together on this. We want it to change."

"Sebastian, give working comedians a chance," Cho said in a video on her Facebook.

Others took to social media to defend Maniscalco.

"Sirius radio did this not Sebastian," one X user wrote. "Jesus Christ the dude is always there for young comics."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Another user said, "TBH this likely has little to do with him, his name is just on the channel. Altho I do miss when Raw Dog was actually raw w/some of the edgiest comics."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"His reps think this is gonna blow over — and they're right," a third added.

"The amount of comedians that think Sebastian Maniscalco is a program director is f---ing sad," another person wrote on X. "He sold his name to be on the channel hes not deciding who gets played."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a statement to Fox News Digital, SiriusXM said, "SiriusXM works together with our creative partners to program the best possible experience for our listeners.

"The launch of Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel, and SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform to deliver a wide range of comedy offerings across our channels."

The company said in a press release announcing the new channel in April that the channel would be "curated and headlined by Maniscalco."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Maniscalco for comment.

World.title: Ohio high school football team pulls off the most amazing half of football ever & the wokes want Sophie FIRED!
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

First Hump Day of October? Sign me up!

We're in the thick of it now, boys and girls. Today is the final day with four MLB games back-to-back-to-back-to-back until ... who knows when? Next March? Next May? 2028? It's anyone's guess. Enjoy it.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

We've also got two college football games tonight, NFL tomorrow and a whole slate of both on Saturday and Sunday. It's all ahead of us right now, folks. Let's lock it in, and not waste a single second.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SENDS A MESSAGE TO THE WOMAN-HATING WNBA PLAYERS WITH HER HAT, CRANKY PRIME & MAGGIE SAJAK!

Let's roll.

Welcome to a Hump Day Nightcaps — the one where a high school football team in Ohio pulled off maybe the most amazing half of football I've ever seen.

Spoiler alert: They managed to possess the football for all 24 minutes. Every single one of them. Animals.

You'll see!

What else? I've got an update on the NASCAR driver who owes an ex-wife $850K after seducing her husband, the wokes are mad at Sophie Cunningham and Caitlin Clark for two hilarious reasons and we've got two postseason pitchers taking very different approaches to the birth of their children this week.

Shockingly, it's caused quite a stir on social media. That almost never happens. We're always so agreeable!

OK, grab you a Fluffernutter in preparation for tomorrow's National Fluffernutter Day, and settle in for a Hump Day 'Cap!

A high school football masterclass

Look at that commercial. Man, what a time to be alive. Watch that, and then pay attention to the garbage we get in between innings of today's baseball game(s).

It's shocking. It's so sad. Our creativity has just gone down the toilet.

Pathetic.

Anyway, I do love a good fluffernutter. Admittedly, it's been, easily, 20 years since I've had one, but man they were elite back in middle and high school. I assume fluff has been all but canceled in today's MAHA world, which is fine. I live with a MAHA mom. Trust me, I get it.

FLORIDA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME ERUPTS INTO VIOLENT BRAWL INVOLVING PLAYERS, COACHES AFTER FINAL WHISTLE

But goodness gracious, they were the best back in the day. Opening up your brown bag in the middle school cafeteria and seeing that mom packed you a fluffernutter sammy was the best feeling.

Simpler times.

OK, let's stay in grade school and get this class started with a couple Ohio high school football team playing keep-away from each other last Friday night.

Amazing:

Scorned NASCAR wife had a pretty loud smoking gun

I went back and watched the entire second, and can confirm that Fairmont did indeed possess the ball all 24 minutes. I've never seen anything like it.

Just ground-n-pound the length of the field — twice — and execute a pair of onside kicks. Wild stuff. Reminded me of my high school's old Wing-T offense.

Those games were absolute slobberknockers every single time. I miss the heck outta them.

Now, some folks are asking about the onside kicks...

The first "onside" kick wasn't visible on the above YouTube stream because the video froze, but the announcers did call it an onside kick.

The second one wasn't so much an onside kick as it was the kicker just drilling the opposing player in front of him and Fairmont pouncing on the ball. Not sure if that was the plan or not, but it worked out.

Regardless, the final stats are staggering:

35:12-12:48 time of possession.

371-108 total yard advantage.

Fairmont finished with 277 rushing yards on 51 (!!!) carries.

37 second half plays for the Firebirds, 158 total yards. 24 minutes off the clock.

I covered a lot of high school football back in the day. I don't think I missed a Friday night in seven years. I came semi-close to one of these games back in 2015 when I watched a huge underdog just run the wildcat for an entire quarter. They gained about three yards per carry, and then converted all the fourth downs. It was incredible. Ate up almost 12 straight minutes.

What a game. What a sport. High school football is the best.

You know what's NOT the best? Cheating on your spouse in a Comfort Inn and letting the whole hotel know about it:

Sophie, Caitlin & paternity leave in October?

So, I wrote about that in last Thursday's Nightcaps, and I'm happy (?) to report that we have our smoking gun in the case.

According to court records obtained by the Daily Mail, the ex-wife of longtime NASCAR spotter Clayton Hughes hired a private investigator months before the two divorced. The PI, Jim Rorie, told a court that he heard Jennifer Jo Cobb and Hughes having "rambunctious" sex in a Comfort Inn on Oct. 2020 after he followed him to the hotel via a tracking device planted on his car.

"There was no doubt about what I was hearing," he told a court, adding that he heard "the squeaking of the bed, quite a bit of that, female tones moaning — and occasionally a male’s voice.

"As the squeaking continued, the tones of a male moaning and saying, ‘Oh f–k’ and ‘Oh my God’ were distinctly heard," Rorie continued. "I believe there was one point where I heard the female yell, ‘Don’t stop.'"

Welp. Probably not the worst thing to happen in a Comfort Inn in Martinsville, but it's certainly up there!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a big Hump Day night. First up? Let's see how the miserable wokes are handling Day 3 of the Indiana Fever's offseason ...

Let me get this straight ...

You've got one insufferable columnist from the woke New York Times saying Sophie Cunningham should be cut because she's too much of a distraction ... because she told ESPN six months ago that men shouldn't be in women's locker rooms?

Okeedokee!

At the same time, you have someone I've never heard of in my life, Charlotte Wilder, getting all bent out of shape because Caitlin Clark hung out with Pat McAfee on College GameDay?

Really?

These people are so far gone, and so beyond broken, it's almost unfathomable.

Almost.

What a bunch of weirdos. We live in such a silly time period. My late grandfather always used to tell me, "You really do realize how [stupid] people are the older you get."

He did NOT use the word stupid, by the way, but I'll let y'all figure that one out on your own.

OK, on the way out, I want to leave the class with a question that's currently dividing the internet ...

If your wife is having your baby in October, are you missing playoff baseball games for it?

So, the best closer in baseball — Mason Miller — missed last night's do-or-die Game 3 for the birth of his child. Meanwhile, Yankees starter Max Fried says he ain't missing a single pitch for the birth of his kid.

Where we stand on this, folks? On one hand, these dudes get paid handsomely for these moments. For October baseball. For the playoffs.

On the other hand ... it's the birth of your child. That's a big deal ... for some, at least.

I wanna hear what YOU think. Let it RIP.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

See y'all tomorrow.

Lemme know! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.
