World.content:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.

Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV.

“It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.”

Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances when she opposed the Trump administration.

She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.”

“I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said.

Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited.

In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader, Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with Trump if he visited Maine, with Trump having recently teased a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”

Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has gone to Maine and backed her at events.

Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024.

Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars on a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority.

Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate.

Collins said she judges all nominees by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade.

“In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said.

Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referring to Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.”

Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the Legislature.

Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats.

Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which included about $1 trillion in unpopular Medicaid cuts.

That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the legislation when it came to final passage. She said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid.

“He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural healthcare fund.

Jackson doubled down.

“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.”

Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She also questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate.

When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s killing of a Mainer this year, saying it happened because “Sen. Collins would not push back against ICE.”

Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said that she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras, as well as training of officers, and that she teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration.

In her closing statement, Collins said: “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.”

Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well.

“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.”

World.title: Florida poll: Republicans lead in the races for governor and Senate
World.content:
Republican Byron Donalds holds a 7-percentage-point advantage over Democrat David Jolly in the Florida governor’s race, according to a new NBC South Florida/Telemundo Station Group poll, while Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is up by 10 points in her matchup against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon.

Donalds, a congressman from the southwest corner of the state, is at 48% in the poll, compared with Jolly’s 41%, in a race in which Donalds has had a commanding financial advantage. (That advantage is just inside the poll’s margin of error, but Donalds has the edge in most of the range of possibilities.)

Moody is at 50% in the Senate race, compared with 40% for Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who got into the general election after a surprise primary victory over Democrat Alexander Vindman in August.

The results come amid broad Democratic optimism about the 2026 elections, with public polling showing the party making races in some typically red states into competitive contests this year. This poll suggests limits to that apparent momentum in other places.

The poll also took a snapshot of the state’s hugely influential bloc of Hispanic voters, largely congregated in South Florida. In 2024, Donald Trump won Hispanic-heavy Miami-Dade County by roughly 11 points, a significant reversal in a part of the state that had long been Democratic-leaning. Joe Biden won the county by 7 points in 2020.

But now, Florida Hispanic voters — including large Cuban, Nicaraguan, Honduran and Colombian populations — appear to be swinging back away from Trump, even as other high-profile Republican candidates hold comfortable leads among Hispanic voters.

Donalds holds a 48%-43% lead over Jolly among Hispanic voters, according to the survey, while Moody is up 47%-40% over Nixon. Trump’s job performance rating, however, is underwater, with 49% disapproving of his job performance, compared with 45% who approve.

Overall, 48% of all Florida likely voters approve of Trump’s job performance and 48% disapprove.

Before Trump’s gains among Florida’s Hispanic population in 2024, Democrats had generally won the demographic in the state by comfortable margins. Democrats argue that recent special election victories in Florida show the party has already started winning back the Hispanic vote, in part because of Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy. Unhappiness with prices and the cost of living has also affected Trump’s ratings among Hispanic voters.

“In legislative races in Florida, we have seen huge swings,” Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NBC News last week, speaking of the committee’s efforts in Florida House races. She said that on immigration, Trump and his party broke a promise “to go after the worst of the worst.”

By far the most important issue identified was inflation and the cost of living, with 30% saying it is likeliest to influence their votes. In both the overall sample and the sample of Hispanic voters, “direction of the state or country” (17%) was the second most important issue. The broader polling data put “immigration enforcement” as the third most important issue (16%), while the Hispanic sample put property taxes (13%) as the third most important issue. Immigration enforcement was the fourth most important issue among Hispanic voters (12%).

Questions about the Trump administration’s push to allow local and state policy to cooperate with federal immigration officials fell along party lines.

Among all voters, 85% of Republicans support the policy, compared with 18% of Democrats and 44% of those identified as independent voters who supported the harsher immigration enforcement tactics.

Property taxes have also been front and center in Florida during the midterms.

The state Republican Party and term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis support a ballot measure, known as Amendment 3, that would increase property tax exemptions to the first $250,000 of a home’s value by 2028. The exemption cap is currently $50,000.

In the poll of all Florida voters, 55% back the amendment, 26% oppose it, and 19% are undecided. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of Republicans supported the idea, compared with 36% for Democrats and 43% for independents.

The overall survey questioned 625 registered voters, all of whom said they were likely to vote in the November elections. They were interviewed over the telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research Inc. from Sept. 28 to Thursday, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The same time frame and methods were used to survey 400 Hispanic registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.

World.title: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
World.content:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night during their only scheduled debate of this fall’s race for governor in Georgia, taking aim at each other on economic issues, data centers and President Donald Trump.

Public polls show Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and a former Biden administration official, and Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, locked in a close race four weeks out from Election Day, with early voting kicking off next week.

The hourlong, town-hall-style debate was largely civil, featuring live and taped questions from voters. Jackson frequently ripped his opponent over her record as mayor, while Bottoms attacked his praise of Trump.

“My opponent has said he wants to be Trump’s favorite governor. He wants to be Trump with a Southern tone. He said there’s not a single policy that he disagrees with Trump on,” Bottoms said in response to a question about the Trump administration’s cuts to federal funding.

“I will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary. I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” she continued.

Jackson responded, “I don’t owe anybody anything,” and said, “Nobody’s ever told me what to do.”

He then invoked Brian Kemp, Georgia’s popular, term-limited governor — the first of multiple times he did so.

“I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents, and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said.

Trump endorsed Jackson’s rival, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, during the Republican gubernatorial primary. But Jackson still attempted to claim the MAGA mantle and leaned heavily into comparing himself to the president. Since winning the nomination in June, he’s backed off that approach and sought to link himself more to Kemp, who had also backed Jones.

Jackson took several shots at Bottoms over her tenure as mayor, accusing her of being responsible for regional inflation in the Atlanta area that he claimed exceeded national inflation rates and pointing to higher crime rates in the city during the Covid-19 pandemic.

“This is the kind of policy that we cannot have in running Georgia, not having people feeling safe to go to work,” Jackson said. “Bad mayors don’t make good governors.”

While the candidates were asked about housing and education, the event focused predominantly on economic issues and affordability, with both candidates repeatedly pressed about how they’d bring down costs. Both focused heavily on tax relief.

Bottoms emphasized her proposals to cut or suspend state or local taxes on a raft of items, like auto insurance, groceries, hygiene products and diapers. Jackson reiterated his promise to cut state income taxes, property taxes and taxes on certain utilities.

Data centers and the controversial surveillance traffic cameras known as Flock cameras also took center stage.

On data centers, Bottoms repeated her desire to implement a pause on new construction. Jackson said he wouldn’t approve new construction as governor without first getting local community approval, establishing environmental standards and getting a commitment that local communities’ power bills would be reduced.

But the two sparred over the issue, as well, with Bottoms accusing Jackson of investing in data centers and Jackson accusing her of having approved building them as mayor.

Bottoms also said she wasn’t opposed to a moratorium on installing new Flock cameras, while Jackson said he was.

The issue of election security — which has hung over Georgia politics for six years — also came up.

Bottoms said she was “deeply concerned about Donald Trump’s rhetoric around our elections.”

Jackson, however, when he was asked whether he thought the U.S. Justice Department should be “overseeing and getting involved” in the state’s elections, deferred to Kemp again.

“I don’t think that’s necessary unless Gov. Kemp thinks it’s necessary,” he said.

Jackson has flooded the airwaves with ads, using tens of millions of dollars of his own money to outspend Bottoms 7-to-1 as of last week.

That disparity has worried many Democrats, who’ve seen this year as a prime opportunity to flip the governorship blue for the first time in 16 years.

Aiding Bottoms is the broader political environment in Georgia and nationally: Trump faces negative approval ratings and voter concerns about his administration’s handling of the economy.

World.title: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
World.content:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University students began a seven-hour sit-in Wednesday in solidarity with Jane Doe, the woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity nearly two years ago.

“Seven hours for the seven hours she endured. Seven hours of solidarity. Seven hours demanding change,” a coalition of Cornell student groups said in a post on Instagram ahead of the demonstration.

Roughly 80 students had gathered inside a campus dining hall named for Pulitzer Prize-winning author Toni Morrison by around 3 p.m. The organizers said the sit-in is part of “Zero Day,” an “economic blackout calling on students to disrupt business as usual by not attending class or spending on campus.”

The protest illustrates the tense mood on the Ivy League campus following Jane Doe’s allegations that she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members last month, leading to renewed national attention on sexual misconduct and collegiate Greek life.

Three of the accused men have publicly denied the allegations through attorneys.

World.title: Union alleges Bureau of Prisons in contempt for failing to reinstate collective bargaining agreement
World.content:
The union representing 30,000 Bureau of Prisons employees is asking a federal judge to hold the agency in contempt, alleging that prison leadership has refused to follow the court's order to immediately restore its collective bargaining agreement.

The contempt request, filed Oct. 6, comes just one week after U.S. District Judge Vernon Oliver in Connecticut granted a motion for a preliminary injunction against the Bureau of Prisons that was sought by the National Council of Prison Locals.

Bureau of Prisons Director William Marshall terminated the collective bargaining agreement on Sept. 25, 2025. He alleged the union posed an "obstacle to progress" and said it was not the "kind of union" he could support.

The judge ruled that the union was likely to succeed on the merits of its argument that the BOP had violated the Administrative Procedure Act by terminating the collective bargaining agreement and ordered the bureau to reinstate it immediately.

In its motion for contempt, the union alleged that bureau leadership is stonewalling and refusing to allow the union to resume its usual operations, including by allowing people to have "official" union time.

In one such example, the motion and an accompanying sworn statement said that a BOP employee who was facing termination asked to be represented by a shop steward at the meeting.

"There ain't no union," a BOP official allegedly told the employee, according to the motion. The employee was terminated on Oct. 5.

In another allegation, the union said that Marshall told people on Sept. 29, hours before the court ruling hit the docket, that he had no plans to enforce the terms of the collective bargaining agreement unless he received direct orders from the White House.

"They have not restored union office space or official time, allowed for union representation in disciplinary proceedings, or taken any of the other myriad specific steps that Defendants themselves told the court would be required if the court entered the requested injunction," attorneys for the union wrote.

"Defendants' noncompliance is total."

In a press release issued by American Federation of Government Employees Local 1237, which represents employees at FCI Mendota, the union alleged that management in that facility had also locked union officials out of their offices.

The Bureau of Prisons declined to comment, citing the pending litigation.

Since the court's original Sept. 29 order granting the union's request for a preliminary injunction, the Justice Department has not formally sought a stay to pause the ruling.

On Oct. 2, however, the Justice Department filed a formal "notice of compliance" with the court. In that filing, it said BOP was "aware" of the court's order and "complying with its terms."

But at the same time, the department also said that it did not understand the court's ruling to mean that the BOP could not proceed with trying to re-terminate the collective bargaining agreement again before it expires in May 2028.

It also added that the Justice Department did not expect the U.S. District Court would be supervising "every alleged failure" by BOP to comply with the collective bargaining agreement.

The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate unions at multiple federal agencies.

In March 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that sought to exclude federal offices involved in national security or intelligence work from having collective bargaining agreements with staff. That order also applied to the Justice Department, which includes the Bureau of Prisons.

But after the order was made public, the BOP allowed its union to continue operating for approximately six months before terminating the collective bargaining agreement.

In doing so, Marshall at the time did not cite national security as a basis for his decision.

World.title: Man eyed Mall of America for attack, pledged allegiance to ISIS, FBI says
World.content:
An 18-year-old man accused of telling an FBI informant he planned to carry out an attack later this month at Mall of America was arrested at gunpoint Tuesday in Richfield, Minnesota, during an arranged meeting to buy an assault rifle, according to a federal criminal complaint filed Wednesday.

Minnesota U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen and FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher Dotson discussed the case involving Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, a Twin Cities resident and U.S. citizen, in a news conference Wednesday afternoon, where Rosen praised the FBI for its "diligence" in thwarting the attack.

"They were able to detect a threat and disrupt it before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people," Rosen said.

In the complaint, authorities say a "confidential human source" exchanged "hundreds of bi-directional messages through multiple social media and encrypted messaging applications" with Mohamud from December 2024 until Tuesday. In those exchanges, Mohamud allegedly "expressed his desire to travel to Somalia" to join al-Shabaab and "fight on its behalf and/or commit a mass casualty attack" in Minnesota.

"The messages this defendant allegedly sent to others were chilling. They document the idolization of ideologically motivated violence, a callous disregard to the sanctity of human life, a blind hatred of people of other faiths and a cold commitment to carrying out his vision of violence in our community," Dotson said. "Mohamud allegedly sought martyrdom in carrying out his plans to murder innocent civilians."

The complaint says the FBI contacted Mohamud's parents in May 2025, but they weren't cooperative.

"The FBI attempted to speak with his parents having seen that this young man was becoming radicalized, and those attempts were rebuffed by the parents," Rosen said. "I just would say to parents all over Minnesota and, for that matter all over America, if you get the indication, especially if you hear from federal law enforcement, that your son or daughter is being radicalized to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, heed those warnings."

In July, Mohamud told an informant he didn't have enough money to go to Somalia, according to the complaint. He allegedly said he would attack in the United States instead, and that if he did, he wasn't doing it "for any worldly matter" but "for the sake of Allah only."

U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen WCCO

Mohamud allegedly went on to say in a direct message to the source that he considered carrying out an attack at Mall of America in Bloomington or Valleyfair amusement park in Shakopee. An FBI affidavit says he wrote that he might buy two pistols online first.

The complaint says Mohamud said he wanted to attack the mall "because it's owned by Jewish." He said he was inspired in part by last year's deadly antisemitic attack at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia.

Last month, Mohamud told the source he wanted to carry out an attack at the mall during the Hmong Arts Celebration on Oct. 24, saying "it will be a lot of people," according to court documents.

In another message last month, the affidavit says Mohamud wrote that he had been watching video of the 2016 attack at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando, Florida, and thought he could do the same.

"I just walk in and shoot," Mohamud wrote, according to the complaint.

Court documents also note Mohamud sent the source a video on Discord in which he allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS.

On Tuesday, Mohamud was arrested during an arranged meeting with the source in the parking lot of a Richfield park, according to Rosen. The affidavit says he had left an undercover employee's vehicle with the rifle, four magazines and 200 rounds of ammunition when he was arrested. The filing describes the weapon as a Norinco AK-47 assault rifle, model Mac-90 Sporter, and the ammunition as about 200 live rounds of 7.62x39-caliber.

"They became aware that this was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched, and in fact, in this young man's case, that radicalization progressed to the point where he planned in the most serious of ways to carry out a mass casualty attack," Rosen said.

Authorities allege Mohamud "knowingly received a firearm and ammunition" with reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and a federal crime of terrorism, including providing or conspiring to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

This story will be updated.

World.title: Christa Pike has pneumonia, unable to move arms after botched execution, lawyers say
World.content:
Christa Pike's attorneys said she has pneumonia, a blood clot, couldn't swallow, and is unable to move her arms or hands once she regained consciousness in a Tennessee hospital, days after the death row inmate survived a botched execution by the state.

"Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove," said one of Pike's attorneys, Randy Spivey, at a Wednesday news conference. "It was extraordinary."

Spivey said he and Pike's other attorneys were told she was brain-dead on Monday and expected her to be removed from life support. But by the next day, she had woken up and started talking, he said.

"I don't have an explanation for what happened," the attorney told reporters after a hearing at Davidson County Chancery Court. He said that Pike was confused and disoriented at first, but she began to remember details of the execution attempt on Wednesday.

In addition to the lung infection, a blood clot in her arm, and an issue swallowing that had prevented her from eating, Pike's arms and hands are "tremendously swollen," said Spivey, adding that "we don't know what function she will regain."

Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S., according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Court grants request for evidence

Before Pike's attorneys shared updates on her health outside of the Davidson County court on Wednesday, they attended an emergency hearing in which they requested Tennessee's correctional department to preserve records and other evidence of her failed lethal injection.

Chancellor I'Ashea Myles granted the order and said the state would be mandated to preserve "relevant evidence" of its failed attempt to put Pike to death on Sept. 30, including "drugs, IV lines, needles, catheters, medical supplies, restraints, gurneys" and anything else in the execution chamber at the time of the procedure.

Myles said waste, such as packing supplies and labels, and all written or digital records, including records of communication through encrypted platforms, witness accounts, and correspondence regarding equipment or drug administration issues, must be preserved, too.

She explicitly directed the state "not to lose, misplace, accidentally delete, any information that may be pertinent to this litigation."

"To any extent that any information or any evidence has already been discarded, deleted, destroyed or no longer exists, I want [the Tennessee Department of Correction] to take an affirmative step to try to claw back that information and put in policies and procedures, while this incident litigation is pending, to ensure that no information is discarded or destroyed," said Myles.

Execution aftermath

Staff had given Pike, 50, two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. Her legal team said on Tuesday that she had regained consciousness and was speaking from her hospital bed.

Pike's attorneys also said Tuesday she was continuing "to receive critical medical care" as hospital workers attempted to clear her system of the lethal drug pentobarbital. Her prognosis remained unclear, they added, but she was expected to face, at minimum, "a long recovery."

The legal team has renewed its calls for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's death sentence, pushing him to change the sentence to life in prison without parole so that the state can't attempt to execute Pike a second time, which is the usual course of action after an inmate survives botched execution proceedings. However, while others have survived botched procedures before, Pike is the only known inmate in the United States' modern death penalty era to remain alive after actually receiving lethal chemicals.

"The state has made no promises that Ms. Pike will not be subject to a future execution," Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's attorneys, said in court on Wednesday. Evidence sought by the defense for the correctional department to preserve could help them build future arguments to prevent that from happening, Ihnen added.

Attorneys for Pike had filed an emergency motion Friday asking that the correctional department be required to "preserve all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence" of the failed execution, which, they said, amounted to "evidence of TDOC [Tennessee Department of Correction] inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol."

They accused correctional staff tasked with handling Pike's execution of failing to properly establish an IV line through which to administer lethal drugs, and then failing to realize she had a "blown vein," allegedly allowing pentobarbital to spread through her body and causing a painful, botched procedure. In court, Ihnen also referenced the secrecy that shrouds execution protocols and proceedings in Tennessee and elsewhere across the U.S., which makes arguing death penalty cases particularly challenging.

"We don't know what they have, because they won't tell us," Ihnen said in court. "And so the preservation order seeks the broadest possible preservation of evidence."

Case history

Lee had denied Pike's request for a commuted sentence before her execution date last week, rejecting her clemency petition in the days leading up to it. In its aftermath, he canceled the one remaining execution scheduled to take place in Tennessee by the end of the year and said an investigation would be conducted to determine what went wrong. The now-former Tennessee correctional commissioner stepped down from his post, although an official statement from the agency claimed it had followed protocols.

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the killing and spent more than three decades on Tennessee's death row. As the only woman awaiting execution in the state for a vast majority of that time, she was alone for almost the entirety of her incarceration. She was the first woman Tennessee attempted to execute in more than 200 years and the first person the state attempted to execute in modern times for a crime they committed at age 18, 19 or 20.

Prior to Pike's botched injection, her case had garnered public interest as human rights leaders and advocacy groups rallied against her death sentence, raising issues with her age at the time of her conviction and long history of mental illness and childhood abuse. But those who strongly support her execution, including prosecutors and jurors in Pike's original trial as well as judges who presided over that case and many of her appeals, have countered that capital punishment is warranted given the horrific nature of her crime. Among them is Slemmer's mother, May Martinez.

World.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend
World.content:
Hurricane, tropical storm and storm surge watches have been issued for parts of the U.S. Gulf Coast as Tropical Storm Isaias was expected to approach that area Friday after becoming a hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center.

Currently swirling in the Gulf, Isaias would be the Atlantic Basin's first hurricane of the season and is its ninth named storm. El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The storm formed with less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, which ends Nov. 30.

Maps show possible path

Tropical Storm Isaias, which grew from Tropical Depression Nine on Wednesday and is pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," is expected to pass to the north of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday before approaching the U.S. Gulf Coast the following day, according to forecasters. It is expected to rapidly strengthen.

A hurricane watch was issued Wednesday for the northern Gulf Coast, from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida, and a tropical storm watch was issued from Bay St. Louis to Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line and from Indian Pass to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge watch was also issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida, according to the hurricane center.

Tropical storm-force winds were extending outward up to 45 miles from the storm's center on Wednesday afternoon. At the time, its maximum sustained winds were 50 mph, according to the hurricane center. A storm's maximum wind speed must rise to at least 74 mph to be considered a hurricane.

The possible path of newly formed Tropical Storm Isaias Nikki Nolan/CBS News

Isaias is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 6 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places on the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle.

Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.

Tropical Storm Isaias is expected to impact the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News/Nikki Nolan

The hurricane center on Thursday warned of "an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts" along parts of the northern Gulf Coast and urged people living in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi and northern Florida to "closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place."

In addition to rain, the hurricane center said Isaias could potentially bring urban flooding and isolated river flooding to places in its path.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."

Beware the "I"-named storm

While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.

The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).

When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

World.title: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
World.content:
This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on

toggle caption i Chang-Fu Zhou/Shandong University of Science and Technology

Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles.

"To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo, a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.

For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.

Many of these fossils wind up at the nearby Paleontological Museum of Liaoning, a facility that Luo and his colleague, Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn, visit each year to examine new finds. A decade ago, a specimen in a thick slab of shale caught their eye.

It was the fossilized bones and soft tissue impressions of an ancient mammal that lived some 165 million years ago. "Early fossil mammals — in fact, they are exceedingly rare," says Luo.

Sponsor Message

This animal, which the team named Megacauda sungei and have described in the journal Nature, was a prize discovery. The remains were so intact that it was possible to determine that it was likely capable of chewing food and then swallowing it, and also suckling — traits that are shared by mammals.

Luo and his colleagues conclude that these evolutionary innovations — and their presence among our ancient mammalian relatives — extend deep into the past to at least the middle Jurassic.

"It's all there in one remarkable fossil," says Luo.

A chihuahua-sized chimera

The fossil was about the size of a chihuahua, but somewhat hard to discern from the rock surrounding it.

"The fossil itself is actually very dark," explains Luo. "The bones are black, the slab [is] dark. And it's kind of difficult to have beautiful photographs."

One of his collaborators, Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong University of Science and Technology, snapped a different kind of vivid image using a technique called X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. "It would make this bone pop out in different colors," says Luo.

The resulting image rendered the skeleton a bright yellow and it showcased a curious combination of characteristics. The back end, which includes the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail, resembles a modern-day platypus.

toggle caption i April Neander/University of Chicago

These features suggest that this animal was likely semi-aquatic and foraged in the water. "The big tail is good for swimming," says Luo.

"However," he continues, "its teeth and the jaw would be very different from platypus. So the head is very much of a predator." Indeed, Luo and his colleagues found a smattering of small salamander bones inside the fossil that they suspect the animal had eaten by first cutting and shearing with its sharp teeth.

A lot to swallow

There was something else that Luo instantly noticed about the fossil. "My eyes zeroed in on these tiny hyoid bones," he recalls.

Sponsor Message

The human hyoid bone sits in the throat, half an inch or so above the Adam's apple, and supports the backside of the tongue.

The team later CT scanned the fossil, including the underside of the skull, which exposed a delicate roof of the mouth as well as a series of bone hooks and ridges.

With this combination of rarely preserved features, "we are able with great confidence to reconstruct the whole muscular skeletal machinery," says Luo.

This reconstruction revealed that the animal was likely capable of doing two things that are unique to mammals.

The first is swallowing food after chewing it. Other vertebrates tend to bite and gulp. But mammals "chew down all the food with our teeth," Luo says. "And then we swallow one bolus of food down to our esophagus at a time."

Consider, for a moment, a carnivore that chews meat, an herbivore that crunches on vegetables, and an insect-eater that chomps bugs. This diverse array of foods all get chewed up and then swallowed down a mammalian throat in a similar way.

Secondly, this fossil appears to have been capable of suckling, which embodies something even more fundamental.

"That ability to suckle mother's milk literally defined our biology," says Luo. "And that's why our group is called mammals. We're named after the mammary glands."

This is some of the oldest fossil evidence of an animal with both these key mammalian abilities.

Small but varied

"It's a fascinating specimen," says Jessica Theodor, a paleontologist at the University of Calgary who wasn't involved in the research. "The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals."

Theodor would like to see some of the images in greater detail, but she says a fossil like this tracks the evolution of lactation, which she likens to a kind of dietary and hormonal conversation between mother and baby.

Sponsor Message

"The conversation is beginning very far back in the Mesozoic — in the Jurassic and Cretaceous," says Theodor. "That's amazing to me that it's this old and this fundamental."

For Luo, this fossil is the latest evidence of how new ways of feeding have helped mammals and their predecessors diversify — even back when they were the little guys on the proverbial block.

"Mammals, they're never dominant in the age of dinosaurs," he says. "But nonetheless, they hold out relatively well compared to all other vertebrates."

By the time of the Jurassic period, there were already proto-mammalian gliders, swimmers, land-dwellers, tree-dwellers and diggers. Each one was making a living in its own distinct way — all united in their shared ability to chew, swallow and suckle.

World.title: Judge orders that Christa Pike execution evidence be preserved
World.content:
Judge orders that Christa Pike execution evidence be preserved

toggle caption i George Walker IV/Pool AP

The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence in connection with last week's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, including log books, medical waste and all messages sent or received by officials associated with the execution attempt.

"Anything in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," Judge I'Ashea Myles said.

The judge also granted a request from Pike's attorneys for "liberal access" to their client, ordering that prison officials will have two hours to respond to requests from lawyers for in-person visits with Pike.

Speaking outside the courtroom, Luke P. Ihnen, an assistant federal defender in Knoxville, told reporters that this was "just a first step of many to preserve and enforce Christa's constitutional rights after this unprecedented botched execution."

Sponsor Message

The hearing came a week after Pike was left hospitalized and in critical condition following the Sept. 30 execution attempt in which she was strapped to a gurney and administered two doses of pentobarbital, a barbiturate widely used in U.S. executions. But several minutes after the first dose, she said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."

Pike's attorneys said that after days of unconsciousness, Pike was awake again, speaking and continuing to receive critical medical care.

Randy Spivey, a post-conviction attorney representing Pike, called his client "a survivor."

"She survived sexual abuse [and] the rapes of multiple men. She survived a suicide attempt when she was 12 and she survived the state's attempt to execute her," he said. "She deserves answers about what was done to her and the people of Tennessee deserve those answers, too."

He said of the botched execution, "all of this was foreseen," because Pike has a medical condition that would make it difficult to insert an IV to deliver the lethal doses of pentobarbital.

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Spivey, who was a witness to last week's failed execution, told NPR that after a second dose, Pike fell unconscious but continued breathing and making sounds like choking. It "went on for so long," he said.

Sponsor Message

Following the failed execution, Tennessee's top prison official, Frank Strada, resigned, and the state's governor, Bill Lee, halted executions through the end of the year and ordered an independent investigation into the state's capital punishment system.

It wasn't immediately clear whether that would affect a second attempt to execute Pike, but speaking at Wednesday's hearing, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General John Ayers said the decision on when or if to schedule a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.

Ihnen, one of the defense attorneys, said it would be "unconscionable that the state would try to execute her again."

toggle caption i Tennessee Department of Correction/via AP

Pike was on death row for a murder she committed at age 18. In 1995, she and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp, who was a minor at the time of the crime, received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.

In a clemency petition filed last month, Pike's attorneys asked that her sentence be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole, citing her history of childhood trauma.

"Local and national media covered Christa's trial in the midst of the 'Satanic Panic' of the 1990s," the attorneys said. "In truth, it was Christa's abusive boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, who was fascinated by satanic imagery."

The media at the time had "focused on the salacious parts of Christa's crime, disregarding the context of her youth, trauma, and mental illness," they added.

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Critics of the death penalty are outraged at what happened to Pike during the attempt to execute her.

"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, said Pike was the first person in the history of capital punishment to survive after being injected with lethal drugs.

World.title: Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?
World.content:
Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?

toggle caption i Eli Kaplan/Getty Images

President Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

It would be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades — and the first by firing squad since World War II.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the news on X Monday night, writing, "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in an order released Tuesday that Hasan's execution will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.

Sponsor Message

But Hasan could delay those proceedings if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts, said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center.

"The fact that the president has approved Mr. Hasan's death sentence is another step closer to his execution," Maher said. "But that does not mean that his execution will be imminent."

For example, Ronald Gray, who committed multiple rapes and murders near Fort Bragg in the 1980s, is still on military death row despite having had his sentence approved by President George W. Bush in 2008.

It's not clear why the Pentagon is moving forward now, or why it specifically chose a firing squad as the execution method. But some death penalty experts that NPR interviewed suspect it could be connected to Tennessee's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, which has dominated headlines and reignited debate over the past week.

"For years now, states have been pushing this rock of Sisyphus uphill … They're spending millions of dollars, and yet they're having botched executions," said Corinna Lain, whose book, Secrets of the Killing State, was published last year. "So this moment in time is one where states are really thinking about: what are we doing and what best serves the death penalty? Whether the answer to that is firing squad is another question entirely."

The White House referred NPR's questions to the Pentagon, which declined to elaborate beyond Parnell's post.

Sponsor Message

In his announcement, Parnell said Trump had acted on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said last September that he was "100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."

"This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth told several media outlets, including The Hill, at the time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."

Hasan was working as an Army psychiatrist in Nov. 2009, when he opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — "God is great" — before killing 13 people and injuring another 32. The attack ended when he was shot by civilian security officers at the scene, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.

Hasan acted as his own lawyer during his 2013 trial, at which he admitted that "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." The American-born Muslim said he had "switched sides" and turned against the U.S. because of its military actions in the Middle East.

The military jury found Hasan guilty on all counts. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death, which triggered an automatic appeals process that ended only when the Supreme Court denied his final petition in the spring of 2025.

Hasan is one of just four people currently on military death row — all of whom were convicted of murder — according to the Death Penalty Information Center. They are all incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

toggle caption i Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/Bell County Sheriff's Department

The military's last firing squad execution was in 1945

The first recorded execution by shooting on what would become U.S. soil happened in Jamestown, Va., in 1608, when one of the colony's early council members, Capt. George Kendall, was put to death for mutiny. Firing squads have been used relatively sparingly since, including during the Civil War.

Sponsor Message

"On the one hand, it is one of our earliest forms of execution," said Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno, who has been studying execution methods for 36 years. "On the other hand, it's always been controversial because people associate it with extreme barbarity and … the Wild West."

The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945: Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, the only U.S. soldier to be executed for that reason since the Civil War.

"They didn't even tell his wife that he had been executed; they just said that he had died in Europe," journalist Charles Glass, who wrote a book about World War II deserters, told NPR in 2013. He said Slovik's case only became public knowledge about a decade later, when an investigative reporter published a book about it in the mid-'50s.

Most of the known U.S. military executions during World War II were done by hanging, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last time the U.S. military carried out an execution of any sort was in 1961, when Private John Bennett was hanged for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.

"We basically have gone out of the business — until now — of executing people through the military justice system," said Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.

The military officially suspended the death penalty after a 1983 court ruling, but reinstated it the following year and specifically designated lethal injection as the standard method. Fidell says that changed with new Army regulations in 2023.

"The regulation was changed to make the choice or the method of execution a matter for the president's discretion," he said. "And obviously, the president has, in this case, approved the use of a firing squad."

Under the current rules, once the president approves an execution, the secretary of the Army decides the time, location and method, to take place within 60 to 150 days.

Sponsor Message

Fidell said he was not surprised by Trump's approval, given his administration's embrace of the death penalty overall and the severity of Hasan's offenses. But he suggested some might find the social media announcement inappropriate.

"The military has lived without executions since 1961, and yet we have here a really serious case," Fidell said. "I think it would have been a lot better had a more formal, dignified means been chosen to disseminate this information."

The Pentagon hasn't held a formal press briefing since May.

The death penalty is already under scrutiny

toggle caption i AP/South Carolina Department of Corrections

Denno, who studies the death penalty, doesn't think the timing of the Pentagon's announcement is a coincidence.

Denno says Pike's case "is probably the worst that's ever happened." But it's far from the only botched legal injection in recent years, she says, pointing to what she calls a pattern of convicts being "tortured unnecessarily" that has prompted some jurisdictions to seek out alternatives.

The Justice Department made firing squads available for federal executions earlier this year, following a directive from Trump. Seven states now have firing squads on the books as an execution method, which Denno says is the highest number ever recorded.

Denno says firing squads are "the least inhumane method of execution that we have," since, when done properly, death can occur in seconds.

But she acknowledges that those have been plagued by issues, too, including last year in South Carolina, when an autopsy revealed that the shooters may have prolonged a prisoner's death by missing his heart.

"There is a humane way to take a life. It's called life without parole," said Lain, the author.

Lain says lethal injections, because of their relative lack of gore, have kept the death penalty "out of sight, out of mind" for many people over the last five decades.

But she sees signs of change. Data analysis by the Death Penalty Information Center shows that death sentences have declined by 90% over the past three decades. Fewer than 50 new ones have been imposed each year since 2015. A 2025 Gallup poll put public support for the death penalty at a five-decade low, with opposition highest among younger generations.

Sponsor Message

"The death penalty in this country is dying its own slow death," she said. She thinks the federal government's embrace of the firing squad, including in Hasan's case, could hasten it even more.

World.title: Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel
World.content:
Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel

toggle caption i Scott Olson/Getty Images North America

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

Less than a month before the midterms, the price of fuel is becoming a powerful election issue .

This week, President Trump issued an executive order aimed at lowering costs for frequent diesel users by making a type of fuel called "dyed diesel" more accessible through the end of the year.

Could this lower the cost of diesel? Let's get into it.

Why is diesel so expensive right now?

Prices for all kinds of oil products have risen this year because fewer ships have been getting through the Strait of Hormuz and transporting crude to refineries worldwide — but the diesel supply chain has been uniquely hit. Ukraine's recent attacks on Russian refineries have taken many of them offline, and Russia has cut back on its diesel exports. China has, too.

Sponsor Message

It's added up to a limited supply of diesel — a fuel that powers much of the industrial supply chain.

So its price has soared; the U.S. average for a gallon hit a record of $6.52 a few weeks ago. The price has eased a bit since then, but a gallon remains about $2.60 higher than this time last year, according to AAA .

When diesel prices rise, inflation is likely to follow, analysts say. Diesel powers much of the industrial supply chain, from agricultural equipment to trucks transporting goods from warehouses to grocery stores.

What is dyed diesel?

The "dyed" part means: red dye. "Red-dyed diesel is diesel with red dye in it. That's it," said Will O'Neill, principal analyst at S&P Global Energy and a follower of all things diesel.

Chemically, this diesel is almost identical to the regular kind you'd find in most gas stations. But it's a different color because it's used, and taxed, differently.

Red-dyed diesel is only meant for off-road vehicles, mainly farm and construction equipment — like a tractor that's used in a field. It's exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon on commercial diesel.

Drivers aren't suppose to use it in vehicles that drive on highways. People who do are subject to an IRS penalty — either $1,000 or $10 per gallon, whichever is more expensive.

The red color makes it easier to catch someone who filled up their tank with the wrong stuff. Using the red-dyed diesel is "effectively a form of tax evasion," O'Neill said.

But the new executive order says dyed diesel will be allowed on highways through the end of the year. The IRS won't penalize anyone who uses it.

Sponsor Message

Will this save people money?

It could help farmers, truckers and other workers who count on diesel to do their jobs. The executive order said this move would put money directly into their pockets "to support their vital service to our Nation."

It essentially expands the ways in which workers can use dyed diesel, sparing them the federal tax. Imagine a farmer who usually puts dyed diesel in their tractor — now they can also legally use it to fill up their cargo van, get on the highway, and take their produce to market.

Plus, a handful of states have said drivers can use red-dyed diesel on their highways. On average , state diesel taxes run about 35 cents a gallon. Allowing drivers to use dyed diesel — and skip both federal and state taxes — could add up to a savings of about 60 cents a gallon.

But because the cost of a gallon of regular diesel is now about $2.60 higher than this time last year, drivers will still be paying a higher price overall

Will this put more diesel on the market?

Technically, this will increase the total amount of diesel that people could use.

But Jaime Brito, executive director of oil markets at Dow Jones Energy, points out that this doesn't mean most people can easily access dyed diesel. It isn't available at most gas stations. "When was the last time that you went to a pumping station and you saw that one of the stations gave you the possibility to feed red diesel into your truck?" he asked.

Instead, people would need to go to a special wholesaler — or might be able to find it at gas stations in rural areas.

In an email to NPR responding to these critiques, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers wrote that the president wants to see prices fall and is taking "historic measures" to alleviate oil supply disruptions.

Sponsor Message

Can the Trump administration do anything else to lower diesel costs?

Over the past month, some politicians have floated the idea of a diesel export ban . The idea was that if the U.S. stopped sending diesel to other countries, maybe that would temporarily increase the supply in the U.S., pushing down the price.

But bottom line: refiners pushed back . It would be bad business for them.

Refiners make money by selling diesel within the U.S. and exporting it around the world, said Jacques Rousseau, who focuses on oil, natural gas, and refined products as a managing director with Clearview Energy Partners.

If there was a diesel export ban, sure, that diesel would stay in the U.S. But then, refineries would wind up with a ton of extra diesel. "Then it'll start going into storage. And then once your storage gets filled, then you have to reduce the overall production of your refinery. So then you just start producing less of everything else too because you have nowhere to put this diesel," Rousseau said.

Ultimately, that could lead to prices for refined oil products, like gasoline — and diesel — going up.

President Trump said late Friday that he was not seriously considering an export ban , and that the U.S. didn't need one anymore, as Europe just released about 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from its own stockpiles.

Analysts told NPR that the only real fix will be ending the wars in Iran and Ukraine — until there's more oil flowing freely around the world again, they said, it's hard to see the price of diesel getting much lower. " There's no silver bullet," said O'Neill. "There's no way to snap your fingers and end up with $4 diesel before the election."

"Barring the rapid and credible conclusion of the wars," he continued, "I don't think that happens."

World.title: How Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has brought the culture wars to the military
World.content:
How Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has brought the culture wars to the military

The New York Times reporter Greg Jaffe says Hegseth has disproportionately blocked promotions of Black and women senior officers, and he's also been purging the military of transgender people. Sponsor Message

World.title: She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'
World.content:
She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'

toggle caption i Sue Julian

Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news on the midterms.

Ellen Allen has mixed feelings about the check from the U.S. Treasury and letter from President Trump that arrived at her house near Charleston, W.Va., on Monday.

"I just can't believe it; I mean, that's crazy," says Allen, who's the executive director of a small nonprofit called West Virginians for Affordable Health Care. She says, in her opinion, sending out these checks is a "political stunt."

NPR first spoke to Ellen Allen in the summer of 2025. She was 63 years old at the time and knew she needed coverage from Healthcare.gov even as generous federal subsidies for her premiums were ending. She has a serious eye condition and needs expensive drops to preserve her vision. She advocated for the Republican-controlled Congress to extend the subsidies. It didn't. She ended up using retirement savings to pay $1,967 every month for her premiums from January through August, 2026.

Sponsor Message

Then her birthday came; she turned 65 and was eligible for Medicare. "I was ready at midnight — the first day I could apply, I did," she laughs.

A second check on the way?

Allen chose traditional Medicare, which means she could soon be getting another check from the U.S. Treasury. Last week, President Trump announced that $90 checks will be sent to 20 million people enrolled in Medicare.

"The $90 is — I mean, that's just nothing," Allen says. In her work, she talks to people about healthcare costs all over West Virginia. "People aren't going to be fooled by this," she predicts. "People are hurting. People are feeling the cost of healthcare all year long."

"If they wanted to do something meaningful, they would work on affordable healthcare instead of just sending out checks every now and then," Allen says.

Both checks are directed to select groups. The $500 checks mailed by the Trump administration last week were only sent to people who live in one of the 30 states that use Healthcare.gov for their insurance marketplace. They also make more than $64,000 annually for an individual, which is too much money to qualify for subsidies. These are people, like Allen, who were likely to be hard hit when Congress failed to extend the extra financial help put in place under President Joe Biden.

Sponsor Message

The $90 checks that will be sent to Medicare beneficiaries are only going to certain people enrolled in Medicare Part B. People in Medicare Advantage plans, which are managed by insurance companies, will not get checks.

Can Trump do that?

The checks are hitting people's mailboxes just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The text of a letter sent along with the money touts the Trump administration's efforts on health policy and criticizes the Biden administration.

"This reads like electioneering," says Kathleen Clark, professor of legal and governmental ethics at Washington University law school in St. Louis, Mo. "This reads as though it's intended to influence votes. That is prohibited by law."

Specifically, it would violate the Hatch Act, "the statute that prohibits using federal power and money to influence partisan political elections," she explains. It may also be a use of funds that's unauthorized by Congress.

The money for Healthcare.gov enrollees is from fees insurance companies paid to participate in the marketplace, and the money for Medicare beneficiaries is from a general improvement fund. Neither of these funds has been used for direct payments to enrollees before.

"It looks like a pretty desperate effort to, in essence, bribe the recipients of this letter to vote in gratitude to Trump in the upcoming midterm elections," she adds.

An empowered executive branch

The checks and letters are arriving in people's mailboxes, whether they're legal or not. Clark notes the Supreme Court has enabled Trump's illegal actions many times in the past. "So, of course, he feels empowered to go ahead and do this," she says.

The White House did not respond directly to NPR's questions about electioneering, whether the action is a violation of the Hatch Act or if it is a "political stunt," as Allen put it.

"This is an out-of-touch criticism," Trump administration spokeswoman Allison Schuster wrote in an email. "Americans were overcharged for the operation of the Obamacare exchange, and President Trump returned their hard-earned money. This President will never stop enabling Americans to take control of their health by implementing policies that put money back in their pockets."

Sponsor Message

'Half a tank of gas'

Some Republicans in recent years have advocated for giving more money directly to people rather than to health insurance companies, although the party has yet to settle on a particular approach.

In any case, sending these checks is unrelated to that effort, says Joseph Antos, senior fellow emeritus at the conservative think tank American Enterprise Institute. There's nothing that requires people to use this money for their health.

"From the perspective of the average senior citizen, when they get a $90 check, it's money," he adds, referencing the forthcoming checks for Medicare beneficiaries. "You can go out to McDonald's and buy probably two hamburgers and a shake for $90 [and] maybe buy a half a tank of gas."

A widening trust gap, poll says

A few weeks from the midterm elections, voters say they are struggling with health costs and want candidates to address them, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonprofit health research organization KFF.

"The cost of healthcare is what's going to be front of mind as they're casting their votes in November," says Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology for KFF. "And what we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all voters on which party voters trust to handle healthcare, but they also have the advantage among independent voters, and that's a really important voting bloc for midterm elections."

She says there is "a widening gap" between the Democratic Party and Republicans when it comes to which party voters trust to handle health costs. "It was just a 10-point margin back in April, and now we're seeing it to be a 20-point margin," she says. The poll found 22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42% who trust Democrats.

Where's the credit for GOP candidates?

Antos, of AEI, calls the Trump administration's decision to send out these checks "inexplicable." He describes the move as politically strange, since a Republican administration that disparages Obamacare is investing more money into it, and "unreasonable from a fiscal standpoint," because of the growing national debt.

Sponsor Message

He also notes that most Americans won't be getting these checks. "How about the average, lower-income worker who has employer coverage?" he asks. "They're not getting anything. Why is that? Is that fair?"

He is doubtful the move will have a political benefit for Republican candidates. "For one thing, Trump is not saying that your local congressman did this for you, Trump is saying he did it for you," Antos says. "I don't get it, and I don't see any advantage to anybody, including Donald Trump."

Despite her mixed feelings, Ellen Allen of West Virginians for Affordable Health Care is planning to deposit the $500 check she just received. "I'm not going to send it back," she says. "I'm going to put it in my health savings account and keep working towards healthcare for all."

World.title: Gut microbes followed migrating humans across continents, new study suggests
World.content:
Gut microbes followed migrating humans across continents, new study suggests

toggle caption i Michael Gurven

The Hadza people are hunter-gatherers who have roamed northern Tanzania for thousands of years.

The indigenous Tsimane people forage, fish and hunt in the Bolivian Amazon, some 7,000 miles away.

These two rural communities, separated by an ocean, may appear to have little in common. But a new study shows that they share remarkable similarities when it comes to the bacteria in their guts.

For stories of life in our changing world, subscribe here to the global health newsletter.

Experts say the new paper in the journal Nature suggests this microbial kinship may have taken shape long ago, before human migration split these groups' ancestors apart.

The study, which relied on stool samples from both groups, also showed that both the Hadza and Tsimane microbiomes were markedly different from city folk, even those living nearby.

Sponsor Message

The findings suggest that some strains of gut bacteria have long coexisted with humans, possibly to their mutual benefit. It's an idea that some scientists say raises questions about the impacts of losing those microbes to modern lifestyles.

"If we were inhabited by very similar microbes over a long period of time, it suggests that our human genomes may have come to expect a certain set of microbes and functions," says Justin Sonnenburg, a professor of microbiology and immunology at Stanford University and the study's senior author. "When you start to lose biodiversity in your gut, there may be big issues for your human biology to adjust to and accommodate."

Other researchers not affiliated with the paper say the hypothesis is intriguing, but not yet proven — and that perhaps there's a reason these microbes tend not to appear in city dwellers' guts.

"Another alternative is that the industrialized microbiome profile may actually be adapted to an industrialized lifestyle," says Andrew Moeller , an associate professor of evolutionary biology at Princeton University. "From a health perspective, is it good or deleterious that industrialized humans have lost a lot of ancestral microbial taxa [groups]? We actually don't know."

Documenting what's been kept and lost is a step towards figuring that out, he says.

Microbes hitchhiked on migrating humans

Sonnenburg has previously contrasted the microbiomes of the Hadza with those of industrialized people. He and his colleagues wanted to compare these two communities with one another. "They're living a lifestyle that's much more similar to the lifestyle our ancestors lived, and so therefore is more hospitable to microbes that were handed down through many generations over the course of human evolution," Sonnenburg says.

Sponsor Message

Still, the major overlap was "startling," he says. In comparing the genetic material in stool samples from dozens of individuals collected by the Tsimane Health and Life History Project , with previous analysis from the Hadza community, Sonnenburg and his colleagues found they had around 1,200 of the same bacterial species living in their guts — a near-90% overlap.

In a typical gut microbiome, hundreds to thousands of species interact with each other — mostly bacteria, along with some fungi and viruses. "The microbes are helping us digest foods in our gut, secreting molecules that get absorbed into the bloodstream," Sonnenburg says. "And our blood, of course, circulates throughout our bodies."

The gut bacteria can influence moods, behavior, and the body's response to infections, affecting fundamental parts of biology and health, he adds.

Microbiomes are dynamic — which means they can also change quickly, depending on what foods we eat and what medicines we take.

So it's remarkable that the Hadza and the Tsimane — isolated communities living very far apart, eating different vegetables, fish and meats — have gut bacteria that are much the same, Sonnenburg says.

He and his colleagues think Hadza and Tsimane peoples' shared microbial profile goes back to their common ancestors in Africa, before some of those humans left the continent , passed through Eurasia and crossed a land-bridge that once connected Russia with Alaska, and eventually settled in the Bolivian Amazon. Later, as sea levels rose, the land bridge disappeared.

"Once the land bridge went away, we had a clear picture that it was going to be very hard for them to exchange gut bacteria through traditional human contact means," says Ben Good , a theoretical biophysicist at Stanford and a study co-author.

Using dating techniques based on the rates at which bacteria change, they determined that on average, the microbial strains likely shared a common ancestor about 17,000 years ago — with some dating much further back. "That is consistent with the idea that these populations in South America, Africa and probably in other parts of the world are not just acquiring microbes from their environment that match their lifestyle, so much as transmitting microbes over generations," Sonnenburg says.

Sponsor Message

Other researchers agree that the findings support the concept that large swaths of the gut microbiome migrated with humans — and likely evolved with them, too.

"If the bacteria and the humans had a shared history for many, many generations, there are more opportunities for selection," says Taichi Suzuki , an assistant professor at Arizona State University not affiliated with this paper, who conducts microbiome research. "We would expect more potential dependencies between [the co-evolved] gut microbes and our own genome, basically."

How the microbiome develops

Babies are born with a blank slate microbiome, and start acquiring gut bacteria right away.

"We first get our microbes from our mother's vaginal canal, mother's skin," says Suzuki at Arizona State, "Then as we develop, we get microbes mostly from other individuals in the household and the community."

This human-to-human transmission occurs through the fecal-oral route — ingesting microscopic particles of poo in the air and dust — and serves the important function of passing along microbes that are specific to humans, says Moeller at Princeton. "Something that might make that less disgusting is realizing how tiny these things are," he says, "They're a micron or less in length, and in principle, you just need one cell to found a new population."

The gut also picks up generalist microbes that exist in the environment by ingesting food, soil and water, Moeller says. For instance, E. coli — a bacteria that's found in many places, and thrives in the bodies of humans and many animals.

Some researchers hypothesize that the microbes that have co-evolved with humans may help protect human health — or at least do less harm. For instance, in a case study, those with African ancestry have been found to have a far lower risk of getting seriously ill from an African strain of H. pylori, presumably because their genomes developed alongside the bacteria, compared with those of other ancestries who are susceptible to developing a deadly stomach cancer. It's an example that shows the potential harms of a mismatch between gut microbes and the human genome, Suzuki says.

Sponsor Message

Around 60% of the gut microbes the Hadza and Tsimane people share are rare or absent from the guts of people who live modern, industrialized lives, according to the paper. "The microbes that inhabit my gut are very unlikely to be the microbes that were handed down through the generations from my great great grandparents," Sonnenburg, the Stanford co-author, says. "They are much more likely to be a product of my current lifestyle and the people that I've interacted with locally."

He thinks losing these ancestral microbes may be harming human health. While proving causation is tricky, "a lot of the arrows are pointing in the same direction, that our modern microbiome has changed in ways that may be propagating inflammation, may be unhealthy for us and leading to inflammatory diseases," Sonnenburg says.

Much scientific work will be needed to prove or disprove the theory. "With regards to the evolutionary questions like, which of [these] microbes have we co-evolved with? Which ones have we lost that would be beneficial to regain? It's still early days for that line of questioning," Moeller at Princeton says.

Still, he adds, determining which gut bacteria have been with humans for a long time helps move the field forward.

World.title: Greetings from Lahore, Pakistan, whose high court offers an oasis for chatter and chai
World.content:
Greetings from Lahore, Pakistan, whose high court offers an oasis for chatter and chai

Diaa Hadid/NPR

I'm always eager for an excuse to visit the Lahore High Court in the British-built quarters of Pakistan's second-largest city.

To me, the high court is a near-perfect specimen of British South Asian colonial architecture: Mughal in its curly arches that frame porticos, the Gothic detail that emerges through the red brick baked on the city's outskirts in pluming kilns.

Within, it's a sea of busy, flapping penguins: Pakistani lawyers in their uniforms of white shirts and black suits rushing between courtrooms.

They take a rest in the main square, all chatter and chai under the banyan trees that still shade the men and women of law.

Sponsor Message

It's a contrast to the wheezy, heavily polluted city. Lahore has far fewer trees outside its elite quarters — a signal of a broader crisis in Pakistan, where there's one standard for the masses and another for those who hold power.
