World.title: Environment minister: ‘The conditions for proceeding with fracking do not exist’
World.content:
Head of the Environment and Natural Resources Ministry (Semarnat) Alicia Bárcena said during an appearance before the Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday that Mexico does not currently have the conditions for fracking, contradicting reports by local media claiming that President Claudia Sheinbaum had authorized pilot tests.

“It is not that fracking pilot tests have been authorized; what has been authorized is testing to verify the availability of deep, saline water, so that the subject can even be discussed,” Bárcena clarified. “Currently, the conditions for proceeding with hydraulic fracturing operations do not exist, nor is there any authorization from the president,” she stated.

Bárcena also said that the country cannot yet move forward with this development due to restrictions regarding water availability, ecosystem protection and the regulation of this natural gas extraction technique.

Fracking is a hydrocarbon extraction method that involves drilling deep into the earth and injecting water, sand and chemicals under pressure to fracture the rock and release gas or oil.

According to Bárcena, a group of scientists gathered by the federal government has revealed that fracking could only be carried out in one place: the Sabinas-Burro-Picachos basin, located between the states of the northern states of Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas.

Bárcena added that the scientists, in collaboration with Semarnat and the Mexican Agency for Safety, Energy and Environment (ASEA), issued a series of recommendations that should be followed before considering fracking: water intended for human consumption or agricultural use should not be used in operations: seismic activity should be continuously monitored; highly toxic or harmful chemicals should be avoided; and the protection of aquifers, drinking water and ecosystems must be guaranteed.

Bárcena further indicated that the government should update regulations applicable to the ASEA, establish guidelines for unconventional wells and develop a standard for treating saltwater.

“So, there is a series of restrictions under which fracking cannot be carried out at this time,” Bárcena concluded.

Water availability remains one of the major obstacles to fracking in the country.

According to Mexican nonprofit CartoCrítica, 100% of the fresh water required for potential development in Sabinas-Burro-Picachos would come from basins or aquifers that currently lack available water resources, raising questions about whether extraction could meet the environmental conditions established by the government.

With reports from La Jornada, Infobae and Proceso

World.title: Future presidents and governors of Mexico now barred from holding 2 passports: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇲🇽 Sheinbaum signs decree barring future presidents and governors from holding dual nationality : The decree formalizes a constitutional reform requiring exclusive Mexican nationality for presidential, gubernatorial and Mexico City mayoral aspirants. The ban on dual nationals takes effect from 2028, after gubernatorial elections in 17 states next June.

: The decree formalizes a constitutional reform requiring exclusive Mexican nationality for presidential, gubernatorial and Mexico City mayoral aspirants. The ban on dual nationals takes effect from 2028, after gubernatorial elections in 17 states next June. ⚡ Government targets 60% public share of electricity generation : Energy Minister Luz Elena González said the CFE’s share fell as low as 40% earlier this century, whereas current legislation guarantees it at least 54%. She said that government investments will allow the public share to reach at least 60% by the end of Sheinbaum’s term.

: Energy Minister Luz Elena González said the CFE’s share fell as low as 40% earlier this century, whereas current legislation guarantees it at least 54%. She said that government investments will allow the public share to reach at least 60% by the end of Sheinbaum’s term. 💰 Over 1 trillion pesos to be invested in electricity projects through 2030 : The figure (US $55.5 billion) covers 2025 to 2030 and includes 794 billion pesos for generation projects. González said renewables’ share of generation will rise from 24% currently to 38% in 2030.

: The figure (US $55.5 billion) covers 2025 to 2030 and includes 794 billion pesos for generation projects. González said renewables’ share of generation will rise from 24% currently to 38% in 2030. ✈️ Sheinbaum suggests mechanical fault caused Nayarit plane crash: Asked about Sunday’s crash of a light plane that Governor Miguel Ángel Navarro used to fly on, the president suggested a “defect” in the aircraft was to blame. The pilot and co-pilot were killed in the crash. Sheinbaum said the federal government has no information about a “threat” against Navarro, though the Nayarit Attorney General’s Office is investigating whether the crash was linked to a possible attempt on his life.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a decree on Wednesday morning that will ensure that candidates contesting future presidential elections in Mexico have only Mexican nationality. The decree — which formalizes a recently approved constitutional reform — will also guarantee that dual nationals can’t be gubernatorial candidates in elections that take place after 2027.

The reform has been criticized by some opposition politicians, including Citizens Movement (MC) party Senator Luis Donaldo Colosio Riojas, who said it “creates two categories of Mexicans in the constitution.”

In defense of the reform, Sheinbaum declared last week that “presidents of Mexico can only have one flag, one homeland, one people to defend.”

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Energy Minister Luz Elena Gonzaléz’s presentation on the government’s target for the public share of electricity generation in Mexico.

Sheinbaum signs decree barring future presidents and governors from holding dual nationality

At the start of her press conference, Sheinbaum announced that she would sign a decree formalizing a constitutional reform that establishes a requirement of exclusive Mexican nationality for those aspiring to the presidency, a state governorship or the mayorship of Mexico City.

She noted that the reform was approved by both houses of federal Congress and a majority of Mexico’s 32 state legislatures.

Sheinbaum also noted that the reform will bar presidential and gubernatorial aspirants from holding double nationality from 2028 — i.e., after gubernatorial elections are held in 17 states next June.

The president held up the decree after signing it, eliciting applause from people present in the National Palace.

Government targets 60% public share of electricity generation

González told reporters that the public share of electricity generation — i.e., power generated by the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) — fell as low as 40% earlier this century due to what she called “a mistaken and irresponsible neoliberal vision.”

However, legislation approved early in Sheinbaum’s term establishes that at least 54% of all electricity supplied to the national grid must be provided by the CFE.

González said that “thanks to the investments we’re making” in electricity infrastructure, “we’re going to finish President Sheinbaum’s administration not just guaranteeing the [CFE’s] 54% [share].”

“Rather, we’re proposing that these investments will allow at least 60% of generation to be in public hands,” she said.

González presented data that showed that more than 1 trillion pesos (US $55.5 billion) will be invested in electricity projects between 2025 and 2030. That figure includes 794 billion pesos for generation projects.

According to the data González presented, the CFE will invest 142.46 billion pesos in generation projects while the private sector will invest 199.1 billion pesos. The remaining 452.5 billion pesos will be invested in public-private electricity generation projects.

González highlighted that the government is investing in renewable energy, including in solar and wind projects. She said that electricity generation using renewable sources will increase from 24% currently to 38% in 2030.

Sheinbaum suggests mechanical fault caused Nayarit plane crash

A reporter asked the president about the crash in Nayarit on Sunday of a light plane that Nayarit Governor Miguel Ángel Navarro Quintero used to travel on.

The pilot and co-pilot were killed in the accident. The Nayarit Attorney General’s Office launched an investigation into whether the crash was linked to a possible attempt on the governor’s life.

Sheinbaum said that her government had no information regarding a possible “threat” against Navarro, a Morena party governor.

Asked about the cause of the crash, the president suggested that a “defect” in the plane was to blame. She said that the federal Security Cabinet didn’t have any information that links the crash to “a situation against the governor.”

World.title: The MND Sheinbaum Index™ for August 2026: Security, employment weigh on president’s performance
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND SHEINBAUM INDEX™

Measuring Mexico’s president beyond the polls

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™, an eight-pillar index designed to give our readers balanced, data-driven insight into the current situation in Mexico across a range of areas under the leadership of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

In this edition of the index — which mainly uses data from the month of August — the headline number is 67.9, representing a decline of 1.4 points compared to the previous score. Despite the decline, this is the second-highest MND Sheinbaum Index™ to date. A detailed summary of the latest results appears below.

The publication of this MND Sheinbaum Index™ score comes six days after Sheinbaum celebrated the second anniversary of being sworn in as president. She now has four years remaining in her six-year term.

Before we look in detail at the latest results and consider the index trend in recent months, here is a short guide to the significance of an MND Sheinbaum Index™ score:

85–100: Exceptional — administration performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— administration performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Excellent — administration performing well across most indicators.

— administration performing well across most indicators. 60–75: Quite good, but room for improvement — meaningful strengths, some areas of concern.

— meaningful strengths, some areas of concern. 50–60: Mixed — passing marks overall.

— passing marks overall. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

MND Sheinbaum Index™ pillars for August 2026

Each pillar is given a stoplight color indicating a strong performance (green: a score above 9.4 out of 12.5), an average performance (yellow: 6.2-9.4) or a poor performance (red: below 6.2).

An upward-pointing arrow ⬆️ indicates that the pillar score improved compared to July. A downward-pointing arrow ⬇️ indicates a deterioration in the pillar score. A pause icon ⏸️ means there was no change in the pillar score compared to the previous month.

As you’ll see below, scores for four of the eight pillars declined in August compared to July. The score for just one pillar improved, while the scores for three pillars were unchanged.

🟢 ⬇️ INFLATION (11.85 out of 12.5)

In August, the inflation pillar was the top contributor to the overall index score for a fourth consecutive month, even though the score declined compared to July.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate rose to 3.26% in August, up from 3.12% in July but still quite close to the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target.

The inflation pillar score consequently declined to 11.85 in August from 12.2 in July.

🟢 ⏸️ LABOR POVERTY (10.25 out of 12.5)

There is no change to the labor poverty pillar score in this edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ as the most recent data remains that published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Aug. 26.

Based on that data, the labor poverty pillar score is 10.25.

The labor poverty rate was 31.9% in the second quarter of 2026, an annual decline of 3.2 percentage points.

In the second quarter of 2026, real incomes rose 8% annually.

For a fourth consecutive month, this pillar was the second biggest contributor to the overall index score.

🟡 ⬇️ SECURITY (9.37 out of 12.5)

The pace of homicide reduction declined in August for the first time since April. The year-over-year decline in homicides was 32.1% in August, per data presented at Sheinbaum’s Sept. 8 press conference, down from a 34.8% reduction in July.

The security pillar score consequently declined to 9.37 from 9.84 in July.

A perfect score requires a 50% year-over-year decline in homicides.

🟡 ⬇️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (8.75 out of 12.5)

Year-over-year economic growth in August was 2.5%, according to preliminary data from INEGI — a slight decline from July’s 2.7% reading.

(Annual economic growth in July was subsequently upgraded to 3.3% in revised final data.)

The economic growth pillar score declined to 8.75 in August from 9.25 in July.

🟡 ⏸️ APPROVAL RATING (8.56 out of 12.5)

Sheinbaum’s average approval rating was 68.5% in August, unchanged from July. Thus, the approval rating pillar score remained at 8.56.

Per El Financiero’s August poll, Sheinbaum’s approval rating was 68%, an increase of one point compared to July.

As there was no new QM Estudios de Opinión/Heraldo Media Group survey in August, we used the approval rating detected by the Enkoll/El País/W Radio poll. The president has a 69% approval rating, according to that poll, which was conducted between Aug. 25 and 29.

🟡 ⬆️ TOURISM (7.16 out of 12.5 — This pillar has a one-month lag)

International arrivals increased 2.9% year-over-year in July, the data period used for this index, up from 2.1% growth in June.

Thus, the tourism pillar score rose to 7.16 from 6.91 a month earlier.

🟡 ⬇️ EMPLOYMENT (6.63 out of 12.5)

Mexico’s unemployment rate was 3% in August, on par with the 3% neutral benchmark, but up 0.1 percentage points from July.

The informality rate rose 0.2 percentage points year-over-year in August, up from an increase of 0.1 percentage points in July. Mexico’s informality rate in August, at 55%, remained very high.

The slight increase in the unemployment rate and the larger year-over-year change in the informality rate meant that the scores for both components of this pillar declined in August.

The overall score of 6.63 is 0.37 percentage points below the score for July.

🔴 ⏸️ BUSINESS CONFIDENCE (5.33 out of 12.5)

Mexico’s business confidence score, as measured by a monthly INEGI survey, was 48.2 in August, unchanged from July. That score is below the neutral benchmark of 50. In late 2024, when Sheinbaum was at the start of her six-year term, the business confidence score was around 52.

In August, the score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar remained steady as the most recent data was once again that published by the Economy Ministry on Aug. 24.

According to that data, FDI in Mexico in the first six months of 2026 increased 2.1% annually, a much slower pace of growth compared with the 10.4% year-over-year gain in the first quarter of the year.

With no changes to the scores for the two components of the business confidence pillar, the overall score remained unchanged at 5.33.

The MND Sheinbaum Index™ trend

In the graph below, you can see how the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score has changed over time.

We have now calculated a total of 11 index scores in the period between September 2024 (the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency) and August 2026. The difference between the lowest score (54.5 in March 2025 — predating the publication of the first MND Sheinbaum Index™ article) and the highest (69.3 in July 2026) is 14.8 points.

The month-over-month decline in the score in August is the first since April after increases in each of May, June and July.

What to watch

The next MND Sheinbaum Index™ will focus on the month of September.

Here are three things to look out for in the September Index:

Inflation: Data for the first half of September indicates that the score for the inflation pillar will decline again in the next edition of the index. INEGI reported on Sept. 24 that the annual headline rate was 3.42% in the first 15 days of September, up from 3.26% in August.

Data for the first half of September indicates that the score for the inflation pillar will decline again in the next edition of the index. INEGI reported on Sept. 24 that the annual headline rate was 3.42% in the first 15 days of September, up from 3.26% in August. Business Confidence: The score for this pillar will increase in the next edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ as Mexico’s business confidence score rose in September compared to August. A trade deal between Mexico and the United States — officials are said to be aiming to reach one before the U.S. midterms in early November — could lead to an additional increase in business confidence later in 2026.

A trade deal between Mexico and the United States — officials are said to be aiming to reach one before the U.S. midterms in early November — could lead to an additional increase in business confidence later in 2026. Economic growth: Sheinbaum predicted that economic growth would pick up in the second half of 2026 and so far she has been correct. Will data show that the momentum continued in September?

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Life on pause: The children left in limbo after their parents’ deportation to Mexico
World.content:
“One thing about me, I loved school.”

Lina remembers herself before her mother’s deportation as the girl who talked to everyone. She played basketball and piano, studied French, painted — and loved school.

Today, at 17, Lina is a U.S. citizen living in Jalisco. She has not been in a classroom for five years.

“I don’t work. I don’t go to school. I don’t talk to anybody,” she said. “I’m just alone in my thoughts all day.”

The documentation gap

Lina is one of an untold number of U.S.-citizen children living in Mexico because of a parent’s deportation. Like many, she has been caught in a documentation gap that can make it difficult to build a life here — even though she is Mexican by birthright.

Under Mexican law, children born abroad to a Mexican mother or father have Mexican nationality. Proving it on paper is another matter.

For Lina and other U.S.-born children of Mexican parents, the national Soy México program can temporarily make that process easier. During a brief annual window, it allows eligible applicants to obtain Mexican documents without some of the costly, time-consuming requirements of the regular process.

For families able to use it, Soy México can eliminate months of cross-border bureaucracy and significant expense. Although Soy México is a national strategy, its practical reach is a patchwork: Dates, eligibility and costs can differ from state to state and even, in Baja California, from one municipality to another. In Jalisco, where Lina lives, Soy México opened this year on Aug. 22 and is expected to continue through late October. It could close earlier if federal funding runs out.

For Lina, it could mean something more fundamental.

“I have a higher possibility of going to school,” she said.

A family scattered

The chain of events that brought Lina here began five years ago when she was 12.

One night in Florida, she heard her older brother crying through the wall and learned that her mother, Hanna, had been arrested and would likely be deported.

“I told my mom, and I cried to her,” she remembered. “I was like, just come home, just come home.”

That night, Lina said, she experienced her first panic attack. The next morning she went to school but couldn’t concentrate and spent much of the day crying with a counselor.

While her mother was detained and eventually deported, Lina and her brothers’ home life unraveled. They moved among relatives and were eventually separated from one another.

‘I don’t know anybody here’

Hanna’s own arrival in Mexico offered little stability. Born in Mexico but raised in the United States from about age 2, she arrived in Matamoros with US $100 and headed for Guadalajara, where her father lived. But he did not answer her calls, and when she finally found him, he offered little of the support she had expected.

“I have nowhere to go,” she remembers telling him after finally finding him. “I don’t know anybody here. I don’t know anything here.”

“In my plans, I never thought of coming and living in Mexico.”

Eventually, Hanna feared her children could be placed in state custody. She arranged for a friend to bring them to Mexico.

Lina arrived already behind academically. She had been withdrawn from school in Florida after completing the first semester of seventh grade. She expected to start again in Mexico.

“I was like, I want to go back to school,” she recalled.

She was prepared to repeat seventh grade if necessary. But Hanna was unable to enroll Lina because Lina did not have a CURP and had no Mexican documentation.

“I had so much hope every time,” Lina said. “‘I get to go back to school, I get to go back to school.’ But there was just no hope of that.”

In school, but not on paper

Lina’s younger brothers encountered the same documentation problem, although their elementary school allowed them to attend class but would not receive credit.

“They received them as listeners only,” Hanna said. “They weren’t getting school credit because they didn’t have their papers.”

Tran Dang, executive director of The Rhizome Center for Migrants — which has assisted the family with the children’s identity documentation and the process for the mother to return to the United States — explained that U.S.-born children of Mexican parents can face nearly insurmountable barriers to establishing their identity in Mexico.

To register in Mexico, the children must present a long-form birth certificate that has been translated, certified and authenticated — requirements that impose a heavy bureaucratic and financial burden on families now living in Mexico. Even minor discrepancies between the names used in U.S. and Mexican documents can stall the process, leaving these children without legal status in Mexico, without identification documents, and unable to enroll in school.

In Lina’s case, the Rhizome Center helped her obtain a U.S. passport, her first government-issued photo ID, making it easier to return to the United States, if necessary. But obtaining and apostilling another Florida birth certificate for Lina would have taken roughly eight months, Dang said. Rather than wait that long, the family decided to wait for Soy México.

José Israel López, coordinator of the Soy México program, said problems involving school are among the most common reasons families come to the program.

“It’s almost the primary issue,” he said: Families arrive because children need to enroll or continue their studies.

A shortcut — but not for everyone

Soy México has operated since 2017. When a U.S. birth record from a participating state can be electronically verified, applicants can bypass the apostille and translation requirements.

Eligible applicants can receive their Mexican birth certificate and CURP the same day. But the program is not a universal solution.

It does not operate year-round, not every record can be verified, and not every U.S. state participates. Texas, notably, does not.

So far this year, 16 children have lacked the documentation or other requirements necessary to complete their Mexican registration, even through the Soy México program. Some of those cases require legal assistance in the United States to resolve problems with U.S.-issued documents — the kind of cross-border assistance the Rhizome Center often provides.

López said demand has been rising, a trend he linked partly to events in the United States. In the program’s first month, about 400 applications were received across Jalisco, according to Civil Registry officials.

With continued deportations bringing more mixed-status families to Mexico, Dang believes more U.S.-citizen children are likely to confront the same problem. At the same time, some U.S. children brought here years ago remain undocumented, never having obtained identification in Mexico. They may not know that organizations like the Rhizome Center exist to support returned and deported families in overcoming the legal barriers they experience to continue their lives.

“It’s in the best interest of the United States and Mexico that these kids do not forgo their future and can enroll in school immediately,” said Dang, Rhizome Center executive director.

Years that documents cannot return

While friends and cousins in the U.S. move toward college, Lina is still trying to get back into a classroom — one of the children Dang describes as “invisible to both countries.”

Lina had once imagined doing an accelerated high school program. If she had, she believes, she would now be nearing graduation, or might already have finished.

“I’m not going to lie, I’ve always been embarrassed to go back to school at my age,” she said. “If I had had it my way, I would have graduated already.”

Her brothers have since returned to the U.S. while Lina remains in Mexico with her mother. In a letter she wrote about her mother’s deportation, Lina found the words for it:

“My mother’s deportation did not only affect her. It changed the course of my life. At times I feel as though my life has been placed on pause while everyone else moves forward.”

Dang argues that this is what can disappear inside a bureaucratic process.

“Oftentimes when you’re dealing with these bureaucracies, government offices are just focused on requirements,” she said. “They’re not thinking about lives. Depriving a child of their education and their future has societal and generational implications.”

Lina, however, has not stopped imagining hers.

“I do want to have a career,” she said. “I want to be somebody big. Not somebody big to other people, but I want to be someone big to myself.”

“I want to really make it out.”

Service box: How Soy México works

What is it?

Soy México allows eligible people born in the United States to a Mexican parent to register their birth in Mexico through a simplified process when their U.S. record can be electronically verified. For a limited time, the program can eliminate requirements such as an apostille and translation, but dates, eligibility and costs vary by state.

What does the applicant receive?

A Mexican birth certificate and CURP, which school-age children can use to enroll in school.

When does it operate?

Soy México is administered through state civil registries, and operating periods vary. Several 2026 campaigns have been concentrated in late summer and fall. In Jalisco, the program opened Aug. 22 and is expected to continue through late October, although it could close earlier if federal funding is exhausted. So far this year, some 400 applications have been submitted in Jalisco through the program.

Does everyone who applies qualify?

No. Applicants still must meet the program’s requirements and their U.S. birth record must be verifiable through the participating system. In Jalisco, 16 children so far this year have had cases that could not be completed through Soy México.

What if the family misses the window?

Registration is still possible through the regular Civil Registry process. Requirements vary by state, but the conventional route may require additional steps such as obtaining an apostille and Spanish translation.

What if the U.S. birth certificate contains an ‘error’?

Mexico typically requires that all legal names remain strictly identical across all official documents. A misspelling of a parent’s name, or a missing maternal last name on a child’s U.S. birth certificate might mean the child must correct the U.S. record before the Civil Registry will register the child’s birth in Mexico.

How long does Soy México take?

Processing times vary. In Jalisco, López said applicants can arrange an appointment by telephone; once the appointment is made and the case is ready to process, documents can be delivered that day.

What documents should applicants bring?

Requirements vary by state. Applicants generally need the U.S. birth certificate, proof of the Mexican parent’s birth/nationality and identification. Families should check with their state civil registry before applying.

In Jalisco, applicants are asked to bring:

Completed application (form provided and/or prepared by the program).

Photocopy of official identification of the person to be registered (if an adult) or of both parents (if the person to be registered is a minor).

Original U.S. birth certificate and/or apostilled birth certificate of the applicant.

Original birth certificate(s) of the Mexican parent(s) in SIDEA format; if a parent is of another nationality, a photocopy of their birth certificate is required.

Where can Jalisco residents apply?

Civil Registry of Jalisco, Prolongación Alcalde 1855, +52 33 3819 2456 ext. 47394, 47364, 47320.

Which U.S. states do not participate?

Connecticut, Guam, Idaho, Kentucky, Maryland, New Hampshire, Nebraska, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, Texas, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: Iván Cazarín, regional CJNG boss known as ‘El Tanque,’ is captured in Zapopan
World.content:
Iván Cazarín Molina — the alleged regional leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) — was captured on Monday by federal authorities, Security Minister (SSPC) Omar García Harfuch confirmed in a social media post.

The detention was the result of a joint operation carried out by Army special forces and the SSPC’s Operations Group, with information from the National Intelligence Center. The National Guard also collaborated, Harfuch said, as did Criminal Investigation Agency investigators from the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR), who identified his movements and located him.

Mejorar cada día la seguridad y garantizar la tranquilidad de las familias de México es la prioridad de la Presidenta @Claudiashein . Con inteligencia, investigación y coordinación, seguimos actuando contra las estructuras criminales que generan violencia.

El 5 de octubre, en Zapopan, Jalisco, fue detenido Iván “N”, alias “El Tanque”, identificado como presunto operador regional del Cártel Jalisco Nueva Generación, con actividades en Veracruz, Oaxaca, Tabasco y Puebla. La detención fue resultado de una operación conjunta de @Defensamx1 @SSPCMexico y @GN_MEXICO_ ejecutada por fuerzas especiales del Ejército Mexicano y el Grupo de Operaciones de la SSPC, con información del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia y el trabajo de agentes de investigación de la SSPC y de la Agencia de Investigación Criminal de @FGRMexico, quienes identificaron sus movimientos y lo localizaron. Las investigaciones lo vinculan con homicidios, extorsión, privación ilegal de la libertad, robo de hidrocarburos, lavado de dinero y tráfico de drogas. También se le señala por su presunta participación en el ataque contra un helicóptero del Ejército Mexicano en Jalisco, en 2015, en el que perdieron la vida integrantes del Ejército y de la Policía Federal.

Fue detenido en flagrancia y se aseguraron un vehículo, un arma de fuego y diversas drogas. En septiembre de 2024, el Departamento del Tesoro de Estados Unidos lo sancionó por sus vínculos con el CJNG y lo señaló como parte del círculo cercano de Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, alias “El Mencho” por lo cual hubo intercambio de información con @DEAHQ

Será puesto a disposición de la Fiscalía Especializada en Materia de Delincuencia Organizada (FEMDO), donde se determinará su situación jurídica conforme a derecho. Reconocemos el profesionalismo y la valentía de las fuerzas especiales del Ejército Mexicano, del Grupo de Operaciones y los agentes de investigación de @SSPCMexico , de los agentes de la Agencia de Investigación Criminal de la FGR y del personal del CNI. Agradecemos a los gobiernos de Veracruz y Jalisco, y a sus gobernadores, @rocionahle y @PabloLemusN, por su apoyo Cada acción tiene un objetivo claro: que las familias de México puedan vivir, trabajar y transitar con seguridad y tranquilidad. — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) October 6, 2026

Cazarín, aka “El Tanque” (“The Tank”), was apprehended in Zapopan, Jalisco, part of the greater Guadalajara metropolitan area and the same city in which the authorities captured alleged fuel smuggler Miguel Ángel Solano Ruiz, aka “Capitán Sol,” just three days earlier.

Prosecutors say Cazarín — whose area of ​​operation covered Veracruz, Oaxaca, Tabasco and Puebla — ran a massive fuel theft network and say they have sufficient evidence to charge him with homicide, kidnapping, money laundering and drug trafficking, as well.

Harfuch identified “El Tanque” as a target related to various criminal activities — including 6.8 tons of marijuana seized in Veracruz in July 2024 and the August 2026 kidnapping for ransom of an employee of the state-owned utility company.

El Tanque was also allegedly involved in the rocket-propelled grenade attack on an Army helicopter in Jalisco in 2015, in which nine law enforcement officers lost their lives.

Six months later, federal authorities announced the capture of Cazarín, identifying him as one of the main operators of the CJNG. However, he was only charged with possession of illegal weapons.

The Latinus website says El Tanque was in prison at least through May 2016 when he was transferred from the Altiplano Maximum Security Prison in México state to Puente Grande in Jalisco, but reported that “it is unknown when he was released.”

By 2021, El Tanque was in Tabasco, where he had allegedly established links with “La Barredora,” a crime gang linked to then state Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena.

In September 2024, the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) identified him as the leader of a fuel-smuggling network and tax evasion scheme in which at least eight other people and 26 companies were involved.

The OFAC said the fuel theft operation generated tens of millions of dollars annually for the CJNG.

With reports from La Jornada, El País, CBS News and Proceso

World.title: Nuevo León Gov. García announces US $600M in data center infrastructure investment
World.content:
Nuevo León Governor Samuel García said he has secured US $600 million in investment to develop industrial facilities, primarily data centers, in his state.

The governor made the announcement during his most recent working tour of New York, which concluded Friday. The source of the investment was not given, but it is known that it will go to projects in the cities of Apodaca and Pesquería, expanding on the ongoing investment boom in the border state that has led to the recent inauguration of several tech, data processing and manufacturing facilities.

Como parte de nuestra gira de trabajo en Nueva York, ayer junto a @eloo2 nos reunimos con @Macquarie, grupo global de servicios financieros de Australia que cuenta con áreas industriales y reservas para parques industriales en Apodaca y Pesquería. Juntos, seguiremos explorando nuevas oportunidades para el desarrollo industrial, infraestructura, energía y tecnología entre Nuevo León y Estados Unidos. ¡Ánimo! 🇺🇸🦁👊🏻 — Samuel García (@samuel_garcias) October 2, 2026

The new capital brings total foreign investment in Nuevo León in 2026 to $136.6 billion, according to the governor. “I have no doubt that by December we’ll reach $140 billion,” he said.

García said that Nuevo León is attractive to investors thanks to its strong infrastructure, energy and water availability, the industrial parks in Apodaca and the tax-free Colombia Customs Office.

“Also coming… are the Volvo industrial facility in Ciénega, the Bobcat industrial facility… the Unilever facility in Salinas Victoria, and we just inaugurated the LEGO facility,” García said. “The most important thing is that multinational companies are building their largest facilities, their biggest factories in the world, in Nuevo León.”

The restrictions of a stressed power grid

Though Gov. Gacría insists that his state’s energy supply attracts investment, power grid limitations are a growing problem across the nation. Querétaro state is a case in point.

Investors have announced several multimillion-dollar data center projects in the Bajío state in recent years, drawn by its proximity to the United States, with tech majors such as Amazon, Cloud HQ, Equinix, Microsoft and Ascenty opening facilities.

But the growth of the data center industry has revealed major bottlenecks in Querétaro’s transmission infrastructure.

In Querétaro, the aging electrical grid has proven insufficient for industrial development, and neighboring towns often experience power outages despite the inauguration of a natural gas-fired power plant in December 2025.

Meanwhile, research from the Mexican Institute for Competitiveness (IMCO) suggests that the grid limitations must be addressed to support the expansion of the data center industry.

With reports from México Industry and El Economista

World.title: Mexico’s fixed capital investment grew 6% in July, the fastest pace in 2 years
World.content:
Fixed capital investment in Mexico — money spent by the private and public sectors on long-term assets such as houses, factories and machinery — increased 6% annually in July, the strongest growth of any month in two years.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported the seasonally adjusted growth rate on Monday in its monthly report on gross fixed capital formation, a measure of fixed capital investment (FCI).

It is the product of a 5.9% year-over-year increase in private sector FCI and a 6.9% increase in public sector FCI.

Annual private sector FCI growth increased 2 percentage points from June to reach its highest level in 30 months, a sign that businesses’ confidence in their long-term economic prospects is improving.

However, public sector FCI growth slowed markedly from June, a month in which the annual expansion was 17.3%.

The overall FCI growth rate was up slightly from a 5.9% annual expansion in June. The month-over-month increase in FCI was 1.4%.

In an X post, Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote that despite the growth in July, FCI was still 2.35% lower than the all-time high reached in July 2024.

In a separate post, she wrote that the FCI growth in July is “good news for Mexico,” but added that the data “is still insufficient to speak of a sustained recovery of investment flows and confidence to invest.”

In the first seven months of July, annual FCI growth was a more modest 1.7%. Siller is predicting 2% year-over-year growth in FCI in 2026.

Mexico recorded annual economic growth of 1.9% in the second quarter of 2026 and 3.3% in July. The economy grew just 0.4% annually in Q1.

Spending on construction projects drives FCI growth in July

INEGI data shows that investment in construction projects increased 6.9% annually in July. Investment in residential projects grew 9.2% compared to a year earlier, while spending on non-residential projects such as factories and industrial parks increased 4%.

Investment in machinery and equipment grew 4.9% annually. Spending on imported machinery and equipment increased 9.9% compared to a year earlier, while spending on “Made in Mexico” machinery and equipment declined 3.1%.

In the first seven months of 2026, investment in construction projects increased 4.1% annually. Investment in machinery and equipment fell 1% in the same period.

Eduardo Valle, an economist at Coppel, said that the increase in investment in machinery and equipment in July is a “good sign” as it “signifies that companies are modernizing or expanding their productive capacity.”

However, the annual decline in spending on Mexican machinery and equipment is concerning, especially given that it occurred at a time when the federal government is aiming to strengthen Mexican industry with its Plan México economic initiative. Spending on “Made in Mexico” machinery and equipment declined 8% annually between January and July, while investment in imported machinery and equipment increased 3.5%.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: Edo Lecturer Found Dead in Hotel, Three Held
World.content:
Key Facts —Who Matthew Uwuigbe, a lecturer at Ambrose Alli University (AAU), died in a hotel room. Business Day reports that he was in medical laboratory science. —What Police say he was found dead when a woman returned from an errand. Three people were arrested, and no cause of death has been announced. —Where The hotel is in the Mosco area of Ekpoma, Esan West Local Government Area, Edo State, Nigeria. His body was deposited at the Oriaifo Memorial Hospital mortuary, according to Premium Times. —When The Edo State Police Command says it received the report on Monday, 5 October 2026. Reports about the case were published on 7 October 2026, and some outlets place the death on Sunday. —As of 7 October 2026, 18:30 GMT

A lecturer at Ambrose Alli University (AAU) in Ekpoma, Edo State, Nigeria, was found dead in a hotel, and police have arrested three people. Police say they received the report on Monday, 5 October 2026, and many readers in the United States have family, study or business ties to Nigeria.

What We Know

Matthew Uwuigbe, a lecturer at Ambrose Alli University, died in a hotel in the Mosco area of Ekpoma, in Esan West Local Government Area of Edo State. Business Day reports that he was in medical laboratory science.

Edo State Police Command spokesperson Eno Ikoedem said the command received the report on Monday, 5 October 2026. According to police, the lecturer checked into the hotel and engaged a 21-year-old woman, whom police describe as a sex worker.

Police say he sent her out to buy water. When she returned, she found him dead in the room, according to the police account.

Police arrested three people: the hotel owner, the hotel manager and the woman. Business Day says the arrests are part of efforts to establish what led to the death.

None of the three has been reported as charged with anything so far. They are in custody as part of the investigation, and nobody has been convicted of any offence.

The body was deposited at the Oriaifo Memorial Hospital mortuary, Premium Times reports. Business Day describes the hospital mortuary only in general terms.

AAU spokesperson Mike Aladenika confirmed that Mr Uwuigbe is a member of staff and said the incident happened outside the institution, as quoted by Premium Times. He said: “We are not denying that he is our staff, but whatever he did and what happened, it is his private life.”

Mr Aladenika also said the woman is not a student of the university. That is the university’s position, and it is separate from anything the police investigation may establish.

File photo: the main road on the Ambrose Alli University campus in Ekpoma. Photo: Nogheghase7 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Not Known

The cause of death has not been announced. Police say the circumstances of the death remain unclear and are still being investigated.

Some Nigerian outlets have used headlines that suggest a cause. Police have not said so, and this report does not draw that conclusion.

It is also not known whether any charges will follow for anyone. No further official findings have been published.

The name of the hotel has not been disclosed in the reports we reviewed. The exact time of the death has not been given, and outlets differ on when police received the report.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

For readers in the United States, the official line so far comes from the Edo State Police Command and the university, and both describe a case still under investigation. Until a medical examination is published, any statement about the cause of the Edo lecturer death should be treated as unconfirmed.

Many American readers have family, study or business ties to Nigeria and follow campus and policing stories from Edo State. Those with links to Ekpoma will want to rely on police and university statements rather than on social media talk.

This report is not a security alert for travellers. It simply records what police and the university have said so far.

The coming days should show whether police announce a cause of death and whether the status of the three people held changes. Related Nigeria coverage includes our report on the Ondo military plane crash and the story of the Bayelsa murder suspect who died in court. More is in our Nigeria section.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Matthew Uwuigbe?

He was a lecturer at Ambrose Alli University in Ekpoma, Edo State. Business Day reports that he was in medical laboratory science.

What caused his death?

The cause has not been announced. Police say the circumstances of the death remain unclear and are still being investigated.

Who has been arrested?

Police arrested the hotel owner, the hotel manager and a 21-year-old woman. They are in custody as part of the investigation, and none has been reported as charged.

What has the university said?

AAU spokesperson Mike Aladenika confirmed that he is a staff member and said the incident happened outside the institution. He said the woman is not a student and called the matter “his private life”.

World.title: Botero Peace Dove Damaged in Museum Fall
World.content:
Culture: Colombia

Key Facts —Who. Fernando Botero’s bronze sculpture “La Paloma de la Paz” (Dove of Peace), donated to Colombia in 2016. —What. The sculpture fell from its pedestal after, according to the museum, a visitor leaned against it to take a photograph. —Where. Room 14 (La Rotonda), third floor, National Museum of Colombia, Bogotá. —When. The morning of Tuesday 6 October 2026; confirmed by the museum and the Ministry of Culture on Wednesday 7 October. —Damage. Scratches, paint loss and dents, mainly on the beak. No one was hurt, and the piece is reportedly off display. —Status. As of 7 October 2026, 17:40 GMT

Fernando Botero’s bronze “Paloma de la Paz” fell from its pedestal at the National Museum of Colombia in Bogotá on the morning of Tuesday 6 October 2026. The Ministry of Culture and the museum confirmed on Wednesday 7 October that the Botero Peace Dove was damaged.

Fernando Botero, who died in 2023, was among Colombia’s best-known artists, and his rounded figures are known worldwide. The National Museum is one of Bogotá’s main cultural sites, so the news matters to travellers as well as art lovers.

What We Know

The sculpture fell from its pedestal in Room 14, known as La Rotonda, on the third floor of the museum. It landed on an iron grille structure on the second floor.

According to the museum, a visitor leaned against the pedestal to take a photograph. The piece had anchor supports at two points on its base to prevent sliding, but, according to the museum, the pedestal lost stability.

The visitor and everyone else present were unharmed. The museum activated its safety protocol, and La República reported that the sculpture was taken off display and moved into storage.

The museum’s Conservation Area found scratches and abrasions with paint loss on the head, tail, wings and base. It also found dents in the metal from the impact, mainly on the beak.

La República reports that the bronze structure remained stable and did not fracture. One outlet adds that the impact was on the left side of the piece.

The Ministry of Culture says the work will have to be treated by a professional in conservation and restoration of movable property. The piece is bronze painted white with a golden beak, stands about 70 centimetres tall and carries museum registry number 8107.

Botero donated the dove in September 2016 as a symbol of the peace process, days before the first signing of the peace accord with the FARC guerrillas. The Ministry of Culture announced in October 2023 that the work would be declared national cultural heritage.

The sculpture moved from the presidential palace, the Casa de Nariño, to the National Museum at the end of July 2026. As our earlier coverage explained, that was before the 7 August inauguration of President Abelardo De La Espriella.

Botero (1932–2023) was among Colombia’s best-known artists, known for his voluminous figures. The museum receives roughly 400,000 visitors a year, according to its website.

The National Museum of Colombia on Carrera Séptima, Bogotá. File photo: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Is Not Known

Neither the ministry nor the museum has given a timetable or a cost for the restoration. They have also not said whether the dove will return to display.

It is unclear whether the museum will change its pedestals or its visitor rules. The insured value of the sculpture has not been disclosed.

Until officials publish more detail, these questions remain open. Readers should treat any restoration dates seen elsewhere as unconfirmed.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The National Museum remains open, but the Peace Dove is off display for now. Visitors planning a trip to Bogotá should not expect to see it on the third floor.

As simple common sense, and not an official instruction, visitors can keep a respectful distance from pedestals when taking photographs. The museum has not announced any new rule.

The episode shows how fragile a national symbol can be. Botero gave the dove to mark a peace process, and its condition now draws attention in Colombia and abroad.

Readers can follow more Colombian news and culture in our Colombia section. That section gathers our reporting from across the country.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to Botero’s Peace Dove?

The bronze sculpture fell from its pedestal at the National Museum of Colombia on the morning of Tuesday 6 October 2026. The museum and the Ministry of Culture confirmed the fall and the damage on Wednesday 7 October.

Why did the Paloma de la Paz fall?

According to the museum, a visitor leaned against the pedestal to take a photograph. The sculpture had anchor supports at two points on its base, but the pedestal lost stability.

How badly is the Botero Peace Dove damaged?

The museum’s Conservation Area reports scratches and paint loss on the head, tail, wings and base, plus dents mainly on the beak. The ministry says a professional restorer will have to treat the piece.

Can visitors still see the sculpture?

No, the piece is off display after the fall, and La República reports it was moved into storage. No date has been given for its return.

World.title: Ondo Crash Wreckage Still Missing in Swamp
World.content:
Searchers in Ondo State have not found the main wreckage of the Nigerian Air Force plane that crashed on Monday, as we first reported. Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa visited the swamp near Igbokoda on Wednesday 7 October 2026 and ordered a sustained search for victims and wreckage.

The crash matters to the large Nigerian-American community, many of whom have relatives in Ondo and across south-west Nigeria. It also draws attention from readers who follow US ties with Nigeria’s military and those who fly in the region.

Who. A Nigerian Air Force ATR 42 (tail number NAF 931); the Air Force says 25 people were aboard and none survived.

A Nigerian Air Force ATR 42 (tail number NAF 931); the Air Force says 25 people were aboard and none survived. What. The main wreckage is not yet located; the Navy is using sonar, divers, drones and two swamp buggies.

The main wreckage is not yet located; the Navy is using sonar, divers, drones and two swamp buggies. Where. A swamp near Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area, Ondo State, Nigeria.

A swamp near Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area, Ondo State, Nigeria. When. The crash was on Monday 5 October 2026; the governor visited on Wednesday 7 October.

The crash was on Monday 5 October 2026; the governor visited on Wednesday 7 October. As of 7 October 2026, 17:45 GMT.

What We Know

The Air Force ATR 42 crashed into a swamp near Igbokoda, in Ilaje Local Government Area, on Monday 5 October 2026. It was flying from Benin City to Lagos.

The Air Force has said 25 people were aboard, 20 passengers and five crew, and that none survived. Governor Aiyedatiwa said on Wednesday that “there is no single survivor”.

Tribune Online cites about 32 people aboard, close to the figure Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo gave earlier. The counts still differ, and we attribute each figure to its source.

The aircraft was an ATR 42, a turboprop built for short regional routes. Reports identify it by the Air Force tail number NAF 931.

File photo of the cockpit of a Nigerian Air Force ATR 42-500MP. It is not the aircraft that crashed. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Search and Recovery

The governor was briefed by the Navy, the Air Force, the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the state emergency agency (SEMA) and local divers. He called the crash a “national tragedy” and ordered the search to continue.

Two amphibious swamp buggies have been deployed to widen access and to excavate the swamp. Navy and community divers search the deeper sections.

The main wreckage had not been located during his visit. Tribune reports that aviation fuel is leaking into the surrounding water.

Clothing, aircraft fragments and human remains have been recovered. The site remains difficult to reach.

The Navy Hydrographic Department has deployed side-scan sonar, which maps an underwater site, on the authority of Vice Admiral Idi Abbas, Chief of Naval Staff. Tribune describes the aircraft as submerged and not yet located.

Rear Admiral Abubakar Abdullahi Mustapha of Western Naval Command and Air Vice Marshal Abubakar Abdul Suleh of Logistics Command lead the assessment. Navy divers and Air Force drone pilots are also searching the mangroves and forest for debris.

The Sun quotes: “The sonar findings are expected to inform the next phase of the recovery exercise, including plans to deploy a swamp buggy…” Ondo officials, NEMA and SEMA were present.

What the Governor Said About the Final Seconds

According to TVC News, Aiyedatiwa said eyewitness accounts indicate the aircraft developed technical problems before it crashed. No investigation has yet confirmed this.

The plane was steered towards a swampy area about 200 metres from the town centre. The governor said this “may have saved the coastal community from a larger disaster”.

This is the governor’s account of what eyewitnesses reported. No investigation has established the cause of the crash.

Aviation Safety Talks

Keyamo and Chief of Air Staff Sunday Kelvin Aneke agreed on Wednesday to deepen ties between the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the Air Force. The areas covered are aviation safety, airworthiness certification, training and capacity building, and information sharing.

Plans include a joint NCAA and Air Force committee, and access to civil aviation training for Air Force personnel. Both institutions keep their statutory mandates.

Keyamo said “it is important that we cooperate in the area of safety”. Aneke said: “We are serving the same government; we are protecting the same Nigerians.”

BusinessDay presented the talks as coming after the Igbokoda crash. The reports we reviewed do not tie the agreement to any finding about the cause.

What Is Not Known

The cause of the crash is not known, and no official investigation findings have been published. It is also not known whether the flight recorders have been found.

Officials have not said when the main wreckage will be lifted. It is also unclear why the Air Force count of 25 differs from the figure of about 32.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The aircraft was on a military flight, and no link to commercial aviation has been reported. No advice to airline passengers in Nigeria has been reported in connection with the crash.

For Nigerian-Americans with family in Ondo, the key developments to watch are the recovery of the wreckage and any official list of those aboard. The planned joint committee has no reported timeline.

We will keep following the recovery and update this story as officials confirm facts. More context is on our Nigeria page and in our Africa coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has the wreckage been found?

The main wreckage had not been located as of the governor’s visit on 7 October. Aircraft fragments, clothing and human remains have been recovered.

How many people were aboard?

The Air Force says 25 people were aboard, 20 passengers and five crew. Tribune Online cites about 32, so the counts still differ.

What caused the crash?

The cause has not been established. Governor Aiyedatiwa relayed eyewitness reports of technical problems, but no investigation has confirmed them.

What is side-scan sonar and why is it used?

Side-scan sonar is a tool that maps an underwater site, and the Navy has deployed it at the crash site. Officials say its findings will inform the next phase of recovery, including a swamp buggy.

Sources: Tribune Online, TVC News, The Sun (Nigeria), BusinessDay, Punch.

World.title: Who Runs South Africa’s Economy, Key Players 2026
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country South Africa had 63.5 million people in mid-2026; GDP US$427 billion (2025).

— Who sets the rules Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana; Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago.

— What happened The Reserve Bank raised its policy rate to 7.25% from 25 September.

— The players Naspers, Standard Bank, Sasol, Eskom, Transnet; Rupert, Motsepe and Oppenheimer families.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 64.6% chance December 2026 inflation exceeds 5.0% (7 October, 8:38 a.m. ET).

— Still open Next rate decision 19 November 2026; local elections on 4 November.

A finance minister, a central banker, two state giants and a few listed companies and families steer South Africa’s money.

The South Africa economy is steered by a small group of players. They are the Treasury, the central bank, two state giants, a handful of listed companies and several wealthy families.

They matter to Americans because the United States bought US$16.5 billion of South African goods in 2025, US Census data show. Several South African companies also list shares in New York.

This guide sets out who controls the money, the mines and the power stations, as of October 2026. Conversions use the Reserve Bank’s rate of R16.61 per US$1 on 7 October 2026.

Treasury and the Reserve Bank Set the Rules

President Cyril Ramaphosa leads the African National Congress (ANC), the party of the anti-apartheid struggle. Since the 2024 election it has governed in a multi-party Government of National Unity.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Kenya confirms first Bundibugyo virus case in Nairobi” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

His record is set out in the Rio Times profile Who Is Cyril Ramaphosa? The coalition’s economic strains are covered in this analysis of unemployment and the November vote.

Enoch Godongwana has been finance minister since 3 July 2024, and held the post from August 2021 to June 2024. He has sat on the ANC’s national executive committee since 1997 and chairs its economic transformation sub-committee.

The National Treasury, which he heads, drafts the budget and manages public debt. His deputies include David Masondo.

The finance minister sets the inflation target in agreement with the Reserve Bank governor. In 2025 the 3% to 6% range used for 25 years gave way to a 3% target, plus or minus one point.

Lesetja Kganyago is governor of the South African Reserve Bank (SARB), whose Monetary Policy Committee sets interest rates. In September 2026 it raised the policy rate by a quarter point to 7.25%, effective 25 September.

The decision was unanimous. The committee pointed to escalating conflict in the Middle East, with little oil getting through the Strait of Hormuz.

It expects headline inflation above 5% in late 2026 and early 2027, then back around 3% towards the end of 2027. The next rate decision is due on 19 November 2026.

Four other ministers matter for business. Kgosientsho Ramokgopa is minister of electricity and energy, and Gwede Mantashe is minister of mineral and petroleum resources.

Parks Tau is minister of trade, industry and competition. Barbara Creecy, the transport minister, oversees policy for railways and ports.

The Listed Giants on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange

Most of the big private companies below are listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE). How it works is explained in the Rio Times guide to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

Naspers calls itself a global consumer internet group and one of the largest technology investors and operators in the world. It is the majority owner of Prosus, a separately listed internet group.

Koos Bekker chairs Naspers, and Fabricio Bloisi, formerly head of Brazilian food-delivery firm iFood, has been group chief executive since July 2024. Phuthi Mahanyele-Dabengwa is listed as CEO of Naspers and an executive director.

Two companies holding special A shares, Keerom and Nasbel, together control more than 50% of the votes in Naspers. Naspers calls this its protection structure, meant to keep the group independent.

Sasol calls itself a global chemicals and energy company. Simon Baloyi is president and chief executive, and Muriel Dube chairs the board.

Standard Bank has a presence in 21 sub-Saharan African countries, it says. FirstRand, Absa, Nedbank and Capitec are the other big JSE-listed lenders, all supervised by the SARB’s Prudential Authority.

Mobile operator MTN Group is another heavyweight, explained in the Rio Times guide What Is MTN Group?

Mining From Platinum to Gold

Mining has shaped South Africa’s economy for more than a century. Anglo American was established in 1917 by Ernest Oppenheimer, according to Valterra Platinum’s company history.

Valterra Platinum, the former Anglo American Platinum, was renamed in 2025; its history says its demerger cut Anglo American’s stake to zero. It calls itself one of the world’s leading integrated producers of platinum group metals.

Its mines are in South Africa and Zimbabwe. Craig Miller is chief executive and Norman Mbazima chairs the board.

Sibanye-Stillwater, Gold Fields, Harmony Gold and DRDGold all have shares listed on the New York Stock Exchange, SEC records show.

African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) mines iron ore, manganese ore, chrome ore, platinum group metals, nickel and coal in South Africa. It also makes manganese alloys in Malaysia and holds a stake in Harmony Gold.

Gwede Mantashe’s department oversees mining rights and announces regulated fuel price changes each month. Coal mined in the country also feeds Eskom’s coal-fired power stations.

State Companies Eskom and Transnet

Eskom, the state power utility, is led by group chief executive Dan Marokane, with Mteto Nyati as chair. Ramokgopa has extended Nyati’s term by three years from 1 November 2026, SAnews reported on 25 September.

For years Eskom imposed rolling blackouts, known locally as load-shedding. On 2 October 2026 it said the country had gone 504 consecutive days without them, since 16 May 2025.

Eskom’s energy availability factor, the share of its fleet able to run, was 68.11% from 1 April to 1 October 2026. Diesel spending fell by R4.79 billion (about US$288 million), or 80.49%, on a year earlier.

Its latest annual results are covered in the Rio Times report on Eskom’s profit.

Transnet, the state freight rail and ports company, is led by group chief executive Michelle Phillips, with Andile Sangqu as chair. Its ports include Durban and Richards Bay.

It is opening parts of the network to private operators. In February 2026 it began seeking a private partner for the Richards Bay dry bulk terminal, Mining Weekly reported.

The company’s finances are covered in the Rio Times report on Transnet’s return to profit.

The Families and Tycoons

Johann Rupert, 76, has chaired Remgro since August 2000 and also chairs the luxury group Richemont. Remgro traces its roots to the 1940s, when Anton Rupert founded a tobacco company.

Remgro is now a diversified investment holding company, with interests mainly in healthcare, consumer products, financial services, infrastructure and industry. JJ Durand has been chief executive since May 2012.

Its latest earnings are covered in the Rio Times report on Remgro.

Patrice Motsepe started Future Mining in February 1994, the first step in ARM’s history, the company says. He retired as executive chairman and has been non-executive chairman since 16 February 2026, ARM told the JSE.

Oppenheimer Generations represents the global interests of the Nicky and Jonathan Oppenheimer family. Its ventures include Fireblade Aviation and the Tswalu reserve.

As the Naspers voting structure shows, control often runs through holding companies. That means it is not always visible on share registers.

The South Africa Economy in Numbers

Statistics South Africa estimates the population at 63.52 million in mid-2026. The World Bank puts 2025 gross domestic product at about US$427 billion.

The economy shrank 0.2% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the first. The SARB still expects a rebound in the second half and growth of 1.2% for the year.

Unemployment stood at 33.6% in the second quarter, so about one in three people in the labour force had no job. Consumer inflation was 4.4% in August 2026.

Food inflation is at its lowest since 2010, thanks to strong harvests and steadier meat prices, the SARB says. Banks’ prime lending rate is 10.75%.

The rand traded at R16.61 per US$1 on 7 October 2026, the SARB’s daily rate shows. The bank called the currency notably resilient throughout the year.

South Africa’s place in the region is covered in South Africa Geopolitics Explained 2026. Daily coverage is collected on the South Africa news page.

What It Means for US Readers

Sasol, Gold Fields, Harmony Gold, Sibanye-Stillwater and DRDGold list shares on the New York Stock Exchange, SEC records show. MTN Group’s US receipts trade over the counter.

The United States imported US$16.5 billion of South African goods in 2025 and exported US$6.3 billion, US Census data show. From January to August 2026, US imports fell to US$7.9 billion, from US$12.5 billion a year earlier.

Since 24 July 2026, most South African goods have faced an extra 12.5% US tariff after a Section 301 trade investigation. The US Trade Representative found South Africa does not effectively ban imports made with forced labour.

Goods already subject to separate US national-security tariffs under Section 232, such as steel and aluminium, are excluded. The 12.5% is charged on top of normal US duties.

For investors, a rate rise and a firm rand cut both ways. Higher rates can draw foreign buyers to government bonds, but they also raise borrowing costs for South African firms.

The government’s 2030 bond yielded 8.18% on 6 October 2026, SARB data show. That is well above the 7.25% policy rate.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction-market platform, runs a market on South Africa’s annual inflation for December 2026. On 7 October at 8:38 a.m. ET, bets priced a 64.6% chance that the rate will exceed 5.0%.

The 4.4% to 4.7% band stood at about 21% on a wide bid-ask spread, the 4.7% to 5.0% band at 13.1%. About US$77,800 had been traded across all bands; at 5:07 a.m. ET, the above-5.0% and 4.7%-to-5.0% bands stood at 65.0% and 17.4%.

The market settles on the Statistics South Africa figure for December, which its rules say is scheduled for 20 January 2027. The SARB’s own forecast also has inflation above 5% around the turn of the year.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the SARB will raise rates again on 19 November. That depends on fuel prices and on how long the supply shock lasts.

The local government elections on 4 November 2026, with special voting from 2 November, could shift the balance inside the coalition. US trade data after August, which would show more of the tariff’s effect, are not yet published.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who runs the South Africa economy?

Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana runs fiscal policy under President Cyril Ramaphosa. Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago leads the committee that sets interest rates.

What is South Africa’s interest rate?

The Reserve Bank’s policy rate is 7.25%, after a quarter-point rise effective 25 September 2026. Banks’ prime lending rate is 10.75%.

Does South Africa still have power cuts?

Eskom said on 2 October 2026 that the country had gone 504 consecutive days without load-shedding. The run began on 16 May 2025.

Which business families are influential in South Africa?

Johann Rupert chairs Remgro and Richemont, and Patrice Motsepe chairs African Rainbow Minerals. Oppenheimer Generations represents the Nicky and Jonathan Oppenheimer family.

Can Americans invest in South African companies?

Yes, Sasol, Gold Fields, Harmony Gold, Sibanye-Stillwater and DRDGold list shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Most other big firms trade on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

What do prediction markets expect for South African inflation?

On 7 October 2026, Polymarket bets gave a 64.6% chance that December inflation will exceed 5.0%. These are bets, not polls or official forecasts.

Sources: South African Reserve Bank, MPC statement, September 2026; SARB, monetary policy and inflation target; SARB, daily rates of 7 October 2026; Statistics South Africa; National Treasury; South African Government, Enoch Godongwana; SAnews, Eskom board chair; Department of Trade, Industry and Competition; Department of Transport; Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources; Electoral Commission of South Africa; Eskom, 2 October 2026; Eskom, leadership; Transnet, board; Naspers, leadership; Naspers, group structure; Sasol, leadership; Standard Bank Group; Remgro, board; Remgro, history; African Rainbow Minerals; ARM, JSE SENS announcement, 16 February 2026; Valterra Platinum, company profile; Valterra Platinum, leadership; Oppenheimer Generations; US SEC, company tickers and exchanges; USTR Section 301 notice, Federal Register; US Census Bureau, trade with South Africa; World Bank, South Africa; Mining Weekly (all accessed 7 October 2026).

World.title: Mexico Population and Ethnic Groups Explained
World.content:
MEXICO · POPULATION

Key Facts — The country Mexico had 130.9 million residents in October 2025, INEGI estimates.

— The numbers Median age 32; growth 0.7% a year since 2020.

— The groups 18.6% identify as indigenous, 1.6% as Afro-Mexican (2025).

— What happened INEGI published its 2025 Intercensal Survey on 22 September 2026.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 3% chance Claudia Sheinbaum leaves office by 31 December (7 October, 8:38 a.m. ET).

— Still open Official CONAPO projections do not yet reflect the new count.

INEGI’s 2025 count shows a Mexico of 130.9 million people that is growing slowly, ageing fast and far from uniform.

The Mexico population reached 130.9 million in October 2025, according to INEGI, the national statistics institute. That is 4.9 million more than the 2020 census found, but growth has slowed to 0.7% a year.

For US readers, Mexico matters as the birthplace of nearly a quarter of US immigrants and as a factory partner. This guide covers size, age, cities, groups, migration and coexistence; daily news is in the Rio Times Mexico section.

How Big Is the Mexico Population in 2026

The latest official count is the 2025 Intercensal Survey, a very large sample rather than a full census. INEGI interviewed a sample of more than 7.3 million homes between 6 October and 14 November 2025.

It estimated 130,911,314 residents as of 15 October 2025. Of these, 130.4 million lived in private homes and just over 517,000 in collective dwellings such as institutions.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “Mexico sells record US$60.6bn to the US in August” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The last full count, the March 2020 census, found 126,014,024 people. INEGI then ranked Mexico the world’s 11th most populous country, below Japan and above Ethiopia.

CONAPO, the government’s National Population Council, still ranked Mexico 11th in July 2026, with almost 133 million people. That projection predates INEGI’s new survey, which points to a somewhat smaller population.

Households are getting smaller. INEGI counted 39.7 million occupied private dwellings in 2025, with an average of 3.3 occupants, down from 3.6 in 2020.

At the 2020 census the most populous state was the State of Mexico, which wraps around the capital, with 16,992,418 people. Colima, on the Pacific coast, was the smallest with 731,391.

In 2025 Mexico City itself had 9.2 million residents and Jalisco, home to Guadalajara, had 8.7 million, INEGI’s state results show.

An Ageing Country With Fewer Births

Half of all Mexicans were 32 or younger in 2025, up from 29 in 2020, 26 in 2010 and 22 in 2000. Women made up 51.9% of residents of private homes.

Older people are a growing share. People aged 60 and over were 12.0% of the population at the 2020 census, against 9.1% in 2010.

The government’s National Population Programme for 2026 to 2030, published in May 2026, makes population ageing a national priority. It also formally recognises the fall in fertility.

Registered births totalled 1,678,532 in 2025, a rate of 47.7 per 1,000 women aged 15 to 49. The rate was unchanged from 2024 but well below the 67.7 recorded in 2016.

Women aged 12 and over had borne 1.9 children on average in 2025, against 2.1 in 2020 and 2.6 in 2000. In July 2026 the interior ministry put the fertility rate at 1.6 children per woman, La Razón reported.

That is below the roughly 2.1 children per woman that keeps a population stable without migration. Regional gaps are wide: Chiapas, in the south, had a median age of 26 in 2025, against 37 in Mexico City.

Cities, States and the Rural South

Mexico is mostly urban. At the 2020 census, 21.4% of people lived in places with fewer than 2,500 inhabitants, the threshold INEGI uses for rural communities.

Almost half, 48.4%, lived in the 145 cities of 100,000 people or more. At the other extreme were 185,243 localities of fewer than 2,500 people.

Mexico City and the surrounding State of Mexico form one continuous metropolitan area, the country’s economic and political centre. Guadalajara and Monterrey are the next big urban poles.

Internal migration is common: 16.8% of residents in 2025 had been born in a different state from the one they lived in. Violence also moves people.

In 2025, 509,900 households included someone who had been forced to move by crime or insecurity, INEGI found. Those households were home to 1.6 million people.

Chiapas had 5.9 million people and Oaxaca 4.2 million in 2025. Both southern states have large indigenous populations.
