World.title: ¿Cómo se mueven los votos desde 2023? Las encuestas por sexo, renta, edad e ideología
World.content:
Vox crece en general y especialmente en un grupo: mujeres jóvenes. El PP tiene fugas por la derecha y el PSOE sobre todo por el centro

Pedro Sánchez ha convocado elecciones anticipadas apelando a la movilización: “Necesitamos una mayoría progresista mucho más amplia”. El presidente necesita recuperar los votos que las encuestas dicen que ha perdido. Pero ¿quién se ha movido exactamente? Analizamos con gráficos qué apoyos ha ganado y perdido cada formación desde las elecciones de 2023.

Jóvenes: Vox gana; Sumar y Podemos pierden

Es uno de los fenómenos de la legislatura: la derechización de los jóvenes. Ya había empezado en 2023 y ahora se ha acentuado. Vox sube 7 u 8 puntos entre los votantes de 18 a 24 años, donde es primera fuerza junto al PP con un 26% de los votos, superando al PSOE (22%). También es primera fuerza entre los 25-34 años, donde roza el 30%. El partido de Abascal crece en todas las edades, pero más en los jóvenes.

PP y PSOE tienen los electorados más envejecidos. Los dos logran resultados mucho mejores entre jubilados que entre veinteañeros. También son llamativas las caídas de PSOE, Sumar y Podemos (combinados): caen más entre los jóvenes. El espacio a la izquierda del PSOE tenía un perfil joven en 2023, pero no tanto ahora.

Cuando cruzamos sexo y edad, se destaca un giro: Vox duplica prácticamente sus apoyos entre mujeres jóvenes, desde los 18 a los 44 años. En el extremo contrario, la izquierda retrocede en general y sobre todo entre los chicos jóvenes.

El PSOE sufre su peor caída entre las rentas bajas, donde Vox logra su máximo apoyo

Este movimiento lo vimos ya en las autonómicas: Vox avanza a barrios de rentas más bajas. Según los datos del CIS, el partido de ultraderecha subiría ocho puntos entre votantes de hogares pobres (menos de 1.100 euros) y solo cuatro entre los más ricos (más de 5.000 euros). El partido tiene ahora un perfil decreciente con la renta: pasa del 21% de apoyo entre rentas bajas al 16% entre las altas.

El PSOE cae por el centro

¿Cómo son los movimientos por ideología? El CIS pregunta la ubicación ideológica en una escala de 1 a 10 (donde el 1 es izquierda y el 10 es derecha). Esos datos muestran claramente dos cambios, uno en cada bloque. El PP cae entre quienes se ubican muy a la derecha (desde el 7 al 10), que es donde más gana Vox. Y el PSOE cae sobre todo perdiendo votos del centro. Esto coincide con el corrimiento a la derecha que vemos en las fugas de votantes: el PSOE pierde votantes en dirección al PP, y el PP los pierde en dirección a Vox.

Vox también crece con no votantes

Otro movimiento interesante son los nuevos votantes: ¿qué harán ahora las personas que se abstuvieron en 2023 o que no podían votar? Son un buen termómetro del momento político. El partido que más cae entre ese grupo es el PSOE, al menos de momento. También caen el PP y ligeramente Sumar. Y el que sube es otra vez Vox.

Metodología. Todos los datos de este artículo proceden de barómetros del CIS. Los datos de 2023 salen del macrobarómetro preelectoral del 23J y los de 2026, de todos los barómetros publicados este año. En los dos casos hemos ajustado la muestra usando “raking” para que la intención de voto total coincida con dos referencias: el resultado electoral en 2023 y el promedio de encuestas en 2026.

World.title: El increíble fraude turístico con más de 800 personas afectadas que sucede a 300 metros de la casa de Maricarmen
World.content:
En los últimos cinco días, turistas de todo el mundo acuden a diario al número 19 de la calle de Menéndez Pelayo en busca de un piso que no existe

Decenas de familias se agolpan frente al número 19 de la calle de Menéndez Pelayo, en el madrileño distrito de Retiro, a la espera de una habitación que no existe. Un grupo ha venido desde Nigeria y está de paso por Madrid para llegar a su destino en Milán; otra familia, desde Marruecos con un bebé en brazos; una pareja que ha viajado por negocios está de paso en la capital; y dos jubilados que han llegado desde Ecuador buscan dónde quedarse la noche de este martes. Sin embargo, un cartel en la puerta lo deja claro: “No existe el alojamiento anunciado en booking.com. Tienen que denunciar el pago en la Comisaría de la Policía Nacional”.

Es un martes por la noche, pero la escena se ha repetido desde el viernes. Por quinto día consecutivo, un goteo continuo de turistas, visitantes, parejas y familias se queda atónito al ver que donde debería haber un alojamiento turístico hay un edificio residencial. Los vecinos no conocen ningún piso que se rente por días o por temporadas.

Se trata de una estafa que ha dejado a cientos de personas en la calle y sin ninguna explicación. Durante cinco días, la gran mayoría ha hecho lo mismo: reservar unas horas antes un apartamento por el que pagan entre 90 y 180 euros por día. Algunos han reservado dos noches, pero la mayor parte solamente busca dormir una. “Es lamentable. No tenemos más opciones”, dice Laura, que acababa de bajar de un taxi con sus maletas y ha pagado 200 euros por adelantado para quedarse tres noches, porque era “la opción más asequible en la zona”.

Se da la paradoja de que no es un sitio cualquiera. A solo cinco minutos andando se encuentra la casa de la que Maricarmen Abascal fue desahuciada hace diez días. El suceso dio pie a una crisis de Gobierno que ha derivado en la convocatoria de elecciones generales anticipadas y ha puesto a los pisos turísticos en la mira de los reales decretos que se llevarán a la diputación permanente en los próximos días.

El piso turístico publicado en Booking seguía colgado en el portal a última hora del martes a pesar del alto número de estafados. En la página se describe como un apartamento de 53 metros cuadrados que incluye “muy buen desayuno”, estacionamiento, baño privado, traslado gratis al aeropuerto, centro de spa y “atención en varios idiomas las 24 horas en la recepción”.

Las fotos que acompañan al texto muestran habitaciones diáfanas con camas king size, una cocina equipada y amplias salas de estar. Por la ventana mostrada en una de las imágenes se observan vistas a un elegante edificio que nada tiene que ver con la zona, pero que ha logrado convencer a más de 800 personas a diario en los últimos cinco días, según un conteo estimado por Cris Bellón, la conserje del edificio. Nada de eso existe.

Lo que existía a las 9 de la noche del martes eran turistas despistados, vecinos indignados y una conserje cansada de dar explicaciones fuera de su horario de trabajo. Después de atender a un hombre que ha acudido desde San Sebastián, se ha acercado a ella una familia de Nigeria que ha intentado pedirle explicaciones en un idioma que no domina. “Es nuestra primera vez en Madrid. Estamos de paso. No sé dónde dormiremos esta noche”, lamenta Mohammed Ndongo, quien viaja con su madre y sus dos hermanos.

Este periódico ha tratado de ponerse en contacto en repetidas ocasiones con la plataforma, pero la llamada es atendida por un agente de inteligencia artificial que impone varios filtros antes de permitir la comunicación con otro ser humano. En paralelo, el anuncio seguía funcionando. Cinco días después tenía una nota alta, de 7,7 y más de 700 comentarios, entre los que se leían “muy contenta con la limpieza y amabilidad del dueño” o “ubicación muy buena, en plena Ría de Ferrol”, un sitio ubicado en la provincia de La Coruña, en Galicia.

Según Booking y Airbnb, los fraudes en las reservas electrónicas de viajes han aumentado en el último año. La primera plataforma asegura haber bloqueado en 2025 14 millones de intentos de phishing, un tipo de estafa en línea que utiliza la suplantación de identidad para engañar a las personas y robar sus datos confidenciales. Pero en los últimos meses ha habido una escalada en las usurpaciones de identidad.

Cada cinco minutos llega más gente. Un taxi se detiene frente a la puerta, baja una persona y se repite la escena. “Mira, otro que llega. ¡Madre de Dios!”, exclama Pilar U., quien ha preferido no dar su apellido y ha pagado una reserva de 154 euros para pasar la noche.

El retrato de casi todos es el mismo: personas que llegan por negocios, familias que hacen turismo o estudiantes que están de paso. “Es una locura. Vienen polacos, rusos, de todos lados. El 90% son extranjeros. No me entienden. Estoy aquí para que, al menos, no molesten a los vecinos”, exclama la conserje. No son ni las diez y la acera ya se ha vuelto a llenar con 50 personas que no saben dónde dormirán hoy.

World.title: Julia, la quiosquera más longeva de Madrid, con 90 años: “Me da la vida”
World.content:
La nonagenaria sigue levantándose a las 4.30 de lunes a domingo para ayudar en el quiosco familiar, uno de los 250 que resisten en una ciudad que tenía el doble hace 10 años

Julia Gallardo nunca había subido a un avión hasta los 90 años recién cumplidos. “Todos los pasajeros me saludaron porque el comandante lo dijo por megafonía. Eso fue una emoción...”, relata con una carcajada jovial al recordar el vuelo que el pasado verano la llevó a Lisboa, como regalo de cumpleaños, para pasar cuatro días en la capital portuguesa junto a sus hijos y nietas. Una estancia que muchos tildarían de breve escapadita, aunque para Julia ha sido un acontecimiento excepcional. Porque esta coqueta nonagenaria nunca tuvo demasiado tiempo para irse de vacaciones. Empezó a trabajar siendo una niña y, en la práctica, aún no se ha jubilado: todos los días de la semana sigue madrugando para ayudar, con denodada implicación, en el quiosco de prensa familiar del madrileño distrito de Hortaleza que regenta su hijo Óscar. “Me levanto a las cuatro y media de la mañana porque soy así, porque me gusta”, precisa con una vitalidad contagiosa la persona más longeva que despacha periódicos en la ciudad de Madrid. “A mí el quiosco me da la vida y, con 90 años, tengo ilusión”, remacha.

A Julia Gallardo cuesta llamarla anciana porque no aparenta, ni de lejos, los 90 años que han transcurrido desde su nacimiento, un 29 de julio del fatídico verano de 1936 en el Madrid de los primeros días de la guerra. “El año pasado salí en el periódico del barrio y pusieron mi edad: los clientes venían al quiosco a decirme que debía ser un error, que no se lo creían”, relata divertida esta mujer minuciosa que todos los días alinea revistas y coleccionables en las vitrinas hasta completar el colorido retablo de papel con el que su quiosco saluda al vecindario cada amanecer. “A las 6.15 abrimos y echo una manita a mi hijo para colocar el género, pero luego me vengo a casa. Bajo de nuevo sobre las 14.00 para que Óscar pueda ir a comer, y ya me quedo allí hasta que cerramos sobre las 18.30, para estar con unos y con otros, para hablar y cotillear. Esa es mi vida”.

Julia, la quiosquera más longeva de Madrid en su quiosco. Inés Arcones

Una vida que no era la prevista desde su cuna de “niña pudiente”. “Mi abuelo era jefe de la estación de Peñuelas y mi familia tenía muy buena posición”, explica Julia, criada en Malasaña junto a la calle “ancha” de San Bernardo. Cuando cumplió 13 años, recibió un golpe que le cambió el rumbo para siempre: su madre murió y su padre, que no tardó en amancebarse con otra mujer, puso a trabajar a Julia en la Real Fábrica de Tapices para tejer alfombras de nudo de lana. “A partir de ahí todo fueron desgracias”, hasta que pudo escapar del hogar paterno por la única salida posible para una joven en aquella España: pasando por el altar.

Con su marido, Alfonso Castillo, joyero de profesión, fue feliz en una “casita” de El Pozo del Tío Raimundo, el enorme asentamiento vallecano que acogía en calles de barro a miles de familias procedentes del éxodo rural. En 1963, la pareja fue agraciada con un piso en la flamante Unidad de Vivienda de Absorción (UVA) de Hortaleza, construida en tiempo récord para alojar a expropiados por los planes urbanísticos del franquismo.

En esa vivienda provisional de 50 metros cuadrados, Julia y su marido criaron a tres hijos y pasaron 40 años esperando un realojo. Entre tanto, Alfonso se quedó sin trabajo y, con la ayuda de un cura obrero, Juan Rey, consiguió la concesión del quiosco de la avenida Virgen del Carmen. “Abrimos el 6 de agosto de 1983”, señala Julia, que recuerda bien la fecha porque, apenas dos meses después, un error médico dejó a su esposo como “a un pelele, aunque esté fea la palabra”.

Julia, la quiosquera más longeva de Madrid en su quiosco. Inés Arcones

Alfonso quedó incapacitado, postrado a una silla de ruedas. Era el titular del negocio familiar, aunque nunca pudo gestionarlo solo. Su hijo Óscar, el pequeño, tomó el relevo en cuanto cumplió la mayoría de edad con la abnegada ayuda de Julia. Óscar ahora tiene 55 años, trabaja todos los días de la semana con jornadas de sol a sol y reconoce que, sin su madre, lo tendría todo más complicado. “Si ella no estuviese, no podría tener el quiosco tantas horas abierto”.

Y esa actividad ininterrumpida es la que permite cuadrar unas cuentas menguantes. Porque durante las tardes, cuando suena el timbre de un colegio cercano, hay peregrinación de niños al quiosco en busca de golosinas, peonzas y cromos de fútbol. “El colegio nos da mucha vida. Vienen madres con sus hijos y les dicen: ‘Julia también nos daba los chupachups cuando nosotras éramos pequeñas”, cuenta la infatigable vendedora, consciente del declive de su negocio, uno de los 250 quioscos de prensa que resisten en una ciudad que tenía el doble de estos establecimientos hace 10 años.

“Si oyes a los que son negativos, a los quioscos nos quedan cuatro días, pero si eres un poco positivo como nosotros, mientras podamos lo iremos llevando”, asegura. Porque ella, mientras el cuerpo aguante, pretende seguir madrugando para desempaquetar periódicos al alba. “Ahora, cuando yo no me vea capacitada, pues tampoco vendré, porque el ridículo no lo hago”, hace saber Julia con su risa rejuvenecedora.

World.title: Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty
World.content:
Investigators from the food and product safety board NVWA have raided the homes and businesses of two livestock traders in Overijssel over suspected fraud and transporting sick animals.

The raids took place on September 30, the NVWA said on Wednesday. Investigators seized business records, phones, used ear tags and a pair of pliers for removing ear tags.

Every cow in the Netherlands must be registered and carry an ear tag with a unique number, so animals can be traced quickly if there is a disease outbreak or meat turns out to be contaminated.

Unregistered animals

At one trader’s premises, 88 animals were registered at a different address or not registered at all. At the other, 19 animals were incorrectly registered. Cattle without the mandatory ear tags were found at both sites.

With help from the police, investigators also stopped a lorry that had left one of the traders’ premises early in the morning. None of the 21 cattle on board were registered to his address. Another 32 cattle belonging to the same trader were found on a farm elsewhere in Overijssel. They had been imported but never registered in the Netherlands.

One trader’s business was registered on paper at the other’s address, keeping it out of sight. Cattle from the Netherlands and abroad were being kept there. Animals may only be gathered for sale or slaughter at approved collection centres, which have strict rules on cleaning and disinfecting livestock trucks to stop disease from spreading.

Sick cows

Inspectors also found a shed of cows in poor condition. Some could no longer stand and others had severe inflammation. One of the traders is suspected of transporting the animals even though they were too sick to be moved. The NVWA believes he then kept them because he could no longer sell them or have them slaughtered.

A vet put three cows down on the spot. The NVWA has taken administrative measures to make sure the rest get the care they need.

Neither trader has been arrested. The criminal investigation is being led by the public prosecution department’s specialist unit for environmental and fraud cases (Functioneel Parket). The NVWA told broadcaster NOS it could not say how it came across the pair.

World.title: MPs back age verification plan for online adult services ads
World.content:
Dutch MPs have backed a plan to introduce compulsory age verification for websites advertising sexual services, to protect children from exploitation.

An amendment tabled by opposition parties JA21 and ChristenUnie would require website operators to check the identity and age of anyone whose image is used in an advert, by comparing photo ID with a photo taken when the order is placed.

The vote went against the advice of justice minister David van Weel, who said he “did not disagree” with the principle of the amendment but questioned if it was the most suitable way to change the law.

Van Weel advised MPs to wait until the cabinet produced its own plan after consulting the Council of State and checking whether the amendment complied with European law.

“The amendment is the fastest way to change the law, but sometimes you end up cutting corners,” he said. The Senate still has to vote on the law.

The child protection organisation CKM said it was pleased the amendment had been passed, after earlier attempts to solve the problem through a voluntary agreement failed.

Voluntary approach failed

An investigation by CKM found that 80% of minors in cases of exploitation and abuse were advertised on legitimate websites.

Major adult services sites signed a covenant eight years ago with the police and prosecution service in which they pledged to alert the authorities to signs of abuse.

The agreement followed the conclusion of a notorious abuse case in Valkenburg, Limburg, in which a 16-year-old girl was forced to have sex with 29 men in a hotel room after another man had posted her details online.

Shamir Ceuleers, head of the CKM, told Nieuwsuur: “These are basically victims of human trafficking. They might not be advertised as underage, but there are enough signs in these adverts that something isn’t right.”

He pointed out that MPs had been trying for five years to make websites legally liable for checking the contents of adverts before they were put online because it was clear self-regulation was ineffective.

“Parliament has been asking for regulation by law since 2021, and with good reason,” he said. “The Valkenburg case is brought up every time, but even today there are underage children [advertised] online and that is unacceptable.”

World.title: Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule
World.content:
An Amsterdam judge has signalled she is likely to back Booking.com in its attempt to make staff work at least two days a week in the office, the Financieele Dagblad has reported.

The travel platform faced off against its works council (an elected employee body whose consent is needed to change working conditions) over whether it is reasonable to require in-office presence at that rate for all its workers.

“Two days is really very little, I’m just telling it like it is,” the judge said during Tuesday’s hearing. For over three years, Booking has held the two-day-a-week rule as a recommendation, but now wants it enforced as a mandatory measure.

The headquarters, on Amsterdam’s Oosterdok, cover more than 65,000 square metres. Booking agreed in 2016 to pay €270 million for the building and its land-use rights, according to filings by its parent company with US regulators. The average attendance rate by staff is 27%, according to the FD.

Dozens of employees sat in on the hearing. The company told the court that making office attendance mandatory was a “small step”, and argued that working only from home can harm staff’s mental health.

The works council disagreed, and one employee told the court he commutes an hour to the office, only to sit on Zoom meetings all day with colleagues in other countries.

The council also spoke about mental wellbeing and said that making office days compulsory could harm staff by taking away their autonomy. A lawyer for the council also noted that Booking is economically thriving regardless of low office attendance.

But the judge seemed to lean towards the arguments of the business. “You might think Dutch judges are strange, but we find working 40% of the time in the office perfectly normal,” she told the courtroom, where the audience was partly international.

The two sides have been given a week to reach an agreement. If they fail, the court will rule at the end of October.

World.title: Unions and cabinet start budget talks on social security reform
World.content:
Unions and employers say they have had constructive talks with ministers as they try to end the impasse over next year’s budget.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said the “real negotiations still have to start”, but initial discussions had been good-natured and positive.

The government needs to plug a gap of around €6 billion in the public finances after it agreed to abandon plans to reduce the welfare bill by cutting the long-term incapacity benefit WIA and shorten the maximum term for unemployment pay (WW).

The three largest trade unions, FNV, CNV and VCP, last week called off a series of planned strikes that were called to press the government to save the social security “safety net”.

FNV chairman Hans Spekman said the unions were prepared to look at ways to make the benefits system more cost effective and save money, but the cabinet had not set a target figure. “We are not being asked to meet an objective,” he said.

The minority government hopes to secure support from the left-wing opposition parties Pro and Volt in order to get the votes it needs to pass its budget through both houses of parliament.

Capital gains tax

But finance minister Eelco Heinen also wants to make concessions to right-wing parties on issues such as the reform of the “box 3” income tax mechanism, so that it taxes capital gains rather than asset values.

Heinen has already had to revise his original plans after right-wing parties were critical of his proposal to bring around 850,000 small investors and savers below the threshold for wealth taxes in order to make up the budget shortfall.

There was another setback for the cabinet in the senate, where the farmers’ party BBB stepped up its demands for the government to go back to the drawing board on nitrogen pollution.

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen unveiled a package of measures before the summer recess to bring down nitrogen compound emissions and protect Natura-2000 conservation areas, including a voluntary buyout scheme.

He warned that there was little room to water down the measures if the government wants to lift the “nitrogen blockade” that has held up construction projects, while the left-wing party Pro has warned it will not accept any weakening of the plans.

BBB block threat

But the BBB says the plans are unacceptable to farms and rural businesses and have warned they will block the budget in the upper house, where they are the second largest party, unless Van Essen withdraws them.

Jetten said during a debate in the Senate that there was little room to renegotiate the package. “It is ultimately up to the BBB in both houses to decide if they want to be work with us on realising the nitrogen measures and whether they want to keep tying it in with the tax plans,” he said.

BBB senator Henk Marquat Scholz told Nieuwsuur his party was “keen to go along with the cabinet, as long as the nitrogen letter is taken off the table.”

World.title: NSC loses last seat in parliament as MEP Dirk Gotink quits party
World.content:
The last elected politician representing Nieuw Sociaal Contract (NSC), the party formed three years ago by former CDA MP Pieter Omtzigt, has resigned in a row over whether to work with a new hardline Eurosceptic group.

Dirk Gotink, NSC’s only member in the European Parliament, quit the party over the decision to explore a possible collaboration with Mona Keijzer’s Project 2029, a right-wing conservative movement that sees the European Union as a federal superstate in the making.

Gotink, 45, said in a post on LinkedIn that seeking closer ties with Keijzer, another former Christian Democrat (CDA) MP, was “incomprehensible”.

“When it comes to Europe, we take a very different stance,” he said. “For me the EU is a precondition for our freedom and prosperity … Sowing doubt about the importance of the EU is not just irresponsible but also goes against the interests of the Netherlands.”

The party’s board said it had invited Keijzer to be a guest speaker at this weekend’s conference in Breda without any promise of entering into a formal partnership. But Gotink said the appearance of the former farmers’ party (BBB) housing minister was a “clear choice of political direction”.

NSC leaderless

Gotink has been the only NSC member in any parliament since the general election last October, when the party lost all 20 seats in the Dutch parliament that it won two years earlier, three months after its foundation. It has had no leader since Omtzigt’s successor, Eddy van Hijum, quit in January.

Gotink said he was grateful for the opportunity given him by Omtzigt, but he would be continuing as an independent MEP within the conservative EPP group.

“He redefined Christian Democrat thinking and tied it to tangible ideas such as basic living standards and the rule of law,” he told AD.nl. “He gave me the chance to contribute as an MEP. I am very grateful to him for that.”

Omtzigt founded NSC in August 2023 with a promise to make government in the Netherlands more accountable through constitutional reform and improve people’s basic standard of living (bestaanszekerheid).

Coalition with PVV

But after the party entered a coalition with the far-right PVV, the right-wing liberal VVD and the farmers’ party BBB, NSC fell apart under pressure from PVV leader Geert Wilders, who accused it of obstructing his asylum policies.

Omtzigt resigned as party leader and stepped down as an MP last year on health grounds, having taken several months off work with burnout symptoms. In a parting press conference he said the “poisonous” political climate in the Netherlands was preventing politicians from tackling the country’s real problems.

Omtzigt had quit the CDA in 2021 following a dispute with the party leadership, which wanted the campaigning backbench MP to be offered a “position elsewhere”.

His efforts to seek justice for families who were wrongly accused of benefit fraud in what became known as the toeslagenaffaire triggered the downfall of Mark Rutte’s third coalition government, which included the CDA, in 2021.

He stood for the leadership of the CDA in 2020 but lost narrowly to Hugo de Jonge, the health minister during the coronavirus pandemic. The third-placed candidate in that race was Mona Keijzer.

World.title: Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims
World.content:
The European Court of Justice has ordered the Dutch government to process the asylum applications of 140,000 Ukrainian refugees, adding to the pressure on an overstretched system.

Ukrainians who fled the country in the wake of the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022 are covered by the European Union’s temporary protection rules, which give them the right to live, work and receive medical care in the Netherlands.

Under Dutch rules they are also required to apply for asylum, but until now the immigration service IND has shelved their applications because the European regulations give them more rights.

The European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Luxembourg said in a judgment last week that the rules requiring the Netherlands to process all asylum claims within 21 months also applied to people who fled Ukraine.

The case was brought by a man from the Chinese Uighur minority who was married to a Ukrainian woman and lived in Ukraine with his wife and child before the invasion.

He won a ruling at the district court in The Hague forcing the asylum minister to rule on his claim by January 2024. The court also imposed a conditional penalty on the government of €100 foe every day that a decision is overdue, up to a maximum of €7,500.

Extra pressure

The government appealed, and the case was referred to the ECJ, which said the man had the right to claim asylum as a third country national through the regular procedure even though he was already protected by the EU rules for Ukrainians.

Asylum minister Bart van den Brink admitted that the decision would put “extra pressure” on the system, but the court also recognised that the Netherlands needed time to process all 140,000 claims.

“For a long time we chose not to process claims from Ukrainians because of the fact that they were already protected,” he told NOS. “It’s also because it was a very large number. Now the court has clearly said we have to do it.”

The Netherlands is one of the few countries in the EU that require Ukrainian refugees to apply for asylum through the regular channels in addition to the EU’s temporary protection rules, which are currently valid until March 2028 but are reviewed every year.

“In hindsight it wasn’t such a good idea to link temporary protection to the submission of a claim for asylum,” asylum lawyer Wil Eikelboom said.

Waiting list

Vluchtelingenwerk, the Dutch refugee council, said the need to have asylum claims processed would cause “more worry and uncertainty” for Ukrainians.

“Returning to Ukraine is not a realistic option at the moment, given that there is no sign of the war ending.” a spokesman told Dutch News.

“Vluchtelingenwerk hopes there will be a clear and above all sustainable plan for Ukrainians in the Netherlands, so that these people, who have already been through so much, know where they stand.”

Van den Brink said the government planned to deal with the Ukrainian applications in reverse order, beginning with people who have just arrived in the Netherlands and then working through the 5,000 who are currently on the waiting list for a first response from the government.

Ricky van Oers, lecturer in migration law at Radboud University in Nijmegen, said European rules allowed the government to take more time to process applications when there was a large number from a single country at once.

“They can also decide to prioritise certain groups, such as families,” he said.

World.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy
World.content:
Novelist Anjet Daanje has been tipped as a serious contender for the Nobel prize in literature and, from her 2022 work The Song of Stork and Dromedary, for very good reason.

Published in Dutch as Het lied van ooievaar en dromedaris, the book is loosely based on the life of Emily Brontë, the author of Wuthering Heights. The work opens in 1847, with a villager laying out the body of Eliza May Drayden, who, like Brontë, has written a book widely derided at the time it was published but would go on to become a classic.

The opening scene is tinged with the Gothic horror of Wuthering Heights, Drayden’s eyes refuse to close for her burial.

The next 650 pages follow 11 interconnect stories that orbit around Drayden, and her sister Millicent, the fictionalised Charlotte Brontë who authored of Jane Eyre. Similar again to Wuthering Heights, all are largely set on the moors in England, though the final story takes the reader to the Daanje’s hometown of Groningen.

Rather than a traditional narrative, the book is written like an expansive biography, incorporating news articles, excerpts from diaries, letters, citations from fictional biographies and even parts of Drayden’s novel.

Each of the tales could be novellas in their own right, vivid and sometimes nail-biting, sending the reader off on tangents such as the mistreatment of two half-German sisters during the Second World War, or a pair of French half-sisters whose shared father creates a wedge between them.

The nature of sisterhood and the relationship between various female characters is one of the central themes of The Song of Stork and Dromedary. The work also reflects on the status of women at different times across the novel’s 200-year span.

Death is another important theme. Drayden’s death, with which the book opens, is an event that brings characters together but also tears them apart.

Anjet Daanje published eight novels before The Remembered Soldier (De herinnerde soldaat) became a hit in 2019. It was longlisted for the Libris Literature Prize, took home the F. Bordewijk Prize and the English-translation, which was published in 2025, was longlisted for International Booker Prize and included on The New York Times Book Review’s 100 Notable Books of 2025.

The Song of Stork and Dromedary took home both the Boekenbon Literature Prize and the Libris Literature Prize, the first book to ever net both awards. It was named the Best Book of the Century by the NRC newspaper. The English translation was published this year.

In 2023, Daanje was awarded the Constantijn Huygens Prize for her oeuvre.

The book was translated by David McKay, who also translated War and Turpentine by Stefan Hertmans and Multatuli’s Max Havelaar. He renders the complicated work thoughtfully, retaining Daanje’s character.

The Song of Stork and Dromedary is compelling and brilliant, and the author is worthy of the highest honour in literature.

The Nobel prize for literature winner will be announced on Thursday by the 18 members of the Swedish Academy.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Cancer diagnoses set to rise by almost a quarter by 2045
World.content:
The number of new cancer diagnoses in the Netherlands is expected to rise by almost a quarter to nearly 170,000 a year by 2045, mainly because the population is growing and ageing, the national cancer centre IKNL said on Wednesday.

The number of people dying of cancer each year is also set to rise, from just over 46,000 in 2024 to just over 57,000. Some 136,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

IKNL said in its new 20-year projections that the age-adjusted risk of getting cancer will stay mostly the same, while the risk of dying from the disease will continue falling.

The increase is driven by the growing number of older people. Five-year survival rates have improved for decades, reaching 72% for women and 69% for men, up from 55% and 42% in the early 1990s.

Skin cancer is set to become the most common form of cancer among both men and women, overtaking breast and prostate cancer. Besides ageing, the rise is mainly down to sun exposure and sunburn earlier in life, IKNL researcher Jaike Schilte-Praagman told NU.nl. People are also getting suspicious spots checked sooner, she said.

The projections do not account for new treatments, and there may be breakthroughs in the coming years. “We don’t know what treatments are still to come, so we can’t include them in our calculations,” Schilte-Praagman added.

“Without targeted measures, demand for cancer care threatens to grow faster than capacity,” IKNL board chair Ernst Kuipers told the website.

At least a third of all cancer diagnoses could be prevented through healthier lifestyles and living environments, according to cancer charity KWF.

IKNL calculated in 2024 that if no young people smoked by 2032 and the adult smoking rate fell to 5%, some 120,000 cases of lung, bladder and oesophageal cancer would be avoided by 2045.

“You can’t just tell people to live more healthily,” Schilte-Praagman said. “The government has a role to play too. It has to create an environment that makes healthy choices easier.”

World.title: Poland to review Paramount takeover of TVN through acquisition of Warner Bros

Poland will examine whether Paramount Skydance can take control of TVN, one of the country’s leading broadcasters, following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns TVN. The review is being conducted under a law that requires state approval for ownership changes of companies designated by the government as strategic and protected from takeovers deemed to threaten the national interest. TVN was added to the list in 2024, following reports of its possible sale. Minister Aktywów Państwowych zajmie się przejęciem TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance#PAPinformacjehttps://t.co/FxxDnozx9i — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) October 6, 2026 Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the largest mergers in the global media market, brings together major US media assets including Paramount’s CBS and MTV and Warner’s HBO, CNN and Discovery Channel. After the deal was completed on Tuesday, Poland’s state assets ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that, because the acquisition would give Paramount Skydance indirect control of TVN, the new owner must notify the ministry of the takeover. The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”. The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojchech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares. “I assure you that it will be an entirely substantive and objective administrative procedure, carried out in fulfilment of a statutory obligation, and nothing more,” Balczun told broadcaster Kanał Zero on Tuesday. The procedure is necessary because the Polish government added TVN and another large private broadcaster, Polsat, to its list of strategic companies in December 2024, bringing them under state protection against takeovers considered aggressive or contrary to the national interest. That move came amid reports that Warner Bros. Discovery was considering selling TVN and that a businessman linked to Hungary’s then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, an ally of Poland’s conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, was seeking to buy it. 🎙️Minister @wbalczun w @OficjalneZero o przeprowadzeniu postępowania ws. przejęcia TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance: bardziej bym skupił się na organie, czyli ministrze aktywów państwowych. To jest odpersonalizowana procedura administracyjna, która wynika z ustawy o kontroli… pic.twitter.com/jp3J9zC0jh — Ministerstwo Aktywów Państwowych 🇵🇱 (@MAPGOVPL) October 7, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at the time the move was intended to protect the broadcaster from hostile foreign takeovers and prevent foreign interference in Poland’s media and elections. TVN, which was originally founded in 1995, has been in American hands since 2015, when it was bought by US broadcaster Scripps, which was in turn acquired by Discovery in 2018. The station, which is known for taking a liberal position on many issues, has long been a target for Polish conservatives. In 2021, the then-PiS government passed a law that would have forced Warner Bros. Discovery to sell its majority stake. However, that was vetoed by then-President Andrzej Duda. Poland is adding the country’s two largest private TV stations, Polsat and TVN, to its list of “strategic companies” under special protection. That allows the government to block the sale of the firms to owners from “hostile states”, says PM @donaldtusk https://t.co/TwK9IFRPrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2024 Some in Poland have expressed fear that Paramount could push TVN in a more conservative direction, as it has been accused of doing with other media outlets it has acquired, notably US broadcaster CBS. Paramount’s owner, David Ellison, is a Trump ally, as are PiS and Poland’s current president, Karol Nawrocki. On Sunday, the Journalists’ Association, a Polish organisation representing journalists, called on TVN’s management to establish an editorial independence council similar to those being created at CNN and CBS under the settlement deal that paved the way for the merger in the US. Media reports claim that President Trump tried to persuade Poland's defence minister to leave the government and form a coalition with the right-wing opposition. We outline what is known so far and how the government, including PM @donaldtusk, has reacted https://t.co/m04H8VgoSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 5, 2026 In July, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) also raised concerns about the potential impact of the merger on TVN’s editorial independence, citing the new ownership structure and the risk of political interference. The NGO called for guarantees protecting the channel as a condition of approval for the takeover from the European Commission. The EU executive, however, approved the deal in July without imposing such conditions, following an antitrust review. The commission’s approval covered the entire European Union, meaning that national competition authorities have no grounds to challenge the deal, Tomasz Chróstny, head of Poland’s consumer protection authority UOKiK, told news service Wirtualna Polska before the transaction was completed. World.title: Poland launches new combat uniforms, including first designed for female soldiers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has launched new combat uniforms for its army. It is the first time that the designs have been updated in 33 years, and also the first time that they include a version specially created for women, who now make up around 16% of soldiers. “A soldier’s safety and comfort during service are paramount,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, announcing the new uniforms, which have been undergoing testing by various branches of the military, “[They are] adapted to the needs of women and men serving in the Polish army, because both deserve not only respect and gratitude, but also the creation of conditions that will encourage service as much as possible,” he added. The new tactical uniform features new camouflage patterns that are intended to better reflect the colours and shadows found in natural environments, “allowing the soldier to remain invisible for as long as possible”. According to the armed forces, testing shows it provides 30% better camouflage effectiveness. The defence ministry says that the outfits, which will be produced completely in Poland, are created from “lighter, more flexible and durable materials” than before. The women’s version features a more “closely fitted shape” with a “choice of tops and bottoms to suit women’s figures”, allowing “greater freedom of movement”. Wreszcie mamy mundur dedykowany dla kobiet – żołnierzy! Dzisiaj w polskiej armii 16% żołnierzy to kobiety, a Wojskach Obrony Terytorialnej to ponad 20%. Nie pozwolę nikomu obrażać i zbijać kapitału politycznego na tym, że próbuje się dyskredytować kobiety w mundurach.… pic.twitter.com/GzJOhkwgTO — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 5, 2026 “For the first time in the history of the Polish military, female soldiers will no longer have to choose the size that fits them from men’s uniforms,” said deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak. She noted that women now make up 16% of soldiers in the army, and as much as 20% of those serving in the Territorial Defence Force (WOT), a volunteer reserve formation. Kosiniak-Kamysz says that the new uniforms, which cost around 1,000 zloty (€228) each, will be rolled out gradually, with 7,500 delivered this year. The defence ministry recently signed an agreement with logistics giant InPost to use its parcel lockers to deliver uniforms to soldiers. Poland has dramatically increased the size of its armed forces in recent years. NATO figures show that the number of Polish military personnel has risen from 101,600 in 2016 to an estimated 263,600 this year. That means Poland now has the alliance’s largest armed forces in continental Europe, ahead of France (202,000), Italy (191,600) and Germany (183,200). In NATO as a whole, only the United States (1.3 million) and Turkey (395,800) have more military personnel. Meanwhile, both the number and proportion of women serving in the armed forces have increased dramatically. In 2015, there were only 4,000 professional female soldiers in Poland, a number that has now risen to almost 37,000. Poland has NATO’s third-largest military and the alliance’s largest in Europe, new figures show. For more, see our full report here: https://t.co/QBBVQ9cqzS pic.twitter.com/TA34KQrJ4k — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2024 “Women soldiers contribute significant value to the functioning of the armed forces,” said General Wiesław Kukuła, chief of the general staff of the Polish armed forces, earlier this year. “They successfully perform not only support tasks, but increasingly often stand alongside male soldiers in strictly combat roles,” he added. “They pilot aircraft and helicopters, serve on ships, operate missile systems, and serve in special units.” “Their service is guided by the overarching principle that it is not gender, but physical attributes, competence and determination that define a soldier ready to succeed.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Sweden to deploy Patriot air defence systems to Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Sweden has announced that it will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine. The decision follows a number of other recent moves to strengthen defence ties between Stockholm and Warsaw, with Poland’s defence minister today hailing Sweden as an “excellent, proven ally”. Sweden is deploying the Patriot air defence system to Poland to strengthen the protection of @NATO’s eastern flank. The Swedish forces will protect the logistics hub in south-eastern Poland that plays a key role in providing military and civilian support to Ukraine 🇺🇦. pic.twitter.com/EjGFYFLGnN — Försvarsmakten (@Forsvarsmakten) October 6, 2026 The Patriot deployment was announced on Tuesday by Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, days after Sweden had also revealed that its Gripen fighter aircraft would patrol Polish airspace from October. “The task for both the Gripen operation and Patriot [system] is to protect NATO’s logistics hub in Poland at the airport [in Rzeszów],” said Kristersson at a press conference alongside foreign minister Maria Malmer and defence minister Pål Jonson “[We will] thus ensure that important equipment comes to Ukraine from all the countries that support Ukraine in its defence against Russia,” he added. “This all strengthens NATO, strengthens Europe and strengthens Sweden.” Jonson added that “repeated violations of allied airspace and Russian attempts to influence support for Ukraine show the importance of protecting the logistics hub in Poland”. Malmer, meanwhile, made clear that the deployment was intended not only to protect supply lines to Ukraine, but “is also part of our contribution to NATO’s deterrence and defence”. Sweden will deploy its Patriots to Rzeszów in December and plans for them to remain there until the middle of next year. It will take over the mission from the Netherlands, which has had two of its Patriot batteries in Poland since last December. Colonel Sofia Westermark, the commander of Sweden’s air defence regiment, told broadcaster SVT that the deployment would be “the most complex operation that Sweden has undertaken as a NATO ally”. The country joined the alliance in 2024. Sweden will deploy Gripen aircraft to Poland to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank. Poland is a close ally and a vital hub for support to Ukraine. Swedish security is built together with our allies in NATO, and by taking responsibility together. (1/3) pic.twitter.com/4WaSp2UqYD — Pål Jonson (@PlJonson) September 30, 2026 Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, thanked both Sweden and the Netherlands for their role in defending Polish airspace and NATO’s eastern flank. “The continuity of this mission is an expression of allied solidarity and shared responsibility for the region’s security in the face of the threat from Russia. Together we are stronger,” he wrote on social media. His deputy minister, Paweł Zalewski, told broadcaster TVN that Patriot systems “are currently the only ones effective against ballistic missiles”, making them vital for protecting Rzeszów. He noted that around 90% of international aid for Ukraine goes through the hub. Poland has also been taking delivery of its own Patriot systems from the United States. The first were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport in 2023. Last year, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries. Dziękuję rządowi Szwecji za podjęcie decyzji o wysłaniu do Polski systemów Patriot. Szwedzi przejmą ochronę hubu logistycznego NATO w Rzeszowie. Dziękuję także Holandii 🇳🇱 za dotychczasowe wsparcie Polski i wschodniej flanki NATO. Ciągłość tej misji to wyraz sojuszniczej… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 6, 2026 Earlier this year, Poland’s airspace was violated by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, which landed in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed the country’s eastern borders, and last month a Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad. Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. The growing threat from Russia has pushed Poland to forge closer military ties with other countries around the Baltic Sea, and above all with Sweden. In 2024, the two countries signed a strategic partnership to enhance cooperation on defence and economic development. Since then, they have held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic; Poland has ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab; and Sweden bought €274 million worth of Piorun man-portable air-defence systems from Polish firm Mesko. World.title: Poland detains senior managers from state oil giant Orlen over pre-election fuel price cuts
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged five current and former senior managers at state energy giant Orlen as part of an investigation into allegations that the company artificially lowered fuel prices in the run-up to the 2023 parliamentary election. At the time, many experts and the then-opposition – which won that election and is now in power – accused Orlen of cutting prices to help the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party’s re-election campaign. Prosecutors say that the decisions made by the executives constituted “a gross violation of procedures” and caused “over 4.1 billion zloty” (€938 million) of financial damage to the company. If found guilty, the accused could face up to 25 years in prison. Prokurator przedstawił pięciu menadżerom Orlen S.A. zarzuty wyrządzenia spółce szkody w wysokości ponad 4,1 mld zł w związku z nierynkowym kształtowaniem cen paliw w 2023 r. ⬇️https://t.co/yjiaX0ehHu — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) October 6, 2026 At the end of August 2023, just over a month before the elections, Orlen, which controls around 60% of Poland’s fuel market, began sharply cutting its wholesale petrol prices as well as the prices at the large network of petrol stations it runs. By early October, the wholesale price of unleaded petrol had fallen by nearly 12.7%, while average prices at petrol stations had dropped by about 10%. The price cuts, however, puzzled experts because oil prices on international markets were rising and the zloty was weakening, both of which would normally push fuel prices higher. The relatively low prices in Poland encouraged some motorists from neighbouring countries to travel to Poland to tank up, while some Polish drivers began stockpiling fuel. Just days after the election, held on 15 October, fuel prices began to rise. State oil firm Orlen's wholesale petrol prices have risen this week after falling in the leadup to Sunday’s elections Some had accused Orlen of artificially lowering prices to help the ruling party’s election campaign and warned they would rise afterwards https://t.co/FLUs1n8EA9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 19, 2023 Figures from the then-opposition accused Orlen of lowering prices to win popularity for the government ahead of the elections. Under the leadership of its then-CEO, Daniel Obajtek, the company had regularly carried out actions seen as beneficial for the ruling PiS party. Obajtek is now a PiS MEP. In October 2023, Krzysztof Brejza, a lawmaker from the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then in opposition and is now Poland’s main ruling party – notified prosecutors of a potential crime. He claimed that strategic fuel reserves had been emptied as part of Orlen’s price-cutting move. Now, after a lengthy investigation, prosecutors have announced that five current and former managers have been detained. One, named only as Michał R. under Polish privacy law, served as a member of Orlen’s board from 2018 to 2024. The others are identified as an executive director, two office directors, and the head of a department responsible for pricing. The National Prosecutor’s Office said that all five had been charged with causing large-scale economic damage, which carries a prison sentence of between five and 25 years. “The charges concern abuse of power and failure to fulfil managerial duties, causing damage to Orlen in the amount of over 4.1 billion złoty in connection with the implemented pricing policy,” wrote prosecutors. They said that the main aim of that pricing policy was to keep the price of fuels below the psychological threshold of 6 zloty per litre, and that this was carried out “in a manner detached from market realities…in gross violation of numerous formal and informal procedures applicable to the managerial staff at Orlen”. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new @FT report on how state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million through a botched effort to buy Venezuelan oil under the former government https://t.co/LlGcgXOvGG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Speaking anonymously to broadcaster TVN, one of the prosecutors involved in the case said that the executives’ actions had implications not only for Orlen’s finances, but also Poland’s national security, given that strategic reserves are meant to be saved for emergency situation. “State security was jeopardised for the sake of politics,” they said. “These reserves are intended, at a time of war, to ensure there is fuel for tanks, to put it simply.” Meanwhile, justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, wrote on social media that Orlen and Obajtek had, by “manually controlling prices”, “acted to the detriment of national assets in order to save the party’s [grip on] power”. Na polecenie łódzkiego wydziału ds. Przestępczości Zorganizowanej Prokuratury Krajowej funkcjonariusze ABW zatrzymali wczoraj 5 byłych i obecnych menadżerów Orlen S.A., w tym byłego członka zarządu spółki z lat 2018-2024. Jesienią 2023 roku Daniel „wszystko mogę” Obajtek ręcznie… https://t.co/qV9qroeBu0 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 6, 2026 Obajtek today rejected the allegations and defended Orlen’s actions under his leadership. He accused the current government of acting to distract from its own failure to keep fuel prices under control. “They couldn’t cope with rising fuel prices so – for show and without any substantive justification – they’re detaining experienced managers thanks to whom fuel cost less than 6 zloty [per litre] in the summer and autumn of 2023,” he wrote on social media. “If I have to answer for the fact that Poles paid little for fuel, then I would be honoured,” he added. However, speaking at a press conference, Żurek declared that, “in a state governed by law there are proper procedures for lowering prices”. Instead, under PiS, there was “a state of lawlessness, a state run like a private fiefdom”. Nie potrafili poradzić sobie z rosnącymi cenami paliw, więc – na pokaz, bez żadnego merytorycznego uzasadnienia – zatrzymują doświadczonych managerów, dzięki którym paliwo latem i jesienią 2023 roku kosztowało poniżej 6 złotych, gdy baryłka ropy była po 100 dolarów, a dolar 4,20… — Daniel Obajtek (@DanielObajtek) October 5, 2026 In a separate case, the European Parliament last year stripped Obajtek of legal immunity to face charges for allegedly using Orlen’s funds to serve his own private interests. Polish prosecutors are also pursuing him for allegedly violating Poland’s press law and falsely reporting his income in a tax return. Last month, the Financial Times reported on how, under Obajtek’s leadership, Orlen lost $230 million (856 million zloty) trying to buy Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, unsecured payments and cryptocurrency transfers. Obajtek, however, argued that he managed to turn Orlen into one of Europe’s largest companies, including diversifying it away from its traditional focus on oil and towards other forms of energy, including gas, hydrogen and renewables. World.title: Poland and Lithuania prepare to evacuate one million Baltic residents to Poland in event of war
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression. On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus. “In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing. “As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added. The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members. Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland. Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise. This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation. Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country. Almost 80% of Poles say they would want Poland to come to the aid of the Baltic states if they were attacked by Russia The poll follows controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure casting doubt as to whether Poland should come to their defence https://t.co/l3dj02ETZ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 10, 2026 The two ministers also used their meeting to discuss their joint response to illegal migration. Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027. “Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. But for now, we have decided that they will remain in place for at least another six months.” Poland is reintroducing controls on its borders with Germany and Lithuania to prevent the “uncontrolled flow of migrants”, in particular those returned by Germany after entering illegally "Poland’s patience is running out," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/Pttd3FvpHA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2025 Katelynas emphasised that “Lithuania and Poland share a common goal: to ensure the protection of our borders and effectively prevent irregular migrants from moving through our countries and across the Schengen area”. He also noted that an agreement between the two countries on cooperation between police, border guard and customs services is currently being finalised. “Poland and Lithuania are like brothers and sisters who support each other and will continue to do so,” said Katelynas. Kierwiński likewise expressed his satisfaction that the two countries “speak with one voice…because this part of Europe, the eastern flank of NATO and the EU, must speak with one voice to address and counter the threats posed by Russian imperialism and the difficult situation beyond our eastern border”. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 Last month, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Poland has already recently suffered airspace violations by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter. It has also been the primary target for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. In response, the Polish government has moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters. The Polish-Lithuanian border area, which sits between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and is known as the Suwałki Gap, is seen as a potential target for Russia in the event of war. Poland and Lithuania held joint military exercises there in 2024 to test their defensive capabilities. World.title: Reports claim Trump tried to change Poland’s government. What do we know?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”. Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue. The context Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners. One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister. Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election. By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner. The meeting The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way. On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”. The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki. In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”. Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so. The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan. “I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation. What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz? Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Tusk and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. “Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk. She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”. What has Poland’s government said? On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base. “In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?” Z tak ważnej rozmowy organizator miał obowiązek sporządzić notatkę. Do @MSZ_RP ona nie dotarła. Czyżby dlatego, że spotkanie służyło też próbie zaangażowania obcego państwa w naszą wewnętrzną politykę? https://t.co/0wL0QZBxPv — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 2, 2026 On Monday, Tusk himself told broadcaster TVN that Kosiniak-Kamysz had informed him about his meeting with Trump immediately after it took place. He added that the subject of the meeting “is too interesting to talk about publicly”, but that military “bases were not the topic of the conversation”. “The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk. Kosiniak-Kamysz himself also confirmed on Monday that the question of a permanent US base in Poland had not been discussed at the meeting. He noted that, in March, that issue was not even seriously on the table, because it was only two months later that Trump announced he intended to send additional troops to Poland The defence minister did not give any further details about the content of the meeting, which he described as “informal”. Rozmowa miała dyskrecjonalny charakter i dlatego czuję się zobowiązany do dyskrecji – powiedział w poniedziałek premier Donald Tusk reporterce @tvn24 @WojcikowskaMaja, pytany o spotkanie ministra obrony Władysława Kosiniaka-Kamysza z prezydentem USA Donaldem Trumpem. World.title: Thousands of protesters trap Polish bishop in church amid anger over dismissal of local priest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest. As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight. „Kościół w Grojcu otoczyło kilka tysięcy osób, parafian i uczęszczających do grojeckiej świątyni. #Aktualnie Okrzyki „jesteśmy z Tobą” dla księdza Józefa Zborka." Materiał od @FaktyOswiecim pic.twitter.com/3zaqlBCDF6 — Sebastian Kościelnik (@S_Koscielnik) October 4, 2026 The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest. They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position. The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so. The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday. On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist. However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony. Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”. News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage. 🔴Sceny pod kościołem. Biskup w eskorcie policji. Jest nagranie Nocna interwencja policji przed kościołem w Grojcu w Małopolsce. Biskup bielsko-żywiecki Roman Pindel wraz z towarzyszącymi mu księżmi został wyprowadzony ze świątyni pod eskortą funkcjonariuszy. Wszystko po… pic.twitter.com/XEXU3LOMXm — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 5, 2026 After the church service had been disrupted, Pindel and several other priests retreated to the sacristy. Social media videos show protesters shouting angrily at the bishop. Some even physically assailed him and had to be pulled away. Once inside, the bishop faced continued verbal aggression. Shortly afterwards, the police arrived, including specialist negotiators. Pindel spoke to the crowd, explaining that the decision to dismiss Zborek had been confirmed by the Vatican and was final. The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal. But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m. Hundreds of people have protested in Kraków’s Kazimierz district against plans to evict residents and businesses – including some of the area's famous bars and galleries – from historic church-owned buildings that will be redeveloped into a luxury hotel https://t.co/Xo3SmkWc9g — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 24, 2026 Subsequently, the Bielsko-Żywiec diocese issued a statement saying that the “aggressive crowd” had “threatened the health and lives of the priests”. It also noted that Zborek had been dismissed after a full canon law process in which he had been able to defend himself and appeal. “We know that many people, especially his parishioners, are experiencing this pain,” they wrote. “However, we ask that you accept this decision in a spirit of faith and in unity with the church.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
