According to lawyer Anna Akopova, her client Lasha Chachanidze suffered a beating at the same Prison No. 6 after he shouted from his cell to express solidarity with Davitadze. The lawyer says authorities transferred Chachanidze and two other prisoners to Prison No. 3 in Batumi.

Akopova says the prisoner has multiple injuries on different parts of his body. According to her, about ten people took part in the alleged assault. The lawyer is demanding a medical examination and the preservation of the relevant video footage, which could establish Chachanidze’s condition when staff took him out of his cell and when they returned him.

The Penitentiary Service categorically denies the allegation and says nothing of the sort happened. The Public Defender’s Office said it had received information about the case and would visit the prisoner.

Saba Skhvitaridze, who authorities detained during pro-European protests, also wrote about the tense situation at Prison No. 6. According to a statement published on his Facebook page, authorities transferred some prisoners to other facilities, placed others in de-escalation rooms and several prisoners went on hunger strike. Skhvitaridze also reported that authorities beat a prisoner and that some prisoners injured themselves.

Giorgi Davitadze remains in the same prison, whose staff he accuses of sexual abuse.

The Prosecutor’s Office investigation, which it launched in December 2025 after the Public Defender’s Office filed a complaint, remains incomplete. The Public Defender’s Office says it continues to monitor the investigation and calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make its findings public as soon as possible.

The Penitentiary Service denies all the allegations, including reports of a hunger strike among prisoners, and insists that “complete calm” prevails at Rustavi Prison No. 6.

The Giorgi Davitadze case

World.title: SJC: Extradition of prisoners from Georgia to Russia must be stopped immediately
World.content:
Following the killing of Dmitry Pushkaryov, who Georgia extradited to Russia, the Georgian Social Justice Center (SJC) said that Georgia should immediately halt the extradition of prisoners to Russia.

The organisation said resuming the practice of extraditing prisoners to Russia was incompatible with human rights.

After Georgia extradited Dmitry Pushkaryov, he was killed in an attack on Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) officers. According to Russian authorities, Pushkaryov killed one officer and wounded three others while attempting to escape.

“The mere fact that Dmitry Pushkaryov was killed does not directly establish that Georgia violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by extraditing him. However, his death raises even more serious questions about how thoroughly the Georgian authorities assessed the risks he faced in Russia, what guarantees they obtained from Russia, whether an independent mechanism existed to monitor compliance with those guarantees, and whether the Georgian side subsequently monitored the person’s situation,” the SJC said.

According to the organisation, the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) indicates that information that emerges after a person’s transfer can also matter when assessing how well-founded the state’s initial risk assessment was.

The SJC believes that continuing extraditions to Russia — particularly without proper public justification, a rigorous individual risk assessment and effective independent monitoring mechanisms — could put Georgia in breach of its international human rights obligations.

The organisation calls on the Georgian government, the Ministry of Justice and the Prosecutor General’s Office to immediately suspend extraditions to Russia. The SJC believes the practice should remain suspended until the situation in Russia changes significantly and the international community reaches a consensus on the issue.

The Centre also calls on the Prosecutor General’s Office to publish statistical data on extradition requests received from Russia since 16 March 2022, the decisions made on those requests and the extraditions carried out.

The organisation is also demanding that the Ministry of Justice explain the legal grounds for changing the moratorium recorded before the European Court of Human Rights in the case of Sumbaev v. Georgia.

The ECtHR found Georgia’s 2021 extradition of Aslan Sumbaev, who faced serious criminal charges in Russia, lawful only after Russia provided official diplomatic assurances that it would prevent torture and ensure proper detention conditions.

“Please also specify what individual guarantees and subsequent monitoring mechanisms were applied in relation to the extraditions that have already taken place,” the Social Justice Center wrote.

World.title: Georgia without an opposition? How ruling party moved to ban its opponents through constitutional lawsuit
World.content:
The ruling party Georgian Dream has asked Georgia’s Constitutional Court to ban five opposition parties. Four of them crossed the five per cent threshold in the 2024 parliamentary elections. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, election stability risks, a total of 784,820 voters — 37.79% of those who took part in the election — voted for the four parties.

What legal grounds does the government cite for seeking to ban the five parties? What does the term “collective United National Movement” mean? How has the list of parties facing a ban changed, and under what conditions does European law allow such a ban? JAMnews examined the Georgian Dream lawsuit, relevant legislation and European practice to answer these questions.

Georgian Dream registered its latest lawsuit with the Constitutional Court on 24 September 2026, under case No. 1979.

The list of parties facing a ban includes Unity — National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia — Lelo, Gakharia for Georgia and Federalists.

As of 5 October 2026, the court has not yet published a decision on whether it will accept the lawsuit for consideration on the merits, and it has not yet set a hearing date.

The First Chamber is hearing the case, with Vasil Roinishvili serving as the reporting judge. Under the law, the court must issue its final decision within nine months of the filing — no later than 24 June 2027.

If the court upholds the lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the electoral threshold in the last parliamentary elections could disappear from the country’s political system.

Under current legislation, the authorities can also ask the court to ban another political organisation that acts as a “successor” to an already banned party.

An election campaign promise

Bidzina Ivanishvili at a Georgian Dream rally, April 2024.

The idea of banning opposition parties did not emerge spontaneously within Georgian Dream. Its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili, publicly stated even before the 2024 parliamentary elections that, after the vote, the government would deliver a “strict political and legal verdict” to the “collective National Movement”.

In other words, the idea of banning the opposition did not emerge after the election. It formed part of the election campaign itself.

“After the election, we will have the opportunity to deliver a strict political and legal verdict to the collective National Movement.”

Ivanishvili also explained why, in his view, this did not happen in 2012. He said the government did not yet have sufficient resources at the time:

“Over these years, we have accumulated enough resources to begin fully strengthening our sovereignty…”

A statement made almost six months before the election gradually turned into a concrete political plan. In August 2024, Georgian Dream openly announced that it needed a constitutional majority in the election to declare the “collective National Movement” illegal. The European Commission included the plan in its report that year.

Then EU High Representative Josep Borrell, speaking in the European Parliament, described the promise to ban opposition parties as one of the worrying developments during Georgia’s election campaign.

Two years later, that campaign promise has turned into a concrete lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

Three lawsuits, three lists — how the number of parties facing a ban grew

The lawsuit changed three times over the course of one year.

The Constitutional Court registered the first lawsuit on 31 October 2025, under case No. 1912. Eighty-eight members of parliament signed it. They sought to ban three political forces:

Unity — National Movement

Coalition for Change

Strong Georgia — Lelo

Later, on 21 April 2026, 89 MPs filed a second lawsuit, No. 1958. They added a fourth party, Federalists, to the list.

The list of parties facing a ban grew again in September 2026.

On 24 September, the Constitutional Court registered lawsuit No. 1979, signed by 88 MPs. This time, the authorities are seeking to ban five parties, including former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s party, For Georgia.

The law gives the Constitutional Court a maximum of nine months to rule on such a case. Each new lawsuit has therefore sparked debate over whether that period starts again from the beginning.

The authors of the lawsuit hope the Constitutional Court will complete the process by January 2027, by which time all five parties would have been banned.

Opposition representatives, meanwhile, argue that Georgian Dream is actually prolonging the process by adding new parties.

On what grounds can a party be banned?

Georgia’s Constitution sets out specific grounds for banning a political party.

It prohibits parties whose goals include overthrowing or forcibly changing the constitutional order, undermining the country’s independence or violating its territorial integrity. The authorities can also ban parties that promote war or violence or incite national, ethnic, regional, religious or social hatred.

Only the Constitutional Court can ban a political party.

The Georgian Dream lawsuit relies on these constitutional grounds and argues that the listed parties’ activities target the state.

A significant part of the argument draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission, known as the Tsulukiani Commission.

One of the lawsuit’s key arguments concerns the opposition parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the 2024 election, parliament and the government.

The plaintiffs also link the opposition parties’ actions to “sabotage”, calls for Western sanctions against the Georgian authorities and attempts to “punish” the country.

The lawsuit, for example, treats the opposition’s refusal to recognise the election results and its view that Georgian Dream is an illegitimate government as “sabotage”.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also cited the legitimacy of the government when explaining why the authorities added Gakharia’s party to the list.

He said that although the party, unlike its “fellow opposition parties”, agreed to take part in parliamentary work, it still does not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government:

“It is true that they entered parliament, but to this day they do not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government. Under these circumstances, the spirit of this political party’s activities is no different from that of the other relevant political parties,” he said.

Why these parties?

The lawsuit explicitly cites the parties’ political influence as a reason for seeking their ban. It also mentions other opposition parties, such as the Republican Party, which does not appear on the list, and says:

“At present, they do not have significant influence on politics or a realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold. Accordingly, at this stage, there is no apparent need to ban them.”

A brief overview of the five parties facing a ban: Политические силы, объединенные “Грузинской мечтой” в единый “черный список”, имеют разное происхождение, историю и идеологию. Некоторые из них действительно произошли из политической семьи «Единого национального движения». Некоторые пытались занять независимое пространство именно между ЕНД и «Грузинской мечтой». Политическое же ядро партии Гиорги Гахария и вовсе вышло из самой «Грузинской мечты». «Единство — Национальное движение» «Единое национальное движение» экс-президента Михеила Саакашвили — самая старая партия в этой пятерке и единственная, имеющая опыт пребывания у власти: в течение 9 лет она являлась правящей партией Грузии. На выборах 2024 года ЕНД официально получила 211 216 голосов — 10,17%. Уже долгие годы партия переживает кризис лидерства и на данный момент находится в режиме переходного управления. В августе 2026 года был создан временный управляющий совет, руководителем которого стал Иракли Павленишвили. Избрание постоянного председателя партии должно состояться позже. Главным лицом, принимающим решения в партии, по-прежнему остается Михеил Саакашвили, который уже пять лет находится в тюрьме. ЕНД позиционирует себя как резко проевропейская и евроатлантическая политическая сила. Её историческое ядро — это политическое наследие правительства Саакашвили. Именно правление ЕНД в 2004-2012 годах является главной мишенью большей части иска «Грузинской мечты» и обвинений комиссии Цулукиани. Coalition for Change Coalition for Change was created ahead of the 2024 elections and brought together several different political forces. The coalition included Nika Melia and Nika Gvaramia’s Akhali party, Zurab Japaridze’s Girchi — More Freedom and Elene Khoshtaria’s Droa. Akhali is a pro-European centre-right liberal party. Girchi — More Freedom has a more distinctly right-libertarian economic platform, while Droa has a liberal and activist profile. In the 2024 election, the coalition received the largest number of official votes among the opposition forces — 229,161, or 11.03%. Most of its leaders had previously been associated with the UNM. The coalition brings together parties that broke away from the UNM or emerged independently at different times. Strong Georgia — Lelo The core of Strong Georgia is the Lelo party, which Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze founded in 2019. Both entered politics after careers in business. A broader coalition formed around Lelo in 2024. It included Ana Dolidze’s For People, Aleko Elisashvili’s Citizens and Levan Tsutskiridze’s Freedom Square. The coalition sought to present itself as an independent alternative to both Georgian Dream and the former ruling UNM. The party has a pro-European, centrist-liberal profile. Economic development, institutional reform and Western integration have remained central themes in Lelo’s programmes. In 2024, Strong Georgia officially received 182,922 votes, or 8.81%. Gakharia for Georgia Giorgi Gakharia’s party stands out from the other four parties in the group because of its origins. Gakharia was not a member of the government under Mikheil Saakashvili. Instead, he served as economy minister, interior minister and eventually prime minister under Georgian Dream. He resigned as prime minister in February 2021 and founded his own For Georgia party in May. The party initially sought to present itself as an alternative to both Georgian Dream and the UNM. It received 7.79% in the 2021 municipal elections and 161,521 votes, or 7.78%, in the 2024 parliamentary election. Gakharia’s case shows how broadly Georgian Dream applies the concept of the “collective National Movement”: today, the category also includes a political force led by one of Georgian Dream’s former leaders. Federalists Federalists are the newest party among the five. Giga Bokeria, Tamar Chergoleishvili and their allies founded the party in August 2024 after leaving European Georgia. Giga Bokeria chairs the party, while Tamar Chergoleishvili heads its Tbilisi organisation. The party identifies individual freedom, human rights, European development, free competition, decentralisation and strong democratic institutions as its core principles. Politically, it is a pro-European and liberal force with a more right-wing economic platform. Federalists did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Bokeria and Chergoleishvili’s group has a long-standing political conflict with Mikheil Saakashvili and today’s UNM.

At the same time, the lawsuit notes that the question of whether these parties are unconstitutional could arise in the future if they gain significant influence over the political process.

Initially, the “Federalists” also fell into the category of parties with “no realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold”. However, in March 2026, they joined the “Opposition Alliance”, a nine-party coalition. In April, Georgian Dream also called for the Federalists to be banned.

Thus, according to the lawsuit, a party’s political influence is one of the factors that the plaintiffs themselves take into account when seeking to ban it.

Представители оппозиционного альянса, март 2026 года

How all opponents of the government became the “collective National Movement”

The “collective National Movement” is neither a party nor a legally recognised political organisation. It is a political term coined by Georgian Dream that it has used for years to group various opposition forces into a single political camp, thereby portraying its opponents as a common “enemy”.

Over the years, the boundaries of this category have gradually expanded. It has come to include not only the National Movement itself (UNM, the former ruling party) and parties that broke away from it, but also forces that positioned themselves as alternatives to both the UNM and Georgian Dream. These include Mamuka Khazaradze’s Lelo and Giorgi Gakharia’s party, even though Gakharia himself previously served as prime minister for Georgian Dream.

The term then expanded further. Irakli Kobakhidze included not only opposition parties but also non-governmental organisations and media outlets as part of the “collective National Movement”:

“They are all in the same pot… All the radical opposition parties, all these radical NGOs, their radical media,” Kobakhidze said.

According to Georgian Dream’s current narrative, the political differences between these forces are not significant. The ruling party portrays them as different parts of a single network controlled from abroad. This logic brings together parties with different histories, leaders and political platforms under the “collective National Movement”.

The rhetoric has gradually acquired a specific political goal. In 2024, Kobakhidze compared removing the “collective National Movement” from the political system with banning the National Socialists in post-war Germany.

A year later, he said: “This crisis within the collective ‘National Movement’ must deepen, and it will deepen, ultimately leading to the complete destruction of the collective ‘National Movement’. Only then will Georgia develop a healthy democratic system.”

What does the attempt to ban the parties mean? Views

Representatives of the opposition parties themselves see the Georgian Dream lawsuit not as a separate legal dispute but as part of a broader process of restricting political competition.

Their main argument is that the government is using the courts to remove from the political arena forces that remain its electoral competitors.

Giorgi Sioridze, a representative of the Strong Georgia — Lelo alliance, points to the fact that the list of parties facing a ban has changed several times. He says that each new lawsuit restarts the nine-month period for considering the case.

He believes this allows the government both to retain the option of banning the parties and to delay a final decision.

Giga Lemondzhava, a representative of Coalition for Change, sees the party ban as a new stage in what he describes as authoritarian politics. However, he says political struggle cannot be ended simply by cancelling a party’s legal registration.

The National Movement takes a similar position. One of its leaders, Levan Khabeishvili, called on the opposition in a letter sent from prison not to focus entirely on the parties’ legal status: “Don’t get hung up on the issue of banning parties! They have banned the country!”

His message is that accepting the legal framework created by Georgian Dream would make the opposition dependent on an agenda set by the government. Political resistance, he argues, should not depend on a party’s registration.

The case of Giorgi Gakharia’s party is particularly notable. For Georgia took part in the 2024 election, later entered parliament and does not support violent struggle against the government. Given all this, the party’s MP Giorgi Sharashidze questions how the main constitutional grounds cited in the lawsuit apply to them:

“Unconstitutionality, calls for violence, calls to overthrow the government… What does any of that have to do with us? … We even entered parliament.”

Giorgi Gakharia, meanwhile, sees his party’s addition to the “blacklist” as part of a broader process. In his view, the authorities are trying to leave no functioning critical opposition within institutional politics:

“Regardless of whether they ban us or not, we will not back down in the struggle to restore Georgia’s democracy and protect its European and Euro-Atlantic path.”

The Federalists’ case exposes another contradiction. The party did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Its leaders previously belonged to former President Mikheil Saakashvili’s political team, but they have been in sharp conflict with both Saakashvili himself and the UNM, the party he founded, for many years. Despite this, the authorities also regard them as part of the “collective National Movement”.

Party leader Tamar Chergoleishvili says banning a political competitor is unacceptable to her regardless of her attitude towards that competitor:

“Of course, we see all the other parties as competitors, but we want to defeat our competitors on a level playing field, through fair competition, not as a result of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s bans.”

Georgian Dream explains the process very differently.

According to the authorities, the issue is not about eliminating political competitors but protecting the democratic system. Georgian Dream MP Levan Machavariani argues that opposition parties that appear different on the surface are actually parts of the same political network. He says dividing them into “radical”, “semi-radical” and relatively “constructive” forces is artificial and serves as a way for a common political centre to assign them different tasks.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze follows the same logic. He says the government promised voters to “neutralise foreign agents” and is now fulfilling that promise:

“We made a promise to voters that we would neutralise foreign agents in our country, and we are genuinely fulfilling that promise.”

Kobakhidze also uses this argument to explain the ban:

“It is very important that the state make a decision on this issue — a decision that serves the national interest.”

When can democracy ban a political party?

Europe has precedents for banning political parties, but authorities treat such bans as an extreme measure, usually in very different circumstances from those in Georgia. Banning five parties at once would be unprecedented.

Under the standards of the Venice Commission, authorities may justify dissolving a party if it uses violence or advocates overthrowing the democratic constitutional order. A peaceful call to change the political system or constitution does not, in itself, justify a ban.

European practice focuses not on how radical a party’s position is, but on whether its goals and actions pose a real threat to the democratic order and whether sufficient evidence supports that conclusion.

European case law also sets a high threshold. Spain banned Batasuna after authorities established its links to the ETA terrorist organisation. In Turkey, in the Refah Partisi case, the court considered evidence that the party sought to establish a theocratic system and had made statements linked to the use of force.

In Germany, meanwhile, authorities ultimately did not ban the NPD in 2017, even though the Constitutional Court found that the party’s goals were incompatible with the democratic order. However, the court concluded that the party lacked the real ability to achieve those goals.

What Europe says about Georgia’s case

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has taken a particularly strong position on Georgia.

Even before the 2024 election, a PACE monitoring delegation said Georgian Dream’s calls to ban the opposition threatened political pluralism.

In 2025, PACE described the planned ban as targeting “virtually the entire functioning democratic opposition” and said such a move would effectively create a one-party system in Georgia.

In June 2026, the Assembly made its position even clearer.

Resolution No. 2664 says the initiative to ban “virtually all democratic opposition parties” is unacceptable. It says implementing the initiative would effectively create a one-party dictatorship in Georgia, which would be incompatible with membership in the Council of Europe. The Assembly called on the authorities to withdraw the lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

The European Commission’s 2025 report also describes “serious democratic backsliding” in Georgia and says legislative and institutional changes threaten political pluralism. The report also notes that the ruling party has effectively consolidated control over the legislative and executive branches of government.

What happens if the parties are banned?

Banning the five parties could have consequences far beyond cancelling their names and legal registrations. The issue is what kind of political competition will remain in Georgia ahead of the next parliamentary election in 2028.

If the Constitutional Court upholds Georgian Dream’s lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the five per cent threshold in 2024 could disappear from the political arena. According to official Central Election Commission figures, nearly 800,000 people voted for them in total — about a quarter of all voters.

The current legislation also allows the authorities to extend restrictions to people linked to the banned parties. The court can prohibit them from establishing or joining other parties, standing as candidates in elections or holding political office. Authorities may also terminate the mandates of sitting elected MPs.

A new party name would not automatically provide a way around the ban. The law already includes the concept of a “successor party”. If a new political force substantially repeats the goals, activities or membership of a banned party, the court can ban it as well.

Under the Georgian Dream scenario, all of this could effectively leave the country without political parties or politicians representing the current opposition.

The process is not taking place in isolation. In recent years, the government has also adopted several laws that have sharply tightened the legal environment for foreign funding, grants and the activities of NGOs and media outlets.

Meanwhile, anti-government protests continue in Georgia, and the political confrontation between the authorities and their opponents remains highly tense.

The 2028 election is key to understanding the political significance of these developments. If the court upholds the lawsuit and the current restrictions remain in force, Georgia could enter the next parliamentary election with all four opposition forces that crossed the threshold in 2024 legally dissolved. The mechanism for quickly banning possible successor parties would already be in place.

Ban on opposition parties in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan’s corruption whistleblowers: protection on paper and in practice
World.content:
Azerbaijan drafts anti-corruption bill

Azerbaijan has drafted a separate bill aimed at encouraging and protecting people who report corruption. The bill was submitted to the Milli Majlis on 5 October and is due to be discussed by a parliamentary committee on 6 October.

The initiative comes amid continuing complaints that police officers demand money from citizens, while journalists investigating corruption are sentenced to lengthy prison terms. Existing legislation already provides protections for people who report corruption. The key question, therefore, is from whom – and how – the state intends to protect citizens after they report such cases.

Protection provided by law

Article 11-2 of the Law on Combating Corruption prohibits disclosing the identity of a person who reports corruption without their consent, as well as threatening them or their relatives. It also prohibits dismissing an employee because they have filed a complaint, transferring them to another position, making unlawful deductions from their salary or obstructing their career progression.

If an employee provides evidence that retaliatory measures have been taken against them, the burden of disproving the allegation falls on the employer. The law also prohibits assigning a complaint for review to the person against whom it was made or to anyone with an interest in the outcome of the investigation.

Information registered through an internal reporting procedure must be examined within 20 working days, after which the person who submitted it must be informed of the outcome. If a complaint concerns the head of an organisation, the person may approach a higher-ranking official or a specialised anti-corruption body. The obligation to investigate reports and inform complainants of the outcome therefore existed before the new bill was introduced.

However, a 2025 report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) points to significant gaps in the implementation of these safeguards. Azerbaijan has no specialised body, unit or official dedicated exclusively to protecting people who report corruption. The authorities were also unable to provide examples of the provision placing the burden on employers to disprove evidence of retaliation being applied in 2023-2024.

The report also notes that public disclosure through the media and social networks is not recognised as a protected channel for reporting corruption. This gap is particularly significant for people who report wrongdoing to journalists rather than to state bodies.

Alleged $300 bribe demand and claim of violence

On 28 August, Gündəlik Naxçıvan reported that a young driver had been detained. According to the outlet, police officers said the driver was under the influence of alcohol. He denied this and said he was willing to undergo a medical examination at a hospital.

Instead of being given a medical examination, he was allegedly asked to pay 500 manats (about $300):

“They told me: either you pay the money now, or they will take both you and the car away.”

According to the outlet, after the driver refused to pay, additional traffic police officers arrived at the scene. Five or six officers allegedly used force against him. Witnesses said the driver suffered a broken arm and ribs as a result.

The complaint therefore concerns not only an alleged demand for a bribe, but also claims that force was used instead of allowing the driver to undergo a medical examination and challenge the allegation against him.

Threats of drug possession and other criminal charges

On 10 September, Gündəlik Naxçıvan published another complaint from residents of Ordubad. People who had returned from Russia said they were taken from their homes and brought to a police station, where they were tested for drugs in a toilet without a doctor present.

One complainant, who asked to remain anonymous, said his test was negative but that he was nevertheless asked to pay 10,000 manats (about $5,882). He said that after being threatened with arrest and torture, he paid 5,000 manats (about $2,941).

Similar allegations have been made in the past. In a Toplum TV report published on 17 December 2025, Shiraz Guliyev, who had returned from Turkey, said he was asked to pay 300 manats (about $176.50) near the Sadarak customs checkpoint on the grounds that he had allegedly dropped a cigarette butt. Guliyev said he told officers that he did not smoke, but was threatened with arrest on charges of resisting police if he refused to pay.

In June 2025, blogger Mehman Huseynov alleged that officers from Baku’s Khatai district police station No 37 beat five teenagers and released them after receiving money from their parents.

Lawyer Khalid Bagirov told Meydan TV that the problem was not the absence of mechanisms for holding officers accountable, but that those mechanisms were not being effectively applied.

What do the official figures show?

The Main Anti-Corruption Directorate under the Prosecutor General’s Office said it reviewed 5,655 complaints in the first half of 2026. A total of 54 criminal cases involving 102 people were sent to court. Of the calls received through the “161” hotline, 4,062 were registered as reports of corruption-related offences.

The figures show that investigations are being carried out. However, the number of cases sent to court does not indicate how effectively people who report corruption are subsequently protected from pressure or retaliation.

This distinction is particularly important in cases involving complaints against the police. A person who complains about an officer with the power to detain them, take them to a police station and formally record offences is seeking more than the return of money. They also need guarantees that those powers will not be used against them in retaliation. Receiving a complaint and protecting the complainant are two separate tasks.

According to an OECD report assessing the situation in 2023-2024, Azerbaijan has made no significant overall progress in combating corruption since 2022. The system for declaring the assets and interests of public officials was not operational, while gaps also remained in declaration forms and procedures for their electronic submission and verification.

In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Azerbaijan scored 30 out of 100 and ranked 130th out of 182 countries. Despite an eight-point increase compared with the previous year, the score remains low in terms of perceived levels of public-sector corruption.

Arrests of journalists investigating corruption

The authorities’ pledge to protect those who report corruption also contrasts with the situation surrounding the Abzas Media case. On 20 June 2025, seven defendants in the case were sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven years and six months to nine years. They included journalists Ulvi Hasanli, Sevinj Vagifgizi and Hafiz Babali, who had investigated corruption.

The defendants rejected the charges against them. Reporters Without Borders described the sentences as the result of a politically motivated trial aimed at silencing those who expose corruption and injustice.

Against this backdrop, several questions arise: Is a person who reports an alleged demand for a bribe protected from retaliation? Is the alleged offence independently investigated, and are the findings made public? And can a journalist who exposes corruption continue their work without facing the threat of imprisonment?

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 8, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020 in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the twelvth day of the Second Karabakh war:

- the ministry of defense of Azerbaijan reported that the Armenian armed forces have been shelling the villages of Goranboy, Terter, and Aghdam regions since the early morning hours. There were killed and wounded. As a result of rocket attacks by the Armenian army in Ganja, several civilian objects, one car and residential buildings were damaged.

- a person who posed as a captured Azerbaijani on social media turned out to be an Armenian

- the ministry of defense of Azerbaijan has published video footage of armored vehicles taken as a trophy, which, while fleeing, were thrown in Horadiz by the Armenian military. Later, the defense ministry published another video footage of war trophies captured from the Armenian Armed Forces.

- Armenian armed forces fire at Azerbaijan’s Barda from 'Tochka-U' high-precision tactical missile system. Another rocket fired by the Armenian Armed Forces at Barda hit a restaurant and a school, injuring seven people. Armenia’s Grad missile launcher which attacked Azerbaijan’s Barda and Tartar destroyed.

- Azerbaijan's Ministry of Defense has published anothervideo footage of the destruction of enemy armored vehicles

- 10 shells fired by Armenians from Smerch MLRS were found in Goranboy.

World.title: Azerbaijani FM stresses importance of Middle Corridor, regional cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov stressed the importance of strengthening the Middle Corridor and regional cooperation, the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry said.

On October 7, Bayramov participated in and addressed a meeting of foreign ministers of the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan held in the Avaza National Tourism Zone in Turkmenistan as part of his working visit to the country.

Bayramov highlighted the importance of holding the meeting ahead of the high-level summit as an opportunity for preliminary discussions on key areas of cooperation.

He noted that Azerbaijan's admission last year as a full-fledged member of the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia demonstrated the deepening integration processes between the countries, based on historical and cultural ties, mutual trust and shared strategic interests.

Against the backdrop of growing global instability, geopolitical competition and disruptions in supply chains, the minister stressed the need to deepen regional cooperation to strengthen the economic and energy security of the countries.

In this context, he highlighted the importance of equal and trust-based political dialogue among the participants of the C6 format, as well as expanding trade and mutual investment.

Touching on cooperation in strategically important transport and energy sectors, Bayramov noted the growing role of the Middle Corridor in establishing sustainable connectivity between East and West and in international trade.

He also emphasized the importance of the developing strategic partnership among the countries in the production and transmission of green energy, as well as transport and digital connectivity projects, for fully realizing the region's potential.

The minister paid particular attention to the environmental agenda. He expressed serious concern over the consequences of climate change, problems related to the Aral Sea and water resources, as well as the sustained decline in the level of the Caspian Sea and its adverse impact on coastal infrastructure and the environment.

He stressed the importance of a systematic scientific approach, information exchange and regional cooperation in addressing these challenges.

In conclusion, Bayramov expressed confidence that the documents and agreements to be adopted following the meeting would provide clear guidance for long-term cooperation.

He reaffirmed Azerbaijan's readiness to actively contribute to strengthening the format and implementing its objectives.

World.title: Rural hospital welcomes first student midwives in more than a decade
World.content:
The central Queensland community of Biloela fought for years for the return of local birthing services after the town's birthing unit was shut down in 2022.

The birthing bypass meant expectant mothers were forced to travel to Rockhampton or Gladstone, more than 120 kilometres away, to give birth, with no midwives at the local hospital.

With maternity care back online as of last month, the town faces its next challenge: attracting and retaining the people who will keep it running.

Emma Rideout, 24, is a registered nurse who grew up in Biloela and is now training to be a midwife at the local hospital.

Emma Rideout is one of three midwifery students based in Biloela. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

Given the hospital's recent staffing struggles, Ms Rideout said working locally was not something she had thought would be possible.

"Midwifery was always something I'd had in the back of my mind that I thought I wanted to try one day. I never thought it would be possible to study [here] and not have to leave," she said.

Ms Rideout is one of three local midwifery students at Biloela. It is the first cohort to be based in the hospital in 13 years.

Emma Rideout is thrilled to progress her career into midwifery without leaving Biloela. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

She said it had already been a fulfilling experience.

"It has been really great to be a part of this team at such a special time … I think it's kind of like pioneering.

"Being born and raised in a rural community and then working at the hospital as a nurse, it's made it very certain for me that that's the kind of setting that I want to work in."

Level two maternity care opened at Biloela Hospital last month after four years on bypass. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Attracting workforce a 'challenge' for regional communities

Central Queensland Health chief executive Lisa Blackler said the viability of Biloela's maternity services relied on attracting and retaining midwives in the area.

She said attracting a workforce to the region was the lifeline that reopened the unit, and retaining it was crucial to keeping it operational.

Lisa Blackler says Biloela's maternity service hinges on having a workforce to staff it. (ABC News: Jasmine Hines)

"You have to have the workforce to deliver the service," Ms Blackler said.

"We have to accept that we will have a transient workforce, but it's how we build the pipeline and get a core sort of foundation of staff that do stay.

"I think if we can attract people like Emma … that is a really positive story … we've got to lean in when people show interest in extending their skills and abilities."

Speaking at a press conference in September to announce the return of birthing to Biloela, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said his government was committed to keeping maternity care online in regional hospitals.

"Queenslanders living in regional communities need to know that they matter, that they count for something, and that wherever it is safe to do so that we restore things and continue to deliver services close to where they live," he said.

Diane Tamariki had been a midwife for almost 30 years before accepting the job of midwifery unit manager in Biloela.

Diane Tamariki oversees the development of the midwifery students at the local hospital. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

She said she was drawn to the opportunity to develop a new model of care in the reopened service.

"It's really hard having to start something from scratch but it's also really rewarding being able to work with the community and help to deliver a service that is much needed."

Ms Tamariki has already laid roots in the community, coaching a netball team, meeting her partner and even buying a home, helping to convince her to stay for good.

"I want to see this grow and to be sustainable," she said.

" The medical workforce has really struggled [to get people in rural areas] and so this is a way of being able to support that but to provide a service to the community. "

Diane Tamariki has taken on coaching a local netball team and says she feels like she is part of the Biloela community. (Supplied: Central Queensland Health and Hospital Services)

While regional recruitment remains a major hurdle for rural health care across the country, Emma Rideout believes the town's rural charm is its greatest selling point.

"There's something really special about working in a rural hospital … you get to care for people in the hospital and then see them downtown and they might pull you up and recognise you," she said.

Emma Rideout says Biloela is a "great little town". (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

"I think it's just a great little town and obviously I am a bit biased being from here but … I would recommend it to anyone. Just come and see what you're missing," she said.

World.title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked protests dies
World.content:
The 87-year-old Spanish woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protest has died.

Maricarmen Abascal was hospitalised after she was evicted from the apartment she had lived in for seven decades.

She was expected to return home as soon as she was discharged, after accepting a deal with the company that owned her apartment.

"Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late," the Madrid Tenants' Union said.

"It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal."

Maricarmen Abascal was taken out of her home on a stretcher in the upscale Retiro neighborhood in Madrid. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Protesters who have been camped out in Madrid's iconic Sol square held a minute of silence after hearing news of her passing.

Her case has drawn tens of thousands of people to the streets in outrage and led the prime minister to call for early elections after failing to pass measures to address the country's housing crisis.

Nationwide housing protests erupt

Taken out of her home on a stretcher in the upscale Retiro neighborhood, Ms Abascal was greeted by protesters and supporters as she was loaded into an ambulance.

Trade unions on Wednesday announced a nationwide general strike over housing issues on November 11.

Housing protests erupt in Barcelona after Spain calls early election Spaniards have staged repeated protests in recent weeks to demand housing relief.

Those protests, along with parliament's rejection last week of decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an early election for November 29.

"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Sánchez said in a post on X.

"A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today."

The tenants' union said people were left with " the example of the fight she waged and the legacy Maricarmen has left behind".

"And, above all, we will honour what she always asked of us: 'Fight, keep fighting for what is yours," it said.

Angel Victor Torres, Spain's territorial policy minister, said Ms Abascal had become a symbol of what was happening to many families as elderly and young people struggled to stay in their homes.

World.title: CA 'actively' looking at women's schedule as Aussie stars raise concerns
World.content:
Cricket Australia (CA) says it will attempt to bring the national women's side back into the peak of summer, after officials met with frustrated senior players.

Multiple players have raised concerns over the women's schedule in recent weeks, which includes four straight years of no home internationals or WBBL during school holidays.

Ellyse Perry and Beth Mooney have also highlighted fears it will stunt the growth of junior cricket.

Australia plays Bangladesh and New Zealand in three one-day internationals (ODIs) and T20s respectively over the next fortnight.

A home ODI series against New Zealand is scheduled for March.

Concerns over summer gap for women's cricket Concerns are growing about the lack of women's cricket in school-friendly slots over summer, amid warnings the schedule will hurt the game's growth among girls.

Among the concerns of players is a lack of consistency in their schedule to build up crowds, along with games on school nights that families largely will not attend.

The issue was raised at a function on Monday night in Brisbane to recognise the Australian team's T20 World Cup win.

"We're looking at that actively," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"[Head of cricket] James Allsopp led the conversation with the Australian women's team about this exact issue, so we're talking, we've got dialogue with them.

"We would love to see more cricket played in this window. We have to understand the global components … but we've got to get more cricket into our summer."

Greenberg's comments come after Mooney was particularly critical of the current schedule.

"We're in a bad time slot and it's a bad time of year for parents," Mooney said earlier this week.

"They're not dragging their kid out to watch a 7pm T20 on a Tuesday night or whatever it is.

"We're not getting crowds, it's not marketed well. There is no big-ticket item where people go, 'the Australian women's team play here at this time every year'.

"We want to be relatable athletes. And if we're not front and centre of the summer, it makes it pretty difficult when it's meant to be a summer sport."

AAP

The Australian-led climate talks in the Pacific will wrap up today, with a push to double the number of homes globally and rooftop solar the main item on the agenda.

After four days of discussions, pre-COP is drawing to a close and there's been a mixed response to the event.

Pacific communities and leaders have welcomed the opportunity to shine a spotlight on their fight against climate change. They've also attracted funding to better adapt to rising seas and more extreme weather events.

But the Albanese government has been criticised for spending $20 million on the event and failing to attract many world leaders.

Only two of the 14 who turned up hailed from outside of the Pacific.

Today's focus will be the launch of a global plan to double the number of homes with rooftop solar to 300 million by the end of the decade. The Australian government will be asked to sign up to the pledge.

World.title: Small SA town's 'out of control' pigeon population
World.content:
Walking down the main street of Pinnaroo in South Australia's Murray Mallee, you may have to watch where you step.

With distant coos of pigeons perched on the ledges of the town's historic buildings, you can see the streets have a few unwelcome guests.

Pigeon excrement has been one of the town's biggest concerns due to safety and hygiene. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

From birds creating drinking water issues at the local primary school to local businesses spending hundreds of dollars a week cleaning their machinery, many say more needs to be done to address the problem.

Hundreds spent on cleaning

For third-generation business owner Roydn Bailey, the pigeon problem is not new, but now it is getting "out of control".

Roydn Bailey says the pigeons have been a problem for 15 to 20 years. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

He estimated his business spent hundreds of dollars a week washing pigeon excrement off his company's machinery.

"We try and park our machines between the rafters to limit the amount of droppings onto our machines because it damages the paint," he said.

Roydn Bailey's machinery shed is filled with pigeon feathers and excrement. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"[The droppings] block our gutters up, which then creates a big problem when we get downpours with water coming in through the roof."

Mr Bailey believed having two grain silos at either end of the township made it the ideal food source for the birds.

Todd Dooley has lived in the area for four years and recalls it being an issue from day one. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

A few metres down the road, Todd Dooley runs the local post office and said you can "hear and see them all the time".

Mr Dooley's child also attends the local primary school and said the pigeons have gotten so bad in recent years that the education department had to step in.

Pigeons congregate on powerlines near the local primary school. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"I know they were shipping in drinking water for the kids for the last couple of years because of the damage done to the tanks, pipes and drinking fountains," he said.

An education department spokesperson confirmed the school relied on rainwater tanks for drinking water and had supplied drinking water to the school on two occasions.

"[Water was supplied] last year while the tanks were temporarily disconnected from the rainwater system as a precaution to ensure they were not affected by contamination from impacted gutters," the department said.

"The department has been working with the school to address issues associated with pigeons and ensure its drinking water supply remains safe and available."

Bird-proofing and pressure cleaning were undertaken at the school in April 2025, while water tanks were replaced this year. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

The department said there was no ongoing weekly pressure washing of the school grounds and the school was "not currently" having drinking water trucked in.

Pest explained

Feral pigeons are descendants of domestic homing pigeons that were introduced to Australia from Europe, making them creatures of habit.

Adelaide Pigeon Control owner John Rohal said the species bred extremely fast.

"It may start with just two pigeons on the roof that you don't seem to mind, but they can breed up to nine times a year, and before you know it, you've got 12 up there," he said.

John Rohal says shooting and trapping are the most effective ways to control pest populations. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

" The amount of damage 12 birds in six months can ruin a house. "

Mr Rohal said eradication was the most effective way to address pest populations.

"I would say your two most effective methods would be shooting and trapping as deterrents don't really work," he said.

John Rohal says feral pigeons form generational habits, meaning they return to the same locations. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"I've gone to places where I've only eradicated five out of 20, and the other 15 have bailed and never returned."

Eradication efforts

Southern Mallee Council chief executive Jason Beaton has been organising eradication efforts via a contractor for the past 18 months.

With harvest around the corner, he said the council was prioritising culling to get on top of the issue.

"It's very effective to start with … but then they do come back, so it's going to be a real ongoing process for us," Mr Beaton said

Residents and the local council say the birds have been a major issue, including damaging solar panels. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"It's the public amenity we're worried about; there's real pride in this community, so to have pigeons hanging around and defecating on your public parks and buildings, that is our biggest impact."

When asked whether the state government has been notified about the ongoing issue, he said it was a council problem they would fix on their own.

Jason Beaton says the eradication efforts will be an ongoing process. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"This has been a localised issue that, as the Southern Mallee people do, we solve our own problems," he said.

World.title: New armed police unit unveiled after Bondi terror attack
World.content:
The NSW Police's specialist Armed Response Command (ARC) will begin taking to the streets of Sydney, 10 months after the Bondi Beach terror attack that sparked its formation.

The ARC's highly-trained armed officers are moving to a phase of public training after months of work behind closed doors at dedicated training facilities.

Officers with long-armed rifles are expected to be seen around city in the coming days ahead of the rapid response unit's formal start date, when 250 officers will be tasked around the clock.

The unit is expected to take over the high-visibility patrols of Operation Shelter, which was ramped up after 15 people were killed during a Jewish holiday celebration at Bondi Beach in December.

'NSW Police are ready'

The NSW government invested $94 million to form the unit as part of a response to the terror attack, which has gone toward rifles, training and specially-built vehicles for the ARC.

After the Islamic State-inspired attack, senior members of the NSW Police travelled to the UK and Germany as part of preparations for the ARC.

The new unit was part of the government's $94 million promise to the NSW Police after the Bondi terror attack. (Supplied: NSW Police)

"Keeping the people of New South Wales safe is our number one priority. That means making sure our police have the people, training and equipment they need to respond to serious threats," NSW Premier Chris Minns said.

"We hope these officers are never called on to respond to a major incident. But if one happens, NSW Police are ready.

"People will start seeing these officers and their vehicles around Sydney as training gets underway. This is about being prepared for the worst and making sure we can keep the community safe."

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said the new unit would be a deterrent to anyone inciting hatred.

"ARC will not only provide a policing rapid response, but it will also be a deterrent for those who wish to commit harm, incite hatred or cause fear.

"No matter where you are located across Sydney, we want all communities to feel reassured that police can be anywhere, at anytime, to keep people safe.

When it officially begins work, the unit will have 250 officers in its ranks. (Supplied: NSW Police)

"The environment in NSW has changed, so the way we police the community has changed and what the community expect from us, has changed."

The unit was part of sweeping reforms promised by the state government in the days after the Bondi Beach terror attack.

The federal government, similarly, proposed legislative changes that culminated in laws prohibiting hate groups.

The ARC will take over from Operation Shelter, which formed in 2023 to respond to an increase in antisemitic and Islamophobic incidents and has been responsible for patrols in the wake of the December 2025 tragedy.

World.title: Aussies hit back at ex-players in build-up to first South Africa Test
World.content:
Travis Head has accused former Australian players of levelling unfair criticism at the current Test squad, saying the game has changed significantly since they played.

Just a day after Matthew Hayden slammed selectors and accused them of promoting "the greatest pile of mediocrity" for calling up Nic Maddinson, Head took his own stand in South Africa.

Australia's vice-captain refused to name particular ex-players or comments, but took issue with commentary about the team's batting at a time when averages have dropped worldwide.

Stats show Test runs drying up Test batters are averaging less, scoring more quickly and getting out more often — and we have the charts to prove it.

Head noted the current side had been through a "sticky situation" with the group of past players, in a clear nod to Justin Langer's dramatic exit as coach in 2022.

"I think [we're] unfairly judged a fair bit from a group of past players … that put the bullet through a lot of players," he said ahead of the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

"But that's what they're paid to do. Some of them need a job, so they go after us, and that's totally fine.

"This group is strong enough to deal with those sort of things. That's how it is.

"It's unfortunate, sometimes, to have some of that feedback from a generation of players that we have huge respect for, but that's the caper."

The suggestion of a generational split between Australia's two best eras of the past 50 years has long bubbled away.

This was particularly the case following Langer's exit after his side's 2021/22 Ashes win, when he rejected a contract offer of only six months.

"They're [ex-players] a very proud bunch of guys," Head said.

"We went through a bit of a sticky situation a few years ago where they stood up and were pretty proud about one of their own (Langer).

"But in saying that …we play for the same cause. We have huge respect for it.

How Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket In 2018, Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket to its very core. Here's how a febrile atmosphere colluded with a team persistently testing the limits of acceptability to change the game.

"It's always a balancing act with … what they say and how you take it."

Test batting averages have dropped by close to 20 per cent from the end of the 2010s, while the Sheffield Shield has witnessed a similar downturn since the mid-2000s.

While critics have pointed to the drop in averages coinciding with the rise of T20 cricket, Head pointed to conditions as a major factor.

"It's pretty obvious to see what the wickets were like back then to now," Head said.

"We have huge respect for what's come before us, but it's a completely different game.

"Sometimes it's commented around unfairly on some of the wickets that teams have played on, whether that be Sheffield Shield or Test cricket.

"We've seen games go quicker than ever. We've got a lot of stats that suggest that the ball's doing a lot more."

AAP

World.title: 'Landmark' child safety racial discrimination class actions to be discontinued
World.content:
A class action accusing Queensland's child safety department of discriminating against First Nations families is set to be discontinued in the federal court after losing funding.

A grandmother who signed up to the class action says she has been once again let down by a failing system.

Cindy – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – said she and her family revisited a traumatic period of their history when they joined the lawsuit in late 2023.

Queensland grandmother Cindy says her grandchildren were removed from her care in an act of discrimination by the state's child safety department. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

The grandmother had hoped for accountability.

"It wasn't really about the payout. It was about how child safety treated me as a grandmother," she said.

Landmark lawsuit filed in five Australian states, alleging 'modern Stolen Generation' Cassie is one of hundreds of claimants to 

She says Queensland's Child Safety Department discriminated against her by not only removing her grandchildren from her care after she followed protocol, but each time she was blocked from getting them back.

"I sat in the gutter and I cried for my kid," she said of the night they were taken.

"They want us to fail as grandmothers, as carers. They want us to fail all the time."

Cindy says it was traumatic to revisit parts of her family's history when they decided to sign up to the class action. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

In Queensland, two separate class actions had been spearheaded by Brett Harold Gunning and Madison May Burns.

The lawsuits claimed Indigenous families were stripped of their cultural identity after children were removed and placed into the system in the care of predominantly white families.

They had been seeking an apology as well as compensation.

Two separate lawsuits were launched in the Federal Court against the Queensland government in 2023. (ABC News: Rachel Riga)

'Draining and stressful'

Cindy is disappointed and angry at the way the case has been handled, including what she believes to have been a lack of communication.

The last update Cindy could find had been sent to her family in September last year, advising them the litigation funder, Therium Capital Management, had "decided it no longer wanted to continue" to fund the case.

Therium Capital Management was contacted for comment.

The case had initially been handled by Bottoms English Lawyers, but changed hands when the solicitor moved firms last year.

A website directing people to sign up to the Queensland class actions remained active in early September. (Supplied)

In his orders, Justice Craig Dowling noted the current firm handling the case, WGC Lawyers, had made "significant attempts" to secure alternative funding.

WGC Lawyers declined to comment when contacted, saying the matter remained before the court.

Both parties have been ordered to draft a notice addressed to the group members to explain the discontinuance has been approved by the court and the reasons for it.

"A failure to provide notice of the discontinuance of proceedings ... has the potential to give rise to further concerns of institutional neglect," Justice Dowling wrote.

The class action alleged widespread racial discrimination by child safety departments against First Nations families. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Interstate, plans for similar actions being spearheaded by a different law firm, Shine Lawyers, remain afoot.

Special counsel Caitlin Wilson said claims had been filed in both Western Australia and New South Wales, while investigations in South Australia and Victoria continued.

The purpose of those actions was not only compensation, but accountability and reform.

"You can't tuck a class action away in a drawer after it's been filed," Ms Wilson said.

" It has to be dealt with. "

Ms Wilson said Shine would consider looking at Queensland again once these proceedings had completely closed.

Shine Lawyers special counsel Caitlin Wilson said similar lawsuits were underway interstate. (ABC News: Edward Gill)

Cindy is not sure she has the strength to go through the process again, even if an action was to be relaunched.

"It is draining and stressful and it's heartbreaking when we've got to tell our stories all the time when nothing is being ... done," she said.

Ms Wilson said she understood group members may not want to be involved in any future action.

"It seems to be a series of unfortunate events that have led to this – but that doesn't mean that there's not a claim to be had," she said.

"It doesn't mean that this isn't a national issue and it doesn't mean that we won't be looking at it again."

Racism an ongoing issue in child safety

Advocates agree there continues to be a need for accountability.

Catherine Liddle is the chief executive of SNAICC – National Voice for Our Children. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

According to SNAICC's most recent Family Matters report and data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are more than nine times more likely to be in out-of-home care or on permanent orders than their non-Indigenous counterparts.

Chief executive Catherine Liddle described those numbers as a "gross" over-representation.

"The fact that people are considering class actions shows how serious it is and how desperate people are to get a change in how governments are treating Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children," she said.

Ms Liddle said children who were removed from the care of their parents often dealt with "serious, lifelong consequences" including difficulty accessing healthcare, education and employment.

A spokesperson for Queensland's Department of Child Safety said it was committed to improving outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families and reducing their over-representation in the child protection system.

They said that included having accepted recommendations to strengthen support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community-controlled organisations that deliver targeted intervention and family support services, as well as working to deliver on Closing the Gap commitments.

Housing Minister Clare O’Neil has defended the government’s credit charge surcharge ban, following an outcry from business groups over the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) decision to scrap credit cards as a payment method.

Housing Minister Clare O’Neil. Alex Ellinghausen

“We have a simple principle, and that is that you should not be charged to use your own money, and that’s a good thing for Australians,” she told Today this morning, but said the government had “real concerns” about the ATO’s proposal.

“Small businesses across the country really struggle to manage their cash flow … and using credit cards to pay tax bill is a way that a lot of people are just managing that issue.”

She said the surcharge changes were still working through the system and were “going to take a little bit of time and finessing”.

World.title: Lawyers reveal Christa Pike’s first words after she woke from botched execution
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty Lawyers reveal Christa Pike’s first words after she woke from botched execution Michael Koziol October 8, 2026 — 6:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Death row inmate Christa Pike was believed to be “brain-dead” and hours from having her life support switched off when she woke up unexpectedly and asked where she was, her lawyers said, as a court ordered Tennessee to preserve all material related to her botched execution. Randy Spivey, her attorney, said the convicted murderer was “angry and confused”, and had massively swollen hands, a blood clot in one arm and pneumonia. She was also unable to swallow and had not eaten. Loading Pike, 50, survived two supposedly fatal injections in Tennessee last week, 30 years after she was sentenced to death for brutally torturing and murdering her classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when she was 18. The case has shocked the world and raised significant questions about the death penalty in the US – along with uncertainty about whether the state of Tennessee will try to execute her again.



A court on Wednesday (US time) ordered the state to preserve and maintain all medical equipment, records and communications relating to the failed execution – with further decisions to come about Pike’s access to a tablet, and whether she should be unshackled from the bed. Speaking to reporters after the court hearing, Spivey revealed Pike had been unresponsive and presumed brain-dead the night before she suddenly regained consciousness and began talking. Christa Pike’s attorneys Luke Ihnen (speaking) and Randy Spivey, left, at a news conference in Nashville on Wednesday. AP Photo/George Walker IV “On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day,” he said. “But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone – including me, including her team, and including the medical team – Christa woke up and began talking.”



Spivey was not in the room when Pike woke up. “Our understanding is the first thing she said was, ‘Where am I and who are you?’,” he said. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty How Christa Pike’s botched Tennessee execution unfolded, minute by minute “She has wanted to know what has happened, and she has asked about several people – she has asked about her team, she has asked about the victim’s family.” Pike was aware of the attempted execution, though was suffering a lot of “cognitive confusion”, Spivey said. “I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.” The attorney said his client faced a long road to recovery. She could not move either of her arms, and doctors did not know if they would regain function.



“The swelling is what I noticed. Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove. The swelling was extraordinary … That’s probably as far as I can go.” Tennessee has temporarily paused executions following the botched attempt to kill Pike. The state has not said whether it would attempt to seek her execution again, though Spivey described the idea as “unimaginable”. Pike’s case is unprecedented, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, a nonprofit organisation that critiques problems with the implementation of capital punishment. Although seven Americans previously survived execution attempts, no drugs were administered in those cases, the centre said. The Pike case is Tennessee’s second failed execution in less than five months, after it abandoned the execution of convicted murderer Tony Carruthers in May. In that case, officials could not establish a proper IV line. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Catholic schools knock back IVF leave in new workplace offer
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandSchools Catholic schools knock back IVF leave in new workplace offer Catherine Strohfeldt October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland’s Catholic schools are ignoring union demands for a generous reproductive leave policy that would put private school teachers on equal footing with their state sector colleagues. The Independent Education Union began championing reproductive leave entitlements for private schools across the country after Queensland’s public sector was awarded 10 days of reproductive health leave in September 2024. Under a fresh wage offer released on Thursday, teachers and non-teaching staff at hundreds of Catholic schools – including All Hallows’, St Joseph’s Gregory Terrace and Marist College Ashgrove – would be entitled to up to five days of reproductive leave annually, with strict caveats. Queensland’s Catholic schools and the teachers’ union are at odds over reproductive leave allowances. Louise Kennerley An employee would need to suffer from “chronic symptoms” of one of eight approved reproductive health conditions or medical procedures, including endometriosis, polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), menopause, or if undergoing a hysterectomy.



The leave would also only be accessible to staff members who had fewer than 10 days of personal leave remaining. In state schools, teachers and non-teaching staff can access their 10-day entitlement for circumstances spanning four categories: chronic conditions, fertility treatments, including IVF, preventative screenings, and treatments such as vasectomies or hysterectomies. Eligible conditions and procedures for reproductive leave under Queensland Catholic schools’ proposed EBA Endometriosis

Adenomyosis

Dysmenorrhea

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)

Hysterectomy

Menopause

Perimenopause

Prostate disease In a statement to a federal review last year, the union said workplace protections for reproductive health, including IVF, were essential. “Lack of support in this area contributes to gender inequality, economic disadvantage, and workplace discrimination,” it said. The Catholic Archdiocese of Brisbane, like other Catholic bodies around the world, opposes assisted reproductive technology treatments, including IVF.



It also works with the Australian Catholic University’s Queensland Bioethics Centre, which provides advice on bioethical issues, including reproductive technologies, end-of-life treatments, and cloning. Related Article Teaching We looked at staff salaries at Brisbane’s private schools. These pay the most Catholic Education Queensland chief executive Allan Blagaich said school staff were informed of its position throughout the bargaining experience, which began in late 2025. “Employers have been guided by negotiating an outcome that is fair and reasonable for employees and that values their important contributions, while keeping Catholic education sustainable and accessible for families,” Blagaich said. Union officials were unimpressed with the offer, which they said skipped workload issues raised by staff and would, in some instances, worsen workplace conditions.



Logan Flexi School teacher Alex Patten, who is also an executive in the Independent Education Union’s Queensland branch, said the offer would leave non-teaching staff paid up to 25 per cent less than their NSW counterparts by the end of the deal. Brisbane teacher Sam McKinnon also said the offer was unfair. Logan teacher Alex Patten (left) and Brisbane teacher Sam McKinnon (right). “It cuts existing conditions, it ignores most of what staff asked for, and it’s being put to a vote without in-principle agreement at the bargaining table,” she said. The schools’ deal promised backpay to the last deal’s expiration in June if an agreement is reached before the end of the month, with the voting window closing on October 29.



Some 25,000 teaching and non-teaching staff members in Queensland will be covered by the collective agreement. They are employed within five diocesan zones and non-systemic Catholic schools, including those in Catholic education bodies such as Marist Schools Australia and Edmund Rice Education Australia.
