World.title: This musical is so good, someone saw it 327 times. Now it’s coming to Australia
World.content:
CultureMusicalsComedy This musical is so good, someone saw it 327 times. Now it’s coming to Australia Nell Geraets October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A dressed-up corpse, fake love letters, trout and Ian Fleming. This more or less sums up one of the most bonkers secret missions in history, known as “Operation Mincemeat”. Naturally, a story this absurd can only be told one way: through song, dance and a pinch of glittery fake blood. The musical Operation Mincemeat, based on that same mission, tells the story of how a group of oddball British agents used a homeless man’s corpse to wrong-foot Adolf Hitler. Operation Mincemeat is the epitome of “stranger than fiction”. Matt Crockett The production – written and composed by British theatre group SpitLip, which is often hailed as the “new Monty Python” – has taken both the West End and Broadway by storm, and sold more than 1 million tickets worldwide. And it’s coming to Australia in 2027. The story begins in 1943. The Allies were on the brink of defeat, so they hatched a plan to dress the body of Welshman Glyndwr Michael, who died after ingesting rat poison, as a British officer and drop him off the coast of Spain, an area rife with Nazi spies. The body was paired with a briefcase filled with various documents corroborating his fake identity, as well as “top-secret plans” that indicated the Allies intended to invade Europe via Sardinia instead of their actual entry point, Sicily. Against all odds, the madcap mission worked, redirecting the Nazis, saving countless lives on both sides and helping to turn the tide of World War II.



Operation Mincemeat takes this scarcely believable true story and transforms it into a fast-paced musical romp through history, delivering Nazi boy band pop songs, a Rocky Horror-esque coroner, and more dialogue about newts’ anuses than you’d ever expect in a World War II tale. As if that weren’t already enough to make your head spin, the 80-plus characters are played by just five actors. “People who’ve been through the British education system had World War II browbeaten into us every day of the year,” says David Cumming, SpitLip’s co-artistic director. “Even in maths, it was like, ‘Two plus Nazi is what?’ But for some reason, we weren’t taught this story. So, we knew it had an interest for the public in that sense, and an interest for us. It’s just such a wild caper. We fell in love with it.” Loading Despite its strangeness (or perhaps because of it) Operation Mincemeat has blown away both the West End – where the show’s run was extended a record 19 times – and Broadway, boasting more than 180 five-star reviews and winning both Tony and Olivier awards. It’s even said that some MI5 and MI6 agents have seen the show and approved. Many of the show’s fans, who call themselves “Mincefluencers”, have seen the show dozens of times, with some attempting to complete “cast bingo” sheets by seeing every combination of main cast members and understudies. One super Mincefluencer has seen the show a whopping 327 times.



“We weren’t really prepared for how much our incredible fan base was going to care about these people,” says Zoë Roberts, SpitLip’s co-artistic director, who adds that she can’t get enough of seeing fans dressed up as the campy death-obsessed coroner Spilsbury. These fans, of which there are thousands across the globe, gather on the Discord app to launch their own “missions”, such as “Operation Charming Man”, which convinced Colin Firth (who starred in the 2021 Operation Mincemeat film) to see the musical, and “Operation Preview One”, in which 300 Mincefluencers serenaded the Broadway cast, complete with an orchestra, at stage door after their first preview. The fans even launched an all-out investigation into the real identity of Hester Leggatt, a favourite of fans, whose wartime role was largely unknown before Operation Mincemeat. This fast-paced musical romp through history will soon tour across four continents. Matt Crockett The musical’s dedicated fan base, paired with its incredibly clever script and absurd source material, meant Operation Mincemeat went from a low-budget fringe production in a 77-seat theatre to a global phenomenon. Next year, the musical will commence a national tour in Australia, beginning in Melbourne in September as part of its world tour. Further Australian cities are yet to be announced. The world tour also includes dates in North America, China, New Zealand and Mexico. The search for the Australian cast will start early next year.



Preposterousness alone can’t get a musical to such heights, however. Among the silliness is a healthy dose of heart. The musical has been applauded for its thoughtful acknowledgement of largely unknown or forgotten people who made a huge difference in World War II: namely Glyndwr Michael. “We had this question mark around how we honour the man at the heart of it, the homeless man whose body it was,” says Natasha Hodgson, another co-artistic director of SpitLip. It wasn’t until the pandemic, when the group saw first-hand what it was like to feel so small in the face of insurmountable terror, that the ending came together. The role of Hester Leggatt, a fan-favourite character in Operation Mincemeat, won Jak Malone a Tony Award in 2025. Matt Crockett “We were like, no matter what, that has to be the thing that lingers when the curtain goes down. These contributions cannot be allowed to be forgotten,” Hodgson says. The musical has also been lauded as “quietly queer” thanks to its gender-blind casting, as well as feminist due to its emphasis on the unsung female heroes.



“The straight dads come for the war, and everyone else comes for the gender swapping,” director Robert Hastie says. “There’s something in this show that quietly offers people a way of facing a world that may define them in ways they’re uncomfortable with. It says: ‘You can defy expectations and label [yourself] as confidently and happily as this show does’.” Related Article Arts Culture wars and a swing to the right: A new take on Gone With the Wind is coming As for Ian Fleming, how does he factor into all this? The James Bond author was an officer in the Royal Navy’s Naval Intelligence Department, and he helped write the “Trout Memo”, which included the very deception “Operation Mincemeat” put into action. According to this document, the deception of an enemy in wartime was comparable to fly-fishing for trout. This mission helped win the Allies the war and thus changed the course of history. Given that, you’d expect a musical about it to be of similar proportions and earnestness as Les Misérables, Hastie says. It couldn’t be further from that. “It’s being told by these five miscast idiots,” he says. “You’re willing them to succeed against all odds, both on stage and in the story. It ought to be very serious, but it’s very, very silly … And then it pulls the rug out from under you again in making you care.”

World.title: The crumbling empire of a builder gone broke turned child safety millionaire
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandChild safety The crumbling empire of a builder gone broke turned child safety millionaire Julius Dennis October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Decades before the company he founded was thrust into the public eye after a child alleged she had been raped by a carer, Levi Te Namu left more than 70 creditors in the lurch overseas before moving to Australia to build his empire. The jet-setting chief executive’s lavish lifestyle was funded by millions in Queensland government contracts for his residential care business, Lighthouse Child and Family Services, which shared investors with another provider singled out by the state for profiteering. The rape allegation, made by a girl with an intellectual disability, turned a spotlight on the company and the debate about who should run, and profit, from the state’s struggling child safety system. Levi Te Namu’s business has drawn the Queensland government’s ire. Lighthouse Child & Family Services / @tenamulevi / Marija Ercegovac Child safety has become a hot-button political issue after the number of children in Queensland residential care soared from 650 at the end of 2015 to more than 2800 by March this year.



As that number swelled, so did the state’s financial burden. In 2025, the government spent $1.12 billion on residential care services – five times what it spent in 2015. And there was no shortage of businesses on hand to profit. Among them was Te Namu’s Lighthouse, which quickly became one of the biggest companies of its kind after launching in 2022. Levi Te Namu’s company left several businesses in Mount Maunganui, on New Zealand’s Tauranga Harbour, in the lurch. 7Michael But before he made millions from Queensland’s child safety system, Te Namu was a builder in New Zealand’s regional North Island city of Tauranga, where he operated a company with his future wife’s family. Compared to his Australian-based business, Miden Construction was a small operation, with just a few builds on the go when the global financial crisis hit.



In 2008, just four years after Te Namu had bought it, the company went under, owing more than $500,000 to various contractors and suppliers and leaving four houses unfinished. While most of those companies have either gone under themselves or been sold, this masthead has spoken to several people who were owed money by Te Namu, with one recalling he disappeared, leaving them to deal with liquidators. Of the $509,600 owed to creditors, just $93,000 was clawed back. Of that, $65,000 was spent on liquidators’ fees. Te Namu did not answer direct questions about Miden Construction. Almost 20 years later, he was winning lucrative state contracts to look after Queensland’s most vulnerable children.



Te Namu started Lighthouse while working for the not-for-profit Uniting Care with his now business partner Joshua Hillman. Josh Hillman’s image on the Lighthouse website includes a watermark suggesting it was created with AI. Lighthouse Child and Family Services To kickstart the business, the pair turned to Micheal Zarafa and Dominic Porter – the high-flying businessmen behind controversial residential care service All Care Australia – for seed money. A Melbourne nightclub operator, Porter’s internet footprint is a mix of party boy and proud dad. In one shot, he’s partying with rapper Travis Scott. In the next, he’s wearing matching Christmas Grinch shirts with his wife and kids.



Porter made headlines when armed criminals broke into his home and shot at him, a month after his bar in Melbourne’s ritzy South Yarra was firebombed during the city’s “bar wars” earlier this year. Zarafa and his wife, Vedrana Zarafa, were major funders of R&B festival Souled Out, which had Jhene Aiko and Vince Staples lined up for its 2025 shows in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane before it was cancelled a week before the event. The Porters with international R&B star Ne-Yo (centre). Instagram/@dominicrporter_ Porter’s wife, Kaitlyn Porter, was also a shareholder in the company behind the festival, and the sole shareholder and director of the company that invested in Lighthouse, D Porter Investments. Once Lighthouse was up and running, Te Namu’s Instagram page began to look something like Porter’s – Disneyland, New York, Japan, cruises, and various fast cars occupied his grid.



And the two were becoming closer in business too, with Te Namu and wife Jessica investing in the South Yarra club The Albion, run by Porter. By late 2024, Lighthouse and All Care Australia were two of the largest residential care providers in south-east Queensland, with Porter telling CEO Magazine that ACA had more than 1000 employees across the country. Levi Te Namu and his family frequently spend time overseas. Instagram/@tenamulevi Then the winds changed. In May 2025, while announcing a $20 million commission of inquiry into the child safety system, the Queensland government said it was auditing one residential care provider that had paid out $5.25 million to three shareholders the previous year. “This same organisation receives tens of millions of dollars from the state government to run residential care services, with financial statements also revealing they increased their management fees by 1000 per cent,” it said in a statement.



Porter told this masthead ACA was that service provider, and that the company stopped receiving referrals from the government around the same time, but he did not respond directly to questions about the fee increase. In opposition, the LNP promised to shake up residential care models. Now in government, it is moving away from individualised placement and support, usually delivered through for-profit providers like ACA, to outsourced delivery contracts, usually using not-for-profit providers, which they claim give children better stability. Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm has been under intense public scrutiny. William Davis However, Porter said he thought Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm was using businesses like ACA to avoid accountability for the state of the system. “I believe for-profit providers have been scapegoated to distract from the government’s own expenditure across the residential care system, particularly expenditure involving the not-for-profit sector,” he said.



Porter said the government pulling away from companies like ACA led to reports of children sleeping on the floor of child safety offices when there was nowhere appropriate for them to go. “My view is that Amanda Camm’s narrative has been misleading, hypocritical, and extraordinarily incompetent,” he said. Camm was on leave when this masthead sent questions to her. Acting minister Ros Bates said the government was fixing a broken system and “mov[ing] away from unlicensed residential care providers that exploded under Labor”. Te Namu and Hillman bought ACA in December 2025, after it had been audited and singled out by the government. Paperwork lodged with ASIC showed Lighthouse could have accessed $24 million in loans to help buy the business and residential care homes it owned.



Te Namu would not say how much money had been borrowed by the company, and said the repayments were commercial-in-confidence. Related Article Child safety ‘Heinous’: Ministers defend reforms after revelation of alleged rape of girl in residential care In February, ACA was transferred to another company owned by Te Namu and Hillman, called Best Life Group. The ACA website has since been taken down, and Te Namu said he had no plans to revive it. He said ACA was still servicing some children when the company changed hands, but he was now focused on Lighthouse. An email seen by this masthead showed the police investigation into the rape allegation ended when the girl involved did not want to provide a formal statement and withdrew the complaint, and Te Namu said the man involved no longer worked at Lighthouse.



Meanwhile, workers at other agencies have told this masthead that large numbers of children in state care are being moved out of Lighthouse residential homes. On October 5, Te Namu said the organisation was caring for 12 children, after operating 41 houses at its peak. He said case referrals to Lighthouse had slowed before the rape allegation. In Queensland, providers can operate without a licence, but must comply with minimum standards. Te Namu said the company had been fighting to get a residential care licence since April, and a decision from the department was delayed from July to October. Te Namu said the rape allegation was disclosed on August 21, before it was reported in the media on August 26. “On 26 August, the department confirmed that the application remained under the licensing delegate’s consideration. It refused the application on 1 September, 2026,” Te Namu said.



A department spokesperson said Lighthouse was considered unsuitable for a licence under the Child Protection Act. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: There is a world where art and sport are discrete – but that’s not Melbourne
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Opinion There is a world where art and sport are discrete – but that’s not Melbourne Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic October 8, 2026 — 6:00am

October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

The longer I’ve thought about it, the more convinced I’ve become that Melbourne’s secret is that it’s integrated. Ours is not a city of discrete neighbourhoods like New York. Not really, anyway. It’s not a city of enclaves and subcultures – “villages”, says Eddie McGuire – like Sydney. It’s not that Melbourne is undifferentiated. It’s highly varied. But it’s that the borders between these variations are subtle and fuzzy. More matters of degree than essence. Probably nowhere is that truer than in sport and the arts, which we will talk about at The Age’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum later this month. There’s a world, perhaps most of the world, where these things are discrete: different concepts appealing to different cohorts, some dwelling in the overlap, many not. In Melbourne, much more dwells there. The Melbourne Football Club has a fan who plays trumpet in the stands, who sometimes can’t make it to games because he has to play with the MSO. If you run an art gallery, no one will blink if you are a passionate Essendon supporter. Bulldogs, maybe. Melbourne sports magnate Eddie McGuire wants to see the railway yards separating the MCG from Melbourne and Olympic Parks covered. Jason South That’s a rarer gift than we know. In Sydney, for instance, even sport alone is stratified. You follow union or league, or neither. But none can be a lingua franca. Tell me what you love and I’ll have a fair chance of guessing which school you went to. That’s not without its benefits: each code has its particularities, its own bespoke culture. But in Melbourne, sport and art mingle seamlessly as participants in a common social drama. They are neither mere sport nor mere art. They are culture itself.



Culture is a rich concept. It is not the same thing as a collection of events. It’s not the sum of its economic parts. It’s more the mysterious thing that knits those parts together, that gives them greater meaning. That’s why I have enormous sympathy with Nick Cave’s tour producer Paul Sloan’s way of looking at Cave’s concert in the Alexandra Gardens. Sloan’s battle to stage it was referenced in The Age earlier this week. Naturally, as the Bad Seeds’ promotor, he has commercial interests at play. But his vision of a show that was “quintessentially Melbourne” is ultimately a cultural one. It’s not a concert as a mere event. It’s about the full integration of a Melbourne artist and the city that produced him. But culture is also fragile. It needs events to sustain it, sure. But events can equally erode it where they exist for their own sake, or are mere facsimiles of elsewhere. I think this is why so many footy fans have such an allergic reaction to the recent phenomenon of blaring out songs after goals; or (more mildly) of announcers introducing the home side player by player to tepid applause; of every break in the game becoming an opportunity for some fan “activation” or other. It’s not that they are new. It’s that they’re not of us. Everyone who has been to watch a major sport overseas will know their origin – usually the NBA or the NFL. And everyone who has done that will know that in our game, they become impositions from different sports with different rhythms that don’t suit. They are the most anaemic imitations of someone else’s culture. As though the consultants who dreamed them up don’t know Melbourne, and don’t care to because they assume it’s a market like any other market. But Melbourne often spurns things that make sense elsewhere. Ask Kyle and Jackie O, or Starbucks. The point is not curmudgeonliness, slavishness to tradition or base parochialism. In sport as in the arts, Melbourne has always embraced the new. It has always tasted what other cultures will offer us. The NFL’s recent visit proved that. State of Origin works here. The Australian Open’s evolution got it exactly right. Our Comedy Festival is one of the world’s best because it distils the best of Melbourne: varied, local and international at once, feeding off the energy of a hub. In a word, integrated.



Somewhere in there is guiding principle. Connecting the MCG and Melbourne Park is a great idea, and an integrating one. But only if it somehow makes the events they host feel like Melbourne being itself: the MCG more the people’s ground not less; Melbourne Park a meeting place not an event space; the arts as comfortable in this new cultural square as sport. And of course, though I don’t dwell on it here, the grassroots of both tended so people can come to these places as participants, not consumers. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly None of this is easy. We live in a world where culture is one of the hardest things to sustain. Where the water cooler once stood, now stands the algorithm, denying us common experiences – or even worse, weakening our desire to have them. The economics are only getting harder, and if it means the Town Hall is an expensive venue, even something like the Comedy Festival is vulnerable. Government money cannot answer all questions, especially if inflation is with us a while. But so often the most fragile things are the most precious. And we have no hope of preserving them, if we can’t recognise what we hold in the first place. Waleed Aly is a broadcaster, author, academic and regular columnist. He is moderating the Sport and the Arts session at the Melbourne Assembly.





Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Lawyers reveal Christa Pike’s first words after she woke from botched execution
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty Lawyers reveal Christa Pike’s first words after she woke from botched execution Michael Koziol October 8, 2026 — 6:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Death row inmate Christa Pike was believed to be “brain-dead” and hours from having her life support switched off when she woke up unexpectedly and asked where she was, her lawyers said, as a court ordered Tennessee to preserve all material related to her botched execution. Randy Spivey, her attorney, said the convicted murderer was “angry and confused”, and had massively swollen hands, a blood clot in one arm and pneumonia. She was also unable to swallow and had not eaten. Loading Pike, 50, survived two supposedly fatal injections in Tennessee last week, 30 years after she was sentenced to death for brutally torturing and murdering her classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when she was 18. The case has shocked the world and raised significant questions about the death penalty in the US – along with uncertainty about whether the state of Tennessee will try to execute her again.



A court on Wednesday (US time) ordered the state to preserve and maintain all medical equipment, records and communications relating to the failed execution – with further decisions to come about Pike’s access to a tablet, and whether she should be unshackled from the bed. Speaking to reporters after the court hearing, Spivey revealed Pike had been unresponsive and presumed brain-dead the night before she suddenly regained consciousness and began talking. Christa Pike’s attorneys Luke Ihnen (speaking) and Randy Spivey, left, at a news conference in Nashville on Wednesday. AP Photo/George Walker IV “On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day,” he said. “But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone – including me, including her team, and including the medical team – Christa woke up and began talking.”



Spivey was not in the room when Pike woke up. “Our understanding is the first thing she said was, ‘Where am I and who are you?’,” he said. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty How Christa Pike’s botched Tennessee execution unfolded, minute by minute “She has wanted to know what has happened, and she has asked about several people – she has asked about her team, she has asked about the victim’s family.” Pike was aware of the attempted execution, though was suffering a lot of “cognitive confusion”, Spivey said. “I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.” The attorney said his client faced a long road to recovery. She could not move either of her arms, and doctors did not know if they would regain function.



“The swelling is what I noticed. Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove. The swelling was extraordinary … That’s probably as far as I can go.” Tennessee has temporarily paused executions following the botched attempt to kill Pike. The state has not said whether it would attempt to seek her execution again, though Spivey described the idea as “unimaginable”. Pike’s case is unprecedented, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, a nonprofit organisation that critiques problems with the implementation of capital punishment. Although seven Americans previously survived execution attempts, no drugs were administered in those cases, the centre said. The Pike case is Tennessee’s second failed execution in less than five months, after it abandoned the execution of convicted murderer Tony Carruthers in May. In that case, officials could not establish a proper IV line. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandSchools Catholic schools knock back IVF leave in new workplace offer Catherine Strohfeldt October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland’s Catholic schools are ignoring union demands for a generous reproductive leave policy that would put private school teachers on equal footing with their state sector colleagues. The Independent Education Union began championing reproductive leave entitlements for private schools across the country after Queensland’s public sector was awarded 10 days of reproductive health leave in September 2024. Under a fresh wage offer released on Thursday, teachers and non-teaching staff at hundreds of Catholic schools – including All Hallows’, St Joseph’s Gregory Terrace and Marist College Ashgrove – would be entitled to up to five days of reproductive leave annually, with strict caveats. Queensland’s Catholic schools and the teachers’ union are at odds over reproductive leave allowances. Louise Kennerley An employee would need to suffer from “chronic symptoms” of one of eight approved reproductive health conditions or medical procedures, including endometriosis, polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), menopause, or if undergoing a hysterectomy.



The leave would also only be accessible to staff members who had fewer than 10 days of personal leave remaining. In state schools, teachers and non-teaching staff can access their 10-day entitlement for circumstances spanning four categories: chronic conditions, fertility treatments, including IVF, preventative screenings, and treatments such as vasectomies or hysterectomies. Eligible conditions and procedures for reproductive leave under Queensland Catholic schools’ proposed EBA Endometriosis

Adenomyosis

Dysmenorrhea

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)

Hysterectomy

Menopause

Perimenopause

Prostate disease In a statement to a federal review last year, the union said workplace protections for reproductive health, including IVF, were essential. “Lack of support in this area contributes to gender inequality, economic disadvantage, and workplace discrimination,” it said. The Catholic Archdiocese of Brisbane, like other Catholic bodies around the world, opposes assisted reproductive technology treatments, including IVF.



It also works with the Australian Catholic University’s Queensland Bioethics Centre, which provides advice on bioethical issues, including reproductive technologies, end-of-life treatments, and cloning. Related Article Teaching We looked at staff salaries at Brisbane’s private schools. These pay the most Catholic Education Queensland chief executive Allan Blagaich said school staff were informed of its position throughout the bargaining experience, which began in late 2025. “Employers have been guided by negotiating an outcome that is fair and reasonable for employees and that values their important contributions, while keeping Catholic education sustainable and accessible for families,” Blagaich said. Union officials were unimpressed with the offer, which they said skipped workload issues raised by staff and would, in some instances, worsen workplace conditions.



Logan Flexi School teacher Alex Patten, who is also an executive in the Independent Education Union’s Queensland branch, said the offer would leave non-teaching staff paid up to 25 per cent less than their NSW counterparts by the end of the deal. Brisbane teacher Sam McKinnon also said the offer was unfair. Logan teacher Alex Patten (left) and Brisbane teacher Sam McKinnon (right). “It cuts existing conditions, it ignores most of what staff asked for, and it’s being put to a vote without in-principle agreement at the bargaining table,” she said. The schools’ deal promised backpay to the last deal’s expiration in June if an agreement is reached before the end of the month, with the voting window closing on October 29.



Some 25,000 teaching and non-teaching staff members in Queensland will be covered by the collective agreement. They are employed within five diocesan zones and non-systemic Catholic schools, including those in Catholic education bodies such as Marist Schools Australia and Edmund Rice Education Australia.
