World.title: This musical is so good, someone saw it 327 times. Now it’s coming to Australia
World.content:
CultureMusicalsComedy This musical is so good, someone saw it 327 times. Now it’s coming to Australia Nell Geraets October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A dressed-up corpse, fake love letters, trout and Ian Fleming. This more or less sums up one of the most bonkers secret missions in history, known as “Operation Mincemeat”. Naturally, a story this absurd can only be told one way: through song, dance and a pinch of glittery fake blood. The musical Operation Mincemeat, based on that same mission, tells the story of how a group of oddball British agents used a homeless man’s corpse to wrong-foot Adolf Hitler. Operation Mincemeat is the epitome of “stranger than fiction”. Matt Crockett The production – written and composed by British theatre group SpitLip, which is often hailed as the “new Monty Python” – has taken both the West End and Broadway by storm, and sold more than 1 million tickets worldwide. And it’s coming to Australia in 2027. The story begins in 1943. The Allies were on the brink of defeat, so they hatched a plan to dress the body of Welshman Glyndwr Michael, who died after ingesting rat poison, as a British officer and drop him off the coast of Spain, an area rife with Nazi spies. The body was paired with a briefcase filled with various documents corroborating his fake identity, as well as “top-secret plans” that indicated the Allies intended to invade Europe via Sardinia instead of their actual entry point, Sicily. Against all odds, the madcap mission worked, redirecting the Nazis, saving countless lives on both sides and helping to turn the tide of World War II.



Operation Mincemeat takes this scarcely believable true story and transforms it into a fast-paced musical romp through history, delivering Nazi boy band pop songs, a Rocky Horror-esque coroner, and more dialogue about newts’ anuses than you’d ever expect in a World War II tale. As if that weren’t already enough to make your head spin, the 80-plus characters are played by just five actors. “People who’ve been through the British education system had World War II browbeaten into us every day of the year,” says David Cumming, SpitLip’s co-artistic director. “Even in maths, it was like, ‘Two plus Nazi is what?’ But for some reason, we weren’t taught this story. So, we knew it had an interest for the public in that sense, and an interest for us. It’s just such a wild caper. We fell in love with it.” Loading Despite its strangeness (or perhaps because of it) Operation Mincemeat has blown away both the West End – where the show’s run was extended a record 19 times – and Broadway, boasting more than 180 five-star reviews and winning both Tony and Olivier awards. It’s even said that some MI5 and MI6 agents have seen the show and approved. Many of the show’s fans, who call themselves “Mincefluencers”, have seen the show dozens of times, with some attempting to complete “cast bingo” sheets by seeing every combination of main cast members and understudies. One super Mincefluencer has seen the show a whopping 327 times.



“We weren’t really prepared for how much our incredible fan base was going to care about these people,” says Zoë Roberts, SpitLip’s co-artistic director, who adds that she can’t get enough of seeing fans dressed up as the campy death-obsessed coroner Spilsbury. These fans, of which there are thousands across the globe, gather on the Discord app to launch their own “missions”, such as “Operation Charming Man”, which convinced Colin Firth (who starred in the 2021 Operation Mincemeat film) to see the musical, and “Operation Preview One”, in which 300 Mincefluencers serenaded the Broadway cast, complete with an orchestra, at stage door after their first preview. The fans even launched an all-out investigation into the real identity of Hester Leggatt, a favourite of fans, whose wartime role was largely unknown before Operation Mincemeat. This fast-paced musical romp through history will soon tour across four continents. Matt Crockett The musical’s dedicated fan base, paired with its incredibly clever script and absurd source material, meant Operation Mincemeat went from a low-budget fringe production in a 77-seat theatre to a global phenomenon. Next year, the musical will commence a national tour in Australia, beginning in Melbourne in September as part of its world tour. Further Australian cities are yet to be announced. The world tour also includes dates in North America, China, New Zealand and Mexico. The search for the Australian cast will start early next year.



Preposterousness alone can’t get a musical to such heights, however. Among the silliness is a healthy dose of heart. The musical has been applauded for its thoughtful acknowledgement of largely unknown or forgotten people who made a huge difference in World War II: namely Glyndwr Michael. “We had this question mark around how we honour the man at the heart of it, the homeless man whose body it was,” says Natasha Hodgson, another co-artistic director of SpitLip. It wasn’t until the pandemic, when the group saw first-hand what it was like to feel so small in the face of insurmountable terror, that the ending came together. The role of Hester Leggatt, a fan-favourite character in Operation Mincemeat, won Jak Malone a Tony Award in 2025. Matt Crockett “We were like, no matter what, that has to be the thing that lingers when the curtain goes down. These contributions cannot be allowed to be forgotten,” Hodgson says. The musical has also been lauded as “quietly queer” thanks to its gender-blind casting, as well as feminist due to its emphasis on the unsung female heroes.



“The straight dads come for the war, and everyone else comes for the gender swapping,” director Robert Hastie says. “There’s something in this show that quietly offers people a way of facing a world that may define them in ways they’re uncomfortable with. It says: ‘You can defy expectations and label [yourself] as confidently and happily as this show does’.” Related Article Arts Culture wars and a swing to the right: A new take on Gone With the Wind is coming As for Ian Fleming, how does he factor into all this? The James Bond author was an officer in the Royal Navy’s Naval Intelligence Department, and he helped write the “Trout Memo”, which included the very deception “Operation Mincemeat” put into action. According to this document, the deception of an enemy in wartime was comparable to fly-fishing for trout. This mission helped win the Allies the war and thus changed the course of history. Given that, you’d expect a musical about it to be of similar proportions and earnestness as Les Misérables, Hastie says. It couldn’t be further from that. “It’s being told by these five miscast idiots,” he says. “You’re willing them to succeed against all odds, both on stage and in the story. It ought to be very serious, but it’s very, very silly … And then it pulls the rug out from under you again in making you care.”

World.title: The crumbling empire of a builder gone broke turned child safety millionaire
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandChild safety The crumbling empire of a builder gone broke turned child safety millionaire Julius Dennis October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Decades before the company he founded was thrust into the public eye after a child alleged she had been raped by a carer, Levi Te Namu left more than 70 creditors in the lurch overseas before moving to Australia to build his empire. The jet-setting chief executive’s lavish lifestyle was funded by millions in Queensland government contracts for his residential care business, Lighthouse Child and Family Services, which shared investors with another provider singled out by the state for profiteering. The rape allegation, made by a girl with an intellectual disability, turned a spotlight on the company and the debate about who should run, and profit, from the state’s struggling child safety system. Levi Te Namu’s business has drawn the Queensland government’s ire. Lighthouse Child & Family Services / @tenamulevi / Marija Ercegovac Child safety has become a hot-button political issue after the number of children in Queensland residential care soared from 650 at the end of 2015 to more than 2800 by March this year.



As that number swelled, so did the state’s financial burden. In 2025, the government spent $1.12 billion on residential care services – five times what it spent in 2015. And there was no shortage of businesses on hand to profit. Among them was Te Namu’s Lighthouse, which quickly became one of the biggest companies of its kind after launching in 2022. Levi Te Namu’s company left several businesses in Mount Maunganui, on New Zealand’s Tauranga Harbour, in the lurch. 7Michael But before he made millions from Queensland’s child safety system, Te Namu was a builder in New Zealand’s regional North Island city of Tauranga, where he operated a company with his future wife’s family. Compared to his Australian-based business, Miden Construction was a small operation, with just a few builds on the go when the global financial crisis hit.



In 2008, just four years after Te Namu had bought it, the company went under, owing more than $500,000 to various contractors and suppliers and leaving four houses unfinished. While most of those companies have either gone under themselves or been sold, this masthead has spoken to several people who were owed money by Te Namu, with one recalling he disappeared, leaving them to deal with liquidators. Of the $509,600 owed to creditors, just $93,000 was clawed back. Of that, $65,000 was spent on liquidators’ fees. Te Namu did not answer direct questions about Miden Construction. Almost 20 years later, he was winning lucrative state contracts to look after Queensland’s most vulnerable children.



Te Namu started Lighthouse while working for the not-for-profit Uniting Care with his now business partner Joshua Hillman. Josh Hillman’s image on the Lighthouse website includes a watermark suggesting it was created with AI. Lighthouse Child and Family Services To kickstart the business, the pair turned to Micheal Zarafa and Dominic Porter – the high-flying businessmen behind controversial residential care service All Care Australia – for seed money. A Melbourne nightclub operator, Porter’s internet footprint is a mix of party boy and proud dad. In one shot, he’s partying with rapper Travis Scott. In the next, he’s wearing matching Christmas Grinch shirts with his wife and kids.



Porter made headlines when armed criminals broke into his home and shot at him, a month after his bar in Melbourne’s ritzy South Yarra was firebombed during the city’s “bar wars” earlier this year. Zarafa and his wife, Vedrana Zarafa, were major funders of R&B festival Souled Out, which had Jhene Aiko and Vince Staples lined up for its 2025 shows in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane before it was cancelled a week before the event. The Porters with international R&B star Ne-Yo (centre). Instagram/@dominicrporter_ Porter’s wife, Kaitlyn Porter, was also a shareholder in the company behind the festival, and the sole shareholder and director of the company that invested in Lighthouse, D Porter Investments. Once Lighthouse was up and running, Te Namu’s Instagram page began to look something like Porter’s – Disneyland, New York, Japan, cruises, and various fast cars occupied his grid.



And the two were becoming closer in business too, with Te Namu and wife Jessica investing in the South Yarra club The Albion, run by Porter. By late 2024, Lighthouse and All Care Australia were two of the largest residential care providers in south-east Queensland, with Porter telling CEO Magazine that ACA had more than 1000 employees across the country. Levi Te Namu and his family frequently spend time overseas. Instagram/@tenamulevi Then the winds changed. In May 2025, while announcing a $20 million commission of inquiry into the child safety system, the Queensland government said it was auditing one residential care provider that had paid out $5.25 million to three shareholders the previous year. “This same organisation receives tens of millions of dollars from the state government to run residential care services, with financial statements also revealing they increased their management fees by 1000 per cent,” it said in a statement.



Porter told this masthead ACA was that service provider, and that the company stopped receiving referrals from the government around the same time, but he did not respond directly to questions about the fee increase. In opposition, the LNP promised to shake up residential care models. Now in government, it is moving away from individualised placement and support, usually delivered through for-profit providers like ACA, to outsourced delivery contracts, usually using not-for-profit providers, which they claim give children better stability. Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm has been under intense public scrutiny. William Davis However, Porter said he thought Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm was using businesses like ACA to avoid accountability for the state of the system. “I believe for-profit providers have been scapegoated to distract from the government’s own expenditure across the residential care system, particularly expenditure involving the not-for-profit sector,” he said.



Porter said the government pulling away from companies like ACA led to reports of children sleeping on the floor of child safety offices when there was nowhere appropriate for them to go. “My view is that Amanda Camm’s narrative has been misleading, hypocritical, and extraordinarily incompetent,” he said. Camm was on leave when this masthead sent questions to her. Acting minister Ros Bates said the government was fixing a broken system and “mov[ing] away from unlicensed residential care providers that exploded under Labor”. Te Namu and Hillman bought ACA in December 2025, after it had been audited and singled out by the government. Paperwork lodged with ASIC showed Lighthouse could have accessed $24 million in loans to help buy the business and residential care homes it owned.



Te Namu would not say how much money had been borrowed by the company, and said the repayments were commercial-in-confidence. Related Article Child safety ‘Heinous’: Ministers defend reforms after revelation of alleged rape of girl in residential care In February, ACA was transferred to another company owned by Te Namu and Hillman, called Best Life Group. The ACA website has since been taken down, and Te Namu said he had no plans to revive it. He said ACA was still servicing some children when the company changed hands, but he was now focused on Lighthouse. An email seen by this masthead showed the police investigation into the rape allegation ended when the girl involved did not want to provide a formal statement and withdrew the complaint, and Te Namu said the man involved no longer worked at Lighthouse.



Meanwhile, workers at other agencies have told this masthead that large numbers of children in state care are being moved out of Lighthouse residential homes. On October 5, Te Namu said the organisation was caring for 12 children, after operating 41 houses at its peak. He said case referrals to Lighthouse had slowed before the rape allegation. In Queensland, providers can operate without a licence, but must comply with minimum standards. Te Namu said the company had been fighting to get a residential care licence since April, and a decision from the department was delayed from July to October. Te Namu said the rape allegation was disclosed on August 21, before it was reported in the media on August 26. “On 26 August, the department confirmed that the application remained under the licensing delegate’s consideration. It refused the application on 1 September, 2026,” Te Namu said.



A department spokesperson said Lighthouse was considered unsuitable for a licence under the Child Protection Act. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: There is a world where art and sport are discrete – but that’s not Melbourne
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Opinion There is a world where art and sport are discrete – but that’s not Melbourne Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic October 8, 2026 — 6:00am

October 8, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

The longer I’ve thought about it, the more convinced I’ve become that Melbourne’s secret is that it’s integrated. Ours is not a city of discrete neighbourhoods like New York. Not really, anyway. It’s not a city of enclaves and subcultures – “villages”, says Eddie McGuire – like Sydney. It’s not that Melbourne is undifferentiated. It’s highly varied. But it’s that the borders between these variations are subtle and fuzzy. More matters of degree than essence. Probably nowhere is that truer than in sport and the arts, which we will talk about at The Age’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum later this month. There’s a world, perhaps most of the world, where these things are discrete: different concepts appealing to different cohorts, some dwelling in the overlap, many not. In Melbourne, much more dwells there. The Melbourne Football Club has a fan who plays trumpet in the stands, who sometimes can’t make it to games because he has to play with the MSO. If you run an art gallery, no one will blink if you are a passionate Essendon supporter. Bulldogs, maybe. Melbourne sports magnate Eddie McGuire wants to see the railway yards separating the MCG from Melbourne and Olympic Parks covered. Jason South That’s a rarer gift than we know. In Sydney, for instance, even sport alone is stratified. You follow union or league, or neither. But none can be a lingua franca. Tell me what you love and I’ll have a fair chance of guessing which school you went to. That’s not without its benefits: each code has its particularities, its own bespoke culture. But in Melbourne, sport and art mingle seamlessly as participants in a common social drama. They are neither mere sport nor mere art. They are culture itself.



Culture is a rich concept. It is not the same thing as a collection of events. It’s not the sum of its economic parts. It’s more the mysterious thing that knits those parts together, that gives them greater meaning. That’s why I have enormous sympathy with Nick Cave’s tour producer Paul Sloan’s way of looking at Cave’s concert in the Alexandra Gardens. Sloan’s battle to stage it was referenced in The Age earlier this week. Naturally, as the Bad Seeds’ promotor, he has commercial interests at play. But his vision of a show that was “quintessentially Melbourne” is ultimately a cultural one. It’s not a concert as a mere event. It’s about the full integration of a Melbourne artist and the city that produced him. But culture is also fragile. It needs events to sustain it, sure. But events can equally erode it where they exist for their own sake, or are mere facsimiles of elsewhere. I think this is why so many footy fans have such an allergic reaction to the recent phenomenon of blaring out songs after goals; or (more mildly) of announcers introducing the home side player by player to tepid applause; of every break in the game becoming an opportunity for some fan “activation” or other. It’s not that they are new. It’s that they’re not of us. Everyone who has been to watch a major sport overseas will know their origin – usually the NBA or the NFL. And everyone who has done that will know that in our game, they become impositions from different sports with different rhythms that don’t suit. They are the most anaemic imitations of someone else’s culture. As though the consultants who dreamed them up don’t know Melbourne, and don’t care to because they assume it’s a market like any other market. But Melbourne often spurns things that make sense elsewhere. Ask Kyle and Jackie O, or Starbucks. The point is not curmudgeonliness, slavishness to tradition or base parochialism. In sport as in the arts, Melbourne has always embraced the new. It has always tasted what other cultures will offer us. The NFL’s recent visit proved that. State of Origin works here. The Australian Open’s evolution got it exactly right. Our Comedy Festival is one of the world’s best because it distils the best of Melbourne: varied, local and international at once, feeding off the energy of a hub. In a word, integrated.



Somewhere in there is guiding principle. Connecting the MCG and Melbourne Park is a great idea, and an integrating one. But only if it somehow makes the events they host feel like Melbourne being itself: the MCG more the people’s ground not less; Melbourne Park a meeting place not an event space; the arts as comfortable in this new cultural square as sport. And of course, though I don’t dwell on it here, the grassroots of both tended so people can come to these places as participants, not consumers. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly None of this is easy. We live in a world where culture is one of the hardest things to sustain. Where the water cooler once stood, now stands the algorithm, denying us common experiences – or even worse, weakening our desire to have them. The economics are only getting harder, and if it means the Town Hall is an expensive venue, even something like the Comedy Festival is vulnerable. Government money cannot answer all questions, especially if inflation is with us a while. But so often the most fragile things are the most precious. And we have no hope of preserving them, if we can’t recognise what we hold in the first place. Waleed Aly is a broadcaster, author, academic and regular columnist. He is moderating the Sport and the Arts session at the Melbourne Assembly.





Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Person killed in Coromandel house fire
World.content:
One person has died in a Coromandel house fire.

Emergency services were called to Wharekaho Road in Wharekaho at 2.25am on Thursday, senior sergeant Chris Painter said.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

A shift manager for Fire and Emergency confirmed to RNZ one person had died.

They said seven fire trucks were sent to the blaze, which was "well involved", and the second alarm was raised.

The fire has now been contained, and one crew is still at the scene dampening down hotspots.

Painter said the person's body was found inside the property.

An occupant of the house alerted emergency services "and is being provided with support", he said. They were not injured.

World.title: Big rockets could launch a dozen times a year in initial Canterbury plan
World.content:
Audio player for " John Holt on Tawhaki's ambitions in the space launch market " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/science-and-technology/1786736%2Fbig-rockets-could-launch-a-dozen-times-a-year-in-initial-canterbury-plan

John Holt on Tawhaki's ambitions in the space launch market Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Large rockets weighing up to 100 tonnes each could be launched a dozen times a year from a planned national aerospace centre near Christchurch.

Tāwhaki and a French company are now working on getting capital, consents and customers from Europe to build the spaceport.

The few details of the attempt to tap the burgeoning world of the space launch market have been released to RNZ.

"Launch facility to cater for up to 100-tonne launch vehicles, with an initial consent for up to 12 launches per year," said an executive summary.

This is much bigger than 13-tonne Electron rockets that go up from Mahia - Rocket Lab is working on a new Neutron rocket that would be heavier than 100 tonne and launch from the US - but just a fifth the size of what Elon Musk's SpaceX launches.

A summary of the spaceport plan features a 30m by 30m rocket pad being built to NASA standards, about 10 kilometres from State Highway 75 beside Lake Ellesmere Te Waihora.

It lists five possible rocket fuels - all of them gas - and not the more environmentally-damaging solid rocket fuels.

A southern hemisphere launch gives private or government or scientific missions greater options into the various orbits, of which low-earth orbit (LEO) is particularly sought-after for the likes of Starlink and other communications satellites, and US military constellations planned to support the Golden Dome.

Many more thousands of satellites are expected to go into LEO in coming years - Musk already has about 10,000.

The summary said Tāwhaki and France's SpaceDreamS now needed to develop a collaboration agreement, secure capital for building and consents, and discuss regulations with the National Space Agency, which is part of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and employment.

The key questions to discuss were around the role of the state - many of the current attempts in various countries to build spaceports have substantial government backing - liability and which launch companies might sign up.

"Collaboration between values-aligned organisations" was a guideline.

Tāwhaki has said it would be okay with launching NZ Defence Force spacecraft, but dual-use military-civilian launches by offshore customers would face more questions.

The partners have been marketing the spaceport in Europe and the US as a "strategically unique launch capability" with "an exceptionally clear launch range" and "access to a wide range of azimuths and inclinations".

Tāwhaki - an iwi-Crown joint venture set up with $35m taxpayer funding - has a runway and hangar at Kaitorete Spit, and benefits from special regulations to carry out tests of the likes of high-altitude unmanned surveillance planes in its airspace.

The centre hooked up with SpaceDreamS at an international aerospace congress in Sydney last year. The French visited the spit and signed a memorandum of understanding "to investigate the feasibility of a collaborative spaceport".

The summary said the firm had staff who used to work for French commercial launch provider Ariane Space and had "access to European launch operators and funded programmes".

The SpaceDreamS website said its "feasibility studies bridge the gap between initial ideas and viable projects".

It says spaceports need a launchpad and control room, and perhaps a site for engine testing and zone for recovering boosters that drop into the sea.

A map shows a Kaitorete spaceport with a 5.5km circle of flight operations around the launchpad extending out over the shallow lake to the west and sea to the east.

The summary said: "Confirmed: Land-use, consents, utilities, infrastructure, airspace, commodities, logistics, security & supporting services."

Experts have said the fuel type of rockets matters.

World.title: Hamilton East: Will the 'city of the future' predict the election again?
World.content:
Audio player for " Rachel Moore on the mood of Hamilton East voters " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1786970%2Fhamilton-east-will-the-city-of-the-future-predict-the-election-again

Rachel Moore on the mood of Hamilton East voters Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The Hamilton East electorate runs east of the Waikato River, from Riverlea and Hillcrest in the south, through Fairfield and Enderley, and then to Rototuna and Flagstaff in the north.

Why is it interesting?

Known as a bellwether seat, the way the party vote goes tended to reflect which parties made up the government.

Former Hamilton East MP, now real estate agent, Jamie Strange, said that is down to how Hamilton is made up.

"It's the youngest population of any city in New Zealand and also if you look at the demographic, if you look at the communities in Hamilton, it is very much representative of New Zealand as a whole."

What happened last election?

National's Ryan Hamilton won the seat in 2023. This came at the same time National came back into power, forming a coalition with ACT and NZ First.

Prior to that, the seat was won by Strange in 2020, who retired prior to the 2023 election. Labour formed the Government during this period.

Who's standing?

Incumbent Hamilton East MP Ryan Hamilton was running again for the National Party, while Georgie Dansey is the Labour Party's choice.

New Zealand First has put up Nicola Laboyrie and The Opportunity Party (TOP) candidate is Naomi Pocock.

What do locals say?

For business owner and registered immigration advisor Arun Jacob, the biggest issue this election was the distribution of social housing.

The 58-year-old had just sold his house in Rototuna North, and said nearby social housing affected its value.

"I think the distribution of social housing and suburbs should be taken care of a bit more well."

He said he's by and large happy with the current MP's performance and was looking for a politician who thought about Hamilton's future.

Arun Jacob. Supplied

"It's good to be on the street level and look at your every day bread and butter issues but I would like my MP to have a larger vision and kind of look at the overall well-being of Hamilton."

Toby Brockelbank, 21-year-old student and editor of university magazine Nexus, said cost of living and housing affordability was key.

"Tenant rights as well and the like changes to kind of support for students financially, things like fees free being removed and that sort of stuff.

Toby Brockelbank.

Asked what he thought about Hamilton's bellwether history, Brocelbank said he hoped both the electorate and the nation swung further left.

"Because the coalition have been really dodgy, especially with the Treaty Principles Bill, kind of like anti-immigrant rhetoric, anti-queer rhetoric, and also just kind of like twats to students."

Kristina Laird. Supplied

52-year-old Kristina Laird was looking at all things education.

"I'm an early childhood teacher so for me I'm very much focused on what can be done for early childhood education."

She's also a mum of children that would be heading to university soon.

"I think it's really important like education and educating everyone. Because how are we going to start change if we can't, especially because I see it at the coalface."

As a business owner, Atul Sharma, was worried about the cost of living .

"Almost in every time we have deliveries, the price are changing, the price are increasing. A lot of companies who used to give us credits, like longer credits of payment, they don't do it anymore. People are cautious in terms of spending. The businesses are cautious."

The 44-year-old owner of Bin Inn in Hamilton East said he believed in minimum wage increases, but it squeezed his margins a little more every time.

Atul Sharma.

"I can't pass every cost to a customer, otherwise nobody will come to buy things. So which means I've got less money left to run my household now."

For Seamus Lohrey, a future MP that listened to the uncomfortable truth was important.

"I used to live on May St and I used to see kids walking to school with no shoes and windows covered with glad wrap, yet that reality is never, ever talked about by any MP. And that's something that makes me really sad because they're meant to accurately represent us and that's a reality of so many people in this electorate too."

May Street. RNZ/Rachel Moore

The 23-year-old student, and Waikato University Students Union president, said the job market, public transport and having an inviting CBD were key issues.

"I think for young people, some of the bigger issues are public transport and having a CBD in city that's inviting and a place that young people want to be. We have a young student university campus and many of whom leave after they graduate and don't contribute to Hamilton because there's just no jobs or opportunities here."

Seamus Lohrey.

Meanwhile, Bernadette Ranson said she didn't have much faith in any of the politicians at the moment.

"I think they're all as bad with each other."

World.title: Will the election have an impact on rents?
World.content:
Audio player for " Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1786726%2Fwill-the-election-have-an-impact-on-rents

Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 9m

Rent prices have been mostly flat in recent years, but is the approaching election likely to change that?

Data from Stats NZ shows that the "stock" measure of rents, which includes existing tenancies, did not move at all over either the month or year to August. The "flow" measure of new tenancies was up 0.9 percent over a year but did not move over a month.

Asking rents were a mixed bag, too. Realestate.co.nz data showed Auckland asking rents up 1.2 percent over a year, Coromandel's down 13.7 percent, Hawke's Bay down 3.5 percent, Wellington up 3.9 percent and Canterbury and Otago up more than 5 percent.

Cotality head of research Nick Goodall said he did not think the election was likely to change the picture much.

Cotality head of research Nick Goodall. Supplied / Cotality

"The thing I'll be looking for is who is going to impact living costs and the broader economy.

"At the moment, the reason the rental market is quite flat in terms of rents not going up anywhere is because we have this imbalance between demand and supply, which is playing out in tenants' favour because there are fewer people out there looking for rental properties and there is quite a bit of supply in terms of rental properties available for rent."

He said more people were living with their parents for longer, or staying in larger flatting situations because of the cost of living.

"You don't necessarily have the household creation rate that we might otherwise when things are a bit better economically and from a cost-of-living perspective."

Audio player for " What the election could mean for renters " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1786726%2Fwill-the-election-have-an-impact-on-rents

What the election could mean for renters Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Policies that addressed supermarket, power and petrol costs were likely to have more of an impact on the rental market if they helped improve household finances than the tax policies that applied to housing itself.

Goodall said he expected rents to stay flat for some time. "I think it's probably quite similar to the broader market, where when things improve economically, when the labour market improves and we see unemployment start to fall as well, that's when I think we might start to see people move out to new household situations again … probably quite similar to the broader market where we're expecting values to continue to track sideways or slightly down for the rest of this year, maybe into early next year.

"When certainty comes back and then once we see some economic growth come through too, I suspect that'll then flow on to the rental market as well."

He said, although investors were generally pleased that Labour had said it would not again phase out their ability to claim interest costs as a business expense, rents were driven more by demand and tenant income rather than landlord costs.

Infometrics principal economist Nick Brunsdon agreed rents were unlikely to move quickly, whatever happened politically.

Infometrics principal economist Nick Brunsdon. Supplied / Infometrics

"We are picking migration to pick up ever so slowly which I think would probably get metro rents back into positive territory but probably not substantially. We don't really have the conditions for it. We've had really strong house building going on in the last boom while interest rates were low. We're actually still building quite a lot of houses at the moment. Those factors help keep a strong supply coming through, which will limit the extent of rent increases."

He said rents had been mostly flat since the spike in 2024, and had been falling in the past nine months.

Healthy Homes rules had increased the standard of rental properties, and that system was still bedding in, he said. "I'm not saying it's perfect but I think we have generally raised the quality of houses and the conduct related to landlords from where it has been historically. I think there has been a permanent shift on the relative power between tenants and landlords."

He said rents were not driven by house prices but demand for rental properties. "The two can move separately."

Tenants' incomes were the biggest factor in rent changes. "For example when the Government increased the student allowance back in the 2010s we saw in Wellington, which is quite a student-oriented rental market, rents increasing by pretty much the amount that student's incomes had increased."

World.title: Indefinite ban on taking sea life from large parts of Auckland and Coromandel coastlines
World.content:
The government has indefinitely banned taking some sea life from large parts of the Auckland and Coromandel coastlines.

The ban followed a review of intertidal species in the two regions, prompted by community tensions over harvesting from rockpools.

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones earlier placed a two-year ban on harvesting from intertidal areas in the northern Hauraki Gulf.

On Thursday, he said harvesting for a large range of marine invertebrates would be banned on Auckland's east and west coasts, Waiheke Island, and Coromandel.

Certain species, including cockles, crabs, kina and pīpī, were excluded from the ban.

Jones said while he was reluctant to close coastlines, it was necessary to protect a broad range of species that were vulnerable to overharvesting.

"Fossicking in a rockpool is a Kiwi tradition. It's a pastime that's been enjoyed by generations of New Zealanders. However, it's being exploited by a selfish few who are taking far too much kaimoana. This behaviour is endangering these fragile ecosystems and putting at risk our beloved coastal areas."

Harvesting in the intertidal zone on beaches, rocky shores and rockpools, the area in and around where the tide comes in and goes out, would be heavily limited with exceptions in place for only certain species that could be taken sustainably, he said.

A 2m depth limit would be used to define the area, meaning areas that were accessible at low tide would be covered by the ban.

New daily limits would also apply outside of intertidal zones, he said.

World.title: David Tamihere wants 'quite huge' compensation payout after murder charges withdrawn
World.content:
Audio player for " RNZ National " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/crime-and-justice/1786318%2Fdavid-tamihere-wants-quite-huge-compensation-payout-after-murder-charges-withdrawn

RNZ national

David Tamihere believes he should be entitled to a "quite huge" payout from the Crown for the 20 years he spent in prison now charges of murder have been withdrawn.

On Wednesday, the Crown decided not to pursue a retrial of Tamihere for the 1989 murders of Swedish backpackers Heidi Paakkonen and Urban Höglin.

Justice Simon Mount discharged Tamihere on the two charges of murder and said he was free to go.

Speaking outside of court, Tamihere said he would be having discussions on the matter of compensation with his lawyers.

"I'd like to do it at the level that was around when I first got convicted ... it's quite huge," he said.

Speaking to Morning Report on Thursday, Tamihere said he had been aiming for a retrial.

"Mainly because the Crown could come up and say anything they want. But my argument since '92 has always been, well, look, great, but put it in front of a jury."

He said when the Court of Appeal ruled against him in 1992 he expected the court "didn't have the power to determine guilt or innocence".

"We went into the appeal hearing then, arguing the evidence that was presented in the trial and the validity of that. The Crown turned up with a whole new story."

"There was a few scumbag tricks that were pulled. And even my lawyer at the time allowed a couple of things to go by the board... that was going to never happen a second time."

He argued the Crown prosecutors and the police had manufactured a case.

"It was the police and the Crown prosecutors. And then like the prosecutors act as the conductors of the orchestra."

He said he had mixed feelings when the charges were withdrawn

"We started the morning off expecting another year of going through to a retrial and all that."

"I'm standing in the dock and the old judge just 'goes, yeah, it's over', you know, 'dismissed, you're free to go'. And it was like, you know, someone had just flicked the switch on it."

He said he was talking to lawyers about potential compensation.

Former High Court judge Hon Rodney Hansen, KC, was appointed to oversee two high profile claims for wrongful murder convictions and imprisonments - Teina Pora, who got $3.5 million and Alan Hall, who was awarded $4.9 million.

Rodney Hansen. Supplied / Shortland Chambers

He said it usually fell to a retired judge or King's Counsel to determine whether an applicant was innocent on the balance of probabilities - a lower threshold than "beyond reasonable doubt" that is required to convict in a criminal trial.

"That's the first hurdle, if you like, that lies ahead of him. And it's the first step that has to be taken in the compensation process."

It could be a long and arduous process, and there was a huge weight of responsibility on those overseeing the claim.

"It's such an important matter. A) for the individual, of course, and B) I suppose some sort of public assertion that where a wrong has been done it will be righted. So yes, it's a very important part of the process and any decision maker entrusted with the job of making it treats it with the seriousness appropriate to the gravity of their task," Hansen said.

Sometimes it could be a very complex and difficult process, he said. Other claims, like that of Pora, were more straightforward.

"I didn't even find that a sort of close-run thing in the end. I concluded that it was so clear that he was innocent, that he had actually proved it to the standard of beyond reasonable doubt, not simply the standard he was required to."

Should Tamihere be found innocent on the balance of probabilities, there would be a number of types of compensation available to him.

David Tamihere appears during a callover at the High Court at Auckland in July. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

These included $150,000 for each year he spent in custody, $100,000 a year for loss of livelihood and $75,000 a year for time spent on restrictive bail or parole.

"There is also provision for an award of a sum to recognise any impropriety in the way that the prosecution or the inquiry itself might have been conducted, so that if there has been irregularity, impropriety, or worse, then an additional sum can be included in the overall package," Hansen said.

It is ultimately a matter for Cabinet to approve a compensation claim.

World.title: David Seymour again hints at retirement age increase if ACT elected
World.content:
ACT leader David Seymour has hinted his party's upcoming fiscal plan will once again contain a commitment to raise the superannuation age to 67.

The party would release its fiscal plan on Sunday, one day ahead of National's, with Seymour signalling a focus on cuts, with no new taxes.

On Wednesday, in another preview of the party's fiscal plan, Seymour announced ACT would scrap the cap on charitable donations being able to receive tax credits.

In a speech to Gravity Credit Management on Thursday morning, Seymour, who had spent three years as an associate finance minister, said the government's promise of a surplus in two years' time relied on "heroic" revenue assumptions, such as the government taking in $12 billion more this year than last year.

"We cannot balance the budget when non-health, non-education, non-transfer spending is over 10 percent higher than it should be."

He attacked budgets by both Grant Robertson (whom he labelled a "spendthrift pinko") and Nicola Willis, saying "extraordinarily" after three of her budgets, New Zealand was two thirds closer to peak Covid spending than pre-Covid spending.

"I regret that we haven't saved more than $14 billion. The fact Labour find it so easy to cosy up to our government's fiscal track is a telling sign," he said.

"Labour and National fight like two bald men fighting over a comb, but they're not so different."

He said the next government would have to assess where efficiency had gone wrong in the past decade, and work out how to be at least as efficient as 10 years ago.

"You might ask why I'm saying this now after being part of the government for three years. Our party signed up for a 2017 baseline exercise three years ago, but most of the government refused to implement it. Today, reality is calling and wants its money back."

While the speech did not set out any definitive policy that would be in Sunday's fiscal plan, Seymour recommitted to ACT's policy to raise the superannuation age of eligibility.

"The superannuation bill is rising at nearly $2 billion each year. Longer lives, fewer kids. Only two taxpayers per superannuitant by mid-century. Something has to give, and it will. The only real question is whether we plan the change and make it gradually on our terms, or let it happen to us fast amidst a fiscal crisis."

While he said raising the age of entitlement was inevitable, the government should do so carefully and slowly, with the conditions that KiwiSaver remained available at 65, that people who had worked more than 20 years in a physical job got early compassionate access, and that tax was taken off KiwiSaver investment returns.

"Adjusting by three months saves about $400 million. Adjusting two years would save over $3 billion a year, nearly three quarters of a percent of GDP," he said.

Labour, the Greens, and New Zealand First are all campaigning to keep the super age at 65.

National, which holds a view it should rise to 67, had softened its language this election, with leader Christopher Luxon saying it "probably" should rise, but acknowledging the lack of political consensus.

While National would still put forward a superannuation policy this election, it had been keen to highlight policies to make KiwiSaver compulsory, and increase the default contribution rates.

Seymour also criticised a "dumpster fire of a policy debate" that New Zealand had descended into, singling out parties' supermarket policies in particular.

World.title: Politicians pin hopes of winning knife-edge race on Auckland this election
World.content:
Audio player for " Why Auckland is central to the election campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1786725%2Fpoliticians-pin-hopes-of-winning-knife-edge-race-on-auckland-this-election

Why Auckland is central to the election campaign Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Politicians have been relentlessly focused on Auckland this election campaign, heavily weighting their time there during what is still a knife-edge race.

Home to a third of the population, it's where elections are won - and lost - which will be particularly fresh in Labour's mind.

Leader Chris Hipkins is keen to avoid a repeat of 2023, when even some safe seats flipped blue or came very close.

"We didn't do as well here at the last election as we hoped to," he told reporters last month.

"We're doing much, much better this election campaign, we're getting a much better reception on the ground, and we're going to be campaigning hard for every vote we can get."

He's not alone - candidates of all stripes have a lot of convincing to do.

Auckland has been on the wrong side of the so-called two speed economic recovery, and the poster child for homelessness, unemployment and a property slump.

Newmarket Business Association boss Mark Knoff-Thomas said this election, the city was being noticed.

Newmarket Business Association boss Mark Knoff-Thomas. supplied

"I think there seems to be a much more concerted effort to focus on Auckland," he said.

"Auckland is - or has been, and should be - the pumping engine room of the New Zealand economy, and it's probably fair to say that at various times in the past, Wellington may have sometimes forgotten that," he said.

Knoff-Thomas said "geopolitical madness" had not helped the city, nor had flip-flopping of policies and settings inevitable with changes of government.

"We are gold standard Olympians at short-termism," he said.

"There is a bit more conversations being had now between parties, especially the major parties. They're opening up to more bipartisan sort of arrangements, which which does bode well, I think, long term."

However the city's mayor, Wayne Brown, suggested he wanted politicians to butt out - particularly following both National and the Greens releasing Auckland-specific transport policies.

Wayne Brown in the RNZ Morning Report studio. RNZ

"It's none of their business, they're supposed to be fixing the economy," he told Morning Report on Wednesday.

"None of those parties even will get a majority to do anything they promise."

Financial mentor Peter Verry, who volunteers for two services in Auckland, said politicians were clearly focusing on the cost of living - and rightly so.

"I think they're all well aware, I don't think they're making light of it or thinking, 'oh this is just a nice little election issue and it'll go away'. It won't," he said.

However he said there was some scepticism about the promises being made.

"I don't think anyone's naive enough to think there's actually this miracle cure, that suddenly even with current or a future government that they can click their fingers and it's all going to come right," he said.

Business closures and unemployment were major issues, Verry said, and several clients had packed up and moved to Australia hoping for a better life.

But not everyone had that option.

Pam Elgar who runs social service organisation Lifewise said she would welcome the opportunity to educate politicians if they came knocking.

Lifewise chief executive Pam Elgar. Supplied / Lifewise

"I don't think the majority of politicians do really fully appreciate some of the pressures that our most vulnerable people, the people that we see, those that are homeless, those that are housing deprived [face]," she said.

Lifewise was collaborating with the Electoral Commission to ensure everyone got a side of democracy with their bite to eat at the organisation's pay it forward cafe.

"We're using Merge Cafe as the address for homeless people, so that they can actually register with that as the address, the papers can come to us and then we will dish them out," Elgar said.

World.title: Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast
World.content:
The most famous race on the Supercars calendar is here, with thousands of fans flocking to Mount Panorama in regional New South Wales for the Bathurst 1000.

Fifty-four drivers across 27 cars will battle over the 1,000-kilometre endurance race in an event that always produces drama.

Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

When is the Bathurst 1000?

The Great Race will be held this Sunday, October 11, at Mount Panorama in Bathurst.

There will be four days of action culminating in the 1,000km race on Sunday.

Here is when each of the key sessions begins in your state or territory.

Bathurst 1000 race, Sunday, October 11

11:30am AEDT: NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania

11am ACDT: South Australia

10:30am AEST: Queensland

10am ACST: Northern Territory

8:30am AWST: Western Australia

1:30pm NZDT: New Zealand

Top 10 Shootout, Saturday, October 10

5:05pm AEDT: NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania

4:35pm ACDT: South Australia

4:05pm AEST: Queensland

3:35pm ACST: Northern Territory

2:05pm AWST: Western Australia

7:05pm NZDT: New Zealand

Qualifying (top 10 advance to shootout), Friday, October 9

4:10pm AEDT: NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania

3:40pm ACDT: South Australia

3:10pm AEST: Queensland

2:40pm ACST: Northern Territory

1:10pm AWST: Western Australia

6:10pm NZDT: New Zealand

How can I watch the Bathurst 1000?

Brodie Kostecki hunting Bathurst pole record Supercars star Brodie Kostecki can surpass Australian motor racing legends Peter Brock and Allan Moffat with a Bathurst record this weekend, but will do it without the support of his engineer.

In Australia, you can watch the race on both free-to-air and pay television, as well as streaming platforms.

The Seven Network is the free-to-air broadcaster, and you can watch it on Channel 7 or via the online streaming platform 7plus.

Foxtel and its streaming platform Kayo will also be broadcasting the race. On Foxtel, the race will be shown on Fox Sports channel 506.

In New Zealand, you can watch the race through Sky Sport.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the Great Race from 10am AEDT on Sunday.

Who is driving in the Bathurst 1000?

There will be 54 drivers across 27 cars contesting this year's Bathurst 1000.

Along with the usual 24 cars across 12 teams that contest every round of the Supercars Championship, the wildcard entries in this year's Bathurst 1000 are: 5 Ben Gomersall/Campbell Logan, 15 Craig Lowndes/Bayley Hall and 34 Nathan Herne/James Moffat.

What weather is forecast for the Bathurst 1000?

Sunday is set to be sunny at Bathurst, but rain threatens to cause chaos at Mount Panorama on Saturday. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Rain affected last year's Bathurst 1000, leading to a wild and thrilling finale at Mount Panorama.

For now, the 2026 drivers can breathe a sigh of relief based on the current forecast.

Sunday at Mount Panorama is expected to be sunny, with a maximum temperature of 26 degrees Celsius.

However, there is a 90 per cent chance of rain on Saturday, which could have a massive effect on the starting grid.

The fifth and sixth practice sessions will be held on Saturday, then the iconic Top 10 Shootout from 5:05pm, local time.

The Bureau of Meteorology is forecasting: "High chance of showers, most likely in the morning and afternoon. The chance of a thunderstorm in the morning and afternoon".

That could make Saturday a very wild and eventful day.

*Forecast from the Bureau of Meteorology correct as of Wednesday, October 7

Who won the Bathurst 1000 last year?

Matt Payne and Garth Tander won an extraordinary edition of the Bathurst 1000 in 2025, despite crossing the line second.

The duo started 18th on the grid, and Payne only took the lead with five laps to go. Payne was overtaken on the last lap by James Golding, who was carrying a time penalty for taking out Cooper Murray late in the race.

Golding took the chequered flag, but dropped to third with the penalty, as Payne and Tander were promoted to the win. It was Tander's sixth Bathurst 1000 win, while it was Payne's maiden triumph on Mount Panorama.

But the late chaotic finale barely touches the surface of what was an unbelievable race that was one of the all-time greats.

World.title: How a virulent series gave rise to Sandpapergate
World.content:
As Australia heads back to South Africa for the first time in eight years, there is no doubt ghosts will stir.

The 2018 series was a catastrophe for Australian cricket.

A sporting nation that prides itself on playing hard but fair was dragged to a set of gallows fashioned from its own hubris, humiliated by a single, square inch of yellow sandpaper.

But as seismic as the fallout was, it is worth remembering just how unpleasant the 2018 series was before the sandpaper even entered the chat.

Aussies headbutt the line, South Africa stir the pot

David Warner exuberantly celebrated a run out on the penultimate day of the Kingsmead Test. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Lee Warren)

Australia and South Africa have always been the fiercest of sporting rivals and, following a dominant 4-0 Ashes win that summer, Australia was primed to take on its next biggest challenger.

But an Australian team provoked into believing they were in for a genuine fight was, in that era, a dangerous proposition.

For decades there had existed, within Australian cricket, a win at all costs mentality that crashed through the line between what was acceptable and abhorrent.

Nathan Lyon said that the Australian team, whose belligerent attitude to competition was already verging towards the unacceptable, would "headbutt the line" whenever they played, "the line" a constantly repeated mark by many associated with that team.

But to paraphrase an American sitcom, Australia were often so far past the line that they couldn't even see it any more. At times, the line was just a dot to them.

Nathan Lyon dropped the ball next to AB de Villiers after he was run out. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

In Durban, Australia were being reminded of that fact repeatedly by a hostile crowd, not dissimilar to what foreign teams expect to receive from the bleachers at the Gabba.

The first flashpoint came with the game on the line, Nathan Lyon petulantly dropping the ball next to a run out AB de Villiers as he lay, sprawled on the ground at the non-strikers end, while David Warner screamed at Aiden Markram up the other end.

Warner was in full attack-dog mode at Kingsmead that day and inevitably took things too far.

As the two teams walked into the dressing-rooms with Australia one wicket from victory after play on the fourth day, a wild altercation took place in the stairwell, with Warner getting into the grill of Quinton de Kock.

David Warner and Quinton de Kock had an altercation during the first Test. (News Video)

The footage of that incident, released on the morning of the final day, was revealed by the sort of grainy CCTV footage used to indict street brawlers, befitting the grimy nature of what was turning into a desperately ill-tempered series.

Warner's aggression, although pretty standard at times throughout his career, was far from entirely unprovoked.

During that Test, a pair of Cricket South Africa officials were photographed wearing Sonny Bill Williams masks, part of a foul, hideous dig at Warner via his wife, Candice that several spectators were using to get under the then-Australian vice captain's skin.

Australia won the first Test by 118 runs, but as the series moved to Port Elizabeth, now known by its Xhosa name, Gqeberha, the Proteas roared back to win by six wickets.

Player of the match Kagiso Rabada took 5/96 and 6/54 and turned a broad shoulder towards Australia's belligerence, literally in one instance by physically barging into Smith after dismissing him and delivering a meaty verbal send-off.

Rabada also gave Warner a fair serve when dismissing him and was promptly handed a ban for an accumulation of demerit points, ending his series.

Much to Australia's frustration though, a high-profile lawyer was recruited by Cricket South Africa to successfully get Rabada's charge downgraded.

Sandpapergate

Steven Smith (right) and Cameron Bancroft (left) tried to explain their actions. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

As the febrile circus moved to Cape Town, English officials Nigel Llong, Richard Illingworth and Ian Gould came into the series as part of a pre-planned switch.

They stood in that third Test having been given some news from the departing team that made them wary. There was a suspicion that Australia were "working a little too aggressively on the condition of the ball", as Gould recounted in his autobiography, a ball that was reverse swinging early and exorbitantly, and had been all series.

The host broadcaster, Supersport, had also been alerted and were paying a little extra attention to how the Aussies were handling the ball in this Test.

What those cameras saw sent shock waves through world cricket as Cameron Bancroft, aged 25 and playing in just his eighth Test, was shown using a square of sandpaper to rough up the ball.

Loading...

He initially denied it, despite the cameras showing, in excruciating detail, the opening batter rubbing the ball with the offending square, before dropping it into his pants when he was alerted to having been rumbled, the TV cameras already having picked up his pitiful attempt at subterfuge.

Australia initially admitted to attempting to alter the ball, but it was only later that it was revealed to have been by sandpaper, which shifted the offence from opportunistic to pre-planned cheating.

Bancroft was banned for nine months. Smith and Warner, 12, and the toxic-trending culture within the Australian men's cricket team was placed firmly under the spotlight.

The subsequent emphatic, 492-run defeat at The Wanderers in Johannesburg handed South Africa a series victory.

That series was South Africa's first victory against Australia since 1970.

The 1970 series was followed by a 22-year absence of Test cricket in the nation as a result of apartheid.

Their 2018 win resulted in a far happier outcome.

Sandpaper scars

South Africa are the reigning world Test champions. (Getty Images: Mike Hewitt)

The victory eight years ago was a crowning one for a South Africa team that realised they could beat Australia, despite the clear inequality imposed by cricket's big three that unceremoniously shoved South Africa off the sport's top table.

This return is hardly groundbreaking.

Australia has been back to play cricket in South Africa twice since 2018 — in limited overs series in 2020 and 2023.

But limited overs cricket holds all the detail and intrigue of a one-line newspaper cartoon-strip.

Test cricket is a novel-length feature, weaving gripping storylines with the drama and prestige that elevates it to a completely different level, the sort of contest that transcends sport and bleeds into the front pages.

Sandpapergate has to be considered, when compared to controversies such as the Bodyline or the D'Oliveira affairs, on the lower end of issues to have garnered comment at government level.

David Warner and Steve Smith both served a 12-month ban for their roles. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Lee Warren)

But it illustrates perfectly what Test cricket can mean.

There will be none of that this time around.

Warner has retired, Bancroft's continued omission is evidenced only by the absence of two genuine openers in the Australian team, while Smith returns, as vice captain no less, and remains a batter of irresistible quality.

And South Africa, despite having played just four Tests to Australia's 10, fewer than any other team in the table, are Australia's closest challengers, sitting in second place.

It's a recipe for another fiercely competitive series, but one that will hopefully not boil over this time, especially knowing that these matches will be filmed for the latest fly-on-the-wall documentary series.

World.title: 'One of the greats' signs off after fourth Roosters premiership
World.content:
Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson has hailed Daniel Tupou as one of the NRL club's all-time greats after the four-time premiership-winning winger announced his retirement.

Tupou is ending his 15-year career on a high after helping the Roosters win Sunday's grand final against Newcastle.

The 35-year-old, who had been coy about his future all season, became just the sixth player in Roosters history to win four premierships with the club.

Across a 307-game, one-club career, the winger scored 198 tries, the third most of any player in premiership history behind Ken Irvine and Alex Johnston.

"When you look at what Daniel Tupou has achieved over 15 seasons, he will stand as one of the greats," Robinson said in a statement.

"But those numbers only tell part of the story of Toops and what he means to this club.

Tupou a Roosters grand final specialist Daniel Tupou is edging closer to becoming the first Roosters player in more than 80 years to win four premierships because he always finds his best on the biggest day of the season.

"Since he made his debut, he has represented what we want a Rooster to be.

"He has been incredibly consistent, selfless and dependable, and whenever there has been a big moment or a tough moment, he has been present.

"Toops revolutionised the aerial game at the Sydney Roosters and became the greatest high-ball specialist of all time."

Tupou's exit comes as the Roosters prepare for a big off-season exodus over the coming weeks.

Fellow winger Mark Nawaqanitawase and second rower Angus Crichton are moving to rugby union, playmaker Daly Cherry-Evans is heading to Super League side Hull FC, and Connor Watson is joining St George Illawarra.

But none of them gets close to having the impact the towering winger has had on the Roosters since his NRL debut in 2012.

As well as four premierships (2013, 2018, 2019, 2026), Tupou has won three World Club Challenges and played Test matches for both Tonga and Australia.

He was part of the Tongan side that defeated the Kangaroos in 2019 in one of the biggest upsets in international rugby league history.

Tupou played 10 times for NSW at State of Origin level between 2014 and 2022.

"We love Toops, we're incredibly proud of him, and his name will always hold a very special place in the history of the Sydney Roosters," Robinson said.

Tupou retires as the greatest try-scorer in Roosters history after surpassing Anthony Minichiello in 2023.

World.title: Lionel Messi scores final goal in emotional farewell to Argentina
World.content:
Lionel Messi has delivered one last masterclass in blue and white as Argentina's captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international ​career by scoring a goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.

The 39-year-old's final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental Stadium was less about football ​and more a national ‌celebration of Messi's service to Argentina.

Landmarks across the capital glowed with the team's sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans ‌poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina's national anthem.

Messi's family watched proudly ⁠from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of ‌1978, 1986 and 2022.

"Even through the worst moments we went through, I never stopped fighting, battling, giving everything I had, wanting to always be here," Messi told the crowd after full-time.

Lionel Messi was emotional as he signed off from international duty. (Getty Images: Marcos Brindicci)

"I love all of you, and I will miss all of you. I am proud to be Argentine."

Hours earlier, a ​massive number 10 shirt ‌emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's home town.

As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route.

When the teams took the pitch, Benin captain Sessi D'Almeida looked lost ​for ‌words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake.

The crowd rose for applause and more fireworks erupted in the stadium as the clock ticked past the 10th minute of the match.

After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home ⁠Argentina's opener.

Otamendi shared 17 years with ‌Messi in the national team, including ‌four World Cups, and was also ending his international career.

Messi then set up Nico Paz, one ‌of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina's number 10 shirt, to score the second goal.

In a fairytale ending, Messi converted ‌a penalty ​for 3-0, his 126th ⁠international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd.

At the final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky to mark the end of his magnificent ⁠Argentina career.

Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international ‌stage into a ‌story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs.

For years, Argentina asked ​Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say thank you.

Reuters

World.title: Are Test cricket batters getting worse? The stats say yes
World.content:
Australia's men's head cricket selector, George Bailey, pointed out some home truths recently when questioned on the woes of Test number three Marnus Labuschagne.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," Bailey said, and he's not wrong.

With the first of three Tests against South Africa beginning on Friday ahead of a mammoth run of matches against New Zealand, India and England, Australia's batting line-up will be scrutinised like never before.

Marnus Labuschagne picked a good time to score a century ahead of the first Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Since the beginning of the Border–Gavaskar Trophy at home in 2024, Australia has played 18 Tests with only three batters averaging more than 40: Steve Smith (49.4), Travis Head (46.25), and Alex Carey (40.3).

Beau Webster (33.5) and Cameron Green (30.16) are the only other batters averaging over 30 during the period.

Australia's bowlers have repeatedly dug the batters out of a hole, with the team winning 13 of those 18 matches.

Darren Lehmann sees clear reasons for the decline in Test batting, with serious consequences for the game (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

But Australia's batters aren't alone: Across all 12 Test-playing nations, the game has undergone a huge transition with batters fading and bowlers dominating.

The rise of T20 cricket, better balls and seaming wickets have all played a part.

ABC Sport has done an analysis of all Test batters over the past 40 years with the help of ABC radio cricket statistician, Ric Finlay.

Steve Smith, Travis Head and Alex Carey have all averaged more than 40 over the past 18 Tests. Marnus Labuschagne is in the 20s. (Getty Images: Phillip Brown)

We've looked at batters from one to seven and found the same patterns across all positions.

We could list a table of 40 years but to make things easy, we've broken it down to five-year periods that include every test played from the beginning of 1987 to the most recent Test between England and Pakistan.

To see the patterns, we're narrowing the numbers down to batting averages, run rates and average balls per wicket.

Looking at these figures, you can see that the average of all batters in positions one to seven peaked in the period between 2002 and 2016 before dropping back to the low 30s.

It's easier to visualise with a chart that shows the year-by-year average as well as a rolling five-year average to even out the yearly variations.

The period between roughly 2003 and 2014 is when averages were highest.

This coincides with a golden period for world-class test batsmen when the likes of Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, Australia's Ricky Ponting, South Africa's Jacques Kallis, England's Kevin Pietersen, India's Virender Sehwag and the West Indies' Shivnarine Chanderpaul, to name just a few, were at their peak.

Ricky Ponting was at his peak in the early 2000s. (ABC News)

The rolling five-year average is now at a 40-year low, but that only tells part of the story.

To understand more about the decline of Test cricket batting, two other charts fill in the picture.

The first is strike rate: how many runs batters score per 100 balls.

Batters' strike rates have increased across the board from 41.34 to 58.13: that's almost 17 runs per 100 balls, which is the equivalent of an extra run per over.

But while batters are scoring much faster, they're also getting far out more quickly.

Bowlers are now taking wickets faster than at any time in the past 40 years.

In 1989, top-order batters were lasting more than 85 balls between wickets in the rolling five-year average, while as of this year, wickets are falling every 58 balls — an all-time low.

From the peak to the current trough that's a fall of more than 32 per cent.

It's no accident that we're seeing so many shortened Test matches, like the two-day match in McKay against Bangladesh in August.

The overall figures are mirrored in virtually every individual batting position with averages on the whole going down.

In other words, we have seen a fundamental shift in the battle between the bat and ball playing out over the past four decades and right now, while batters are scoring more quickly, the bowlers are on top.

The same is true for Australia's one to seven batters.

Again we see the early 2000s peak in averages when Ricky Ponting, Matthew Hayden, Justin Langer, Damien Martyn and Adam Gilchrist were in their pomp.

The combined batting rolling average for positions one to seven is now at a 40-year low.

The strike rate rolling average is at an all-time high, although only marginally ahead of that early 2000s era.

But the balls per wicket figure rolling five-year average has dropped alarmingly from its starting high of 98.33 to its current all-time low of 54.26

That's a fall of almost 45 per cent.

To put it another way, opposition bowlers are taking Australian wickets almost twice as quickly as they were 40 years ago.

So, why is this happening?

Former Australia coach and batter, Darren Lehmann, who's currently coaching English country side Northamptonshire, highlights four major changes in cricket that are all linked.

Darren Lehmann (right) as coach of Australia in 2014, with the current head of selectors, George Bailey, and the late Rod Marsh. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour)

The first is the rise and rise of T20 cricket.

"Now they [batters] just don't leave balls," he told ABC sport.

"They have to score off more, so they play more shots to more risky balls in Test cricket,"

"Hence they go at balls they shouldn't go at, which they normally wouldn't have 20 years ago."

The second reason, Lehmann said, was the state of Test wickets around the globe, which he said were spinning and seaming more and earlier.

"They've got more in them and that is a by-product of making sure you get results," he said.

Lehmann said the balls used in Test Cricket, the Kookaburra and Duke, had added an extra layer of lacquer, which meant they stayed harder and the seam stayed prouder for longer, creating more movement.

"Blokes are playing shots to balls they shouldn't because they're trying to score before they get one that gets them out," Lehmann said.

The fourth reason bowlers are on top of batters is the one that ties it all together: data analytics.

"You're honing in on the weakness of players better than you did in the past and you're relentless with that.

"So, if a bloke can't cover drive or doesn't play well off the front foot, you now target that area with more balls, and you don't go away from that."

Mitchell Starc can be relied on to take wickets. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

"If a bloke gets out to a left-armer all the time, well you get Mitchell Starc straight on."

Sooner or later, the batter's lack of patience, the moving ball and seaming wicket combined with the bowler's knowledge of their opponent's weakness will result in a wicket.

Cricket's delicate balance between bat and ball has fundamentally shifted and the cost is two-day test matches like the Boxing Day Ashes test, which cost Cricket Australia millions.

Lehmann said wickets needed to get flatter or lacquer taken off balls in order to shift the balance back towards batters.

"There are consequences: two-day games in Test cricket can cost people their jobs."

Failing Test batters can also lose one of the most coveted jobs in Australian sport.
