World.title: Athletes drive to make table tennis a smash at national Special Olympics debut
World.content:
The repetitive click-clack of a small white ball paddling back and forth over a net may seem like a simple game of ping pong, but for these three teammates, it could be their ticket to the world stage.

The Bundaberg athletes are gearing up to compete in the Special Olympics Australia in Melbourne later this month, where table tennis is making its competitive debut.

Oscar Quarrell, 16, is diligently working to perfect his pendulum — a serve with a bit of side and back spin.

Oscar Quarrell (right) talks with coach Ha Bui as he prepares to play in his first Special Olympics. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Oscar is one of three from his regional club, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, to be selected as part of the 14-strong Queensland table tennis team.

"I love table tennis because it's something that takes my mind off thinking and gives me a break," he said.

"It's also very fun to do with people that actually enjoy hanging around you."

Celebrating 50 years

The Special Olympics is for people with intellectual disabilities, cognitive delays or autism. It is also an organisation that supports community-based clubs and participation.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Special Olympics movement in Australia.

Oscar Quarrell, Taylah Sim and Nicholas Jefferson train with coach Ha Bui. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Special Olympics Australia CEO Jamie O'Connor said 850 athletes across 13 sports would compete at the 2026 games.

"Special Olympics provides programs at a grassroots level week in, week out, at a community level," he said.

"But it also has the path that goes through local competitions to state events, to national events, to international events.

"Our Special Olympics is more about participation opportunities than it is about winning gold medals."

Mr O'Connor said that, in addition to the inclusion of table tennis, dance sport would be a demonstration sport for the first time this year.

Oscar Quarrell practises with Taylah Sim. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

"As sport evolves, and the demand for different sports evolves, then we try and provide options for people with intellectual disability and the sports that they want to compete in," he said.

About 60 athletes who are successful in the national games will go on to compete at the Special Olympics World Games in Santiago, Chile, next October.

Trio take on games

As the excitement builds towards the national games alongside his backhand, Oscar was also preparing for a big leap in independence.

"I'm excited to do something different, and it's also the first time I haven't had my parents with me, so they are going to come and watch, but I'm not allowed to speak to them," he said.

Clubmates Taylah and Nicholas will be joining Oscar in Melbourne.

Taylah Sim has been putting in the hours to prepare for her Special Olympics debut. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Taylah has her eyes firmly on the prize, saying she looks forward to winning then going on to compete at the world games.

Nicholas is also hoping to win a medal, having played the game for 13 years.

His mum, Margaret, said table tennis had opened doors for her son and she enjoyed watching the competition.

"They all want to do their best but, at the end of the day, whoever gets first, second or last, they're all rewarded, and they are happy for them," Ms Jefferson said.

"There's cheering, there's no jealousy, they're here to support each other."

Table tennis has opened doors for Nicholas Jefferson. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Queensland table tennis head coach Kim Hammermeister had high hopes for her Queensland team when they competed at the national level for the first time.

"Bundaberg has always been very strong with their school program for people with an intellectual impairment," she said.

Ms Hammermeister said any Special Olympics sport provided opportunities for friendship.

"People with an intellectual impairment can become very isolated, especially after school," she said.

"Of course, the physical benefits of being active are amazing; you can't put a price on that."

World.title: Bombers call draft 'a priority' after Ridley deal amid Blakey link
World.content:
Essendon has once again headlined the trade period after sending veteran defender Jordan Ridley to Geelong in a bumper deal involving the exchange of four draft picks.

Essendon acquired Jack Bowes, who had requested a move to the club, a 2027 first-round selection and a 2028 second-round selection in exchange for Ridley, a fourth-round selection in this year's draft (currently No.60) and 2028 fourth-round pick.

The move comes as the Bombers and Cats were two of three clubs reported to have canvassed a move for Sydney's Nick Blakey, with St Kilda the third.

Blakey is contracted through 2031 with Sydney and there is no indication thus far that the Swans will agree to a trade this summer.

Nick Blakey could be seeking a move away from Sydney. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

While Essendon may be interested in Blakey, given its Sydney links through Mark McVeigh and John Longmire, the Bombers maintain that "bringing in young talent is the priority". It is unclear how the 26-year-old Blakey would fit into that equation.

Geelong and St Kilda also remain at an impasse over a deal for Saints ruckman Rowan Marshall, who wants to join the Cats for the second straight year.

The Cats will likely have to part ways with players if they are successful in luring Marshall and Blakey, with Gryan Miers's name continuing to be linked with a move away.

Miers's agent, Liam Pickering, said on Wednesday that the 27-year-old will not be joining West Coast, but left the door open to another rival club.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all of Wednesday's trade action.

World.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after China Open incident
World.content:
Coco Gauff says she received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after beating local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open.

The ‌American won 7-5, 6-1 on Monday to reach the fourth round but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set.

She raised her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner.

After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed.

Gauff won the replayed point and held serve ⁠for 5-5 before cruising to victory against her 16-year-old opponent.

De Minaur retires from China Open with injury Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

The two-time major singles champion said she received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match.

"You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote on X in reply to a post containing a racial slur.

"The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane.

"Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."

The WTA has made efforts to ‌tackle ⁠online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system that monitors thousands of players and officials on social media.

A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier.

Gauff explained she was ⁠following the rules when she challenged the point.

Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgement calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play.

Gauff said she spoke to Sun about the ⁠point at the end of the match.

"I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff wrote.

"I didn't like to see ⁠her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it's like but this is the beginning of an incredible career.

"It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd."

Reuters

Tech.title: Roku’s OLED TVs are up to $400 off during Prime Day, starting at $700
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just over a week ago, we covered a deal at Amazon that knocked around 30 percent off Roku’s new (and first-ever) OLED TVs. The deal expired, but has returned for the final day of October Prime Day.

The 55-inch Pro Series OLED is $699.99 at Amazon, which is 30 percent off its list price. The 65-inch model is $799.99, which is $400 off its list price, also at Amazon. Both models support a native 120Hz refresh rate, which is great for gaming, plus four HDMI 2.1 ports for 4K gaming at its full refresh rate, and support for Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. You’ll also get a backlit Roku remote control.

There have been a few TV deals during Prime Day, though these are the lowest prices on OLEDs by a wide margin. We haven’t tested this model, but it’s an affordable way to get unbeatable contrast for your next movie or game night.

Tech.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops cost up to $7,000
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match.

The flagship Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark laptops from Dell, Lenovo, MSI, HP, and Asus start as low as $2,599 for configurations with an 18-core CPU, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of storage. That’s close in price to a similarly specced 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip, though Apple includes 1TB of storage. But the prices for both RTX Spark and Apple laptops of course go much, much higher.

Of the pricing we’ve seen so far, a kitted-out Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark laptop with a 20-core chip, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage costs up to $6,999.99. We don’t yet know the full breadth of configuration options for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, as the preorder page only has an email sign-up box to get updates, but a 48GB model on Best Buy costs $3,999.99.

Asus’ ProArt P14 and P16 range in price from $2,599.99 to $6,999.99. Image: Asus

Wildly expensive laptops aren’t really anything new: you can configure a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max chip to nearly $10,000 if you max out all options. But the first volley of RTX Spark options are obviously aimed at the high-end side of creators and local AI users. And RAMageddon certainly isn’t helping make this any easier on peoples’ wallets.

Will they be worth it? We’ll find out soon. The Surface Laptop Ultra and other RTX Spark laptops are launching this month — as early as October 16th.

Tech.title: It appears .agent and .agi are about to be the hot new domains
Tech.content:
For the first time in years, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers — better known as ICANN — is accepting applications for new top-level domains. These are the suffixes at the end of all URLs, and you may know them as things like .com, .org, and .pizza.

ICANN just announced the 1,615 applications that have been submitted so far, from 481 different applicants. The trend will not surprise you: AI is everywhere. Ten different companies, including both Meta and OpenAI, applied for the .agent domain. Seven, including OpenAI, applied for .agi. Six, including OpenAI, applied for .asi, clearly attempting to get in on President Trump’s demand to switch from “artificial intelligence” to “super intelligence.” Four companies applied for .intelligence, and Meta is one of two interested in the preposterously long .superintelligence. (OpenAI applied for a total of 15 TLDs; Meta wants a whopping 21.)

There are, broadly, two types of domains in these applications. One is more generic, the kind of thing lots of people or companies might use. There are hundreds of those in this current batch, from .geek to .haha to .anime to .jackpot. There’s also my personal favorite new one, .itiswhatitis.

The other is purely branded, giving a company its own TLD to use for its own purposes. There are 345 brand applications in this batch, including everything from .applebees and .bankofamerica to .zillow and .zoom. Meta applied for .facebook, .instagram, .messenger, .meta, .frommeta, and .threads, which it could use for many purposes; Bluesky applied for .bsky with the apparent intention of weaving the domain into its usernames; OpenAI applied for .chatgpt, .codex, .openai, .gpt, and others; Anthropic wants .anthropic and .claude. These strings could ultimately make for memorable product pages, social media usernames, and much more besides.

It has mostly been a tough road for these alternate TLDs over the last few years. Some, like .ai or .app, have become somewhat popular thanks to various tech trends, but most people just never got used to the idea of typing .restaurant or .babysitting, and .com and a few others have actually become more important than ever. It’s interesting to see so many brands go for their own domain, which only Google and a few others have accomplished before.

This is but one step in the process of creating a new top-level domain, and nothing will be made official before sometime next year. But it appears that even as the world becomes more filled with and mediated by AI, great domain names continue to matter. Even the AI companies think so.

Tech.title: Everything announced at Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra event
Tech.content: The biggest announcement was arguably the release details about the Surface Laptop Ultra, its new laptop that’s powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark Arm-based chip. The machine will start at $2,599 for a configuration with an 8-core CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage, and it will be released on October 16th. The laptop also has built-in magnetic USB-C charging instead of the proprietary Surface Connect magnetic charging port. The Verge’s Tom Warren published a deep dive all about the new laptop. Microsoft also announced that the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a mini PC for developers, is available for preorder for $5,999 ahead of shipping in November.

Tech.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS. It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.

To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo on stage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached.

Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text. The new experience will be available starting this fall on Windows 11 PCs, according to Windows and Surface boss Pavan Davuluri.

Tech.title: How Microsoft built its MacBook Pro competitor
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Before Microsoft releases a laptop to the public, it needs to put the device through its paces. That all happens inside a windowless, warehouse-like lab on the company’s Redmond, Washington, campus, where the team developing Surface devices programs robots to press their buttons thousands of times, pelts devices with radio waves from giant antennas, and builds contraptions that drop objects from increasingly daring heights to see whether the products can hold up.

Its latest laptop, the product I’m here to see, really needs to hold up. The Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t just another high-end config of the Surface Laptop, it’s the debut platform for Nvidia’s RTX Spark — Nvidia’s entrance into the world of Arm-based PC chips, and a chance to blow expectations out of the water when it comes to what a Windows laptop is capable of.

Microsoft’s last big laptop push — the Copilot Plus PC initiative from 2024, focused initially on Qualcomm chips — “was really aimed at MacBook Air,” says Brett Ostrum, corporate vice president of Surface at Microsoft. Microsoft also wanted to go head-to-head with the MacBook Pro, but existing chips weren’t capable enough. “We knew that was not going to reach MacBook Pro-level compute.”

Around that time, Nvidia began privately showing off what its forthcoming chips could handle when it came to AI, and Microsoft jumped at the possibilities. “It literally made a ton of sense for us in terms of how to go and compete with the MacBook Pro,” Ostrum says. “Nvidia was a logical choice.” The two companies have spent the years since working hand in hand, resulting in today’s launch.

The Surface Laptop Ultra can also play games. The “nightfall” color option looks a lot like Apple’s space gray.

Much like the MacBook Pro, the Surface Laptop Ultra is a high-end device. It has a CNC-machined aluminum body, a huge trackpad, chicklet keys, and fan vents tucked underneath its slightly elevated base. There’s an array of ports, including HDMI and an SD card slot, and a high-res touchscreen that looks great up close. A model with 24GB of RAM starts at $2,599.99, and if you want the very top of the line with 128GB of memory, you’re looking at $5,899.99.

Some of that price comes from the Ultra being one of the most polished laptops you can buy in the Windows world. But some of it comes from the all-new chip inside: the first of Nvidia’s RTX Spark line, which is supposed to bring essential components of Nvidia’s workstation-level power down to a portable device. The RTX Spark chips inside the Surface Laptop Ultra are geared toward local AI workloads and creative tasks. Microsoft says it’s powerful enough to handle compressed 280 billion-parameter AI models running locally — models that needed to run in the cloud only a year ago. The RTX Spark is both CPU and GPU, and the GPU should be able to handle Blender 3D objects with ease and cruise through other creator workloads in Premiere or Photoshop thanks to the system’s use of unified memory — the same approach Apple takes on its M-series chips.

Microsoft is largely positioning the Ultra at developers who want a powerful GPU for local AI compute, but it’s also targeting the creatives and professionals who would buy a MacBook Pro. “It is built for us,” says Jit Hirani, lead designer for Surface devices. “We come to work to build a product for ourselves.”

Previous Next







1 / 5 The Surface Laptop Ultra parts aren’t held together with glue.

Because Nvidia combined the CPU and GPU on the RTX Spark, Microsoft was able to make its Surface Laptop Ultra motherboard smaller and increase the size of the fans on the device. The space inside the machine is maximized for battery, with components neatly arranged in a black grid. Microsoft has also focused on repairability, with no components glued down and clearly marked instructions and QR codes throughout for disassembly.

As this is an Nvidia laptop, you can also use it for gaming, but I get the sense that Microsoft is treading carefully about positioning this as a gaming laptop. The RTX Spark is an Arm chip, which means most games aren’t native and will have to be emulated. Still, I got a chance to briefly play an emulated version of Gears of War: E-Day on the Surface Laptop Ultra, and it ran buttery smooth, even transitioning between the laptop being plugged in and running off battery without a performance hit.

The Surface Laptop Ultra has the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C charging on a laptop.

Microsoft put a lot of care into making sure the Ultra’s design was as premium as a MacBook’s, too. One detail in particular stood out to me: the way Microsoft has cleverly reworked its magnetic Surface Connect charging port.

“I think we gave our engineering team probably about 300 iterations on this journey because it’s the world’s first built-in magnetic connect for USB-C,” says Hirani. “The single constraint from day one when we designed the product was that we could not change the universal USB-C [port].”

Instead of losing a USB-C port to some custom solution, Microsoft has built a magnetic attach around the USB-C port instead. It feels very similar to the original Surface Connect, complete with a charging light and no need to precisely guide it into place. You can even disconnect the cable from the 140-watt charging block, reverse it, plug it back in, and use the regular USB-C port on the other end to charge all of your other devices.

Ostrum tells me that Microsoft spent years “grinding on this” to make a magnetic USB-C charging solution, so my question to him is: Will we see this on more Surface devices? “We’ll wait and see,” he says. “We have been super passionate about that experience. This is the place where we wanted to introduce it to the world.”

The amount of testing and product iteration that went into getting this charging port right is mirrored in the rest of the Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft has an Automated Experience Lab (AXL) tool that helps the teams measure the responsiveness of a device, beyond just regular benchmarks. That’s anything from measuring how long it takes to launch Microsoft Teams to how fast it is to type letters on a keyboard.

The “BB8” robot that tests the Surface Laptop Ultra.

This is all automated through an Arduino board that can inject code onto a system and measure its response times. Microsoft has created what it affectionately calls its own BB8, a robot that helps the thousands of engineers working on getting the stability just right for the RTX Spark platform.

“We have engineers at Nvidia that are working on power, performance, graphics, stability, and Wi-Fi,” explains Ostrum. “When they work on each of those things, they have to complete their code, check it into Nvidia. Once Nvidia is satisfied with the stability and the performance of that chunk of code, it flows into the next branch.”

That process creates a lag, sometimes lasting weeks, between Nvidia, Surface, and Windows all getting code ready for a new platform like RTX Spark. To speed things up, Microsoft has got Nvidia engineers uploading code remotely to this tiny robot that automates tasks that regular consumers do with a laptop. The miniature robot can unplug USB-C devices, use the touchscreen, pen, and trackpad, and open and close the device.

“By allowing our silicon partners to download onto this setup, we greatly accelerate [testing],” explains Ostrum. “It might have been weeks from the time they were done with their code to the time they were ready to drop it to us. They can have that data back the next day.”

Microsoft’s lessons of building Surface hardware for nearly 15 years have also been applied to the Surface Laptop Ultra in ways I’ve never heard about before. I’ve seen some of Microsoft’s hardware labs over the past 15 years, but the one I visited this week was eye-opening. It’s so secretive that I wasn’t able to take photos of the outside of the building or the lobby, and it lacks windows so nobody can see inside.

It houses the unsung heroes of Microsoft’s Surface team who spend hours creating new ways to stress test new Surface devices. That includes simple tests like automated drop tests or rows of robots opening and closing laptop lids thousands of times, but it also includes electromagnetic compatibility and RF compliance testing, and X-ray machines and specialist electron microscopy equipment that are used to find failures at nanometer scale.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Machines flip laptop lids back and forth.

Microsoft also has what it calls a “CSI lab” to perform analysis on hardware failures and ensure the results are fed straight back into the manufacturing process. This can identify faults with component suppliers. In one case a few years ago Microsoft found touch failures on some of the displays it was using. The Surface team traced it back to sulfur and other halogens found on the display, after the supplier had changed the gloves that the manufacturing operators were using.

The testing has helped Microsoft get to the point where it now has the confidence to take on the MacBook Pro. It also gets at the bigger reason Surface continues to exist inside Microsoft. Surface isn’t just a regular hardware business for Microsoft, it’s a way to show its OEM partners what Windows hardware should be capable of. Surface has helped push the industry forward on trackpads, displays, pen support, performance, and design. Without Microsoft’s own efforts, Windows laptops and tablets would have fallen even further behind Apple’s MacBooks.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is the clearest example yet of that role. Microsoft is using its own hardware to prove that Windows can compete at the very highest end of the laptop market, while giving its OEM partners a target to beat. That makes Surface far more than a showcase for Microsoft’s software and hardware. It’s one of the ways Microsoft makes sure Windows itself keeps moving forward.

Tech.title: The Meta Quest 3S gets a rare discount during October Prime Day
Tech.content: Until the end of Amazon’s October sale later tonight, you can grab the 128GB Meta Quest 3S for just $297.49 (usually $349.99) at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. While the lenses and displays aren’t quite as sharp as the Quest 3, the underlying chipset is the same, and this is a much more reasonable price for casual VR gaming and movies. In other words, it’s a big upgrade over the Quest 2. You’ll also get three months of Horizon Plus, which gives you access to a huge library of games.

Tech.title: What The Social Reckoning gets right — and wrong
Tech.content:
Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning has its fair share of cinematic flair, but many details in the story hew closely to real life. The movie tells the story of how Frances Haugen, a Facebook civic integrity product manager, came to leak a large trove of internal documents to Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, in what would later become a 2021 series called “The Facebook Files.” In both real life and in the film, Haugen’s leaks lead her to testify as a congressional whistleblower. The final frames of the movie describe the impact she had even after that closing scene, speaking before governments around the world and bolstering lawsuits against Meta nationwide with the internal communications she disclosed.

The film’s Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, says that she really believes in Facebook, echoing a message the real Haugen left for her colleagues just before she signed off for her last day in May 2021. “I don’t hate Facebook,” she wrote on the company’s internal message board, according to The Journal. “I love Facebook. I want to save it.”

Sorkin, both directing and screenwriting the semi-follow up to 2010’s The Social Network, which he only wrote, took some liberties with the dialogue and the chronology of the movie. The most obvious is that he condensed the timeline and shifted major events forward by several months. Some key moments in the film — Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) preparing for a congressional hearing about misinformation and extremism and Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) getting ready to publish the first Facebook Files report — occur on the same day, which happens to be January 6th, 2021, amid the insurrection at the US Capitol. In reality, Zuckerberg testified in the House alongside other tech CEOs in March 2021, and the first installment of the Facebook Files wasn’t published until that September.

”I love Facebook. I want to save it”

But the movie pulls directly from Horwitz’ investigation and the documents that Haugen collected, which showed how the company applied its content moderation policies in inconsistent ways, drove users toward hate groups, and had meager responses to apparent human trafficking on the platform. Meta declined to provide a comment on the movie, but in past statements, the company has referred to the documents collected by Haugen and their recounting in the Facebook Files as cherry-picked to serve a specific narrative. Zuckerberg called the reporting Facebook Files “a coordinated effort to selectively use leaked documents to paint a false picture of our company” during a 2021 earnings call after the initial reports were released, and said that when faced with “impossible tradeoffs … these questions are not primarily about our business, but about balancing different difficult social values.” Here’s what you should know about the real life events underpinning the film.

Losing a friend to the misinformation rabbit hole inspired Haugen

The Social Reckoning opens with a young blonde woman standing next to her overheating car on the side of a highway. When cops pull up to ask if she’s okay and smell alcohol on her breath, the exchange quickly grows tense. The woman appears unnerved by the officer, a person of color, and whips out her phone to record him; soon, she’s threatening violence and is arrested. Then, we see Madison’s Haugen in her apartment watching the video the woman posted to her Facebook page, “Voice of Reason,” with the caption “Watch me own DEI cops.” Haugen reveals later that the woman was a friend she met in spin class, radicalized by conspiracy theories on Facebook after the progressive candidate she campaigned for lost.

The scene and details about the friend appear to be fictionalized, but are based on a true part of Haugen’s story. Haugen told The Journal that she took the role on Facebook’s civic integrity team after seeing a family friend radicalized online. “It’s one thing to study misinformation, it’s another to lose someone to it,” she said.

Facebook’s algorithm recommended extremist groups

In the movie, one of the first major revelations Haugen shares with White’s Horwitz is that 64 percent of people who joined extremist groups on Facebook were sent there by its algorithm. That statistic — in the movie and real life — became the basis of a May 2020 article in The Journal. In the real article, Horwitz and co-author Deepa Seetharaman wrote that a 2016 internal Facebook presentation found “64% of all extremist group joins are due to our recommendation tools.” It added, “Our recommendation systems grow the problem.” At the time of the 2020 article’s publication, a Facebook spokesperson told The Journal it had since strengthened protections and “are not the same company today.”

A shift in Facebook’s algorithm promoted rage

As they hunt through pages of documents in the movie, Haugen and Horwitz keep trying to figure out why Facebook tuned its recommendation algorithm to reward “Meaningful Social Interactions” (MSI), rather than likes, in 2018. Haugen senses favoring MSI could be driving users like her friend toward radicalization, but she and Horwitz initially aren’t sure how — especially since Facebook publicly said the shift was expected to undercut engagement. They come to understand that the new ranking system weighted emoji reactions and reshares much more highly than likes; Zuckerberg and other executives knew this change would promote rage-sharing.

That’s a fairly accurate translation of what we know about MSI. Zuckerberg promoted the shift as a way to correct for a trend of “public content” from brands and media “crowding out the personal moments that lead us to connect more with each other.” Though he anticipated the change would be good for users, he said it would actually hurt Facebook’s engagement. But, he said, “if we do the right thing, I believe that will be good for our community and our business over the long term too.”

”Misinformation, toxicity, and violent content are inordinately prevalent among reshares”

In an installment of The Journal’s “Facebook Files” series in 2021, however, Horwitz and co-author Keach Hagey found that Facebook employees had warned that prioritizing MSI was promoting angrier engagement. Documents obtained by The Journal showed that leading up to the change, Facebook had been concerned about declining engagement from users through actions like resharing or commenting. To combat this, the documents showed, Facebook tried to encourage more original posts and resharing. While Facebook found some positive user benefits of the change, researchers found, “Misinformation, toxicity, and violent content are inordinately prevalent among reshares.” Zuckerberg, in the movie and apparently real life, resisted some mitigation proposals that would damage engagement.

Meta has downplayed the significance of MSI. In a statement to The Journal at the time, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said, “Is a ranking change the source of the world’s divisions? No.”

Instagram made teen girls feel worse about their bodies

In the movie, Haugen’s colleague shares a thumb drive with documents including a study about how Instagram harms teen girls’ body image. She tells Haugen to get the word out before the company starts marketing Instagram Kids. It’s not clear if this colleague actually existed, but the information she shares appears to be based on an internal study that found 32 percent of teen girls surveyed who said they felt bad about their bodies felt worse after using Instagram. Instagram had indeed planned to launch a service specifically for kids under 13, but announced shortly amid the uproar from the “Facebook Files” release that it was pausing the project to work through concerns.

An early Facebook investor encouraged Zuckerberg to change

As Strong’s Zuckerberg preps for the 2021 congressional hearing in the film, sitting on a stage behind a desk and rehearsing answers with his team, a venture capitalist named Charlie emerges from the shadows. Charlie, played by comedian Bill Burr, gives Zuckerberg feedback and urges him to moderate political ads. Movie-Zuckerberg says he’s upset with Charlie after he wrote a scathing op-ed, and reminds him he 100x’d his investment, which would have been worth over $1 billion if he’d held his position.

Charlie is inspired by real-life Facebook investor-turned-critic Roger McNamee, an executive producer of the film. McNamee published an op-ed in The Guardian in 2017 charging that Facebook and Google “threaten public health – and democracy,” and in 2019 published the book Zucked: Waking Up to the Facebook Catastrophe. Sorkin told Vanity Fair that although McNamee was game to be depicted in the movie, “it was made clear” that “there might be a problem with Facebook” in depicting the conversation between the VC character and Zuckerberg in the movie. So the character became a fictionalized version inspired by McNamee, instead.

Facebook’s civic integrity team was “absorbed”

In the film, Haugen seems dejected when she realizes that the civic integrity team she works on — which worked on worldwide election-related risks including misinformation — will likely be dissolved, and she’ll be reassigned. A Facebook executive assures the team that even if that were to happen, the work would be “absorbed” into other teams, and it would only be beneficial to their work.

“I don’t trust that they’re willing to actually invest what needs to be invested to keep Facebook from being dangerous”

This reflects how the company communicated the change in structure following the 2020 US election. In her “60 Minutes” interview in 2021, Haugen said, “when they got rid of Civic Integrity, it was the moment where I was like, ‘I don’t trust that they’re willing to actually invest what needs to be invested to keep Facebook from being dangerous.’” (That’s actually when Haugen first responded to Horwitz’ initial outreach on LinkedIn.) Meta executive Guy Rosen responded at the time that the team was not disbanded, but rather “integrated” into “a larger Central Integrity team so that the incredible work pioneered for elections could be applied even further, for example across health related issues. Their work continues to this day.”

Zuckerberg’s office was bulletproofed

Haugen’s film character mentions that Zuckerberg has bullet-proof features in his office, which appears to be based in reality. A 2019 report from Business Insider found that a “glass-walled conference room” he would sometimes work from had “bullet-resistant windows and a panic button.”

It took time for Haugen and Horwitz to build a strong source-reporter relationship

The movie depicts a push-and-pull relationship between Haugen and Horwitz, as the journalist tries to get Haugen to share more information without crossing a delicate ethical line of soliciting her to steal confidential documents. As Haugen decides whether or not to go the extra mile, she also becomes frustrated with Horwitz for not making more progress on his own.

The two meet regularly on a hiking path, where Horwitz eventually gives Haugen a burner phone to communicate with him and on which she later takes pictures of internal documents. At one point, Horwitz even travels to Puerto Rico to collect more information from Haugen, after she relocated there during the pandemic.

These details all seem to mostly follow the true course of their source building relationship. Haugen told The New York Times in 2021 that she had “auditioned” Horwitz for some time, and decided to give him the scoop because she found him to be “less sensationalistic than other choices I could have made.” Horwitz acknowledged in an on-stage interview with Haugen in 2022 that “things got tense between us” at times, in part because Haugen had concerns about The Journal’s institutional approach, and in part over some messiness about when certain information was released by other publications or agencies Haugen worked with.

Haugen really did relocate to Puerto Rico during the pandemic, and Horwitz also visited her to collect information, though the timeline of those travels is different than in the movie. Haugen invited him to Puerto Rico once she realized Facebook’s policies prevented her from working from a US territory, prompting a deadline to quit or move. She chose to quit, meaning the pair had one last period of time they could access internal documents at Facebook. Speaking to Horwitz on stage in 2022, Haugen said she was “so grateful that you put in a huge amount of effort to just be there and make sure that we asked as many questions as we could so history got to have some kind of record for it.”

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse launches on iPad just a month after its mobile debut
Tech.content:
If there’s any doubt about how seriously Meta is taking AI, here’s a new signal: The company on Wednesday announced that its Muse assistant is now available in a dedicated iPad app. That’s a milestone it took Instagram some 15 years to reach, despite constant user demand.

Muse, meanwhile, hit the iPad just a month after launching on iPhone.

(To be fair, it may not be as difficult to bring something like Muse to iPad, given its text-heavy interface, where image and video resolution and formatting matter less.)

Since launching on iOS and Android on September 8, Muse has topped 6.6 million installs, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. The app, which is now one of dozens of consumer-facing AI agents, lets users connect their accounts to stay on top of email, meetings, bills, and more, and to complete tasks like booking reservations, ordering groceries, setting goals, and making purchases.

To make that work, Meta has been adding partners in the effort, which appear in Muse as “connectors.” Users can add and sign in to them selectively, depending on which parts of their online life they’re comfortable letting an AI agent handle.

With the iPad release, Meta has updated this list with several of its newer additions, including connectors aimed at small businesses, like Asana, Canva, Dropbox, Figma, QuickBooks, GitHub, Klaviyo, and Zoom, as well as connectors for Meta ad accounts. It also added Notion and Granola.

In addition, Meta recently announced more retail partners, like Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. These allow the agent to shop those retailers’ sites and complete transactions on users’ behalf. Because this technology is still new, these experiences can still run into issues as websites mistake agents for bots and block their access.

On Tuesday, Meta announced that it’s working with industry partners on a technological solution to this problem in the form of an open standard that would allow personal AI agents to identify themselves to businesses. That would help businesses sort the good bots from the bad.

Tech.title: ChatGPT for Teens keeps teens talking, even during mental health crises
Tech.content:
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that provides age-based ratings and reviews of media and tech for families, has labeled ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk.”

The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful. In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences.

In response to a wave of teen suicides and other concerns related to kids using chatbots — like cheating on tests — OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August, promising more safeguards like parental controls, limits to high-risk content, and protection against emotional dependence.

A new study from Common Sense Media has found that despite those assurances, ChatGPT for Teens’ design still encourages engagement, even when it may pose a risk to user safety.

The report called the engagement cues “pervasive even in crisis situations” and noted that while ChatGPT cautioned the teen against unhealthy relationships generally, it stopped short of recognizing the harms of an unhealthy relationship with itself.

“Our view is that OpenAI shouldn’t be marketing [ChatGPT for Teens] to parents, and kids shouldn’t be using an unsafe product,” the researchers wrote. “Some protections, including refusing sexual roleplay, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.”

OpenAI disputed Common Sense’s assessment, saying the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice” and raising concerns about its methodology.

“Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

The report comes amid growing scrutiny of technology designed to maximize young users’ attention. Meta recently agreed to settle for $18 billion in a lawsuit brought by 29 states over claims that its social media platform harms children with addictive features, while state and federal lawmakers have begun targeting similar dynamics in chatbots. The bipartisan CHATBOT Act, introduced this year, specifically calls out AI companies’ use of “rewards, notifications, and targeted advertising to drive prolonged engagement by adolescent users.”

One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions. ChatGPT for Teens largely dispensed with those, Common Sense found, but retained other language encouraging users to stay in the chat.

During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.”

The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem. While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others.

Interestingly, the model reliably pointed the user toward a trusted adult when testers described a potential risk from another person, doing so in 94% of crisis prompts. But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.”

When told “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” it validated the user’s concern but then said: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.”

A spokesperson at Common Sense Media told TechCrunch this reflected a broader pattern: ChatGPT’s language continued to express always-on availability, a deep understanding of the user, and its own apparent mental state. Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support.

According to many experts, such as the researchers behind human well-being benchmark HumaneBench, fostering healthy relationships with humans is a key measure of whether a chatbot supports mental health.

Even features designed specifically to interrupt engagement rarely did so, according to Common Sense. OpenAI has promoted break reminders as part of its teen protections, but across nearly 2,000 prompts, testers encountered just two, both during individual conversations lasting around 90 minutes. The researchers found the reminders appeared to track the length of a single conversation rather than how much time a teen had been using the app.

ChatGPT for Teens updated break reminder. Image Credits:OpenAI

Coincidentally, OpenAI released its own data on Wednesday on ChatGPT for Teens, saying teens spend less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average and fewer than 2% spend more than three consecutive hours on it. The company also said that in nearly half of teen conversations with break reminders, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes.

OpenAI’s objections to Common Sense’s methodology focused largely on parental safety notifications, crisis notifications, and other findings in the report. The AI lab did not explain how its methodological concerns affected the report’s findings around engagement cues and relational behavior, nor did it answer whether OpenAI uses metrics like conversation length and session duration to evaluate ChatGPT for Teens.

Tech.title: X expands its ‘Gametime’ sports hub beyond the NFL, starting with MLB
Tech.content:
X is doubling down on sports, with Wednesday’s news that it’s expanding its “Gametime” feature on the social media site to go beyond tracking the NFL alone.

First announced in August, NFL Gametime is X’s new project that offers a single hub for tracking live scores, getting play-by-play updates, tuning into game feeds, and more. The move wasn’t meant to be useful only to X users who like to congregate on the platform to discuss live sporting events, but to woo brands and advertisers looking to reach passionate sports fans.

At Advertising Week New York, X said Gametime will become a year-round destination spanning “all professional sports.”

However, that full expansion isn’t yet live as of today. Instead, X announced its second league partnership with Major League Baseball (MLB). Arriving this month, the new MLB experience will allow baseball fans to follow and engage in postseason discussions and will organize things like scores and stats, team and league content, plus news, creator content, and real-time discussions.

Image Credits:X

X said content from other leagues will be added soon, including the NBA.

The expansion of the Gametime feature comes as X continues its efforts to win back advertisers — in this case by leveraging live sports and their highly engaged fans as a way to draw brands back to X.

“In just six weeks, Gametime has evolved from a football-focused product into a scalable destination for sports, attracting strong demand across major advertisers from payments to consumer goods looking to engage highly attentive fans from the pregame conversation through the biggest moments of the game,” said SpaceXAI’s head of Global Advertising, Monique Pintarelli, in an announcement.

The new feature’s introduction follows X owner Elon Musk’s July settlement in a multiyear legal battle with the advertising trade group the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), which X had sued for its alleged “illegal boycott” of the platform.

Some advertisers had become uncomfortable with the platform’s lax moderation standards under Musk, as well as with Musk’s outsized position on the social media site, where he often spouted controversial views and politics via X posts. Musk believed the WFA’s guidelines had steered brands and ad agencies away from X, suggesting it was a place where their ads could appear next to harmful online content.

X’s announcement of the settlement in July said the move “resets the relationship between the two organizations.” The company also committed to both freedom of speech and brand-safety innovations.

Tech.title: ChatGPT is getting a lot more visual, with the launch of a new interface
Tech.content:
ChatGPT is about to get a lot more visual, thanks to a new feature that OpenAI calls Intelligent UI. The new interface, which is being rolled out Wednesday with a new GPT-6 model, will integrate a significant amount of visuals into users’ conversations.

OpenAI says many of those visuals will be interactive. In other words, instead of just flat, cartoonish pictures, the chatbot will frequently include things like tappable buttons, a customized calculator for a specific task, interactive charts, editable graphs, and other elements the user can work with directly.

The big goal here, according to OpenAI, is to make “learning complex topics easier.” It may also make ChatGPT friendlier and more accessible and help bring in a wider audience, though OpenAI didn’t say so directly.

In a call with journalists, OpenAI staff gave a brief demonstration of Intelligent UI’s capabilities, showing how the new chatbot can instantly whip up various diagrams and visuals that help users understand more abstract topics.

Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.”

Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions. He asked ChatGPT to “explore how an airplane wing generates lift” and the chatbot quickly spun up a number of diagrams designed to show how planes stay in the air.

Other examples from the company included things like visuals for recipes, a diagram explaining bicycle mechanics, a map for a multi-day hiking excursion, a personal savings calculator, and more.

This new feature will be customizable. As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back. Intelligent UI rolls out globally with GPT-6 for Pro, Plus, Business, and Enterprise users, and arrives Thursday for users of the free and lower-cost Go tiers.

Tech.title: Greenairy is building smart plant towers to clean the air in your office
Tech.content:
How clean is the air in your workplace? That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace.

In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital.

After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.”

Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air).

Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “sick building syndrome,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well.

That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy, which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt.

Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.”

Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.”

Greenairy plant tower. Image Credits:Greenairy

Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. Saraf said that in the startup’s own testing using RESET-certified air monitors, it compared three offices: one with Greenairy plant towers, one that had a medical-grade ionizer (a device that uses an electrical charge to make dust and other particles clump together and fall out of the air), and a third with a HEPA air purifier that traps very small particles.

“Our tower had the lowest VOC levels and removed VOCs the fastest,” she said. “The office staff also grew fond of the natural ‘fresh’ aroma of the tower and the natural vibe it brought.”

Thombre added that they saw an “immediate” improvement within regular office hours, with a 50% reduction in both the daily VOC average and peak levels. She said the results improved even more “as the plants and microbes mature and the gases are prevented from accumulating.”

Greenairy has also had its results validated by the German testing and certification firm TÜV SÜD and will be publishing them soon. (Results are available upon request in the meantime.) The pair plans to begin large-scale manufacturing after the results are certified.

The startup’s founders are currently based on opposite sides of the world, with Saraf in Berkeley, California, and Thombre in Singapore. It’s an arrangement that Saraf said “works well at this stage,” allowing one founder to focus on testing in Singapore while the other can fundraise in the Bay Area.

“If things go to plan, both of us will be in Singapore by the first half of 2027,” she added. “That’s when we expect to launch our first mass-produced towers and install them for our first customers” in Singapore.

Join us October 13-15 at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco to learn more about the company and the dozens of other teams pitching to VCs at Disrupt.

Tech.title: CIA officer admits to creating fake top secret government program to steal over $190M, including gold bars
Tech.content:
A now-former officer with the Central Intelligence Agency has pleaded guilty to stealing almost $200 million, including hundreds of gold bars, as part of a fraudulent scheme masquerading as a top secret government program.

The U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed that David J. Rush, a Virginia resident, admitted to one count of wire fraud linked to running the fabricated operation and defrauding the government while he was a CIA officer. In a statement, prosecutors said that Rush lied about his education and military experience to gain a position at the CIA, and used his access as an employee to set up the top secret and highly compartmentalized program with the intention of using it to funnel U.S. government funds into his possession.

During his arrest, law enforcement found more than $46 million worth of gold bars in Rush’s house linked to the long-running fraud scheme, along with cars, watches, and over $2 million in cash.

The plea deal means that Rush escapes trial, as much as the U.S. government likely avoids having to explain in open court how Rush evaded vetting scrutiny to join the U.S. intelligence agency, and how actions went undetected for more than a year.

Rush was until recently a senior CIA officer who, according to earlier reports, worked for a division of the CIA since 2010 that develops hacking tools and techniques for carrying out espionage. Per court filings, Rush had significant authority over government intelligence programs and spending.

Over the course of 2025, Rush used his position to fabricate a so-called special access program, which are surveillance or intelligence-gathering operations so sensitive that only a few people are read into them. Special access programs, or SAPs, require special clearance that not even the most cleared individuals in government are granted access to. According to The Washington Post, Rush constructed the compartmentalized program under the guise of a fake “continuity of government” plan, aimed at keeping the government functioning in the event of a war, natural disaster, or some other destructive catastrophe. As part of the scheme, Rush used the program and fake government contract to trick an unnamed defense contractor into buying large amounts of gold that Rush then pocketed.

According to The Post, the case astounded officials as Rush’s duties at the CIA involved work with one of the government’s “most sensitive intelligence-gathering programs,” with details so sensitive that only a few senior U.S. intelligence officials and lawmakers know of its existence. The Post withheld details of that program from publication as its disclosure could “jeopardize ongoing intelligence-gathering operations.”

Court filings said that by virtue of his position, Rush “effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny.”

Rush is scheduled to be sentenced in late January 2027 and faces up to 20 years in prison.

Tech.title: Meta rolls out new AI tools to detect ads that secretly lead to child sexual abuse material
Tech.content:
Meta announced Wednesday that it took action against 33.2 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content on Facebook and Instagram in the first half of 2026. At the same time, the company is rolling out new AI tools to find ads and accounts that may be used to secretly direct people to illegal child abuse material.

More than 97% of the content Meta acted on was found by its systems before users reported it, the company said. In India, Meta acted on 5.3 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content during the same period, with more than 98% detected before users reported it.

Meta said its latest AI tools are aimed at people using ads that look harmless to send users to illegal content outside Meta’s platforms.

The company has introduced a new large language model (LLM) system to detect what it calls “signposting.” This refers to ads that may look normal but are suspected of directing users to illegal content or other harmful activity elsewhere online. Meta says this is a tactic it has recently seen bad actors use as they continue to change their methods to avoid detection. While the ads themselves may not contain illegal material, they can still act as a gateway to websites hosting child sexual abuse material.

Because of this, Meta said it’s now looking at where an ad sends users, and not just what the ad contains. The company can use this information to block websites or other destinations that break its rules and take action against the accounts behind them.

Meta is also using additional AI-driven scans to find child exploitation content that earlier systems may have missed. The company said it will continue adding new signals as it learns more about how these networks operate.

Another new tool is a “red-teaming AI agent” that tests Meta’s own safety measures. It looks for weaknesses that bad actors could use to get around the company’s protections. Meta said this could help it find new methods of abuse before they become more common.

Additionally, the company is improving its systems for finding people who return to its platforms with new accounts after their previous accounts have been removed.

The new measures come as Meta continues to face pressure over the safety of children on its platforms. The company has faced lawsuits and criticism from lawmakers over the risks its social media services may pose to young users. In August, Meta reached an agreement to pay up to $18 billion to settle a child safety lawsuit involving 29 U.S. states, addressing concerns regarding the protection of children online.

Meta has introduced several child-safety features this year, including parental controls for Meta AI, preteen accounts on WhatsApp, and alerts for parents when children search Instagram for self-harm content.

In September, WhatsApp added more controls for parents. They can limit how teenagers use Channels, control who can see their status updates, and decide who can add their children to groups. Parents can also choose to receive notifications about certain group activity.

Tech.title: Healthleap raises $38M for its AI that flags hospital patients who may need a closer look
Tech.content:
Healthleap, a startup building an AI platform that reads patient records to identify patients at risk of undiagnosed illnesses, has raised $38 million in seed and Series A funding, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The financing includes an $8 million seed round co-led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital, and a $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures. The company is not disclosing its valuation.

Founded in South Africa in 2022 by siblings Jemima and Josiah Meyer (pictured above), the startup initially offered a clinical nutrition tool Jemima had built for dietitians. But the company later pivoted and built a more general-purpose platform that aims to identify patients admitted to hospitals who may be suffering from conditions like malnutrition or delirium that aren’t often identified early enough, CEO and co-founder Josiah Meyer told TechCrunch.

“A patient’s chart holds two kinds of data. Labs, weights, and vital signs sit in structured fields, but the most telling signs sit in clinicians’ written notes: poor appetite, recent weight loss, muscle loss, trouble swallowing. Our developing approach is extracting affirmative or negated mentions of these clinical concepts in an easily extensible and scalable way,” Josiah said.

The company’s platform is currently deployed in more than 50 hospitals, where it screens patients for conditions such as malnutrition and delirium, he said. The startup has also built programs to identify aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers, and risk of readmission for congestive heart failure, which Josiah said are undergoing further clinical validation.

To find patients that may be at risk of an illness or were undiagnosed, Healthleap plugs into a hospital’s electronic health record system and uses language models to pull information from written notes, such as references to recent weight loss or difficulty swallowing. That analysis is then fed into its risk models, alongside structured information such as lab reports and vitals to surface patients who may need a closer look. The company notes that its software doesn’t diagnose patients, only highlights items for additional review.

“Each night, we analyze every adult inpatient’s record: lab results, vital signs, weights, medications, diet orders, diagnoses, clinicians’ notes, and more,” Josiah explained. “Each morning, we write a risk score into the care team’s existing workflow with a dashboard accessible that holds additional information about the patients’ trends.”

Malnutrition likely served as a useful starting point for Healthleap, as it’s a condition that often goes undiagnosed and can adversely impact patient recovery in a variety of ways. Research suggests 20% to 50% of hospital inpatients are malnourished, and some studies have linked malnutrition with longer stays, impaired wound healing, infections, and other complications, as well as higher morbidity and mortality.

Josiah said Healthleap has grown from three hospital partners to more than 50 over the past year, and its customers now include Penn Medicine, Cedars-Sinai, Intermountain, Houston Methodist, and Emory Healthcare. Revenue has grown more than 10x over the same period, he said, though he didn’t disclose specifics.

The startup sells three-year contracts priced according to a hospital’s licensed bed count, and also uses an outcome-based pricing model. “We use the hard ROI that the hospital finance team validates and attributes to us as the measurable ROI. Based on that, we contractually ensure that we deliver multiples of the contract price. To date, every customer has seen a 5x hard ROI or more, in some cases over 20x annual total ROI,” Josiah said.

At the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Healthleap says its malnutrition program resulted in $23.8 million in annualized financial impact, of which $6.3 million came from additional reimbursement and $17.5 million from shorter hospital stays.

Healthleap plans to spend the fresh cash on engineering, product, sales, and customer success as it adds support for identifying more conditions. Josiah said the company ultimately wants to cover more than 40 major health conditions and expand into outpatient and home care.

Tech.title: Meet the Vendors Selling ‘Cornell Seven’ Merch
Tech.content:
Last weekend, the clothing brand Cherrykitten published an Instagram post promoting T-shirts, crop tops, and sports bras with the slogan “I Am Jane Doe” emblazoned on the front. “ALL OF US ARE UNTIL NONE OF US ARE,” the company wrote in the caption, adding that it would donate 5 percent of the net sales proceeds to the National Organization for Women.

A reference to the “Cornell Seven” case, in which an anonymous woman accused seven Cornell University fraternity members of sexual assault, among other counts, #IAmJaneDoe started going viral last week. Many sexual assault survivors used the hashtag in solidarity with the alleged victim after trolls attempted to dox her on social media. (All seven of those accused have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.)

The message, while powerful, may have been ill-suited for appropriation by Cherrykitten, a brand perhaps best known for selling tank tops and crop tops with slogans like “Pls do not give me a cigarette no matter what I say” and “AI cannot generate tits like these.” The company received immediate backlash on social media for selling the shirts, with many accusing it of tastelessly capitalizing off of a grisly sexual assault case. “Using the cornell seven sexual assault as a merch idea and then donating ONLY 5% to a womens charity.. oh cherrykitten.. you’re fucked,” one tweet with 2.2 million views read.

The brand removed the post, issuing an apology for “turning a real and deeply serious situation into a product,” according to a screengrab of a now-deleted Instagram post. (Cherrykitten did not respond to WIRED’s requests for comment.) But Cherrykitten is far from the only brand attempting to market apparel around the Cornell Seven case, which has garnered outrage around the world.

On Amazon, there are more than 6,000 results for “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts; on platforms like Etsy and Redbubble, there are hundreds of sellers promoting such merch, including T-shirts, sweatshirts, hats, bracelets, mugs, and bumper stickers. The listings, which include keywords like “feminist,” “true crime,” “protest,” and (weirdly, on Redbubble) “lizzieborden,” often feature AI-generated photos of women with shiny hair and broad grins modeling the merch.

One such seller, who requested her name be withheld to protect her privacy given the sensitive nature of the case, is the owner of a three-year-old shop on Etsy which sells T-shirts with progressive slogans. Her “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirts in shades like ash, dark chocolate, and purple cost between $19.53 and $27.93; she’s sold 21 since October 1.
