Tech.title: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
Tech.content:
Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom, recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch.

They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case.

The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food.

“Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence, the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence.

Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments, suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world.

Tech.title: The New ChatGPT Is More Show Than Tell
Tech.content:
When you ask a chatbot a question, you’ll often get a wall of text back, maybe with an image or two pulled from the web. That may no longer be the case soon, as OpenAI overhauls how ChatGPT answers prompts.

On Wednesday, OpenAI unveiled an “Intelligent UI” update for ChatGPT that generates visual, custom elements—when helpful—for answering a user's questions. The company's new experience is powered by its recent GPT-6 model, which rolls out to paid users today and to free users tomorrow.

Courtesy of OpenAI

I got a quick test of the user interface before launch, and these visual elements felt like a welcome change. When I asked for a diagram of a slug, ChatGPT generated an anatomy-focused visual with buttons I could press for each different part, from the upper tentacles to the muscular foot. I also generated a San Francisco apartment affordability calculator with movable sliders to adjust income and other expenses, showing what percentage of my take-home pay different units would cost.

My favorite part of this quick hands-on with ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI was an airplane seat explorer. I’m not a fan of sitting in the exit rows, so I asked ChatGPT to generate a custom tool to compare the cabin layouts between four different Alaska and Delta planes. In its output, I could tap any seat on the map for more details, and ChatGPT highlighted the exit rows in green.

While useful in some results, every ChatGPT answer won’t suddenly include a chart or graphic. “We have a design team that spent a lot of time figuring out when adding a diagram, chart, or buttons adds value versus when it's starting to feel cluttered,” says Aarush Selvan, a product manager at OpenAI. If a user isn’t interested in visuals, they can tell ChatGPT to generate fewer of those outputs.

These visual results are similar to what Google announced earlier this year for Search when it expanded the bespoke results users may see. Google’s version is called “generative UI.” One example: If you want to better understand deep space, Search can output an adjustable graphic that breaks down how black holes work, using multiple sliders.

Tech.title: GPT-6 for All: Your ChatGPT Answers Are Getting a Very Visual Makeover
Tech.content:
OpenAI has been working this year to make ChatGPT more than a text-only service. Now, it’s rolling out a new intelligent user interface to bring interactive graphics, images and other visual displays into your AI answers, powered by GPT-6. The interface will be available to free users this week.

If you ask ChatGPT to explain the offside rule in soccer, the chatbot could create interactive graphics that let you adjust each player’s position on the field to see where the boundary lines would be in each scenario. You can also have the AI plan your dinner party menu and grocery list, with a slider you can adjust based on the expected number of guests. ChatGPT creates these custom images and graphics, but they’re based on information pulled from online sources, which should be cited in each answer.

Your next answer from ChatGPT might have more images and interactive elements. OpenAI

This new UI is powered by OpenAI’s latest flagship model, GPT-6. In addition to the new answer format, all ChatGPT users will have access to GPT-6 this week. It’s rolling out to Plus and Pro users on Wednesday, with plans to bring it to free users later in the week.

More from CNET

More complex tasks for AI models — like deep reasoning, image generation and running AI agents — eat up users’ allotted tokens or usage limits. OpenAI told CNET that while there’s more information in these AI images, it doesn’t expect this new visual interface to “meaningfully” change usage because “by and large it’s very efficient.” We’ll have to wait and see if that proves true for most users.

Despite being the company that made tech history with its text-synthesis AI model, OpenAI has worked to move its chatbot beyond text alone. It has invested in its voice mode, with new AI voice models that are better at conversation and language translation. Its image generation efforts, including ChatGPT Images 2.5, are also bolstering the company’s efforts to create more multimodal experiences for customers. The idea is to give users more options to customize how they use ChatGPT. But for now, this new intelligent user interface is limited to text prompts, though you can use voice-to-text to dictate your requests, OpenAI says.

Tech.title: Amazon Knows You Have a Goldfish Named Ziggy, Even if You Don’t
Tech.content:
Websites have long kept personalized information about their customers, and it can be useful. Bath & Body Works might alert you to a sale on its three-wick candles, or your local theater can tell you when the musical Six comes to town.

Few shopping sites have more information about customers than Amazon — currently on day two of its October Prime Day sales — which knows your book preferences, your shoe size and even which cereals you might buy at Whole Foods. But there’s something unnerving about seeing your Amazon personal purchase history distilled into a dossier of factoids — especially when some of them are wrong.

The Amazon About You page, a list of facts the company gathered from your purchases, made the news Tuesday after a post by Threads user fangirlinmegan was picked up by TechCrunch. In the Threads post, the user points out that, in addition to Amazon knowing that she “prepared for a Bluey-themed 2nd birthday celebration” and “consistently repurchases cat hairball treatment,” the giant shopping site has declared, under product preferences, that she “has flat buttocks.”

More from CNET

“I mean it ain’t wrong, but damn did you have to call me out like that?” she wrote on Threads.

How to find out what Amazon knows about you

Naturally, that sent other Amazon customers running to check out what personal data Amazon’s About You page keeps about them. It’s easy to find.

On your phone, log in to Amazon, tap the icon that looks like a little person (or chess pawn) in the bottom menu bar, then tap “shopping preferences,” then “about you.”

On a laptop or desktop, log in and hover over where it says “Hello” and shows your name in the upper-right corner of the page. Click on “account” under the “your account” heading, and then look far down under “ordering and shopping preferences,” and click on “your shopping preferences.” Once there, scroll down to “manage your information” to see your Amazon About You page.

An ‘established coffee routine’

My personal Amazon dossier was pretty boring. It knows that I “consistently replenish household essentials,” which was probably gleaned from my recurring Subscribe and Save orders for Bounty paper towels and Charmin. It knows what city I live in and that I have one child, though it underestimated said child’s age by almost a decade.

It knows my family is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” (Yes, and ouch.) Actually, my little summary makes me sound pretty classy. I did not know that my devotion to coffee and reading meant that I had an “established coffee routine” or that I “value classic and literary fiction.”

I also apparently “maintain a comprehensive beauty routine.” If “comprehensive beauty routine” means slapping on lipstick when I remember, and occasionally trying out a free foundation sample from Sephora… nailed it!

A fish called Ziggy

I may be boring, but other people have fairly hilarious Amazon dossiers. CNET Editor-in-Chief David Katzmaier shared a screenshot of what Amazon knows about him, and hoo, boy, did it really dig deep into his aquarium situation. The e-commerce behemoth knows he has a fish tank with a waterfall and a pond with goldfish that eat only algae, owns a snail, has a fully grown blue crayfish and even has a betta fish with bent fins.

It’s intriguing to track how Amazon garnered this information. If you buy fish accessories, just like I buy coffee and books, it’s not a huge leap to figure out you own fish. But the specificity (bent fins? the color of the crayfish?) is a bit shocking to see.

Most entertaining on Katzmaier’s list is Amazon’s confident declaration that he “owns a goldfish named Ziggy.” How exactly would it know the name of a goldfish? I can see how it might know the name of a cat or dog, as people do order ID tags, personalized beds or even Christmas stockings for their furry friends. But for a fish? And to make it more intriguing, he says the goldfish is not named Ziggy. But he knows where Amazon might have picked up that idea.

“We don’t actually have any fish named Ziggy, but my kid changed one of our Alexa smart speakers’ wake words to ‘Ziggy’ so I think that explains it,” he said. “The rest of this list is accurate.”

Amazon isn’t exactly hiding that it collects and curates this info. An Amazon representative pointed me to an article published in May on the company’s Amazon News site that shows and explains the preferences page.

And if you don’t want Amazon thinking about the shape of your butt, or are seeking privacy for Ziggy the goldfish, you can make those changes. I found it easy to delete or update some of the information Amazon had on me that I didn’t want used for personalization. Once you’re on your preferences page, clicking a specific statement lets you delete it.

It’s light, compact and requires minimal brain power to operate, which is a big boon during blurry-eyed early mornings.

Nikita praised the eco-friendly design, but was just as taken with the rich, flavorful coffee this one-of-a-kind machine produced. Picture a Keurig, minus the plastic K-Cups piling up in landfills. The tabs run about $1 each and are available through Amazon or directly from Lavazza.

More from CNET

Pods are sold in bundles of 48 and cost $1 each. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Tech.title: 6 Prime Day Kitchen Deals Our Experts Tested (and Would Buy Again)
Tech.content:
Amazon’s October Prime Day sales are your shot to upgrade your kitchen without paying out the rear — including on coffee makers, air fryers, blenders and more culinary essentials.

Amazon has thousands of deals during its sitewide sale, but they are not created equal. Many seem tempting but aren’t worth it, even with the markdown. I’ve been testing kitchen gear for years, and I know how to see through the hype. I’ve sorted through hundreds of offers on the most impressive kitchen tech we’ve personally tested, using Amazon price history trackers to make sure the deals are as good as they sound.

Below are the six best Prime Day kitchen deals, all of which I’d recommend to family and friends without hesitation.

More from CNET

Nikita Ephanozv/CNET $90 (save $40) Lavazza Tabli plastic-free pod espresso machine Get it now $90 at Amazon Expert Take Lavazza recently introduced the first-ever pod coffee maker that brews compostable rounds made from pressed coffee — no aluminum, no plastic and no waste. Our coffee expert reviewed the Tabli last week and found that it made authentic-tasting espresso shots with little hassle. He loved its eco-friendliness, but was equally impressed by the rich, flavorful coffee this first-of-its-kind brewer churned out. Think Keurig, but without plastic K-Cups filling up the landfill. The tabs, which you can also buy on Amazon or through Lavazza, cost about a buck each. Bottom Line Considering the fanfare surrounding this innovative new single-serve espresso system, which launched only a couple of months ago, we were pleasantly surprised to see it go on sale so quickly. The Tabli would make an excellent gift for a college student or environmentally conscious coffee drinker on your holiday list.

Zojirushi $121 (save $69) Zojirushi Micom 3-cup rice cooker Get it now $121 at Amazon Expert Take Of the many rice cookers I tested, Zojirushi was the most precise and landed at the top of our list for cooking custom rice. The only thing keeping it from the top spot was the high price you pay for that performance. Not so when you snatch the Micom 3-cup cooker for $121 during Prime Day. Cheaper rice makers rely on Fuzzy Logic technology alone, which determines when water has completely evaporated from the cooking chamber. Zojirushi combines that tech with precise temperature control to cook fussier grains like brown rice perfectly. It includes settings for various rice and grain types, including GABA brown, which cooks rice slowly to activate gamma-aminobutyric acid, a nutrient shown to improve calm and focus. It also includes long-grain white rice and steel-cut oat programs, since those grains require precise time and temperature to get right. Bottom Line This compact rice cooker typically sells for $190 but is down to $121 right now. If you cook rice as much as I do — two or three times per week — it's worth springing for a high-end model. Be warned that a 3-cup cooker is best for smaller families, though 3 cups of uncooked rice still equates to roughly 18 side dish servings.

Vitamix $295 (save $205) Vitamix Propel Series 510 blender Get it now $295 at Amazon Expert Take All Vitamix blenders pack big power, but the Propel Series has a little extra — at least compared to the VX series (formerly called the Explorian). It has 2.2 peak horsepower, so it can handle just about anything you drop inside. Unlike the manual-only VX, the Propel has three built-in automatic programs for smoothies, frozen desserts and hot soups for hands-off blending. It’s also one of the quietest and lightest Vitamix blenders, which makes it feel user-friendly. These blenders aren’t cheap, but as CNET’s Anna Gragert, who uses a 19-year-old Vitamix without issue, can attest, they really last. Bottom Line This is the cheapest we've ever seen the Vitamix Propel 510 drop on Amazon. The powerful blender retails for $500 with an average tag of $433 on Amazon. It's only been down to $300 twice before during flash sales. It comes with a five-year warranty.

Pamela Vachon/CNET $153 (save $27) Ninja Crispi glass-bowl air fryer Get it now $153 at Amazon $153 at Best Buy Expert Take Simply put, this is the best air fryer we’ve tested, and it’s currently at its lowest price ever on Amazon. The Crispi broke the air fryer mold when it launched, with a modular build that’s easier to store and a glass bowl cooking chamber that’s easy to clean and PFAS-free. If you’ve used a nonstick air fryer basket, you know how quickly it accumulates a layer of gunk that’s hard to remove. Not so with the Crispi. As a bonus, the cooking chamber comes with a tight-fitting lid that makes storing leftover food simple and intuitive. The Crispi has as much power as you’ll ever need from an air fryer and features uncomplicated cooking controls. If there is one ding on this model, it’s that the cooking chamber is lower than some we’ve tested, meaning you might struggle to fit a whole chicken or large cut of meat without breaking it down first. For more cooking capacity, try the Ninja Crispi Pro — also on sale for Prime Day. Bottom Line Our favorite air fryer at its lowest price ever on Amazon — what's not to love? The Ninja Crispi has significant advantages over pod-style nonstick air fryers, and thanks to its outsized popularity, it rarely goes on sale.

Technivorm $270 (save $100) Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV coffee maker Get it now $270 at Crate & Barrel Expert Take The Dutch coffee maker company Technivorm has sold exceptional brewers for decades, earning it cult status among coffee snobs. The KBGV drip coffee machine has clean lines and sharp angles that give off both a vintage and laboratory feel. Retro design aside, in our testing, this brewer consistently delivers perfectly balanced coffee, heating water up to a precise temperature as it hits the grounds. Bottom Line Technivorm's brewers often sell for $400, so snatching up one of its most popular models for $270 is a no-brainer if you were already planning to upgrade your home setup. The KBGV is currently listed for $366 on Amazon and seldom drops below $300.

Ninja/CNET $88 (save $42) Ninja Blendboss personal blender Get it now $88 at Amazon Expert Take The BlendBoss is the latest addition to Ninja’s blender lineup, and it quickly became our top pick. When we tested it against several others, we found it pulverized ice into snow in 15 seconds — as fast as any — and made quick work of turning dense frozen fruit into healthy smoothies. The blender comes in a range of colors — great for gifting — and has a quirky design unlike any other personal blender I’ve seen. Bottom Line This is one of few times the BlendBoss has been discounted since it launched earlier this year. The small and powerful blender typically sells for $130 but it's down to $88 for Prime Day.

What’s the single best kitchen deal?

That largely depends on your kitchen needs. For me, the powerful Vitamix Propel 510 for $295 is simply one of the best prices we’ve seen on any of the brand’s iconic blenders in some time. I fully expect that deal to expire or sell out long before Prime Day ends.



Is Prime Day a good time to buy kitchen gadgets?

Absolutely. The kitchen category really pops off during Prime Day sales, and we’re seeing discounts of 40% to 60% on some of our favorite gear, making them easy to recommend right now. The next opportunity to save big will be Black Friday, but price hikes can happen at any time, so there’s no guarantee we’ll see deals as good as today’s again.

Tech.title: Mark Your Calendars to See October’s Meteor Showers, Views of All 8 Planets and More
Tech.content:
If you live where the leaves change, October is probably the prettiest month of the year. That goes for the sky, too. This month features an action-packed lineup of meteor showers and celestial showcases.

You can see all eight planets this month

Mercury is visible just before sunset for several days in October. Stellarium

Every planet in the solar system is easily seen at some point this month, with Mercury being the most difficult. That’s not unusual, thanks to its proximity to the sun. Here’s a quick rundown on the best times to view each planet in October.

Mercury: Mercury is in elongation (the farthest it can get from the sun) on Monday, making that day and the two or so days before and after the best possible time to view Mercury.

More from CNET

Venus: Venus spends most of the month being right next to the sun, making it virtually impossible to see. However, by the end of the month, it begins to separate from the sun, making it visible just after sunset. The best view is on Oct. 31, and the view is only set to get better going into November.

Mars: Mars will be visible in the night sky every night in October. It rises from the eastern horizon right around 2 a.m. and stays there until the sun comes up.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are going to be pretty close together all month, so most of the same rules apply, except that Jupiter rises about 2 hours later than Mars on most nights in October.

Saturn: Saturn is living its best life in October. It’s visible almost right at sunset ET and stays visible in the night sky until sunrise.

Neptune: Neptune is also visible every day in October and follows a very similar path to Saturn. It rises in the east, streaks across the sky, and sets in the west right around sunrise. They’re actually pretty close together in the night sky every night during the month, so if you can find Saturn, Neptune isn’t far off, but you’ll definitely need magnification to see it.

Uranus: Uranus is visible the entire month and follows a very similar path through the sky as Saturn and Neptune, but its trek happens later at night. It rises on the eastern horizon about 2 hours after Saturn and follows it across the sky, but never really catches up, ending up in the high western sky when sunrise comes.

Oct. 7: Draconids Meteor Shower

The Draconids meteor shower is in the Draco constellation near Vega. Stellarium

The Draconids meteor shower is a minor meteor shower that occurs every year around the first week of October. It officially starts on Tuesday and runs until Saturday, making it one of the shortest meteor showers of the season. It peaks on Wednesday evening and continues into the middle of the night. It’s fed by the 21P/Giacobini-Zinner comet, which is part of the Jupiter family of comets.

Draconids meteors appear to originate from the Draco constellation. It sits high in the western sky in the northern hemisphere this time of year, with a slight lean to the north. If you’re using a sky map app, all you need to do is find Vega, and you’re already in the right neighborhood to catch Draconids.

The peak is a little tame, at around 10 meteors per hour most years, but it has a history of surprising astronomers. In 1933 and 1946, Draconids spat out thousands of meteors an hour in what were two of the most intense meteor showers of the 20th century. On the plus side, the moon is below the horizon for this meteor shower, so you won’t need to worry about light pollution from the moon.

Oct. 10: The last good chance to see the Milky Way

The Milky Way captured with the Tiny1 camera. TinyMOS

The very best time to view the Milky Way is at a new moon in the warm months of the year, from May to August. This is when the Milky Way is high in the sky all night, giving night owls great views and plenty of time to photograph it. The problem is that it’s best viewed on nights with a new moon between midnight and 4 a.m. local time, which can be a bit late for some folks.

September and October are great for this because the Milky Way is at its highest point between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. local time, giving the early birds a chance to snap some sweet photographs of the Milky Way. After October, the Milky Way is too low on the horizon to allow really good pictures of it until the following May. So, if you have a camera and are in some place that’s dark, the new moon on Saturday is probably your last chance to capture a striking photo before next spring.

Oct. 21: Orionids meteor shower

The Orionids meteor shower will be low to the horizon in the east when its peak occurs.

Orionids is the better-known of the two October meteor showers. This one officially started on Friday and runs until Nov. 7. It’s possible to spot a meteor from Orionids any night during the month, but the shower reaches its peak on the evening of Oct. 21. Meteors for this shower come from the 1P/Halley comet, which also feeds the Eta Aquariids meteor shower that happens every year in May.

This is a slightly more active meteor shower than the Draconids, and you can expect about 10 to 20 meteors per hour. The moon is set to be about 76% full that night, so you can probably expect to see fewer meteors thanks to lunar light pollution. The Orion constellation, where the meteor shower will appear to originate, doesn’t pop up over the eastern horizon until after midnight, so make sure to pack some coffee if you’re staying up late for this one. If you can find the stars Betelgeuse, Capella and Rigel, then you should be able to find Orion easily. They’re in the same general area.

The Orionids meteor shower is best known for its bright, fast-moving meteors, which leave long trails that can last for over a minute and sometimes result in fireballs. Their brightness will be a boon, with the three-quarters-full moon in the sky hindering viewing.

Oct. 26: The Hunter Moon

A full moon rises behind the Washington Monument. NASA/Bill Ingalls

October’s full moon falls close to Halloween this year, perfect for spooky views. According to The Old Farmer’s Almanac, October’s full moon reaches its peak on Oct. 26 at 12:12 a.m. ET. It’ll also be over 90% full for a couple of days before and after, giving you a solid five days to check it out.

October’s full moon isn’t quite a supermoon. A full moon is only classified as a supermoon when the moon is in perigee and full at roughly the same time, and October’s full moon misses the mark by a couple of days. October’s full moon is the last normal full moon of the year. November and December close out 2026 with supermoons before January opens with the final supermoon of this cycle.

Oct. 27: The moon eclipses the Pleiades

The moon will eclipse the Pleiades before either rises in the sky, but most people will still get to see part of it. Stellarium

Pleiades is one of the best star clusters to view in the night sky. They’re known as the Seven Sisters, and in terms of clusters of stars, it’s one of the easiest to see. The exception is on Oct. 27, when the moon will cross in front of them, blocking them almost entirely from view. When this happens depends on where you’re located.

The moon begins passing in front of them before sunset in eastern time, and moves out of the way around midnight. Those on the East Coast will start the night in the middle of this little eclipse, while those on the West Coast will glimpse it at the very end. Finding it should be simple enough since the moon is the easiest thing to see in the night sky.

All month: Constellations and asterisms

The sky is continuing its rearrangement from summer into autumn, and there are tons of constellations to gaze at over the course of the month. Many of September’s constellations appear again, including both Dippers, Aquarius, Pegasus, Pisces and many others. October plays host to a few new ones in the night sky cycle, including Taurus, Cetus, Auriga and Orion, which will appear low on the horizon as they begin their months-long ascent into the sky for the winter.

There are some smaller asterisms to observe as well, including the Coffin of Delphinus, the Circlet of Pisces and the Northern Cross. We recommend using a sky map to find them all, as there are quite a lot. That’s good news, because even if you don’t go out during one of the big events in October, you’ll still have plenty of objects to look for in the night sky.

Tech.title: Google’s Next Android XR Device Is Arriving Ahead of Meta’s VR Glasses, at a Similar Price
Tech.content:
The once familiar landscape of VR headsets is starting to melt. As smart glasses flood the zone, VR devices are changing form. And devices that are almost VR, too. Meta’s glasses-like headset, called Meta VR Glasses, is coming next year for $1,299, but the Xreal Aura, a pair of display glasses with a computer puck that also turns into an AR/VR device, is coming even sooner for $1,279.

Xreal announced the Aura’s price on Wednesday, but not a release date. It should be coming in the next month or two, though, and I’ve had a chance to try it several times over the last year. It’s currently only available to preorder if you placed a $100 hold for the right to order one earlier this year, but more options to buy are coming in a few weeks, according to the company.

Xreal’s Project Aura supports hand tracking, and it works just like it does on VR headsets to pinch, scroll and control apps. Scott Stein/CNET

What Xreal Aura can do

I found the Xreal Aura to be one of the most fascinating devices I’ve tried in a while, because it bridges some of the gaps between glasses, AR and VR. The Aura is a more advanced pair of Xreal display glasses (which I’ve reviewed in various forms over the last few years) connected to a processing puck that runs Android XR, floating apps and experiences into the world with micro-OLED displays. The displays are effectively mirrored down from the top of the glasses and projected over transparent lenses that have layers of dimming. Google’s visually aware Gemini AI can run at the same time, recognizing apps that are open and things in the real world around you.

More from CNET

The Aura has a larger 70-degree field of view than previous Xreal glasses (which top out at 57 degrees), which allows more viewing space and more apps to be laid out. It’s less than standard VR, but in my demos, it felt like it approached usefulness close to what VR headsets can offer. It also has hand tracking via external cameras, and can float 3D experiences and even VR apps in Android XR into the room surprisingly well.

The $1,279 starting price for Xreal Aura includes 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM. There’s also a $1,500 version with 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM.

The Aura comes with its own travel case. The processor puck it uses is about the size of a phone. Scott Stein/CNET

Meta VR Glasses and Xreal Aura compared

Meta’s VR Glasses have a similar, yet different, proposition. They’re more like sliced-off Apple Vision Pros and use pass-through cameras to let you see the outside world rather than actually transparent lenses. But they also have eye tracking in addition to hand tracking, and can work with Meta Quest controllers and Quest apps. Their 84-degree field-of-view micro-OLED displays are more expansive and higher-res than the Aura’s. Meta’s VR Glasses have only one storage config we know of (128GB), but also have a MicroSD card slot that can store apps too.

Both the Xreal Aura and the Meta VR Glasses connect with external processing pucks that are roughly phone-sized, both using Qualcomm Snapdragon XR Elite chipsets. Both also have the unique ability to port in other USB-C video-out devices, floating a phone screen, laptop, iPad or Steam Deck right alongside other apps. Clearly, a phase change in form is underway.

Google’s got more glasses coming

Google’s got lots of Android XR devices planned, including a line of Gemini-powered smart glasses made with Samsung, Warby Parker and Gentle Monster coming sometime before the end of the year. But the Xreal Aura is Google’s next Android XR product on deck since its Samsung Galaxy XR partnership last year, and can do a lot of the same things in a smaller form for less.

Between the Meta VR Glasses and the Xreal Aura, it already feels like the distinctions between “VR” and “AR” are starting to melt away. But at their almost-identical near-$1,300 prices, they’re also setting the tone for what these gadgets will cost going forward. Valve’s Steam Frame VR headset is over $1,000, and Snap’s upcoming Specs AR glasses cost $2,195. At these prices, although far less than Apple’s $3,699 Vision Pro, they’re also far more expensive than Meta’s Quest VR headsets. If you’re considering spending up on the idea of immersive displays that can be used for work or taken on the go, though, you should stay put and see how these devices perform when I review them.

Tech.title: Shopped With CVS Online? You Could Be a Part of a $20.5M Settlement
Tech.content:
The pharmacy chain CVS is getting ready to settle a $20.5 million lawsuit against it, despite its claims that it has done nothing wrong. The lawsuit alleges that the pharmacy disclosed private health information, browsing data and more from those who shopped on its websites (cvs.com and cvshealth.com) or mobile apps to advertising company Criteo and other third parties.

Potential class members of the lawsuit should have received an email notification in September (PDF) about the case, which entitles them to either $5 or $10 in payment, depending on whether they can provide specific documentation. That said, the payments may be reduced depending on the number of qualified class members, according to the official settlement website.

Eligibility is also straightforward. If you made a purchase at CVS online or in its mobile app prior to July 27, you’re considered a class member and are eligible for payment.

More from CNET

As is typical with class-action lawsuits, potential class members may also opt out of the settlement. Opting out of the settlement will prevent payment but allow you to maintain your right to sue the company directly. The final date to opt out of the settlement is Nov. 1.

The final hearing is set for Dec. 1, and if the court approves the settlement, payments will be issued 120 days after approval. Class members can be paid via check, PayPal, Venmo or Zelle.
